rows.summary:
The Bombay High Court held that the Income Tax Department had not complied with the statutory requirements of section 245 of the Income-tax Act before adjusting Tata Communications Ltd.’s refund against outstanding demands. The case arose in AY 2019-20 and concerned a refund/stay-of-demand dispute; the court specifically criticized the Department’s approach to treating its order as not covering matters dealt with by the ITAT on the ground that the Union of India was not a party, calling that justification unacceptable and inconsistent with the conduct expected of a model litigant.

From a compliance perspective, the key requirement reaffirmed is that before any refund is adjusted against a tax demand under section 245, the Department must follow the procedure mandated by that section rather than simply making an adjustment unilaterally. The judgment signals that authorities cannot rely on technical arguments to avoid the effect of a High Court order where the substance of the dispute requires compliance, and that departmental actions in refund adjustment matters are subject to judicial scrutiny. No specific monetary thresholds, rates, or filing deadlines were stated in the excerpt, but the operative compliance point is that refund adjustments must be lawfully and transparently made in conformity with section 245 and the court’s direction, especially where related stay/refund proceedings are already pending or decided.

rows.summary:
The Bombay High Court held that a writ petition could be maintained in Bombay even though the challenged income-tax order had been passed by Delhi authorities, because the assessee was based in Mumbai and part of the cause of action arose there. For compliance purposes, the more important ruling is that a notice under section 148 and a reassessment order under section 147 issued in the name of an amalgamated company that had already ceased to exist are **void and without jurisdiction**; this is not treated as a mere procedural defect.

The Court specifically rejected the argument that the defect could be cured under section 292B, and it also held that the assessee’s participation in the reassessment proceedings does **not** validate the proceedings or create any estoppel against law. In practical terms, if a company has been amalgamated before reassessment proceedings are initiated, tax notices and reassessment orders must be issued, if at all, in the name of the surviving entity; action taken against the non-existent predecessor entity is invalid.

The case concerned AY 2012–13, and the Court’s decision was pronounced on April 9, 2021 and published on April 24, 2021. The ruling reinforces a key compliance control point for corporate restructuring: once an amalgamation takes effect, the company should ensure tax records, PAN-related communications, and litigation notices are promptly aligned with the successor entity’s name so that any future assessment or reassessment proceedings are not directed at a dissolved legal person.

However, shares issued to shareholders of an amalgamating company in terms of a scheme of amalgamation does not fall within the sweep of the deeming provisions of s. 56(2) (viib). The so-called excess value of assets vested on amalgamation cannot be notionally termed as premium over the face value for the purposes of the deeming provision (AS-14 issued by the ICAI & CBDT Circular No 3/2012 dated 12-6-2012 referred) (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Income from other sources DCIT v. Nos. 2081/Ahd/2018 dated April 13, 2021 )(AY. 2013-14) 56(2)(viib) : Income from other Sources – Excess over Fair market Value of Shares – Deemed Income – Not applicable – shares issued under a scheme of amalgamation. Facts: The assessee company filed its return of income for AY 2013-14 in question which was subjected to scrutiny assessment. In the course of assessment proceedings, it was gathered by the AO that one M/s. Kalavir Estate Pvt. Ltd. (KEPL) amalgamated with the assessee company under the scheme of amalgamation.
rows.summary:
The ITAT Ahmedabad held in **DCIT v. Ozone India Ltd.** that **section 56(2)(viib)**, which taxes a private company on **excess share premium received over fair market value**, does **not apply** where shares are issued to shareholders pursuant to a **scheme of amalgamation**. The case involved **AY 2013–14**, with the tribunal’s decision **pronounced on April 13, 2021** and published on **April 24, 2021**.  

On the facts, the assessee-company had filed its return for AY 2013–14, and during scrutiny the Assessing Officer found that **M/s. Kalavir Estate Pvt. Ltd. (KEPL)** had amalgamated into the assessee under an approved amalgamation scheme. In that process, the assessee issued shares to the shareholders of the amalgamating company. The tax department sought to treat the value arising from the amalgamation as **deemed income** under section 56(2)(viib), effectively characterizing the issuance as if there were an unjustified premium over face value.  

The tribunal rejected that approach, stating that the purpose of section 56(2)(viib) is to tax **unexplained or excessive premium received by private companies on issuance of shares where the shares do not carry corresponding underlying value**, not to cover share issuance mandated by an amalgamation scheme. It held that the **notional excess of assets vested on amalgamation cannot be treated as share premium** for this deeming provision. The decision also referred to **AS-14 issued by ICAI** and **CBDT Circular No. 3/2012 dated 12-6-2012** in support of the treatment of amalgamation accounting and share issuance as distinct from taxable premium.  

For compliance teams, the practical takeaway is that where shares are issued **solely because of a bona fide amalgamation approved under a scheme**, the transaction should not ordinarily be exposed to **section 56(2)(viib)** tax on alleged excess fair market value. However, the ruling is limited to the facts of amalgamation-related issuance and does not change the general rule that **unjustified share premium in ordinary equity issuances** can still be scrutinized under section 56(2)(viib).

This ITAT Mumbai decision concerns **section 50C of the Income-tax Act**, which deems the **stamp duty valuation** of transferred property to be the sale consideration for **capital gains** purposes when the stated sale price is lower than the stamp valuation. The Tribunal stated that the **third proviso to section 50C**, inserted by the **Finance Act, 2018**, creates a tolerance band under which section 50C will **not apply if the difference between stamp duty value and actual consideration does not exceed 5%**; this tolerance was later **increased to 10% by the Finance Act, 2020**. Although those amendments were described as prospective, the Tribunal held them to be **curative in nature** and therefore applicable **retrospectively from 1 April 2003**, the date section 50C was originally introduced.

For compliance purposes, the practical effect is that where a property transfer’s **stamp duty value is up to 10% higher than the declared sale consideration**, the declared consideration should be accepted at face value and the **anti-avoidance substitution mechanism under section 50C should not be triggered**. The case was an appeal for **Assessment Year 2011–12** in the matter of **Maria Fernandes Cheryl vs. ITO (International Taxation 2(3)(1), Mumbai)**, with the Tribunal’s pronouncement dated **15 January 2021** and publication on **17 April 2021**. The ruling is relevant to taxpayers and tax teams handling **immovable property transfers**, especially where there is a small gap between contractual consideration and stamp duty value, because it supports using the statutory tolerance band rather than mechanically substituting stamp value for capital gains computation.

rows.summary:
The Supreme Court held that Section 18 of the Limitation Act applies to proceedings under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 because Section 238A of the IBC makes the Limitation Act applicable “as far as may be.” As a result, where a corporate debtor makes a written and signed acknowledgement of debt before expiry of the limitation period, that acknowledgement can extend the limitation period for filing an insolvency application. The Court also clarified that an entry in the debtor’s books of account, including a balance sheet entry, can constitute an acknowledgement of liability under Section 18, provided it is read together with the notes annexed to or forming part of the balance sheet and the auditor’s report.

This decision specifically reverses the NCLAT Full Bench ruling in V. Padmakumar v. Stressed Assets Stabilisation Fund, which had taken a contrary view on balance-sheet acknowledgements. The Court reaffirmed the basic limitation principle that once time begins to run, it cannot be stopped except by a legally recognized process. For compliance purposes, this means companies facing potential debt enforcement or insolvency exposure should treat balance-sheet disclosures, related notes, and auditor commentary as potentially legally significant acknowledgements that may revive or extend limitation periods for creditors. The judgment was pronounced on April 15, 2021 and published on April 17, 2021.

The Bombay High Court in **Sadruddin Tejani v. ITO** interpreted the **Direct Tax Vivad se Vishwas Act, 2020 (DTVSV Act)** and held that the scheme is aimed at resolving **disputed tax liability**, not disputed income. The Court said that where a declarant is an **eligible appellant** and the case is **not covered by section 4(6)** and does **not fall within any disqualifications in section 9**, the **Designated Authority cannot reject the declaration filed under section 4(1)**.

The Court further stated that the Designated Authority must process the declaration and issue **Form 3 under section 5(1)**, setting out the amount payable in accordance with **section 3** of the Act. In this case, the refusal to accept the declaration was held improper because the record did not show that the taxpayer fell into any of the statutory exclusion categories. The Court therefore **quashed the rejection order**.

The decision reinforces that declarations under the scheme must be evaluated strictly against the statute’s disqualification rules, and once a valid declaration is filed by an eligible appellant, the authority is required to move the matter forward rather than deny it administratively.

rows.summary:
The Supreme Court in **DCIT v. Pepsi Foods Ltd.** examined the **third proviso to section 254(2A)** of the Income-tax Act, which had provided for **automatic vacation of a stay granted by the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT) after 365 days**, regardless of who caused the delay in hearing the appeal. The Court held that this rule was **unconstitutional** because it was **discriminatory and manifestly arbitrary**: it could punish an assessee even when the ITAT could not hear the appeal in time for reasons beyond the assessee’s control, and it could also benefit the Revenue even when the Revenue itself was responsible for the delay.

As a result, the Court struck down the offending operation of the proviso and directed that the provision be **read down** by deleting the word **“even”** and the words **“is not”** after the phrase **“delay in disposing of the appeal”**. In practical compliance terms, a stay granted by the ITAT **does not automatically lapse merely because 365 days have passed**; the stay will stand vacated **only if the delay in disposing of the appeal is attributable to the assessee**. This means the focus shifts to **fault-based delay** rather than a strict time-based expiration.

For corporate taxpayers with pending appeals and stay orders before the ITAT, the decision materially affects **stay-of-demand management**: companies no longer face automatic loss of stay solely due to passage of time beyond 365 days if they are not at fault for the delay. At the same time, the ruling preserves the possibility of vacation of stay where the assessee’s conduct is responsible for delaying disposal. There is **no new filing deadline or compliance formality created by this judgment**, but it is important for legal and tax teams to document which party caused any adjournments or hearing delays so that stay protection can be defended if challenged.

The Bombay High Court considered a charitable trust’s request for relief from delayed filing of **Form 10B** for **AY 2018-19** under **sections 11 and 119(2)(b)**. The court noted that **CBDT Circular No. 2/2020 dated 03.01.2020** had delegated power to the **CIT** to admit belated Form 10B applications only if the delay was **up to 365 days** for **AY 2018-19 and onwards**, and held that this one-year cap was **not arbitrary or irrational**. The Bombay High Court in **Macrotech Developers Limited v. PCIT** interpreted the **Direct Tax Vivad se Vishwas Act, 2020** and specifically the ineligibility rule under **section 9(a)(ii)** concerning pending prosecutions. The Court held that the exclusion from filing a declaration under the scheme applies only where, **as on the date the declaration is filed, a prosecution is pending in respect of the tax arrear attributable to that same assessment year**; it does **not** bar a taxpayer from using the scheme merely because there is some prosecution pending for that assessment year on a different, unrelated issue.

In practical compliance terms, companies should assess eligibility for the scheme by tying any pending prosecution to the **specific tax arrear being settled**, rather than treating any prosecution for that assessment year as an absolute bar.

rows.summary:
This Delhi High Court ruling in **CIT v. D. K. Garg** concerns **Section 68 of the Income-tax Act** and the treatment of **accommodation entries**, **cash credits**, and the taxpayer’s attempt to claim the benefit of **peak credit**. The Court held that an accommodation entry provider who seeks peak-credit relief must make a **full and candid disclosure of all facts within his knowledge** about the credit entries in the relevant accounts; this includes explaining **the source of every deposit**, **the destination of every payment**, and the movement of funds through the account structure. In practical terms, the assessee must be able to show that money was moved **through banking channels** from the creditor’s bank account to the assessee’s bank account, that the **identity of the creditors** is established, and that the money later paid out from the assessee’s account returned to the creditors’ accounts; this is the **primary onus** on the assessee under Section 68.

The decision is especially relevant to entities or individuals involved in **entry-providing / paper-entity transactions** or other arrangements where cash is introduced and converted into cheques or bank transfers. The Court emphasized that a taxpayer cannot claim the benefit of peak credit merely by asserting that only the highest outstanding balance should be taxed; instead, the taxpayer must first produce a clear and credible explanation of the entire transaction flow and the linked accounts involved. Where the taxpayer fails to do this, the unexplained credits remain liable to be treated under Section 68. The case date is **AY 1995–96**, with the judgment pronounced on **4 August 2017** and published on **16 August 2017**.

rows.summary:
The Supreme Court’s decision in **ADIT v. E-Funds IT Solution Inc.** addresses when a foreign company will be treated as having a **Permanent Establishment (PE) in India** under **Article 5 of the India–U.S. DTAA (1990)** for tax purposes. The tax authority had held that the U.S. companies had a **fixed place PE in Delhi** and were therefore taxable in India on income earned through that alleged PE; the CIT(A) also upheld the assessments, additionally reasoning that the companies had **service PE** and **agency PE** status under Article 5.

The Supreme Court explained the law on **fixed place PE, service PE, and agency PE**, and rejected the idea that mere **close association, dependence, or integrated business relationship** between the U.S. company and Indian group entities is enough to create a PE. It held that the correct test is whether the foreign enterprise itself has a sufficiently permanent **place of business in India through which its own business is carried on**, and that the **functions performed, assets used, and risks assumed** test is **not the proper test** for determining a location/fixed-place PE. The Court therefore clarified that a foreign company does not automatically become taxable in India just because related Indian entities perform support functions or because there is operational dependence between the entities.

For compliance purposes, the key practical takeaway is that **foreign enterprises using Indian affiliates or service providers are not automatically exposed to Indian PE risk solely because of group linkage or business dependence**. PE exposure must be assessed based on the actual facts showing whether the foreign company has a **fixed place**, **service presence**, or **agency relationship** in India within the meaning of the treaty, rather than relying on generalized notions of economic presence or business integration. The judgment is dated **October 24, 2017** (pronouncement), with publication on **October 25, 2017**.

rows.summary:
This circular explains how the GST return filings for July and August 2017 were to be handled during the initial rollout period, when the normal monthly return sequence under sections 37, 38, and 39 of the CGST Act, 2017 and rules 59, 60, and 61 of the CGST Rules, 2017 was temporarily disrupted. Ordinarily, registered persons had to file outward supply details in FORM GSTR-1 by the 10th of the next month, inward supply details in FORM GSTR-2 by the 15th, and the monthly return in FORM GSTR-3 by the 20th; however, the GST Council extended the filing dates for GSTR-1 and GSTR-2 for July and August 2017 and allowed a simplified return in FORM GSTR-3B for those two months, to be filed by the notified due dates after payment of tax.  

The circular also notes that taxpayers using transitional credit under section 140 of the CGST Act for their July 2017 liability had to file FORM GST TRAN-1 on or before 28 August 2017, and that this credit would be posted to the electronic credit ledger and could be used to discharge tax liability. Because FORM GSTR-3B was filed instead of the normal return sequence while the GSTR-1/GSTR-2 due dates were extended, the circular says the system would later reconcile the information furnished in GSTR-1 and GSTR-2 with the amounts reported in GSTR-3B once those returns were filed.  

For compliance purposes, the key point is that the simplified GSTR-3B filing did not replace the underlying reporting obligations permanently; it was an interim mechanism for the initial GST months, with reconciliation to follow once the regular statement/return data became available. The document is addressed to all Principal Chief Commissioners/Chief Commissioners/Principal Commissioners/Commissioners of Central Tax and all Principal Directors General/Directors General, indicating that field formations were expected to apply and oversee this reconciliation framework.

rows.title:
CGST dated 27.08.2017 is issued to clarify classification and GST
                            rate on lottery
rows.desc: Circular No.06/06/2017-CGST F. No. 354/149/2017-TRU Government of India Ministry of Finance Department of Revenue Tax Research Unit ***** New Delhi, the 27 th August, 2017 To, The Principal Chief Commissioner/Chief Commissioners/ Principal Commissioner/ Commissioner of Central Tax (All) / Director General of Systems Madam/Sir, Subject: - Issue related to classification and GST rate on lottery tickets – regarding Supply of lottery has been treated as supply of goods under the Central Goods and Services Tax (CGST) Act, 2017. 2. Accordingly, based on the recommendation of the GST Council, the GST rate for supply of lottery has been notified under relevant GST rate notification relating to CGST/IGST/UTGST/SGST. However, entries in the respective notifications mention classification for lottery as “-”. 3. In this connection, references have been received, inter-alia, stating that due to discrepancy in code allotted, i.e., lottery is defined as goods but code allotted for lottery is under services, the assessees are not able to upload return or deposit tax in time. 4. The matter has been examined. It should be noted that the process of filing return is linked with rate of tax specified for supply. Further, there is complete clarity about rate of tax on lotteries. As mentioned above, in GST, lottery is goods and the classification indicated in relevant notification for lottery is “-”, which means any chapter. 5. That being so, it is clarified that the classification for lottery in respective CGST, IGST, UTGST and SGST notifications shall be ‘Any Chapter’ of the First Schedule to the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 (51 of 1975) and tax on lottery should be paid accordingly at prescribed rates, 12% or 28%, as the case may be. (Ruchi Bisht) Under Secretary (TRU)
rows.summary:
This circular, issued on 27 August 2017 by the Ministry of Finance, clarifies how lottery tickets are to be classified and taxed under GST because assessees were encountering return-filing and tax-payment problems due to a coding mismatch. The circular states that, under the CGST Act, 2017, supply of lottery is treated as a **supply of goods**, even though the GST rate notifications had shown the classification entry for lottery as “-”. For compliance purposes, the government clarifies that this “-” should be read as **“Any Chapter” of the First Schedule to the Customs Tariff Act, 1975**, and that lottery must be taxed under the applicable GST rate notifications accordingly.

The circular specifically resolves the issue that the lottery description was appearing as goods while the code allotted in the system was under services, which had prevented some taxpayers from uploading returns or depositing tax on time. It emphasizes that return filing is linked to the rate of tax applicable to the supply, and that there is no ambiguity on the applicable lottery tax rate. The prescribed GST rate for lottery is confirmed as **12% or 28%, as the case may be**, depending on the relevant notified category.

This clarification applies to the GST framework under **CGST, IGST, UTGST, and SGST** rate notifications and is directed to all Central Tax field formations and systems officials. From a compliance standpoint, entities dealing in lottery tickets should ensure their tax classification and return-filing treatment align with the “Any Chapter” classification and the correct notified rate, so tax can be paid and returns filed without system errors or delay.

rows.summary:
This circular clarifies the rules for exporting goods or services without payment of integrated tax by furnishing either a bond or a Letter of Undertaking (LUT), under section 168(1) of the CGST Act, 2017, in response to inconsistent interpretations of Notification No. 16/2017–Central Tax dated 7 July 2017 and earlier GST circulars. The key policy clarification is that the LUT facility is no longer limited to manufacturer exporters: **any registered person** may use LUT **if** they received foreign inward remittance in the preceding financial year equal to **at least 10% of export turnover, and in any case not less than Rs. 1 crore**; the circular states this effectively means the exporter must have received **whichever is higher: Rs. 1 crore or 10% of export turnover** in the previous financial year. If that threshold is not met, the exporter must export under a **bond** rather than LUT.

The circular also clarifies the process for using and accepting the bond/LUT. The bond must be **executed on non-judicial stamp paper** for an amount determined as per the relevant bond format, and the exporter is required to furnish a **bank guarantee** along with the bond only to the extent required by the proper officer, not as a blanket requirement for all exporters. It further states that the LUT can be furnished on the exporter’s own letterhead in the prescribed format, and it must be accepted by the jurisdictional Assistant/Deputy Commissioner. The circular instructs tax officers not to insist on unnecessary guarantees or documentation beyond what the notification and circular require.

Another important compliance clarification is that the LUT/bond is a **pre-export** undertaking: it must be furnished **before exports are made** under the zero-rated/without payment route. The circular also explains that exports under bond/LUT are subject to the condition that the exporter will comply with the export provisions, including export of goods or services within the prescribed time limits and maintenance of proof of export. If the exporter fails to comply, the bond can be enforced for tax, interest, and any other applicable amount. The circular is intended to create uniformity across field formations, so compliance teams should ensure exporter eligibility is checked against the prior-year remittance threshold and that the correct instrument—LUT or bond—is used before undertaking exports without payment of integrated tax.

rows.summary:
This circular clarifies the bond/LUT procedure for **exports of goods or services without payment of integrated tax** under **rule 96A of the CGST Rules, 2017**. It was issued by the **CBEC GST Policy Wing on 7 July 2017** under **section 168(1) of the CGST Act, 2017** to ensure uniform implementation after complaints from exporters and field offices about difficulties with the prescribed process. The core requirement is that any registered person making such zero-rated exports must furnish either a **bond or a Letter of Undertaking (LUT) in FORM GST RFD-11** before exporting without IGST payment.

The circular then distinguishes who may use an LUT and who must furnish a bond. It points to **Notification No. 16/2017-Central Tax dated 01-07-2017**, which specifies the class of exporters eligible to export under LUT, together with the applicable conditions and safeguards. **Exporters not covered by that notification must furnish a bond instead of an LUT.** The circular also reiterates that the **procedure for submission and acceptance of the bond was already laid down in Circular No. 2/2/2017-GST dated 4 July 2017**.

For the bond itself, the document requires that it be executed on **non-judicial stamp paper** of the **value applicable in the State where the bond is furnished**. A key clarification sought by the field was whether export bonds should be a **running bond with debit/credit facility** or a **separate one-time bond for each consignment/export**. The circular notes this issue and explains that the bond mechanism is intended to operate as a running bond, so exporters do not have to execute a fresh bond for every shipment.

For compliance teams, the practical effect is that exporters making zero-rated supplies without IGST must first check whether they qualify for LUT under the 1 July 2017 notification; if not, they must arrange a bond in RFD-11 on the correct state stamp paper and follow the prescribed submission/acceptance process from the earlier circular. The circular is not imposing a new tax rate or deadline, but it does require adherence to the LUT/bond framework as a precondition to exporting without paying integrated tax.

rows.summary:
This circular, issued on 5 July 2017 by the Central Board of Excise and Customs (GST Policy Wing), assigns “proper officer” status for specific GST functions under the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 (and related rules) to designated Central Tax officers, for matters other than registration and composition. It applies by virtue of section 2(91) of the CGST Act, read with section 20 of the IGST Act and subject to section 5(2) of the CGST Act, and it is intended to clarify which officer rank may legally exercise particular powers under the Act/rules.

For Principal Commissioners/Commissioners of Central Tax, the circular assigns the functions under section 67(7) and the proviso to section 78. For Additional or Joint Commissioners of Central Tax, it assigns powers under sections 67(1), (2), (5), and (9); sections 71(1) and (2); the proviso to section 81; the proviso to section 129(6); and rule 139 sub-rules (1) to (4) and rule 140(2). For Deputy or Assistant Commissioners of Central Tax, the circular assigns a broader set of functions, including sections 54(5), (6), (7), and (10); section 60(1), (2), and (3); sections 63, 64(1), and 65(6); and multiple powers under section 74, including sub-sections (1), (2), (3), (5), (6), (7), (9), and (10), with the listing continuing on the next page. 

From a compliance standpoint, the practical impact is that taxpayers and company compliance teams must ensure that notices, orders, demands, recovery actions, inspections, access requests, search/seizure-related actions, refund-related actions, and other proceedings under the cited provisions are handled by the correct officer rank, because authority is being formally allocated to those officers. The circular does not set new monetary thresholds, tax rates, or filing deadlines; instead, it is an internal administrative authorization that determines which GST officer is empowered to act under the listed sections and rules, effective from the date of the circular itself, 5 July 2017.

Various communications have been received from the field formations and exporters on the issue of difficulties being faced while supplying the goods or services for export without payment of integrated tax and filing the FORM GST RFD -11 on the common portal (www.gst.gov.in), because of which exports are being held up. 2. Whereas, as per rule 96A of the Central Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017, any registered person availing the option to supply goods or services for export without payment of integrated tax shall furnish, prior to export, a bond or a Letter of Undertaking. This bond or Letter of Undertaking is required to be furnished in FORM GST RFD-11 on the common portal. Further, Circular No. 26/2017- Customs dated 1 st July, 2017 has clarified that the procedure as prescribed under rule 96A of the said rules requires to be followed for the export of goods from 1 st July, 2017. 3. Another issue being raised by various stakeholders is that the Bond/Letter of Undertaking is required to be given through the proper officer which is to be furnished to the jurisdictional Commissioner as per sub-rule (1) of rule 96A of the said rules. Taking cognizance of the fact that a large number of such Bonds/Letter of Undertakings would be required to be filed by the registered exporters who would be located at a distance from the office of the jurisdictional Commissioner, it is understood that the furnishing of such bonds/undertakings before the jurisdictional Commissioner may cause hardship to the exporters. 4. Thus, in exercise of the powers conferred by sub-section (
rows.summary:
This circular addresses practical problems exporters were facing after GST implementation when supplying goods or services for export **without payment of integrated tax** and then trying to file **FORM GST RFD-11** on the GST common portal. The government notes that these difficulties were causing export shipments to be held up, so it clarifies the procedure for furnishing the required **bond or Letter of Undertaking (LUT)** under **rule 96A of the Central Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017**.

The core requirement is unchanged: any **registered person** choosing to export **without paying integrated tax** must furnish, **before export**, a **bond or LUT** in **FORM GST RFD-11**. The circular also confirms that, for **export of goods**, the rule 96A procedure applies **from 1 July 2017**, consistent with **Circular No. 26/2017-Customs dated 1 July 2017**.

The new operational relaxation is that the bond/LUT does **not** need to be physically filed before the **jurisdictional Commissioner**, which had created hardship because many exporters are located far from that office. Instead, the circular allows this filing to be handled through the **proper officer** / jurisdictional tax administration mechanism in a way that avoids travel and administrative delay, so exporters can complete the requirement more easily and prevent export disruption.

For compliance purposes, the document is important because it confirms that exporters using the **zero-rated export without IGST payment route** must still ensure a valid **bond or LUT is in place before export**, but the process is being administratively simplified to reduce delays. The effective date tied to the export procedure is **1 July 2017**, and the requirement remains to use **FORM GST RFD-11** on the GST portal.

The petitioner contended that it was unable to access the GST portal and, consequently, could not submit its response to the show cause notice or participate in subsequent proceedings. During the initial hearing, the Special Government Pleader for State Tax sought time to ascertain the factual position. At the subsequent hearing, the Department admitted that certain technical glitches prevented the petitioner from accessing the GST portal. Taking note of this admission, the High Court held that the issuance of the cancellation notice and suspension of registration were legally unsustainable as the petitioner had been denied an effective opportunity to respond, contrary to the principles of natural justice. Accordingly, the Court set aside both the impugned show cause notice and the suspension order while reserving liberty to the Department to initiate fresh proceedings strictly in accordance with law. The writ petition was disposed of without any order as to costs. A single benchmark ensured consistent valuation and reduced disputes about the rates charged by individual banks. This distinction arose before the Bombay High Court in a petition filed by Bajaj Finance Ltd. The Court sought a clear examination of the boundary between permissible assistance to borrowers and activities involving objectionable advertisements or assurances concerning the extinguishment of loan liabilities. Significantly, the order is interim. It neither declares all debt management services unlawful nor gives unrestricted approval to their activities. They allegedly represented that borrowers could get rid of their loans, obtain reduced interest rates or even avoid repayment altogether, with legal and other assistance being provided. The approval comes nearly three years after regulatory restrictions on Paytm Payments Bank disrupted its wallet services and forced the company to reassess its payments business. rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has issued a revised framework for domestic money transfer (DMT) services that does two main things: it caps cash transfers under DMT at **Rs 10,000 per transaction** and **consolidates/streamlines the existing DMT rules** into a single updated set of requirements. For compliance purposes, this means any entity offering domestic money transfer services must ensure that no individual cash transfer exceeds the Rs 10,000 ceiling, and systems, agent processes, and transaction controls should be adjusted to prevent acceptance or processing of higher-value cash transfers.

The change applies to **domestic money transfer services**, so the operative compliance question is whether your business is involved in receiving cash from a sender and remitting funds to a beneficiary within India through DMT rails. The document indicates a broader regulatory cleanup as well, meaning firms should review the consolidated rules rather than relying on fragmented prior instructions; the consolidation suggests earlier DMT directions may have been reorganized or superseded to the extent inconsistent with the new framework.

No separate deadline date, phased implementation schedule, or numerical threshold beyond the **Rs 10,000 per transaction cap** is visible in the provided text. A compliance team should therefore focus immediately on confirming that onboarding, transaction monitoring, agent training, customer communications, and transaction-limit controls all reflect the new ceiling, and should verify whether any legacy procedures for higher-value cash remittances must be discontinued or reclassified under other payment products.

rows.summary: This article reports on a proposed Reserve Bank of India change to the priority sector lending (PSL) framework that would make it easier for banks to count certain loans toward PSL targets and reduce dependence on borrower certificates. The draft is described as widening the lending options eligible for PSL classification, which should help banks rely less on certificates as proof that a loan qualifies; for compliance teams, the key takeaway is that documentary substantiation for PSL eligibility may become less rigid if the proposal is finalized. The piece does not provide the exact draft rule text, numerical PSL targets, or any implementation date/deadline in the content shown, so there is no specific effective date to calendar from this document alone. It does, however, indicate a likely procedural shift: banks may need to update internal PSL classification and verification processes to reflect broader eligible lending avenues and potentially revised evidence requirements once the RBI’s final version is issued.

The article reports that Piramal Finance’s CEO, Jairam Sridharan, expects the revised co-lending framework to preserve “pure origination” arrangements, but to make it difficult or impossible for lenders to continue using loan origination as an upfront monetisation strategy. In particular, he says structures where an originator books a loan and then immediately recognises profit by assigning it or co-lending it to investors based on the net present value of future cash flows “may not survive” under the new rules. For compliance purposes, the key point is that any business model relying on immediate profit recognition from direct assignment or co-lending of originated loans may need to be reworked, while straightforward origination-only arrangements are expected to remain permissible.

The piece also provides current scale and exposure data for context: Piramal Finance’s co-lending book is around Rs 5,000 crore and is growing at an annualised 20–25%, and the company says it is currently participating purely as an investor rather than originating much business for banks. The company also notes revolving credit exposure of around Rs 2,000 crore, equal to 2% of its Rs 1 lakh crore book, which is relevant as a size-of-exposure indicator rather than a new requirement.

Separately, Sridharan flags the proposed insurance distribution norms as creating an estimated 18–24 basis point drag on return on assets, although Piramal says it has a natural hedge through its 50% ownership in an insurance business. The article also mentions AI-led lending operations, stating that AI-driven disbursements were Rs 102 crore and collections handled entirely by AI without human intervention were Rs 172 crore, but it does not describe any new regulatory obligations tied to those AI figures. Overall, the only clear compliance-impacting change discussed is the anticipated tightening of co-lending rules, especially around upfront monetisation of originated loans through assignment or co-lending structures.

rows.desc: Articles 6 min read Explained: IRDAI's four-part motor insurance structure; what changes from December 15 The new framework requires customers to record which optional covers they want, while insurers must disclose the premium charged for each component separately. ETBFSI Research ETBFSI Updated On Nov 12, 2026 at 12:00 PM IST Read by 100 Professionals var news_msid = 135719372; console.log(news_msid); Set ETBFSI as your preferred source on Google Copy Link Share on WhatsApp Share on Linkedin Share on X Share on Telegram Share on Facebook IRDAI's four-part motor insurance framework separates third-party liability, occupant liability, personal accident and own-damage cover, with only specified components remaining mandatory.Insurers must disclose premiums separately for each component and obtain customers' recorded choices through a standardised option form.Existing third-party policyholders can add occupant liability cover during the policy period by paying an additional premium to the same insurer.The new framework gives insurers flexibility to price optional covers while mandating standardised policy wordings, customer disclosures and Bima Sugam integration from December 15.Motor insurance buyers will have greater clarity over the protection they purchase from December 15, when insurers introduce a four-section policy structure separating compulsory third-party liability from cover for passengers, personal accidents and damage to the insured vehicle. The new framework requires customers to record which optional covers they want, while insurers must disclose the premium charged for each component separately.The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) has directed general insurers to adopt the new structure for private cars and two-wheelers, following a Supreme Court order in the case of National Insurance Company Ltd versus Thungala Dhana Laxmi and others. The framework, set out in a November 2 circular, prescribes standardised policy wordin
rows.summary:
IRDAI has directed general insurers to move, from **December 15**, to a **four-part motor insurance structure** for **private cars and two-wheelers**. The policy will now be split into **third-party liability**, **occupant liability**, **personal accident cover**, and **own-damage cover**, with only the legally required third-party component remaining mandatory; the other covers will be optional and must be explicitly selected by the customer. Insurers must **itemize and disclose the premium for each component separately** rather than presenting a single bundled price, and they must obtain the customer’s **recorded choice** for the optional covers through a **standardized option form**.

The framework was issued in an **IRDAI circular dated November 2, 2026**, and was introduced in response to a **Supreme Court order in National Insurance Company Ltd. v. Thungala Dhana Laxmi and others**. It also requires insurers to use **standardized policy wordings**, improve customer disclosures, and integrate the process with **Bima Sugam** beginning on the effective date. A further operational change is that **existing third-party policyholders** will be allowed to **add occupant liability cover during the policy term** by paying an **additional premium to the same insurer**, rather than waiting for renewal. The document emphasizes that insurers will have flexibility to price the optional covers, but they must comply with the standardized structure and disclosure requirements once the framework takes effect.

rows.summary:
Bank of Baroda (BoB) said the transition to the expected credit loss (ECL) framework will create a significant one-time capital hit and a smaller but continuing increase in credit costs. Management quantified the one-time impact at about 125 basis points of capital, or roughly Rs 12,500 crore, and said the bank has already set aside a Rs 2,500 crore floating provision specifically for the ECL transition that may be adjusted in line with regulatory guidelines. After that existing buffer is applied, the remaining one-time impact over a five-year period could be around 25 basis points at best.

BoB also said the recurring impact of ECL on credit costs is expected to be 30–35 basis points on a gross basis and 20–25 basis points on a net basis. Despite this expected pressure, the bank has kept its overall FY27 credit-cost guidance unchanged at below 0.6%. Management noted that, excluding prudential provisioning made during the quarter, credit cost in Q2 FY27 was 0.18%.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that this is not a new operational requirement imposed on customers; it is an accounting/regulatory capital transition affecting BoB’s provisioning, capital planning, and credit-cost reporting over the next several years. The statement indicates the bank is already building additional provisioning buffers and will align the Rs 2,500 crore floating provision with regulatory treatment as permitted.

rows.title: RBI consolidates domestic money transfer rules, specifies transaction limits
rows.desc: Articles 3 min read RBI consolidates domestic money transfer rules, specifies transaction limits The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has consolidated its framework for domestic money transfers, prescribing transaction limits for cash-based remittances, mandating additional authentication for senders and requiring banks to strengthen monitoring of unusual fund transfers. Shrishti Sharma ETBFSI Published On Nov 11, 2026 at 06:37 PM IST Read by 100 Professionals var news_msid = 135738757; console.log(news_msid); Set ETBFSI as your preferred source on Google Copy Link Share on WhatsApp Share on Linkedin Share on X Share on Telegram Share on Facebook * Cash pay-out transfers from bank accounts will be capped at Rs 10,000 per transaction and Rs 25,000 per beneficiary per month.* Cash pay-in through Business Correspondents (BCs), ATMs and other channels will be limited to Rs 5,000 per transaction and Rs 25,000 per remitter per month.* Walk-in customers can remit up to Rs 50,000 through NEFT at bank branches.* Banks and BCs must register remitters using verified mobile numbers and self-certified officially valid documents, with every transaction requiring additional authentication.The Reserve Bank of India on Wednesday issued the Reserve Bank of India (Domestic Money Transfer) Directions, 2026, consolidating the existing instructions governing domestic money transfers through formal banking channels.The directions, effective immediately, apply to scheduled commercial banks, including regional rural banks, urban co-operative banks, state co-operative banks and district central co-operative banks, as well as authorised payment system operators and participants, including banks and non-banks, to the extent applicable to their respective services.The domestic money transfer (DMT) framework was introduced to facilitate small-value fund transfers through formal banking channels, particularly for individuals such as migrant workers who may lack access to conventional banking facilitie

rows.title: Tata Sons-Noel Rift Widens Over Succession Calls
rows.desc: Articles 2 min read Tata Sons-Noel Rift Widens Over Succession Calls Appointments at Trent, Voltas and Tata International reignite oversight concerns within the group kala vijayraghavan and sagar malviya Published On Nov 12, 2026 at 07:59 AM IST Read by 100 Professionals var news_msid = 135752672; console.log(news_msid); Set ETBFSI as your preferred source on Google Copy Link Share on WhatsApp Share on Linkedin Share on X Share on Telegram Share on Facebook Mumbai: Tata Sons has been blindsided by leadership succession decisions at some Noel Tata-led group companies, which have appointed new chairpersons without seeking the holding company's customary approval, people close to the matter said.The appointments, made after Noel Tata stepped down as chairman after turning 70 earlier this month, have brought into sharper focus the rift between Tata, who heads Tata Trusts, and Tata Sons, led by chairman N Chandrasekaran, over authority and the holding company's role in succession decisions at group companies.While the people cited above said Tata Sons' approval has always been sought for such appointments, legal experts said such approval would be legally mandatory only if the company's articles of association specifically provide for it. The Companies Act, 2013, does not require a promoter or holding company to approve the appointment of a chairperson. Advt The appointments of Bahram Vakil as chairman of Trent and Tata Investment Corporation, Sunil D'Souza as chairman of Voltas, and TV Narendran as chairman of Tata International were made without prior approval from Tata Sons, sources said.The holding company is likely to take up the matter at its next meeting, they said, adding that the emergence of parallel power centres within the conglomerate is a concern. Tata Sons and Noel Tata declined to comment.Tata was in control of strategic decisions and business plans at the group companies he chaired, officials said. rows.summary:
SEBI’s Nodal Co-ordination Cell issued an informal guidance response to Share India Securities Limited on August 17, 2026, in answer to a June 22, 2026 request concerning whether securities bought under Discretionary Portfolio Management Services (D-PMS) may be pledged. The firm explained that, under its D-PMS setup, clients maintain demat accounts with an approved custodian, trades are executed through empaneled brokers, and the securities purchased remain in the client’s beneficial ownership and are held in the client’s name in the demat account; the specific practical question was whether a client can pledge those securities, either directly or by routing instructions through the portfolio manager to the custodian.

The document is an interpretive guidance request rather than a rulemaking or enforcement order, so it does not announce a new regulation, fee, threshold, or deadline. Its substance is that the requester is seeking SEBI’s view on the permissibility and regulatory implications of pledging client-held securities purchased through the D-PMS framework, including whether the portfolio manager may facilitate or permit such pledging despite the securities being the client’s property. The text provided stops at the formulation of Query 1 and does not include SEBI’s answer, conditions, or any final compliance direction. For compliance purposes, the only concrete operational facts stated are that the assets are held in the client’s demat account with an approved custodian, the trading is routed through empaneled brokers, and the issue concerns possible pledge instructions from the client directly or through the portfolio manager.

SEBI has issued an informal guidance response dated July 17, 2026 to Integrated Enterprises (India) Private Limited, a registered Depository Participant (DP), in reply to its May 8, 2026 request for an interpretive letter under SEBI’s Informal Guidance Scheme, 2025. The company had asked whether a DP that is **not registered as a custodian** may levy any form of **“custodial charge”** on investors merely for holding securities in dematerialised form, in light of the SEBI Circular dated January 28, 2005, as read with the SEBI Master Circular for Depositories dated December 3, 2024.

The material compliance point is that the request concerns the **permissibility of charging investors for demat holdings**, specifically whether a DP can characterize or impose a fee as a custodial charge when it is not actually registered and regulated as a custodian. The document identifies the affected entity as a **Depository Participant servicing clients’ demat holdings and transfers** and levying charges under its tariff sheet, so the practical issue is whether such a charge is consistent with the SEBI framework governing DP fees and investor charges.

The excerpt provided does **not yet contain SEBI’s final interpretive conclusion or any operational directions**, so there are no additional deadlines, effective dates, numeric thresholds, or procedural changes stated in the visible text beyond the date of the application and the date of the informal guidance letter. For compliance purposes, the key takeaway from the visible portion is that the question is about whether a DP without custodian registration can impose a custody-style charge on demat clients at all, and the answer—once the rest of the letter is reviewed—would determine whether the firm must stop, amend, disclose, or restructure that fee.

rows.summary:
SEBI issued an informal guidance letter on June 4, 2026, in response to Saint-Gobain Sekurit Automotive Private Limited’s request for a “no action” view under the SEBI (Informal Guidance) Scheme, 2025 regarding the SEBI (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011. The specific question was whether Regulation 10(1)(d)(iii) of the Takeover Regulations would apply to the transfer and vesting of shares currently held by Saint-Gobain India Private Limited—26.74% of the equity of Saint-Gobain Sekurit India Limited, consisting of 2,43,59,490 shares—into Saint Gobain Sekurit Automotive Private Limited under a proposed demerger scheme.

rows.desc: Page 1 of 5 GENERAL MANAGER DEPARTMENT OF DEBT AND HYBRID SECURITIES POLICY AND DEVELOPMENT – 1 SEBI/HO/DDHS/DDHS-RACPOD1/P/OW/2025/0000025190/1 September 23, 2025 To, Ms. Rashmi Jain, Company Secretary and Compliance Officer, Tata Realty and Infrastructure Limited, E Block, Valtas Premises, TB Kadam Marg, Chichpokli, Mumbai-400 033 Ma’am, Subject: Request for informal guidance by way of an interpretative letter on applicability of Chapter IV and Chapter VA of the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 under the provisions of SEBI (Informal Guidance) Scheme, 2003 by Tata Realty and Infrastructure Limited 1. This has reference to your letter dated June 09, 2025, seeking an interpretative letter under the SEBI (Informal Guidance) Scheme, 2003. 2. Vide the said letter it has been inter-alia stated that Tata Realty and Infrastructure Limited is a public limited company incorporated under the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013 and is a wholly owned subsidiary of Tata Sons Private Limited, having only Non-Convertible debentures (‘NCDs’) listed on BSE; with no other listed specified securities. Further, based on your audited financial statements, the value of outstanding listed NCDs as on March 31, 2025 is Rs.535 crores. Page 2 of 5 3. In view of the above, you have sought an interpretive letter under the SEBI (Informal Guidance) Scheme, 2003 from SEBI on the following: 3.1. Query 1: As on March 31, 2025, the outstanding value of the listed NCDs of the Company were Rs.535 Crores. Hence, would the company be classified as a HVDLE w.e.f April 01, 2025? 3.2. Query 2: As on March 31, 2025, the outstanding value of the listed NCDs of the company were Rs.535 crores. Hence, would the company be under statutory obligations to comply with Regulation 3(3) of SEBI Listing Regulations which mandates the company to comply with the provision of Chapter IV of the SEBI Listing Regulations or considering that regulation 15(1A) restricts its applicabilit
rows.summary:
SEBI’s letter responds to Tata Realty and Infrastructure Limited’s request for informal guidance under the SEBI (Informal Guidance) Scheme, 2003 on whether Chapter IV and Chapter VA of the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 apply to it. Tata Realty stated that it is a public company and wholly owned subsidiary of Tata Sons Private Limited, that it has only listed non-convertible debentures (NCDs) on BSE and no other listed specified securities, and that the outstanding value of those listed NCDs was Rs. 535 crore as of March 31, 2025. Based on that fact pattern, the company asked whether it would be classified as a “high value debt listed entity” (HVDLE) from April 1, 2025, and whether it would then have to comply with Regulation 3(3), which makes Chapter IV applicable, or whether Regulation 15(1A) limits that applicability.

For compliance purposes, the key issue is the threshold/value test: the company’s outstanding listed debt of Rs. 535 crore as of March 31, 2025 is above the HVDLE threshold, so the question is whether the Chapter IV obligations attach starting April 1, 2025. The submission specifically frames the compliance concern around the interaction between Regulation 3(3) and Regulation 15(1A), i.e., whether being an HVDLE triggers the full governance/disclosure requirements in Chapter IV despite the general restriction on applicability in Regulation 15(1A). The document excerpt provided does not include SEBI’s final substantive answer, but it clearly establishes the operative facts, the relevant date (March 31, 2025 for the outstanding amount and April 1, 2025 as the potential effective date), and the exact compliance question: whether a listed-debt-only issuer with Rs. 535 crore outstanding NCDs must start complying with Chapter IV and Chapter VA of the SEBI LODR framework.

Rajagopal Sundaram Alternate Assets Limited, Sundaram Towers, 1 st and 2 nd floor 46, Whites Road, Royapettah, Chennai, 600014 Dear Sir, Sub: Request for Informal Guidance by way of interpretive letter under the provisions of Securities and Exchange Board of India (Informal Guidance) Scheme, 2003 in connection with the provisions of Securities and Exchange Board of India (Alternative Investment Funds) Regulations, 2012 (“AIF Regulations”) Ref: Your letter dated April 23, 2025 1. In the context of your letter under reference, you have, inter alia, stated that Sundaram Alternate Assets Limited (‘the Applicant’) is a SEBI registered Portfolio Manager bearing registration no. INP000006271 and also the Investment Manager for Sundaram Alternative Investment Trust, a Category III Alternative Investment Fund (“AIF”) having registration no. IN/AIF3/16-17/0291 and Sundaram Category II AIF having registration no. IN/AIF2/17- 18/0340, and have sought an interpretive letter under the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Informal Guidance) Scheme, 2003 (“Informal Guidance Scheme”) from SEBI in respect of the following query – i. Please clarify whether during the extended period, the close-ended Alternative Investment Fund is permitted only to liquidate its existing portfolio investments or allowed to make investments in portfolio companies. Page 2 of 4 2. Our Comments: The submissions made in your letter have been considered and without necessarily agreeing with your analysis, our views on the issues raised in your letter are as under: 2.1. In terms of Regulation 13(5) of AIF Regulations, extension of the tenure of the close ended Alternative Investment Fund may be permitted up to two years subject to approval of two-thirds of the unit holders by value of their investment in the Alternative Inve
rows.summary:
SEBI has issued an informal guidance letter dated **July 9, 2025** in response to Sundaram Alternate Assets Limited’s request regarding the **extension of tenure for close-ended Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs)** under the **SEBI (Alternative Investment Funds) Regulations, 2012**. The applicant, which is a SEBI-registered portfolio manager (**registration no. INP000006271**) and the investment manager for **Sundaram Alternative Investment Trust** (Category III AIF, **registration no. IN/AIF3/16-17/0291**) and **Sundaram Category II AIF** (**registration no. IN/AIF2/17-18/0340**), asked whether, during the extended period of a close-ended AIF, the fund may only liquidate existing investments or whether it may also make new investments in portfolio companies.

SEBI’s comment cites **Regulation 13(5)** of the AIF Regulations, which allows a close-ended AIF’s tenure to be **extended for up to two years** if approved by **two-thirds of the unit holders by value of their investment** in the AIF. SEBI’s guidance indicates that, during the extended tenure, the AIF is **not restricted only to liquidation** of its existing portfolio; rather, it is also **permitted to make investments in portfolio companies**. This means compliance teams should treat the extension period as a continued investment period, not a wind-down-only period, unless the fund’s own constitutive documents or other applicable rules impose stricter limits. The letter is issued as an **interpretive response under the SEBI (Informal Guidance) Scheme, 2003**, and addresses the specific operational question raised by the applicant for its close-ended AIFs.

rows.summary:
This notice sets out registration and accommodation procedures for the Seventh Annual International Research Conference on Securities Markets (7th IRCSM) 2026–27, titled “Technology, Trust, and Transition: Securities Markets Reimagined for a Digital Future,” to be held February 10–12, 2027. Participants must complete separate forms and make separate payments for registration and accommodation; the registration form must be filled out first, and applicants must choose the correct fee link under the Registration tab for either “Indian Participants” or “International Participants.” The notice emphasizes that the participant’s name must be entered with correct spelling because the same name will appear on the participation certificate and later changes will not be accepted.

For accommodation, participants must calculate the number of nights they intend to stay and use the “plus (+)” function in the accommodation form to select and pay for the appropriate number of days. NISM will verify the check-in and check-out dates against the payment made and will provide campus stay accordingly. Campus accommodation is available only from February 10, 2027 through February 13, 2027, with a maximum stay of 3 nights. The accommodation form offers two payment subcategories: single occupancy for a single room, or double occupancy if the participant is staying with a spouse/parent; in the double-occupancy case, the accompanying spouse/parent must also have their registration fees paid. The notice specifically prohibits female participants from sharing a room with a male participant unless that person is a spouse, parent, or close relative.

The document also states that selected paper presenters are required to pay registration charges, but their accommodation will be complimentary. Presenters are instructed to wait until the research paper results are announced before making accommodation-related decisions. Finally, NISM reserves the right to cancel, postpone, modify, or otherwise change the conference arrangements, indicating that attendees should monitor for updates and be prepared for administrative changes.

This document is not a rulemaking or notice with binding regulatory deadlines; it is a public investor-awareness campaign message from SEBI (“Samajh Se Investing Simple,” i.e., invest with understanding). Its core instruction is that investors should first understand products and facts before investing, rather than relying on tips or hype, and that they should start with small amounts, begin investing early, and stay invested with patience. The campaign explicitly promotes informed selection among regulated investment products, naming mutual funds and SIPs, stocks, REITs, InvITs, commodities, and bonds as categories investors should learn to recognize and evaluate before choosing the right investment approach.

The communication also emphasizes fraud prevention: investors are warned to “beware of investment frauds” and not depend on tips, but instead make decisions based on facts. It presents “facts” and “understanding” as the basis for investment behavior, urging people to plan first and invest later rather than acting impulsively. No specific effective date, compliance deadline, filing obligation, threshold, or rate is provided in the content.

For a compliance team, the relevant takeaway is that this is a SEBI investor-education initiative that may be used as a basis for internal investor communication, education, or conduct messaging, especially around suitability, product understanding, and anti-fraud awareness. The content does not impose new operational requirements on regulated entities in the text provided, but it does reinforce the expectation that market participants encourage informed investing and steer investors toward regulated products rather than unverified advice.

Here's a list of FAQs for the SEBI Investor Awareness Test: 1.What is the SEBI Investor Awareness Test (Level 1) ? Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) in association with National Institute of Securities Markets (NISM) has introduced this examination with an aim of fostering Financial Literacy and Investor awareness among the Investment public. This initiative seeks to empower individuals with essential knowledge about basic concepts of savings and Investment. By equipping potential investors with the necessary skills and insights, the regulator aims to enhance financial literacy and promote informed decision-making. This exam aims to empower prospective investors, enabling them to make informed choices and navigate the complexities of financial markets effectively. 2.Who can take the SEBI Investor Awareness Test (Level 1)? Anyone who is keen on learning about the Indian Financial Markets may take the exam. There is no eligibility requirement with regards to age as well as educational qualification to take the SIAT exam. 3.How can I register for the SEBI Investor Awareness Test (Level 1)? It describes the portal’s functional sections: an AI Tools & Quantum Computing knowledge area with toolkits, tutorials, and expert-led sessions intended to help the securities market prepare for emerging cryptographic threats and automated cyberattacks; an Advisories & Circulars section containing FAQs, regulatory advisories, SEBI circulars, alerts, and cybersecurity guidance; a Security Incidents & Reporting section for reporting incidents and sharing breaches, Indicators of Compromise (IOCs), Indicators of Attack (IOAs), and public threat information; and a Vulnerabilities & Threat Intelligence section that integrates sources such as Cyber Swachhta Kendra (CSK) and the Market Security Operations Center (MSOC) to identify and mitigate threats before they affect market functions or investor data.

Instead, the practical compliance implication is that securities-market participants should use the portal as the central reference point for cybersecurity advisories, incident reporting, vulnerability intelligence, and educational materials, and should monitor the portal for future SEBI advisories, circulars, alerts, FAQs, and incident feeds that may create binding obligations. rows.title: Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPI)
rows.summary:
The document appears to summarize SEBI’s responses to comments on proposed changes for Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPIs), and it indicates that SEBI is **not accepting several requests to relax the compliance framework**. On the proposal relating to **identification/validation of SWAGAT-FI status for existing FPIs**, commenters asked that existing FPIs not be required to provide additional proof because it would increase burden and paperwork; SEBI **disagreed**, saying the verification requirements will instead be aligned with the **existing exemption criteria under the Additional Disclosure Framework**, which the industry has already implemented. In practical terms, FPIs seeking the relevant status will still need to demonstrate the required conditions—such as diversification, independence of fund managers, regulator confirmation, blind pool status, and absence of segregated portfolios—but SEBI’s stated approach is to use a familiar verification model rather than introduce an entirely new process.

On **re-KYC and fee/payment periodicity**, commenters wanted the current periodicity to remain unchanged and opposed additional re-KYC requirements, arguing that material changes such as UBO updates would be caught through ordinary monitoring and that longer fee blocks would reduce SEBI’s flexibility. SEBI **disagreed with removing the re-KYC requirement**, stating that **material change reporting obligations remain in force** and that the additional re-KYC requirement is being retained for FPIs, consistent with treatment of other investors. The document also clarifies that there is **no yearly fee requirement currently**; instead, the proposal is to **increase the fee block period from 3 years to 10 years**, and this 10-year block is intended to **coincide with the re-KYC cycle**, rather than changing the underlying ability of SEBI to adjust fees.

A third item begins addressing comments that **FPIs should not be allowed to facilitate single demat accounts**, but the text provided is truncated, so the specific final regulatory outcome for that point is not visible in the excerpt. Based on the visible portions, the compliance takeaway is that SEBI is **preserving core identity, ownership, and status-verification controls for FPIs**, while trying to implement them through standardized existing frameworks rather than eliminating the obligations.

rows.summary:

rows.title:
The Information Technology Department (ITD) of SEBI is the enabler of technology landscape in the organisation. ITD is committed to its vision of leveraging technology in partnership with every department of SEBI to achieve the following goals: 
1.	Development and implementation of Enterprise wide solutions like Portals and gateways, Network Infrastructure, Private Cloud Infrastructure, Mail and messaging solution, Data lake, Document Management system, SAP Solution etc. 
2.	Facilitating Ease of doing Business for market intermediaries by enhancing the digital interfaces between them and SEBI in respect of a large range of functions such as Regulations, Compliance and Reporting. 
3.	Developing Data Warehouse system for surveillance, inspections and supervision activities. 
4.	Driving data analytics practice at SEBI. 
5.	Ensuring deployment of strong cyber security measures and information technology (IT) resilience in the market Infrastructure to facilitate uninterrupted trading and privacy of investor data. 
6.	Undertaking IT inspections and audit for MIIs and intermediaries. 
7.	Development of framework for information interchange with various government agencies. 
8.	Facilitating innovation in markets through SEBI’s Innovation Sandbox Framework.

rows.desc: Compilation of Informal Guidance relating to SEBI (PIT) Regulations, 2015 for the period Oct 2015- Sept 2026 Oct 13, 2026| Clarifications on Insider Trading Compilation of Informal Guidance relating to SEBI (PIT) Regulations, 2015 for the period Oct 2015- Sept 2026
rows.summary:
The document is a compilation of informal guidance issued by SEBI relating to the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015, covering the period from October 2015 through September 2026, and published/dated October 13, 2026. On the face of the material provided, it does not introduce a new standalone rule, amendment, threshold, deadline, or procedure; rather, it is a reference compilation of clarifications on insider-trading compliance under the PIT Regulations. For a compliance team, the relevant takeaway is that the document is intended to collect SEBI’s informal interpretive guidance over that period and should be used to understand how SEBI has interpreted existing obligations under the insider-trading framework.

Because the provided content contains only the title and date, it does not specify any particular entities, transactions, disclosure forms, trading windows, UPSI handling rules, pre-clearance thresholds, or reporting deadlines that were changed or newly required. It likewise does not identify any one listed company, intermediary, employee category, designated person group, or connected person as newly affected. In practice, the compliance implication is limited to confirming that this is a compilation source for interpretation of the PIT Regulations rather than an operative circular imposing fresh compliance duties in the text supplied.

These Directions are issued under Section 18 read with Section 10(2) of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007. Yours faithfully, (Sara Rajendra Kumar Neti) Chief General Manager-in-Charge Encl.: As above 2 Reserve Bank of India (Domestic Money Transfer) Directions, 2026 Table of Contents Chapter I – Preliminary ........................................................................................................ 3 A. Short Title and Commencement .................................................................................... 3 B. Applicability .................................................................................................................... 3 Chapter II – Conduct of Business ....................................................................................... 3 C. Payment of amounts transferred from a bank account (Cash Pay-out Service) ............. 3 D. Payment of amounts to be credited to bank accounts (Cash Pay-in Service) ................ 4 E. Operational Safeguards and Monitoring ......................................................................... 4 F. Inter-bank Settlement ..................................................................................................... 4 G. Charges ......................................................................................................................... 5 H. Customer Grievance
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has issued the **Domestic Money Transfer (DMT) Directions, 2026** to harmonize and consolidate the existing instructions on domestic money transfer. The directions are issued under **Section 18 read with Section 10(2) of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007**, and were released by RBI’s Department of Payment and Settlement Systems in the circular dated **November 11, 2026**.

The directions apply to **all Scheduled Commercial Banks**, including **Regional Rural Banks, Urban Co-operative Banks, State Co-operative Banks, and District Central Co-operative Banks**, as well as **authorised payment system operators and participants**, whether **banks or non-banks**. In other words, the framework is not limited to banks; it also governs payment system entities that offer or participate in domestic money transfer arrangements.

The document is structured around two main service models: **cash pay-out services**, where amounts transferred from a bank account are paid out in cash, and **cash pay-in services**, where amounts are accepted in cash for credit to a bank account. It also sets out requirements on **operational safeguards and monitoring**, **inter-bank settlement**, **charges**, and **customer grievance handling**, indicating that compliance obligations extend beyond transaction processing to include control systems, settlement discipline, pricing practices, and complaint redressal.

As far as the excerpt provided shows, the key change is the **replacement/consolidation of prior RBI instructions into a single 2026 direction set**; the excerpt does not itself specify new thresholds, fee caps, transaction limits, dates for phased implementation, or numerical compliance standards. For compliance purposes, affected institutions should treat this as the governing RBI framework for DMT going forward and review the operative chapters for any specific procedural controls, settlement timelines, fee disclosures, grievance timelines, or restrictions that apply to their exact role in the DMT chain.
