rows.summary:
The RBI has issued a consolidated **Master Direction on Cyber Resilience and Digital Payment Security Controls for authorised non-bank Payment System Operators (PSOs)**, dated **November 5, 2026** (reference **DPSS/2026-27/475 CO.DPSS.CSD.No.S825/01-01-078/2026-2027**). The purpose is to create a **single reference document** for PSOs by consolidating earlier guidance issued on the subject, specifically the **December 31, 2019** circular on cyber security controls for third-party ATM Switch Application Service Providers and the **January 10, 2020** guidance on **system audit of payment systems operated under the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007**. The Master Direction is aimed at ensuring non-bank PSOs are resilient to existing and emerging **information systems and cyber security risks**, and it covers governance arrangements for **identification, assessment, monitoring, and management** of those risks, along with baseline security measures to support **system resiliency** and **safe, secure digital payment transactions**.

The document states that affected entities should **endeavour to migrate to the latest security standards**, which means existing controls are not frozen at the current baseline if stronger or newer standards are available. It also clarifies that the existing RBI instructions on **security and risk mitigation for card payments, Prepaid Payment Instruments (PPIs), and mobile banking** continue to apply unchanged. Where there is any **discrepancy in applicability** between the consolidated Master Direction and earlier directions, the revised Master Direction is intended to serve as the single reference point, so compliance teams should align policies and control frameworks accordingly.

No specific monetary thresholds, technical percentage thresholds, or explicit implementation deadlines are stated in the excerpt provided, but the compliance obligation is to treat this as a **binding consolidated framework** applicable to **authorised non-bank PSOs** and to ensure internal cyber resilience, digital payment security, and audit-related controls are updated to match the consolidated directions and any higher/latest standards referenced by RBI.

rows.title: Foreign Exchange Management (Export and Import of Goods and Services) (Second Amendment) Regulations, 2026
rows.desc: Published in the Official Gazette of Government of India Extraordinary Part III, Section 4, on November 02, 2026 RESERVE BANK OF INDIA FOREIGN EXCHANGE DEPARTMENT CENTRAL OFFICE Mumbai 400 001 Notification No. FEMA 23(R)/(2 )/2026-RB November 02, 2026 Foreign Exchange Management (Export and Import of Goods and Services) (Second Amendment) Regulations, 2026 In exercise of the powers conferred by Section 7, Section 8, sub-section (6) of Section 10 and sub-section (2) of Section 47 of the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 (42 of 1999), the Reserve Bank of India makes the following amendments to the Foreign Exchange Management (Export and Import of Goods and Services) Regulations, 2026 [Notification No. FEMA 23(R)/2026-RB dated January 13, 2026] (hereinafter referred to as 'the principal regulations'), namely: 1. Short title and commencement: - (1) These regulations may be called the Foreign Exchange Management (Export and Import of Goods and Services) (Second Amendment) Regulations, 2026. (2) These regulations shall come into force from October 01, 2026. 2. In the principal regulations, in regulation 2, sub-regulation (1), after clause (d), the following shall be inserted, namely: - “(da) “resident individual” means a person resident in India who is a natural person.” 3.1 In the principal regulations, in regulation 3, in sub-regulation (2), the following shall be inserted as provisos (a) and (b), namely:- “(a) the exporter of services shall be deemed to have submitted the EDF when such exporter, being a resident individual, provides information required in relation to the receipt of payment for such services to the Authorised Dealer for crediting the account of the exporter. (b) the exporter of services shall be deemed to have submitted the EDF when such exporter, being a person other than a resident individual, provides information required in relation to the receipt of payment for such services to the Authorised Dealer for crediting the account of the exporter if
rows.summary:
This amendment to the RBI’s Foreign Exchange Management (Export and Import of Goods and Services) Regulations, 2026 took effect on **October 1, 2026**, even though it was published in the Official Gazette on **November 2, 2026**. It is issued as the **Foreign Exchange Management (Export and Import of Goods and Services) (Second Amendment) Regulations, 2026** under FEMA, 1999. The change first adds a formal definition of **“resident individual”** in regulation 2(1)(da), meaning **a person resident in India who is a natural person**.

The substantive compliance change is in **regulation 3(2)** on Export Declaration Form (EDF) submission for **exporters of services**. Under the new provisos, an exporter of services will be **deemed to have submitted the EDF** when the exporter gives the Authorised Dealer the information needed for the **receipt of payment and crediting of the exporter’s account**, rather than requiring a separate EDF submission in the usual way. The amendment draws a distinction between **resident individuals** and **all other persons** (such as companies, LLPs, partnerships, and other non-individual exporters): a resident individual is covered by proviso (a), while a non-resident-individual exporter is covered by proviso (b) subject to the condition stated in the text provided.

For compliance teams, the key operational point is that service exporters who are **resident individuals** now satisfy the EDF filing requirement through the payment/crediting information they provide to the bank, so internal export documentation and banking workflows should be aligned to ensure that the required receipt-of-payment details are furnished accurately and promptly to the **Authorised Dealer**. Any entity exporting services should review whether it is treated as a **resident individual** or as another type of person, because the amendment changes the compliance path for EDF submission and therefore affects how the company or exporter documents export proceeds and bank reporting under FEMA.

rows.title: Implementation of Section 51A of UAPA, 1967: Updates to UNSC’s 1988 (2011) Taliban Sanctions List: Amendment of 05 Entries
rows.desc: RBI/2026-27/303 DoR.AML.REC.255/14.06.001/2026-27 October 30, 2026 The Chairpersons/ CEOs of the Commercial Banks, Small Finance Banks, Payment Banks, Urban Co-operative Banks, Rural Co-operative Banks, Regional Rural Banks, Local Area Banks, Non-Banking Financial Companies, Asset Reconstruction Companies, All India Financial Institutions Madam/Dear Sir Implementation of Section 51A of UAPA, 1967: Updates to UNSC’s 1988 (2011) Taliban Sanctions List: Amendment of 05 Entries Please refer to Chapter IX on “Requirements/obligations under International Agreements - Communications from International Agencies” of the Reserve Bank of India - Know Your Customer, Directions, 2025 dated November 28, 2025 (amended time to time) (“Directions”), as applicable, as per which, regulated entity shall ensure that in terms of section 51A of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) (UAPA) Act, 1967 and amendments thereto, it does not have any account in the name of individuals / entities appearing in the lists of individuals and entities, suspected of having terrorist links, which are approved by and periodically circulated by the United Nations Security Council (UNSC). 2. In this connection, Ministry of External Affairs (MEA), Government of India has informed about the UNSC press release SC/16494 dated October 29, 2026 wherein the Security Council Committee established and maintained pursuant to Security Council resolution 1988 (2011) has enacted amendments to the ‘Taliban Sanctions List’, which includes names of individuals and entities associated with the Taliban. 2.1 The Security Council Committee pursuant to resolution 1988 (2011) enacted the amendments specified with strikethrough and/or underline in the entries below on its 1988 List of individuals and entities subject to the assets freeze, travel ban and arms embargo set out in paragraph 1 of Security Council resolution 2816 (2026), and adopted under Chapter VII of the Charter of the United Nations. 2 A. Individuals TAi.007 Name: 1
rows.summary:
This RBI communication requires all regulated entities covered by the RBI KYC Directions, 2025—specifically commercial banks, small finance banks, payment banks, urban co-operative banks, rural co-operative banks, regional rural banks, local area banks, NBFCs, asset reconstruction companies, and all India financial institutions—to continue ensuring, under Section 51A of the UAPA, 1967, that they do not maintain any account in the name of any person or entity appearing on the UNSC-approved lists of suspected terrorists/terror-linked parties. The circular updates the UNSC’s 1988 (2011) Taliban Sanctions List, following MEA intimation of UNSC press release SC/16494 dated October 29, 2026, and states that the Security Council Committee established under resolution 1988 (2011) has amended the Taliban Sanctions List; those amendments are reflected in the attached list entries using strikethrough and/or underline.

The substantive change in this communication is that five entries on the Taliban Sanctions List have been amended. The document excerpt provided begins the listing of the revised entries and explicitly notes that the list is subject to the asset freeze, travel ban, and arms embargo measures under paragraph 1 of UNSC resolution 2816 (2026), adopted under Chapter VII of the UN Charter. For compliance purposes, the key obligation is to compare customer names and beneficial ownership against the updated sanctions list immediately and to ensure no account is opened or continued in the name of any listed individual or entity.

The document does not state a separate implementation deadline in the excerpt provided, but because it is an update to the UNSC list and is issued under the RBI KYC framework, institutions should treat it as an immediate screening and controls update. Compliance teams should therefore refresh sanctions-screening databases, review any existing customer relationships against the amended names, and follow existing UAPA/UNSC escalation, freezing, and reporting procedures if any match is found.

This RBI communication directs all regulated entities covered by the RBI KYC Directions, 2025 — including commercial banks, small finance banks, payment banks, urban and rural co-operative banks, regional rural banks, local area banks, NBFCs, asset reconstruction companies, and all India financial institutions — to continue applying Section 51A of the UAPA, 1967 by ensuring they do not maintain accounts in the names of persons or entities appearing on the UNSC’s approved terrorist sanctions lists. The update is based on MEA intimation regarding UNSC press release SC/16490 dated October 26, 2026, which amended entries on the ISIL (Da’esh) and Al-Qaida Sanctions List under resolutions 1267 (1999), 1989 (2011), and 2253 (2015), read with Chapter VII of the UN Charter and Security Council resolution 2734 (2024). The RBI states that three entries have been amended, with the specific changes shown in the underlying UNSC list using strikethrough and underline; the excerpt provided begins the first amended individual entry, QDi.340 for Emilie Edwige Konig (DOB 9 Dec. 1984, POB Plo...), but the text supplied is cut off before the full amended particulars are shown.

For compliance purposes, the key operational requirement is that institutions must compare customer and beneficiary names against the updated UNSC list and ensure no accounts, services, or ongoing relationships exist for listed persons/entities, consistent with their existing sanctions screening and UAPA obligations. The document does not announce a new standalone deadline, rate, threshold, or filing date; rather, it is an implementation/update notice that becomes relevant immediately upon circulation because it refers to the current UNSC amendments and the existing obligations already contained in the RBI KYC Directions. Compliance teams should therefore use the latest UNSC amended list entries, update sanctions-screening systems and watchlists to reflect the 03 amended records, and confirm that any positive matches are handled under the institution’s existing freeze/escalation/reporting procedures required by law and the RBI directions.

rows.summary:
This RBI communication directs all regulated entities covered under the RBI KYC Directions, 2025—specifically commercial banks, small finance banks, payment banks, urban co-operative banks, rural co-operative banks, regional rural banks, local area banks, non-banking financial companies, asset reconstruction companies, and all India financial institutions—to apply section 51A of the UAPA, 1967 in light of changes to the UN sanctions list. The update is triggered by MEA information referencing UNSC press release SC/16488 dated October 26, 2026, which states that the Security Council, acting under resolutions 1267 (1999), 1989 (2011), and 2253 (2015), removed three entries from the ISIL (Da’esh) and Al-Qaida Sanctions List after considering delisting requests under paragraph 75 of resolution 2734 (2024). As a result of the delisting, the assets freeze, travel ban, and arms embargo applicable under paragraph 1 of UNSC resolution 2734 (2024) no longer apply to those three removed entries.

For compliance purposes, the practical requirement is that entities must promptly update their sanctions screening/monitoring controls and account review processes so they do not continue to treat the delisted names as sanctioned persons under the UN/UAPA framework. The document reiterates that regulated entities must not maintain accounts in the names of individuals or entities appearing on the UNSC-approved lists of persons suspected of terrorist links, and the change here is specifically the removal of three names from that list, not the addition of new names. The communication is dated October 27, 2026, and it operates as an implementation update under the RBI KYC Directions, 2025 as amended from time to time.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **“Commercial Banks – Forthcoming Instructions) Second Amendment Directions, 2026”** on **October 23, 2026**, under **Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**. These amendments are directed at the **minimum capital requirements for operational risk** in the RBI’s **Commercial Banks – Forthcoming Instructions, 2025**, specifically **Chapter IV** of those Directions.

The key compliance change is that **Chapter IV, as amended, will take effect from April 1, 2027**. Until that date, the amended operational risk capital framework is not in force. The amendment states that **Paragraph 29 is replaced entirely**, and the revised text clarifies how the **Business Indicator (BI)** constituents — **ILDC, SC, and FC** — are described, with reference to **Table VIII** and the schedules in the prescribed financial statements format. It also says that an **indicative mapping of BI items to financial statement schedules and line items** will be issued later, so banks should not expect a finalized mapping in this amendment itself.

A critical compliance instruction is that the mapping is expressly stated to be **indicative**, not binding as a final taxonomy, but where the measurement, classification, or presentation of an item under the **Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks - Financial Statements: Presentation and Disclosures) Directions, 2025** differs from the treatment required under these operational risk directions, banks **must ensure that the items used for ORC computation are aligned with these operational risk directions**. In other words, when calculating **Operational Risk Capital (ORC)**, banks cannot simply rely on the financial statements presentation rules if those rules produce a different measurement/classification/presentation outcome. Compliance teams should therefore review the bank’s BI/ORC calculation methodology, identify any items whose accounting presentation may differ from the ORC treatment, and be prepared to adjust the computation framework before **April 1, 2027**.

rows.summary:
This circular expands where compounding applications for certain FEMA contraventions may be filed and processed. Previously, applications involving **Overseas Investments** and **Borrowing and Lending, and Guarantees** were being received at the **Central Office of the Reserve Bank of India**; under this circular, the Reserve Bank has **delegated compounding powers to select Regional Offices** for these matters as a customer-service measure. The circular applies to **Authorised Dealer Category-I banks and other Authorised Persons** and is issued with reference to the RBI’s earlier **A.P. (DIR Series) Circular No. 17/2024-25 dated October 1, 2024** and the **Master Directions on Compounding of Contraventions under FEMA, 1999 dated April 22, 2025**.

For **Overseas Investment** matters, the delegation covers compounding applications for contraventions under the **Foreign Exchange Management (Transfer or Issue of Any Foreign Security) Regulations, 2000** notified under **FEMA 19/RB-2000**, as amended, and the **Foreign Exchange Management (Transfer or Issue of Any Foreign Security) Regulations, 2004** notified under **FEMA 120/RB-2004**, as amended. The document indicates that the change is not a change in substantive law or thresholds, but a **change in the authority handling compounding**: instead of all such applications going to Central Office, the designated Regional Offices may now compound these contraventions.

The same delegation also extends to contraventions relating to **Borrowing and Lending, and Guarantees** transactions, which were likewise previously centralized at the Reserve Bank’s Central Office. Compliance teams should therefore route applicable compounding applications in accordance with the revised RBI process and confirm whether the relevant matter falls within the jurisdiction of a **select Regional Office** rather than the Central Office. The circular does not state a new monetary threshold, penalty rate, or filing deadline; its operative requirement is the **procedural redirection of compounding applications** to the newly delegated Regional Offices.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy) Eleventh Amendment Directions, 2026

To ensure alignment with the latest leverage ratio framework (‘leverage ratio 2017 standard’) issued by the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, there is a felt need to amend these Directions. 2. Accordingly, in exercise of the powers conferred by Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 and all other provisions / laws enabling the Reserve Bank of India to issue instructions in this regard, the Reserve Bank being satisfied that it is necessary and expedient in the public interest so to do, hereby, issues the Amendment Directions hereinafter specified. 3. These instructions shall be called the Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy) Eleventh Amendment Directions, 2026. 4. These Amendment Directions modify t he Directions as under: 4(1) Paragraph 262 shall be substituted with the following, namely: “262. The definition, minimum requirement, and the scope of application of the leverage ratio shall be as under: (1) The Basel III leverage ratio is defined as the capital measure (the numerator) divided by the exposure measure (the denominator), with this ratio expressed as a percentage: Leverage Ratio= Capital Measure Exposure Measure (2) The minimum leverage ratio for a domestic systemically important bank (D-SIB) shall be 4 per cent and 3.5 per cent for other banks. Branch of a global systemically important bank (G-SIB) in India ( hereinafter referred to as ‘G-SIB Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy) Eleventh Amendment Directions, 2026 2 branch’) shall maintain a leverage ratio of 3.5 per cent p
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Commercial Banks – Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy, Eleventh Amendment Directions, 2026** on **October 23, 2026** to update **Chapter VII: Leverage Ratio framework** of the existing 2025 capital adequacy directions so they align with the Basel Committee’s latest **“leverage ratio 2017 standard.”** The amendment is made under **Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and formally replaces **paragraph 262** of the 2025 Directions.

The key substantive change is a new paragraph 262 that restates the leverage ratio framework and minimum requirements. It defines the **Basel III leverage ratio** as **capital measure divided by exposure measure, expressed as a percentage**, and sets the minimum leverage ratio at **4.0% for domestic systemically important banks (D-SIBs)** and **3.5% for other banks**. It also states that **branches of global systemically important banks (G-SIBs) in India** must maintain a **3.5% leverage ratio**.

For compliance purposes, the amendment affects **commercial banks subject to the RBI Directions**, with specific obligations varying by bank type: D-SIBs face the higher **4% minimum**, while all other banks, including **G-SIB branches in India**, are subject to the **3.5% minimum**. The document does not specify a separate phase-in timetable or reporting deadline in the text provided, so the practical compliance requirement is to ensure the bank’s leverage ratio calculation and ongoing capital monitoring are aligned immediately with the substituted paragraph 262 and the Basel III leverage ratio definition.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks - Miscellaneous) Amendment Directions, 2026** under **section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and other enabling powers. The amendment is addressed to **small finance banks** and specifically refers to **Section C on “Limits for Non-Option Derivative Contracts” of Chapter IV** of the **Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks - Miscellaneous) Directions, 2025**.

The only substantive change is that **Section C on “Limits for Non-Option Derivative Contracts” (paragraph 37 of the 2025 Directions) has been deleted in its entirety**. The document does not replace that section with any new cap, formula, reporting rule, approval process, or other substitute requirement, so the prior paragraph 37 limits are no longer in force under these directions.

The amendment is titled the **Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks - Miscellaneous) Amendment Directions, 2026** and **takes effect immediately upon issuance**, i.e. **19 October 2026**. For compliance purposes, small finance banks should treat the deleted section as removed from the applicable directions from that date and ensure internal policies, limit frameworks, product approvals, and derivative dealing documentation are updated accordingly so they no longer rely on the superseded paragraph 37 language.

rows.summary:
The RBI’s **Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks - Miscellaneous) Second Amendment Directions, 2026**—issued under **Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and related enabling powers—makes a single but important change to the **Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks - Miscellaneous) Directions, 2025**. Specifically, it **deletes Section C of Chapter IV, titled “Limits for Non-Option Derivative Contracts” (paragraph 37 of the 2025 Directions)**. As a result, the prior RBI-prescribed limits applicable to commercial banks for non-option derivative contracts under that section are removed from the 2025 framework by this amendment.

The amendment is titled the **“Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks - Miscellaneous) Second Amendment Directions, 2026.”** It **takes effect immediately upon issuance** and is dated **October 19, 2026**. For compliance purposes, this means commercial banks should treat the referenced paragraph/section as no longer operative from the effective date and should update internal policies, operating limits, and any control or reporting references that relied on the deleted limits to ensure they do not continue applying a superseded RBI requirement.

rows.title: Master Directions on Relief/Savings Bonds
rows.summary:
This Master Direction consolidates and updates all operative RBI instructions on Relief/Savings Bonds as of June 30, 2018, and supersedes earlier scattered guidance by placing the current rules in one location; it was issued on July 2, 2018 and is stated to be updated whenever rules, regulations, or policy change. It applies to the designated Receiving Offices named in the circular: State Bank of India, all nationalized banks except Punjab and Sind Bank and Andhra Bank, Axis Bank Ltd., ICICI Bank Ltd., HDFC Bank Ltd., and Stock Holding Corporation of India Ltd. (SHCIL). The first operational change concerns broker enrollment/registration: Receiving Offices may use a simple registration process, under which a broker submits a request on business letterhead along with business data, and the Receiving Office must allot a code number that the broker must quote on all bond applications tendered for brokerage claims. The document also addresses appointment of sub-agents by Receiving Offices and notes a concern that some offices have engaged other banks as brokers/agents for receiving applications while those intermediaries use RBI’s name in publicity material and billboards, indicating that such arrangements and branding use are being scrutinized or should not misrepresent RBI involvement.

The directions also cover brokerage payment/rates for Savings Bonds and nomination facilities for Relief/Savings Bonds, with the detailed instructions contained in the later sections and appendix of the Master Direction. From a compliance perspective, the key obligation is to follow the updated RBI-prescribed procedures exactly, ensure only properly enrolled brokers are used for brokerage claims, and ensure the broker code system is implemented so applications can be tracked and brokerage paid only where properly claimed. Because the directions are a living compilation updated by RBI, compliance teams should treat this as a standing requirement to monitor subsequent amendments on the RBI website rather than a one-time circular.

rows.title: Master Direction – Operational Guidelines for Primary Dealers (Updated as on November 22, 2018)
rows.summary:
This update to the RBI Master Direction on Operational Guidelines for Primary Dealers reiterates and clarifies several existing operational requirements for primary dealers (PDs) in government securities markets. First, PDs must follow the RBI’s rules for submitting non-competitive bids in G-Sec auctions, as set out in RBI/2008-09/479 dated May 22, 2009, as amended from time to time. It also confirms that PDs may sell securities allotted in primary issues on the same day they are received, but only in accordance with the specific circulars cited in the direction: IDMC.PDRS.No.PDS.1/03.64.00/2000-01 dated October 6, 2000; RBI/2005/461–IDMD.PDRS.4777/10.02.01/2004-05 dated May 11, 2005; and RBI/2012-13/133-IDMD.PDRD.188/03.64.00/2012-13 dated July 16, 2012. For such same-day sales, PDs are permitted to use brokers to execute the sale contracts.

A key settlement requirement is that primary auction settlement is independent of secondary market settlement and must therefore be funded separately. Successful PDs must ensure sufficient funds are available in their RBI current account on the auction settlement day before 3:00 p.m. to cover their auction subscriptions. If funds are short, the deficiency will be treated as an instance of “SGL bouncing,” which triggers the applicable penal provisions. Compliance teams should therefore treat auction-day liquidity management as a standalone obligation, not something that can be covered by secondary market settlement balances.

In the secondary market, PDs are required to act as market makers in Government securities by quoting two-way prices in G-Sec on the NDS-OM platform, in the OTC market, and on recognized stock exchanges in India, while also taking principal positions in the secondary market. The direction also imposes annual turnover targets: PDs must achieve a minimum turnover ratio of 5 times for Government dated securities and 10 times for Treasury Bills/Cash Management Bills, measured against average month-end stock holdings. For outright transactions specifically, the minimum turnover ratio is lower but still mandatory: at least 3 times for Government dated securities and 6 times for T-Bills/CMBs. The turnover ratio is defined as total secondary-market purchases and sales during the year divided by average month-end stocks.

The document also begins a separate requirement on short-selling in the secondary market, stating that PDs must comply with RBI-issued guidelines on that activity, but the excerpt provided cuts off before the full rule text. For compliance purposes, the material obligations visible in this excerpt are the funding deadline of 3:00 p.m. on auction settlement days, the prohibition on failing to fund primary auction obligations without incurring SGL bouncing treatment, the mandatory market-making function, the specified annual turnover ratios, and adherence to the cited RBI circulars governing same-day sale of auction allotments and non-competitive bidding.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India [Conduct of Government Business by Agency Banks (ABs) – Payment of Agency Commission and Oversight of ABs] Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s 2026 Directions on “Conduct of Government Business by Agency Banks (ABs) – Payment of Agency Commission and Oversight of ABs” set out the framework for appointing agency banks, paying commission for government business, and monitoring compliance. The directions are issued on April 30, 2026, and apply to agency banks conducting Government business under RBI appointment; the document’s operative details govern which government transactions are eligible for agency commission, how they must be reported, and what documentation is required to claim payment. It also specifically distinguishes transactions that do **not** qualify for commission, so banks need to check each transaction type against the eligibility rules rather than assuming all government collections or payments are compensable.

A major substantive part of the directions is the commission framework for government business: the RBI specifies the rates of agency commission, clarifies when a **single challan is to be treated as a single transaction**, and lays out the exact procedure ABs must follow to submit commission claims. The directions also require ABs to report government transactions to RBI in the prescribed manner, which is tied to the commission claim process, and to submit specified supporting documents when seeking payment. The document additionally includes clarifications on commission claims and introduces a penalty mechanism in the form of **penal interest for wrong claims of agency commission**, meaning banks may face financial consequences if they claim commission incorrectly or inconsistently with the directions.

For compliance purposes, the key operational issue is that the directions are not just fee-setting rules; they create an end-to-end control regime over government business conducted by agency banks. ABs must ensure their transaction tagging, challan treatment, reporting, and claim support are aligned with RBI’s prescribed rules, especially for transactions linked to Government schemes, which receive separate treatment in the directions. The final chapter on oversight indicates RBI will supervise government business conducted by ABs, so banks should expect ongoing monitoring of appointment compliance, transaction reporting, claim integrity, and adherence to the eligibility rules for agency commission.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India [Disbursement of Government Pension by Agency Banks (ABs)] Directions, 2026 (Updated as on June 24, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Disbursement of Government Pension by Agency Banks (ABs) Directions, 2026”** (issued **April 30, 2026** and updated **June 24, 2026**) sets out the operating rules that **agency banks** must follow when paying government pension, including central, state, and related government pension disbursements routed through banks. The directions apply to **all agency banks authorized to disburse government pension**, and they replace/organize the compliance framework around pension payment timing, implementation of government orders (including **dearness relief (DR)** changes), error recovery, special handling for vulnerable pensioners, reimbursement, and life-certificate processing.

A core obligation is that agency banks must **promptly implement government orders** relating to pension changes, especially **DR and similar revisions**, and must keep themselves updated through the Government’s published orders available on the relevant government website. Banks are required to ensure pension is disbursed in line with the government’s instructions and at the prescribed time each month; the directions emphasize that pension should be credited **on the due date prescribed by the government/RBI framework**, not delayed by internal bank processing. Compliance teams should treat this as a strict operational requirement, because the directions place responsibility on the paying bank to avoid delayed credit and to ensure government-issued revisions are reflected without avoidable lag.

The document also addresses **recovery and refund of excess pension payments**. Where an excess payment occurs due to an error attributable to the **agency bank**, the bank is responsible for arranging recovery/refund in accordance with the directions and the applicable government instructions. Where the excess arises from a **government-attributed error**, the bank must still follow the prescribed process for correction, but the obligation and recovery mechanics differ from bank-attributed mistakes; this distinction matters for liability allocation, reporting, and reconciliation. Compliance staff should ensure the bank has controls to identify whether an overpayment originated from bank processing or from government input, because that affects how the excess is recovered and who bears the operational burden.

A separate chapter provides special instructions for **old, sick, disabled, and incapacitated pensioners**. These pensioners must be allowed to withdraw pension through the permitted modes set out in the directions, and banks are expected to use customer-friendly procedures to facilitate payment when the pensioner cannot personally visit the branch in the normal manner. The directions also require banks to **display the relevant withdrawal instructions prominently in branches**, so staff and customers can see how such pensioners may access their pensions. This is a branch-level compliance obligation, not just a back-office one, and should be reflected in staff training and inspection checklists.

The directions further cover **reimbursement of pension payments** made by agency banks and the associated documentation/processing expected for claiming reimbursement from the government system. In addition, the document contains a dedicated chapter on **life certificates**, indicating that banks must follow the prescribed life-certificate verification and submission process as a condition for continuing pension payments. For compliance purposes, the most important takeaway is that agency banks must maintain end-to-end controls over pension implementation: timely application of government orders, accurate monthly disbursement, proper handling of overpayments and recoveries, accessible procedures for vulnerable pensioners, visible branch instructions, and correct reimbursement and life-certificate processes.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks - Internal Ombudsman) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Commercial Banks – Internal Ombudsman Directions, 2026** were issued under **Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** to strengthen internal grievance redress and require a meaningful review of customer complaints before final rejection by an apex-level authority inside the bank. The Directions take effect **immediately**, but compliance with **clause 7(2), clause 14(2), and clause 14(4)** is permitted until **June 30, 2026**. RBI also reserves the right to **suspend any or all provisions** of the Directions, either generally or for a particular regulated entity, and to extend any such suspension by further order.

The Directions apply to **Commercial Banks** that had **10 or more banking outlets in India as of March 31, 2025**, regardless of whether the bank is incorporated in India or abroad. For this purpose, “Commercial Banks” covers **banking companies other than Small Finance Banks, Payment Banks, and Local Area Banks**, as well as **corresponding new banks** and **State Bank of India**. Accordingly, institutions below the 10-outlet threshold as of that date are outside the scope, while qualifying banks must implement the internal ombudsman framework required by the Directions.

The document specifically signals that banks must maintain an **Internal Ombudsman mechanism** as part of their customer complaint handling process, with review occurring **before rejection** so that complaints are not summarily dismissed without an internal apex-level reconsideration. Because the excerpt provided does not include the later operational clauses, a compliance team should expect additional detailed requirements in the full Directions on appointment, role, escalation workflow, and reporting, and should treat the immediate-effective provisions plus the June 30, 2026 implementation deadline as mandatory planning dates for any in-scope commercial bank.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks - Internal Ombudsman) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Small Finance Banks - Internal Ombudsman Directions, 2026** are issued under **Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** to strengthen internal grievance redressal by requiring an apex-level internal review before customer complaints are rejected. The Directions take effect **immediately on January 14, 2026**, except for **clause 7(2), clause 14(2), and clause 14(4)**, which must be complied with **no later than June 30, 2026**. RBI also reserves the power to **suspend any or all provisions** of the Directions, generally or for a specified regulated entity, and to extend any such suspension period.

These Directions apply to **Small Finance Banks that had 10 or more banking outlets in India as of March 31, 2025**. They also apply to any Small Finance Bank that reaches that **10-outlet threshold after March 31, 2025**, but only **from six months after it first meets the eligibility criterion**. In other words, compliance teams at SFBs should first determine whether the bank meets or later crosses the 10-outlet trigger, because that determines whether and when the internal ombudsman framework becomes mandatory.

Substantively, the framework is intended to ensure that customer complaints are **reviewed by an internal ombudsman before rejection**, rather than being declined solely through ordinary complaint-handling channels. The document therefore requires banks in scope to maintain or enhance an internal grievance redress process with an **apex-level internal review function** that can independently assess complaints proposed for rejection. While the excerpt provided does not include the operative details of clauses 7 and 14, the document clearly signals that some specific implementation requirements tied to those provisions have a later compliance date of **June 30, 2026**, so affected banks should treat those as deferred mandatory steps and ensure their implementation plans and policies are aligned accordingly.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Payments Banks - Internal Ombudsman) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Payments Banks - Internal Ombudsman Directions, 2026** are intended to strengthen internal grievance redress by requiring an **apex-level internal review before customer complaints are rejected**. The Directions take effect **immediately on January 14, 2026**, except for **clause 7(2), clause 14(2), and clause 14(4)**, which may be implemented later but must be complied with **no later than June 30, 2026**. The RBI also reserves the right to **suspend any or all provisions** of the Directions, either generally or for a specific regulated entity, and to extend any such suspension from time to time.

These Directions apply to **Payments Banks** that have **10 or more banking outlets in India as of March 31, 2025**. They also apply to any Payments Bank that reaches that threshold **after March 31, 2025**, but in that case the obligations begin **six months after the bank first meets the eligibility criteria**. In practice, compliance teams at affected Payments Banks need to assess their outlet count as of the March 31, 2025 cutoff and continuously monitor whether they cross the threshold later, because eligibility triggers a delayed but mandatory implementation timeline.

The document’s stated regulatory purpose is not merely procedural; it is to ensure complaints are not rejected without a meaningful internal review at the highest level within the bank. For compliance purposes, the key operational requirement is to confirm that the bank’s internal grievance handling framework includes the mandated Internal Ombudsman review mechanism and that the delayed-effective clauses are fully in place by **June 30, 2026** at the latest. The excerpt provided does not include the substantive definitions or the later clauses themselves, so the material obligations visible here are the applicability test, commencement date, RBI suspension power, and the deadline for the specified deferred provisions.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies - Internal Ombudsman) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Non-Banking Financial Companies (Internal Ombudsman) Directions, 2026** are intended to strengthen customer grievance redressal in NBFCs by requiring an **apex-level internal review before a complaint is finally rejected**. The Directions take **immediate effect**, but **clause 7(2), 14(2), and 14(4)** do not have to be implemented until **June 30, 2026** at the latest. The RBI also reserves the right to **suspend any or all provisions** of the Directions, either generally or for a specific regulated entity, and to extend any suspension period.

These Directions apply to specified **NBFCs**, but explicitly **exclude** Housing Finance Companies, Core Investment Companies, Infrastructure Debt Fund-NBFCs, NBFC-Infrastructure Finance Companies, Non-Operative Financial Holding Companies, Primary Dealers, and Mortgage Guarantee Companies. Applicability is determined **as of March 31, 2025**, and the document begins listing categories such as **deposit-taking NBFCs**; the full regulation should be checked for all thresholds and subcategories covered, but the key compliance point is that the regime is targeted at NBFCs meeting the prescribed applicability criteria on that date. For in-scope entities, the core obligation is to maintain an Internal Ombudsman framework that allows customer complaints to be **reviewed before rejection**, rather than simply denied at the first-line grievance stage.

From a compliance perspective, the key operational dates are: **effective immediately upon issuance on January 14, 2026**, with a **hard compliance deadline of June 30, 2026** for the specified clauses. NBFCs that fall within scope should assess whether their current grievance-redress process already includes the required **independent internal review mechanism**, and if not, they will need to implement or revise procedures, governance, and escalation workflows to ensure complaints are routed for review before rejection. The document’s stated policy objective is not merely procedural formality; it is to ensure **speedy and meaningful resolution of customer complaints** through a higher-level internal authority within the NBFC.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Bank Prepaid Payment Instruments Issuers - Internal Ombudsman) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Non-Bank Prepaid Payment Instruments Issuers – Internal Ombudsman Directions, 2026”** require covered non-bank PPI issuers to strengthen their internal grievance redress framework by creating an **apex-level internal review mechanism** before customer complaints are finally rejected. The purpose is to ensure **speedy and meaningful resolution of complaints**, with an internal ombudsman-style review of grievances that would otherwise be denied.

These Directions apply to **non-bank prepaid payment instruments issuers** with **more than one crore (10 million) prepaid payment instruments outstanding as of March 31, 2025, or any time thereafter**. The text also indicates the Directions apply to **specified categories of PPI issuers under clause 4(1)(h)**, so compliance teams should assess applicability based on the formal definition in the instrument, not just business size. The Directions are issued under **Section 18 of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007**.

The Directions take **immediate effect** upon issuance, but three specific provisions are subject to a later compliance deadline: **clause 7(2), 14(2), and 14(4)** must be complied with **no later than June 30, 2026**. Compliance teams should therefore distinguish between obligations that are effective immediately and those that have the six-month implementation window. The Reserve Bank also reserves the power to **suspend any or all provisions** of the Directions for a specified period, either generally or for a particular regulated entity, and may **extend any suspension from time to time** by further order.

In practical terms, affected PPI issuers need to ensure they have an internal process that permits **review before rejection of customer complaints** by an internal authority at the highest level within the issuer. Because the document is a formal RBI direction rather than guidance, failure to meet the applicable deadlines or applicability threshold would create a direct compliance issue for in-scope issuers.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Credit Information Companies - Internal Ombudsman) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Credit Information Companies (Internal Ombudsman) Directions, 2026** apply to all **Credit Information Companies (CICs)** and are intended to strengthen the CIC internal grievance redress system by requiring an **apex-level internal review before customer complaints are rejected**, so complaints are handled more speedily and meaningfully. The Directions take effect **immediately on January 14, 2026**, **except** for **clause 7(2), clause 14(2), and clause 14(4)**, which must be complied with **no later than June 30, 2026**. The RBI also reserves the power to **suspend any or all provisions** of the Directions, either generally or for a specific regulated entity, and to **extend any suspension** from time to time by order.

From the portion provided, the document begins defining key terms for implementation. It identifies the **“Competent Authority”** as the **Managing Director / Chief Executive Officer of the CIC**, indicating that senior management will have an explicit role in the complaint-handling framework. It also defines **“Complaint”** as a written representation or one made through the prescribed channel/mode (the text shown cuts off before the full definition), which signals that the obligations will turn on formal complaint intake and processing methods established by the Directions.

For compliance purposes, the material points are that CICs must ensure their internal grievance process is structured to allow an **independent or higher-level internal review before refusal/rejection of complaints**, and they should be prepared to implement the delayed provisions by **June 30, 2026**. Because the Directions are issued under **Section 11 of the Credit Information Companies (Regulation) Act, 2005**, they have statutory regulatory force for CIC operations. The excerpt provided does not yet include the full mechanics of appointment, tenure, reporting, escalation, or complaint timelines, so additional sections would be needed to identify the complete operational obligations.

rows.title: Master Direction - Reserve Bank of India (Internal Ombudsman for Regulated Entities) Directions, 2023
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **“Master Direction – RBI (Internal Ombudsman for Regulated Entities) Directions, 2023”** on **December 29, 2023**, to consolidate and update the internal-ombudsman framework previously set out separately for banks, NBFCs, non-bank system participants, and credit information companies. It applies to **all Scheduled Commercial Banks (excluding RRBs), all NBFCs, all Non-Bank System Participants, and all Credit Information Companies** addressed in the circular, and it is intended to strengthen the internal grievance-redress architecture by reaffirming the Internal Ombudsman as an **independent, apex-level authority for consumer grievance redress** within each regulated entity. The RBI states that the framework was reviewed in light of the integration of the three RBI Ombudsman schemes and to improve customer service standards, indicating that this direction is meant to harmonize and reinforce existing complaint-handling requirements rather than create an entirely new concept.

For compliance purposes, the key substance is that regulated entities covered by the direction must maintain an Internal Ombudsman mechanism that operates as a meaningful final internal review layer for consumer complaints, with the Ombudsman positioned independently from the business and complaint-handling functions. The document does not, in the excerpt provided, specify numerical thresholds, complaint types, appointment timelines, or reporting deadlines, but it clearly signals that the RBI expects the mechanism to function “as envisaged” and not merely as a formalistic process. The direction is issued under the RBI’s statutory powers, meaning it has mandatory regulatory force for covered entities and should be treated as a compliance obligation affecting governance, complaints escalation, and consumer grievance resolution processes.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Credit Valuation Adjustment Framework) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Commercial Banks – Credit Valuation Adjustment (CVA) Framework Directions, 2026** (issued **October 7, 2026**) establish the prudential capital treatment for **CVA risk** for covered commercial banks, replacing the prior framework through a formal repeal clause. The directions apply to **commercial banks** within RBI’s scope and set out when they must calculate capital for CVA risk, how exposures are to be brought into scope, and how CVA hedges may be recognized for capital purposes. In particular, the document creates a structured framework for CVA risk capital charges under a **Basic Approach (BA-CVA)**, with a **reduced version** and a **full version**, and also includes an **alternate treatment** and rules for converting the resulting charge into **risk-weighted assets** for regulatory capital reporting.

For compliance purposes, the key operational requirement is that affected banks must determine their CVA capital charge using the prescribed BA-CVA methodology and the detailed scope rules in the later chapters, rather than relying on an ad hoc internal measurement approach. The directions specifically address the **capital treatment of CVA hedges**, meaning banks must evaluate whether hedging instruments qualify and how they affect the calculated CVA charge. The framework also imposes **disclosure and reporting requirements**, so institutions will need to ensure their regulatory reporting processes and public/management disclosures align with the prescribed CVA treatment. The table of contents shows that the document contains separate chapter-level rules for **scope of application**, **capital requirements**, and **reporting/disclosure**, indicating that compliance teams should expect both calculation requirements and governance/reporting obligations, not just a formula change.

The document’s effective date is tied to its issuance on **7 October 2026**, and it includes a dedicated **repeal chapter**, which means prior RBI CVA framework provisions are superseded to the extent specified in this instrument. From a compliance implementation standpoint, banks should identify all derivative and other positions that fall within the CVA framework, map them to the applicable BA-CVA treatment, confirm hedge eligibility under the new rules, and update capital reporting systems so the resulting CVA capital charge is reflected correctly in regulatory capital and risk-weighted asset calculations. Since the table of contents also references an **Annex 1**, compliance teams should review that annex for any technical formulas, asset classifications, or reporting templates that may be necessary to implement the framework precisely.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks - Minimum Capital Requirements for Market Risk) Directions, 2026
rows.desc: DOR/2026-27/472 DOR.MRG.REC.227/21-01-002/2026-27 September 21, 2026 Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks - Minimum Capital Requirements for Market Risk) Directions, 2026 Table of Contents Chapter-I: Preliminary ........................................................................................................... 3 A. Short title and Effective Date ......................................................................................... 3 B. Applicability ................................................................................................................... 3 C. Definitions ..................................................................................................................... 3 Chapter-II: Boundary between the banking book and the trading book ................................. 5 A. Scope of the trading book ............................................................................................. 5 B. Restrictions on reclassifying instruments between the regulatory books ....................... 5 C. Treatment of internal risk transfers ................................................................................ 6 C.1 Internal risk transfer of credit risk from banking book to trading book .................. 6 C.2 Internal risk transfer of general interest rate risk (GIRR) from banking book to trading book ................................................................................................................... 7 C.3 Eligible hedges for the CVA capital requirement .................................................. 8 Chapter-III: Scope of application of market risk ................................................................... 10 A. Exclusion of certain structural foreign exchange positions from Net Open Position .. 10 Chapter-IV: Calculating risk- weighted assets for market risk ............................................... 16 A. Risk-weighted assets and capital requirements .....................................
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Commercial Banks – Minimum Capital Requirements for Market Risk” Directions, 2026** set the supervisory framework for how commercial banks must classify positions, measure market risk, and calculate the resulting capital requirement. The document applies to the **commercial banks in scope under the RBI framework** and is organized around the boundary between the **banking book** and **trading book**, treatment of **internal risk transfers**, the **scope of market risk application**, and the **calculation of risk-weighted assets (RWA) and capital requirements** for market risk.

A key compliance theme is that banks must maintain and apply a disciplined distinction between instruments held in the banking book versus the trading book, and they are restricted in how they can move instruments between those books. The directions also govern **internal risk transfers** from the banking book to the trading book, including transfers of **credit risk** and **general interest rate risk (GIRR)**, and set rules for what counts as an **eligible hedge for the CVA capital requirement**. That means banks cannot rely on informal or opportunistic repositioning of exposures; any reclassification or internal transfer must fit the regulatory criteria in these directions and be supportable for capital purposes.

The document also addresses the **scope of market risk exposure** by identifying certain **structural foreign exchange positions** that may be excluded from the **Net Open Position** calculation, but only where the regulatory conditions for that exclusion are met. For compliance teams, this means FX positions that are part of the institution’s structural balance-sheet management must be reviewed carefully to determine whether they may be excluded, and if so, whether the exclusion is properly documented and consistently applied.

Finally, Chapter IV establishes how banks must compute **risk-weighted assets for market risk** and the related capital requirements, indicating that the directions are intended to be used operationally in capital measurement and regulatory reporting. The excerpt provided does not include the detailed formulas, thresholds, or specific effective-date text beyond the issuance date shown at the top (**September 21, 2026**), so a compliance team would need the full chapter text to identify the exact calculation mechanics, any implementation deadlines, and any transitional arrangements. Still, the document clearly requires banks to align their book classification, internal risk transfer treatment, FX structural position treatment, and market-risk RWA calculations with the RBI’s prescribed methodology.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks - Capital Charge for Credit Risk – Standardised Approach) Directions, 2026 (Effective from April 1, 2027)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Commercial Banks – Capital Charge for Credit Risk – Standardised Approach” Directions, 2026** (issued **April 27, 2026** and **effective from April 1, 2027**) establish the RBI’s updated framework for how **commercial banks** must calculate and apply **capital charges for credit risk** under the standardised approach. The directions apply across a broad range of exposure types and are organized into detailed rules covering **sovereigns, foreign sovereigns and central banks, public sector entities, MDBs/BIS/IMF, banks, corporates, subordinated debt/equity/other capital instruments, retail, MSMEs, real estate, NPAs, fund investments, specified categories, unhedged foreign currency exposure, other assets, off-balance sheet items, and securitisation exposures**. They also set out the framework for **external credit ratings**, including which rating agencies are eligible, how ratings are mapped and used, and how to handle long-term and short-term ratings, unsolicited ratings, multiple ratings, issuer-not-cooperating cases, and the use of issue ratings for issuer/other claims.  

From a compliance perspective, the directions require banks to follow explicit **general instructions and due diligence requirements** before assigning risk weights, including ensuring exposures are classified correctly and that any reliance on external ratings or credit risk mitigants meets the RBI’s standards. The document further lays down detailed rules for **credit risk mitigation**, including the legal certainty required for mitigation arrangements, how to treat **maturity mismatches and currency mismatches**, and the conditions for recognizing **collateral, on-balance-sheet netting, and guarantees** as valid forms of mitigation. The final chapter states that prior relevant directions are being **repealed**, meaning banks will need to transition their capital charge computation and related internal controls to this new framework by the **April 1, 2027** commencement date.  

For compliance teams, the key implication is that this is not a narrow amendment but a **full replacement framework** for determining risk weights and capital treatment for credit risk under the standardized approach. Banks will need to review their exposure classification logic, rating dependency controls, collateral and guarantee documentation, off-balance-sheet treatment, and securitisation capital calculations to ensure they align with the new directions before the effective date.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks - Asset Classification, Provisioning and Income Recognition) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **“Commercial Banks – Asset Classification, Provisioning and Income Recognition Directions, 2026”** on **April 27, 2026** as **DOR/2026-27/398 / DOR.STR.REC.No.6/21.06.011/2026-27**. This document is the governing prudential framework for **commercial banks** on how to classify assets, recognize income, and make provisions, and it also introduces an **Expected Credit Loss (ECL)-based provisioning framework**. For compliance purposes, the key point is that it is not merely a guidance note: it is a set of binding directions that will affect banks’ credit impairment methodology, loan classification controls, provisioning calculations, and related reporting and governance processes.

The document is organized into a preliminary chapter, then rules for **classification as non-performing assets (NPAs)**, followed by a detailed chapter on **ECL-based provisioning**. The content shown indicates that the RBI is setting out the criteria for when an exposure must be classified as an NPA and the prudential norms that apply once a bank makes that determination. It then moves into a formal framework for calculating ECL, including **fair valuation on transition**, **initial recognition and subsequent measurement**, how to determine a **significant increase in credit risk (SICR)**, how ECL is measured for different financial instruments, the **period over which lifetime ECL is measured**, **probability-weighted outcomes**, and the use of the **effective interest rate**. A compliance team should treat this as a significant change to credit-loss governance because these topics imply new model, data, documentation, and controls requirements for expected-loss estimation.

Because the table of contents shows a dedicated section on **applicability**, compliance should confirm which entities within the bank group are covered and whether any branches, subsidiaries, or specific categories of commercial banking activity are excluded or subject to special treatment. The document also includes a definitions section, which will be important because the operational meaning of terms such as asset classification categories, default/NPA triggers, SICR, lifetime ECL, and effective interest rate will drive policy drafting and model calibration. In practice, the bank should expect to review and potentially revise its credit policy, accounting policy, provisioning methodology, internal escalation triggers, and management reporting so that they align with RBI’s required classification and impairment approach.

From a compliance standpoint, the most material obligations indicated by this draft are: determine when an exposure becomes an NPA under RBI-prescribed norms; apply the RBI’s prudential treatment once an asset is non-performing; build and maintain an ECL methodology that reflects **initial recognition, subsequent measurement, and SICR-based staging**; and ensure provisions are measured using the specified framework rather than legacy loss-incurred approaches. Since the document’s excerpt does not show the detailed thresholds or transition dates beyond the issuance date, the immediate action item is to review the operative chapters for any **effective date, implementation timeline, transitional arrangements, model governance expectations, or provisioning percentages** that will determine when the bank must change its systems and reporting.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Prudential Norms on Declaration of Dividend and Remittances of Profits) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Commercial Banks – Prudential Norms on Declaration of Dividend and Remittances of Profits Directions, 2026** (issued as **RBI/2025-26/387, DOR.ACC.REC.No.427/21.02.067/2025-26 dated March 10, 2026**) establish the prudential framework commercial banks must follow before declaring dividends or remitting profits. The directions apply to **commercial banks** and specifically distinguish between **banks incorporated in India** and **foreign banks operating in India in branch mode**, with separate rules for dividend declaration and profit remittance. The document is organized around board oversight, eligibility criteria, dividend/profit limits, reporting, restrictions, penalties, and repeal/saving provisions.

For **boards and management**, the RBI requires explicit **board oversight** over any proposed dividend declaration or profit remittance, meaning the decision must be assessed against the prudential conditions in the directions rather than treated as a routine distribution matter. Banks must satisfy the prescribed **eligibility criteria** before any payment is made; if those conditions are not met, dividend or remittance is not permitted. For **banks incorporated in India**, the RBI sets the **quantum of dividend payable** through prudential limits, so compliance teams must verify that the proposed dividend amount falls within the applicable ceiling and is supportable by the bank’s financial position and regulatory status.

For **foreign banks operating in India in branch mode**, the directions instead govern **remittance of profits**, and the RBI also specifies categories of **profits that are ineligible for dividend payment or remittance**. That means not all profits can necessarily be taken out of India, and compliance must ensure the amounts proposed for remittance are drawn only from profits that qualify under the RBI’s rules. The directions also establish a **reporting system**, so banks will have to file the prescribed information to the RBI in the manner and form required before or in connection with distribution/remittance decisions.

The RBI further provides for **restrictions on payment of dividend and remittance of profits**, meaning even otherwise eligible banks can be barred from making distributions if regulatory conditions are not met. The document also includes **penal consequences for non-compliance**, indicating that violations may trigger supervisory or enforcement action in addition to the underlying prohibition on payment/remittance. Finally, Chapter III contains **repeal and saving provisions**, so compliance teams should check which prior RBI instructions have been superseded and whether any transitional or grandfathering treatment applies to actions already taken or pending when these directions took effect.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Miscellaneous) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on October 19, 2026)
rows.summary:
This RBI circular, **Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Miscellaneous) Directions, 2025** (dated **November 28, 2025**, reference **DOR/2025-26/174 / DOR.SOG(SPE).REC.No.93/13-04-001/2025-26**), consolidates and sets out binding directions for **commercial banks** on several operational and governance matters, with a significant focus on the **Depositor Education and Awareness Fund (DEAF)**. The document is structured into chapters covering applicability and definitions, board governance requirements, DEAF credit/refund/registration/claim procedures, and returns/reporting, so compliance teams should treat it as a formal operating rulebook rather than a guidance note.

A key set of obligations applies at the **board level**: banks must have **board-approved policies**, the board is assigned specific oversight responsibilities, and the board must conduct periodic reviews of the relevant compliance areas. This means the bank’s senior governance framework is expected to explicitly approve, monitor, and periodically reassess the policies and procedures covered by the directions, rather than leaving them solely to operational teams.

The most substantive operational requirements concern the **Depositor Education and Awareness Fund**. The directions define how amounts are to be **credited to the Fund**, how **refunds and interest** are to be handled, and the **registration guidelines** and **procedural requirements for transfer and claims**. Banks will need to ensure that dormant/unclaimed balances are transferred to the Fund in the manner prescribed by the RBI, that eligible refund claims are processed according to the specified procedure, and that any interest treatment tied to DEAF balances follows the new framework exactly. The inclusion of separate sections for credits, refunds, registration, and claims indicates that banks must maintain controls across the full DEAF lifecycle, from identification of eligible balances through transfer and eventual customer claim resolution.

The directions also impose **return/reporting obligations** (“Returns”), meaning banks will need to file whatever periodic or event-based reports the RBI specifies in the final text and ensure the underlying data is accurate, traceable, and reconciled to internal records. Because the document is titled as “Miscellaneous” directions and is expressly issued as a Reserve Bank of India direction for commercial banks, compliance should assume these are **mandatory requirements** effective from the date stated in the circular unless the operative chapters specify staggered implementation or separate deadlines. Where the final text includes precise thresholds, timelines, or filing formats for DEAF transfers, refunds, registration, or returns, those should be treated as direct compliance triggers for the relevant banking operations and IT/workflow teams.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Forthcoming Instructions) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Commercial Banks – Forthcoming Instructions” Directions, 2025** is a comprehensive prudential capital framework for **commercial banks**, issued as RBI/DoR/2025-26/173 dated **November 28, 2025**. Its table of contents shows that it will govern three major areas: **counterparty credit risk capital for derivative transactions**, **capital requirements for exposures to central counterparties (CCPs)**, and **minimum capital requirements for operational risk**. From a compliance perspective, this is not a narrow clarification; it is a framework-setting direction that will affect how banks compute regulatory capital, determine exposure measures, and apply internal controls and reporting around derivatives, CCP clearing, and operational-risk capital calculations.

For **derivative transactions**, Chapter II introduces the **Standardised Approach for Counterparty Credit Risk (SA-CCR)** as the method for computing the **default risk capital charge**. This means affected banks will need to use the RBI-specified standardized counterparty credit risk methodology rather than ad hoc or legacy approaches for qualifying exposures. Compliance teams should expect operational requirements around correct trade classification, netting set identification, replacement cost and add-on calculations, and consistent application of the approach across all applicable derivative portfolios.

Chapter III sets out the **capital treatment for exposures to CCPs**, with separate rules for **qualifying CCPs (QCCPs)** and **non-qualifying CCPs**. Banks that clear through CCPs will need to distinguish whether the CCP meets the qualifying criteria, because the capital treatment differs materially depending on that status; exposures to **QCCPs** and **non-qualifying CCPs** are addressed in separate sections, and the chapter also includes specific requirements for recognizing **net replacement cost in close-out netting sets**. In practical terms, this implies the bank must have documented procedures to identify the CCP category, apply the correct exposure measure, and maintain evidence supporting any netting recognition used for capital purposes.

Chapter IV begins the framework for **minimum capital requirements for operational risk** and specifically includes an **interim arrangement**, indicating that the RBI is putting in place transitional treatment while the full operational-risk requirements are implemented. Even though the excerpt provided does not show the detailed formulae or phase-in dates, the presence of this chapter means commercial banks should prepare for updated operational-risk capital calculations, likely with transitional compliance steps and supervisory expectations during the interim period. Overall, the document is aimed at ensuring banks update capital computation processes, systems, and governance to align with RBI’s forthcoming standardized rules for derivatives, CCP exposures, and operational risk.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks - Climate Finance and Management of Climate Change Risks) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on October 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Climate Finance and Management of Climate Change Risks) Directions, 2025** on **November 28, 2025** (reference **DOR/2025-26/172** and **DOR.SFG.REC.No.91/30.01.021/2025-26**). The document is structured to impose two broad sets of requirements on **commercial banks**: first, governance and risk-management expectations for **climate finance and climate-related risks**, and second, a specific regulatory framework for **acceptance of green deposits**. The directions state a new/updated framework rather than a one-off disclosure requirement, so compliance teams should treat them as ongoing operational, treasury, product, disclosure, and board-governance obligations.

A central requirement is that the **board of directors** must oversee climate finance and climate risk management, meaning the bank cannot leave these matters solely to management-level committees. The directions require the board to approve and monitor the bank’s framework for dealing with climate change risks, which would typically include identifying exposures, setting internal controls, and ensuring appropriate reporting to senior management and the board. In practice, this means climate-related financial risks must be embedded into governance, strategy, and risk management rather than handled as a purely ESG or CSR matter.

The document creates a dedicated **Framework for Acceptance of Green Deposits**. Banks that choose to accept green deposits must have a formal **policy** approved by the board, and the framework governs how such deposits may be offered, priced, deployed, and reported. The directions specify rules for the **denomination, interest rates, and tenor** of these deposits, and require a **financing framework** that identifies the eligible use of proceeds, how funds will be tracked, and what internal controls apply. Green deposit proceeds must be used only for the stated green purposes under the framework; banks therefore need strong ring-fencing, tracking, and auditability so that deposited funds are not diverted to non-eligible activities.

The directions also require **third-party verification/assurance** and an **impact assessment** for the green-deposit framework. That means banks must obtain external confirmation that the proceeds are aligned with the stated green-use criteria, and they must assess and evidence the environmental impact of funded activities. In addition, the directions impose **reporting and disclosure** obligations, so banks must be prepared to disclose their green deposit framework, how proceeds were deployed, and the relevant impact/assurance information in a way that is transparent to regulators and depositors. This implies operational obligations around documentation, audit trails, internal certification, and periodic public/regulatory reporting.

Finally, the document includes **repeal and saving** provisions and states that other existing provisions may continue to apply as saved or supplemented by the new directions. For a compliance team, the key action is to map these directions against existing deposit-product approvals, treasury pricing, environmental/ESG claims processes, internal control frameworks, and board reporting, then determine whether the bank is offering—or intends to offer—green deposits and whether its climate-risk governance already meets the RBI’s expectations. Because the document content provided here is only the table of contents and headings, it does not expose the detailed numerical limits, specific tenor bands, interest-rate caps/floors, or exact reporting formats; however, those will be the critical implementation details to verify in the operative chapters before launch or ongoing compliance certification.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Managing Risks in Outsourcing) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Commercial Banks – Managing Risks in Outsourcing) Directions, 2025”** (issued **November 28, 2025**) replaces/sets a formal outsourcing-risk framework for **commercial banks** subject to RBI supervision, with the rules organized around board oversight, senior management accountability, and controls over outsourced financial services. The document establishes that each covered bank must have a **board-approved outsourcing policy** and a governance structure that clearly assigns responsibility for approving, monitoring, and reviewing outsourcing arrangements, including ongoing risk management and oversight of vendors/service providers. A key compliance theme is that outsourcing does **not** transfer responsibility away from the bank: the bank remains accountable for the outsourced activity, must maintain effective supervision, and must ensure the arrangement does not impair prudential control, customer protection, or regulatory compliance.

A central requirement is that **certain activities cannot be outsourced** at all; while the excerpt does not list the prohibited items, the directions expressly create a category of activities that banks are barred from delegating, so compliance teams must identify those exclusions in the operative text before entering any arrangement. For permitted outsourcing of financial services, the bank must implement an authorization process, maintain clear accountability lines, and ensure senior management performs active oversight, supported by a documented governance framework and a bank-wide outsourcing policy.
