Finally, the directions contain **repeal and saving provisions** and state that application of **other laws is not barred**, so compliance teams should treat these directions as additive to, not a substitute for, other applicable corporate, accounting, and banking law requirements.

If you want, I can also turn this into a **compliance checklist** for board, finance, and secretarial teams.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks – Miscellaneous) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on October 19, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Small Finance Banks (Miscellaneous) Directions, 2025** on **November 28, 2025** under RBI/DoR/2025-26/204, and these directions apply specifically to **small finance banks (SFBs)**. The document is a consolidated compliance framework covering board governance, depositor education fund obligations, and related procedural/reporting requirements, so SFBs should treat it as a binding operational and governance direction rather than a high-level guidance note. The title and table of contents indicate the directions take effect from the stated commencement date in Chapter I and are organized into multiple mandatory chapters, beginning with applicability and definitions, then board responsibilities, and then detailed rules for the Depositor Education and Awareness Fund (DEAF).  

A major compliance theme is the **role of the Board**: SFBs must have **board-approved policies** and the board is assigned specific oversight responsibilities, with periodic **board reviews** required. This means the bank cannot rely only on management-level procedures; policies and their implementation must be formally approved and monitored at the board level. For compliance teams, this implies documentary evidence of board approval, regular review cycles, and an internal control structure that demonstrates the board is actively supervising the relevant regulatory areas covered by the directions.

The document also contains a detailed chapter on the **Depositor Education and Awareness Fund**, including definitions, the rules for **credits to the fund**, **refunds and interest**, **registration guidelines**, **procedural guidelines for transfer and claim**, and **returns**. The presence of separate sections on credits, refunds, registration, claims, and returns indicates that SFBs have affirmative obligations not only to transfer applicable amounts into the fund but also to maintain processes for depositor claims, handle refunds with interest where applicable, and submit required regulatory returns. In practical terms, compliance teams should expect obligations around identifying eligible dormant/unclaimed amounts, transferring them correctly to the fund, maintaining records sufficient to support later claims, and ensuring the bank can process and report these items in the format and timelines prescribed by the RBI.  

Because the excerpt provided ends at the table of contents, it does not show the exact thresholds, time limits, interest rate treatment, or filing deadlines; however, the structure makes clear that those details are contained in the later chapters and are mandatory for SFB operations. A compliance officer should therefore review the full text immediately for the exact operational rules on what amounts must be credited to DEAF, how refunds and interest are calculated, what registration and claim procedures must be followed, and what returns must be filed, along with the precise commencement date and any transition provisions.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks – Climate Finance and Management of Climate Change Risks) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on October 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued these Directions on November 28, 2025, for **small finance banks (SFBs)**, establishing a formal regulatory framework for **climate finance, management of climate-related risks, and acceptance of green deposits**. The document applies specifically to SFBs and requires board-level governance over climate-related matters, including oversight of the bank’s climate finance strategy, risk management approach, and compliance with the green deposit framework.

A central requirement is that each SFB must have a **board-approved policy** governing green deposits and related climate-finance activities. The policy must cover the bank’s approach to accepting green deposits, the sectors or projects that may be financed with the proceeds, the process for use-of-proceeds tracking, and mechanisms for monitoring compliance with the permitted end use. The directions also require banks to establish a **financing framework** that sets out how eligible green projects are identified, evaluated, monitored, and reported, together with internal controls to ensure that funds are not diverted to non-eligible purposes.

The framework imposes conditions on the **denomination, interest rates, and tenor** of green deposits, meaning SFBs cannot structure these deposits arbitrarily and must follow RBI-prescribed parameters. Proceeds from green deposits must be used only for specified green uses under the bank’s approved framework, and banks must maintain evidence showing that the funds were applied accordingly. The directions also introduce requirements for **third-party verification or assurance** and **impact assessment**, so banks will need external or independent confirmation of the green nature of the financed activities and reporting on the environmental outcomes achieved.

In addition, the directions impose **reporting and disclosure obligations**. SFBs must make relevant disclosures about their green deposit mobilization, deployment of proceeds, verification/assurance status, and impact performance, so compliance teams should expect periodic reporting obligations as well as possible public disclosures. The document also includes **repeal and saving provisions**, indicating that earlier RBI instructions on the same subject are being replaced or superseded while preserving actions already taken under the prior framework where applicable. No specific implementation date, compliance deadline, or numerical threshold is visible in the excerpt provided beyond the issuance date, so a compliance review should verify the operative commencement date and any annexed standards or limits in the full text before implementation.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks – Managing Risks in Outsourcing) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Small Finance Banks – Managing Risks in Outsourcing) Directions, 2025”** were issued on **28 November 2025** under circular number **DOR/2025-26/202 / DOR.ORG.REC.No.121/21-04-158/2025-26**. They are a dedicated outsourcing-risk framework for **small finance banks (SFBs)** and set out how outsourcing arrangements must be governed, approved, monitored, and controlled; the document is organized around board oversight, outsourcing of financial services, risk management, and governance requirements.

At a high level, the directions require each SFB to have a **board-approved outsourcing policy** and a clear governance structure that keeps the bank accountable for outsourced activities even where day-to-day work is performed by an external provider. The board is expected to approve the policy, oversee the bank’s outsourcing framework, and ensure management maintains effective controls over outsourced arrangements. Senior management must implement the policy, monitor vendor performance and risks, and ensure that outsourcing does not dilute the bank’s responsibility to customers, regulators, or the Reserve Bank of India.

The directions specifically address **outsourcing of financial services**, and they also identify **activities that must not be outsourced**. Although the excerpt does not list those prohibited activities, the document clearly establishes that not everything can be delegated to third parties and that the bank must retain control over critical functions. Any outsourced arrangement must be authorized, documented, and subject to ongoing oversight, with the bank remaining fully accountable for compliance, conduct, and risk outcomes.

The directions also require a structured **risk management and governance framework** for outsourcing. That includes maintaining an outsourcing policy, defining management responsibilities, and ensuring that outsourced services are integrated into the bank’s broader risk-management system. The compliance significance is that SFBs cannot treat outsourcing as a mere procurement issue: they must manage it as a regulated operational-risk and control issue, with board-level visibility and continuing monitoring.

Because the provided excerpt stops at the table of contents and section headings, it does **not** provide the detailed operative thresholds, procedural steps, reporting deadlines, or specific prohibited activities. A compliance team should therefore treat this as a signal that the full directions impose a comprehensive outsourcing-control regime on SFBs, and should review the complete text for any detailed requirements on due diligence, contract terms, audit/access rights, exit management, subcontracting, data security, incident reporting, and regulator access.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on October 1, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Small Finance Banks – Responsible Business Conduct Directions, 2025** set out a consolidated, bank-wide conduct and customer-protection framework for **small finance banks (SFBs)**, replacing and updating earlier RBI instructions on customer service, customer protection, deposit accounts, lending conduct, inclusion, and related operational requirements. The document is organized into chapters covering institutional governance, branch-level service standards, customer guidance and protection, financial inclusion/accessibility, payment and remittance services, deposit liabilities, responsible lending, and miscellaneous/repeal provisions, and it is accompanied by annexes prescribing the **format of a comprehensive notice board**, a **quick-rate disclosure table**, **inventory forms**, and **claim-settlement forms** for accounts with and without nominee/survivorship arrangements.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that the directions impose an integrated set of obligations on SFBs rather than a single standalone rule: banks must maintain an internal institutional framework for responsible conduct; ensure branch operations and customer interactions meet prescribed service standards; provide customer-facing disclosures and protection measures; and implement accessible products and services for financial inclusion. The document also specifically regulates **payment and remittance services**, **deposit accounts and other liabilities**, and **responsible lending conduct**, meaning the bank’s onboarding, account maintenance, grievance handling, disclosures, credit underwriting, and recovery practices must all align with the RBI’s conduct expectations. Where the directions prescribe customer disclosures, the bank must use the RBI-mandated formats, including the annexed notice-board presentation and rate disclosure summary.

The title indicates that this is the **2025 Directions**, and the document is marked **“Updated as on July 1, 2026,”** so compliance teams should treat the July 1, 2026 update date as the latest incorporated version of the framework reflected in the text provided. The document reference is **DOR/2025-26/201 DOR.MCS.REC.No.120/01-01-033/2025-26**, issued **November 28, 2025** by the Reserve Bank of India. Because the excerpt provided shows only the table of contents and annex listings, it does not disclose the substantive thresholds, rates, or operational formulas, but it clearly signals that those details are contained in the chapter text and annexes, especially **Annex II (“Rates at a Quick Glance”)** and the claim-settlement forms in **Annex IV–VI**.

From a compliance-action standpoint, SFBs should expect to review and likely update branch notice boards, customer disclosures, account-opening and deposit-liability processes, nominee/survivorship claim procedures, inclusion/accessibility practices, payment/remittance operations, and lending conduct controls to match the new consolidated directions. The presence of separate settlement claim forms for accounts **with nominee/survivorship clause** and **without nominee/survivorship clause** suggests that banks must maintain different documentary workflows depending on account structure. In short, this is a comprehensive RBI conduct manual for SFBs that standardizes how they must interact with customers and manage retail banking products and claims, with the operative details embedded in the chapter text and annexures.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on October 1, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Small Finance Banks – Know Your Customer Directions, 2025** are AML/KYC compliance directions issued under the RBI’s supervisory powers and are specifically applicable to **small finance banks** in India. They are intended to prevent banks from being used for **money laundering (ML)**, **terrorist financing (TF)**, and related illicit activity, while preserving the integrity and stability of the financial system. The document is organized into chapters covering preliminary provisions, general requirements, customer acceptance policy, risk management, customer identification and due diligence, recordkeeping, reporting to the Financial Intelligence Unit–India, obligations arising from international agency communications, other instructions, and repeal/savings provisions.

From the excerpt provided, the document indicates a comprehensive framework for **customer acceptance, identification, and ongoing due diligence**, meaning covered banks must have formal internal controls for onboarding and monitoring customers rather than relying on one-time KYC at account opening. It also imposes **record management** obligations and **mandatory reporting requirements to FIU-India**, which typically means suspicious or threshold-based transaction reporting must be done in the prescribed manner and timelines under the AML regime. The directions also address compliance where there are **international agreements or communications from international agencies**, signaling that banks must respond to sanctions/terrorism-related or cross-border regulatory instructions as required by law.

The document is labeled **“Updated as on December 29, 2025,”** and the underlying directions were issued on **November 28, 2025** under reference **DOR/2025-26/200 DOR.AML.REC.No.119/14.01.007/2025-26**. Because only the table of contents and introductory text are shown here, the specific thresholds, timelines, exceptions, documentary requirements, and any precise procedural steps are not visible in the provided excerpt; however, the chapter structure makes clear that the directions likely replace or update prior RBI KYC instructions for small finance banks, and compliance teams should treat them as the controlling KYC/AML rule set for that bank category. If you share the full text, I can produce a clause-by-clause compliance summary with all operative requirements, deadlines, and implementation obligations.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks - Financial Statements: Presentation and Disclosures) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Small Finance Banks – Financial Statements: Presentation and Disclosures) Directions, 2025”** (DOR/2025-26/198, DOR.ACC.REC.No.117/21.04.018/2025-26, dated **November 28, 2025**, and shown as **updated on July 01, 2026**) is a comprehensive accounting and disclosure framework for **small finance banks (SFBs)**. It governs how SFBs must prepare and present their **standalone balance sheet and profit and loss account**, what must be disclosed in the **notes to accounts**, how **consolidated financial statements** are to be presented, and certain additional accounting treatments and control-related disclosures. The document is organized into: preliminary provisions; prescribed formats and instructions for the balance sheet and P&L; guidance on issues tied to particular Accounting Standards; detailed note-disclosure requirements; consolidated financial statement rules; and other operational instructions such as inter-branch account provisioning, Nostro reconciliation, reserve fund appropriations, and fraud provisioning.

From a compliance perspective, the key practical point is that these Directions apply specifically to **small finance banks** and require them to follow RBI-prescribed formats and disclosure conventions in their financial statements, rather than relying only on generic accounting presentation. SFBs must ensure their financial reporting package includes the mandated line-item structure, the required notes and explanations, and any special treatment required for defined transactions or balances. The document also signals that RBI expects not just form compliance but substance-based disclosures, including additional explanatory information in the notes and explicit treatment of problem balances and operational exceptions. Because this is an updated 2026 version of a 2025 direction, compliance teams should assume the document supersedes earlier presentation/disclosure instructions to the extent specified in the operative text and that any implementation timing would depend on the commencement/applicability provisions in Chapter I, Section A/B.

The directions also address specific end-of-period financial reporting and control topics that typically create compliance risk: **inter-branch account net debit balances**, **unreconciled Nostro account items**, **transfers to or from reserve funds**, and **fraud provisioning**. These provisions indicate that banks must not leave such balances or exceptions untreated; instead, they need to apply the prescribed provisioning, reconciliation, and accounting treatment set out in the relevant chapters. For a compliance team, the operational implication is that finance, treasury, operations, and internal controls teams should verify that the bank’s chart of accounts, note-disclosure templates, consolidation process, and exception-management workflows align with the RBI format and any instructions in the notes/guidance sections. The document is therefore not merely descriptive accounting guidance—it is a binding regulatory reporting framework that affects both the content of published financial statements and the underlying closing, reconciliation, and provisioning processes supporting them.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks – Treatment of Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks – Treatment of Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters) Directions, 2025** on **November 28, 2025** (DOR/2025-26/197; DOR.FIN.REC.No.116/20-16-003/2025-26). These Directions are specifically addressed to **small finance banks** and are intended to create a **non-discriminatory, transparent, and natural-justice-based process** for classifying borrowers as wilful defaulters, while also putting in place a system for **sharing credit information** so lenders can avoid extending further institutional finance to such borrowers. The RBI states that it is acting under **Sections 21 and 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and **Section 11 of the Credit Information Companies (Regulation) Act, 2005**.

From the portions provided, the document is organized to cover: the **board’s role**, the **treatment of wilful defaulters**, **reporting of wilful defaulters and large defaulters**, **preventive measures and auditor responsibilities**, and **repeal/other provisions**, with prescribed reporting formats in **Annex I** for large defaulters and **Annex II** for wilful default cases. For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that small finance banks are being placed under a formal RBI framework requiring them to identify, classify, report, and maintain records on borrowers who are either wilful defaulters or large defaulters, rather than handling such matters solely through internal policy.

The introduction makes clear that the RBI expects the classification process to be **transparent and fair**, with **natural justice** protections built in. That means a bank cannot simply label a borrower a wilful defaulter without following the process mandated by the Directions, and the purpose of the regime is not only enforcement but also **warning the financial system** by disseminating the relevant credit information. The material provided does not yet include the detailed operational thresholds, timelines, or classification criteria, but it does show that the Directions will impose specific governance, reporting, and preventive-control obligations on small finance banks and their auditors once the full chapters are applied.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks – Resolution of Stressed Assets) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on October 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Small Finance Banks – Resolution of Stressed Assets Directions, 2025** (issued **November 28, 2025**, and updated **as on July 1, 2026**) set out the mandatory framework small finance banks must follow for identifying, reporting, resolving, and provisioning for stressed exposures. The directions apply to **small finance banks (SFBs)** and govern how they must handle borrowers showing stress, including the need for **board-approved policies** covering recognition of stress, escalation, resolution options, monitoring, and governance responsibilities. They also require **early identification and reporting of stress**, meaning banks must detect deterioration in asset quality before default or outright non-performance and ensure that such cases are tracked and reported internally and, where applicable, to the Reserve Bank.

The document establishes a formal **resolution process** once stress is identified, including a defined **review period** during which the lender(s) must evaluate and finalize a viable resolution plan. Where multiple lenders are involved, the directions require an **Inter-Creditor Agreement (ICA)** so creditors can coordinate decision-making and implementation of the resolution plan; the plan must be formulated and executed within the regulatory timelines set out in the directions. If the resolution plan is not implemented on time, the bank becomes subject to **additional provisioning** under Chapter IV, meaning higher capital/provisioning charges are imposed as a penalty for delay. The directions therefore create a strong compliance incentive to complete resolution within the prescribed period rather than defer action.

The framework also includes **disclosure obligations** and **supervisory review** requirements, so SFBs must maintain records and reporting sufficient for RBI oversight and for any internal or external disclosure obligations specified in the directions. Although the excerpt provided does not include the detailed numeric thresholds or timelines in the later chapters, the title and table of contents indicate that the document further covers **prudential norms applicable to restructuring** in Chapter V, meaning any restructuring undertaken must comply with RBI’s prudential treatment rules. For compliance teams, the key operational takeaway is that SFBs need documented governance, prompt stress recognition, disciplined resolution timelines, coordinated creditor action where relevant, and readiness for enhanced provisioning if implementation is delayed.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks – Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on October 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
This RBI direction, issued on **November 28, 2025** and updated as of **July 1, 2026**, sets the Income Recognition, Asset Classification, and Provisioning framework specifically for **Small Finance Banks (SFBs)**. It applies to the entities covered by the SFB licensing and supervisory regime and replaces/standardizes how these banks must recognize interest income, classify assets, and make provisions for credit exposures, with the document organized around board oversight, prudential lending, disclosures, asset classification, automation, and non-performing asset rules.

From a compliance standpoint, the key point is that SFBs must operate under RBI-prescribed rules on **when income may be recognized, when an account becomes an NPA, how regularization near the balance sheet date is treated, and how special cases are classified**, rather than relying on internal discretion. The document also specifically addresses the **automation of income-recognition, asset-classification, and provisioning processes**, meaning banks are expected to build or maintain systems that can apply these rules consistently and accurately rather than handling classification manually or opportunistically.

The directions also impose governance obligations on the **Board of Directors**, which must oversee prudential lending standards and consumer education, and they require certain **disclosures** so that asset quality and provisioning practices are transparent. Although the excerpt does not list the detailed thresholds or provisioning percentages, the structure shows that the document contains explicit rules for **classification as non-performing assets**, treatment of **accounts regularized near the balance sheet date**, and **specific categories of NPAs**, all of which are material for credit policy, MIS, impairment/provisioning, and financial reporting controls.

For compliance teams, the practical impact is that SFBs should review their loan origination, monitoring, delinquency tracking, system automation, board reporting, and disclosure controls against the RBI framework in force as updated **July 1, 2026**, to ensure their internal policies map exactly to the mandated classification and provisioning process.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks – Asset Liability Management) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Small Finance Banks – Asset Liability Management Directions, 2025”** is a new binding framework issued on **November 28, 2025** under reference **DOR/2025-26/194, DOR.LRG.No.113/13-10-002/2025-26**. It applies specifically to **Small Finance Banks (SFBs)** and sets out the RBI’s expectations for governance, policy approval, liquidity risk management, and asset-liability management (ALM) processes. The document is structured to cover board accountability, liquidity risk governance, risk measurement and monitoring, and related operational controls, so compliance teams should treat it as a core prudential requirement rather than a guidance note.

At the board level, the directions assign the **Board of Directors primary responsibility for approving and overseeing ALM and liquidity risk management**. The board must approve the bank’s relevant policies, internal limits, and review mechanisms, and is expected to ensure that management has a clear strategy for identifying, measuring, monitoring, and controlling liquidity risk. In practical terms, this means the bank’s ALM framework cannot be left to treasury or risk teams alone; it requires documented board-level ownership, periodic review, and formal approval of the parameters under which liquidity risk is managed.

The liquidity risk chapter makes clear that SFBs must maintain a **formal governance framework** for liquidity risk, backed by a written liquidity risk management policy and an articulated strategy for managing liquidity across normal and stressed conditions. The directions require the bank to identify liquidity exposures, assess them using both a **flow approach** and a **stock approach**, and continuously monitor them through defined internal controls and reporting. This implies that compliance teams should expect the RBI to look for evidence of end-to-end liquidity measurement processes, not just static ratio compliance, including systems for cash flow projections, asset liquidation assumptions, and ongoing monitoring of funding concentrations and mismatches.

Although the excerpt provided does not include the later chapters in full, the table of contents shows that the directions also address **risk monitoring** and likely further detailed ALM controls beyond the introductory framework. From a compliance standpoint, the key takeaway is that these directions formalize a comprehensive ALM regime for SFBs, with obligations centered on governance, policy approval, liquidity risk identification and measurement, and ongoing oversight. Any SFB subject to the directions should review its existing ALM and liquidity management architecture to confirm it has board-approved policies, documented risk limits, management reporting, and procedures capable of supporting RBI scrutiny under the new 2025 framework.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks – Classification, Valuation and Operation of Investment Portfolio) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on October 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Small Finance Banks – Classification, Valuation, and Operation of Investment Portfolio Directions, 2025** set the prudential and accounting rules Small Finance Banks must follow for their investment books, replacing and consolidating prior RBI instructions on investment classification, valuation, and portfolio operations. The document applies to **Small Finance Banks (SFBs)** and governs how they must classify investments at purchase, value them over time, transfer securities between books, and manage compliance controls through board-approved policies and internal systems. It was issued on **November 28, 2025**, and the version supplied is **updated as of May 18, 2026**; compliance teams should treat the updated text as the current operative version and verify whether any transitional provisions or implementation dates in the body of the directions differ from the issue date.  

At a high level, the directions require each SFB’s **Board** to approve and oversee an investment policy framework that defines the bank’s investment objectives, risk appetite, classification approach, valuation methodology, and operational controls. The rules organize investments into specific accounting buckets — **Held to Maturity (HTM)**, **Available for Sale (AFS)**, and **Fair Value through Profit and Loss (FVTPL)**, with **Held for Trading (HFT)** as a sub-category under FVTPL — and require banks to classify securities consistently based on the nature of the instrument and the bank’s intent and business model. The document also contains specific guidance for **investments in associates and joint ventures**, indicating that these holdings are subject to their own recognition and measurement treatment rather than simply being managed like ordinary debt or equity securities.  

The directions also regulate **initial recognition** and subsequent valuation, meaning the bank must recognize investments at the correct transaction date/cost basis and then remeasure them according to the category into which they are placed. For compliance purposes, the important point is that the bank cannot freely treat investments as a passive treasury matter: classification, fair valuation, and any movement between categories must follow RBI-prescribed rules and be supported by documented internal procedures. The policy framework and accounting treatment should therefore be aligned with the bank’s financial reporting, risk management, and treasury operations so that valuation gains/losses, amortization, and any trading activity are recorded in the proper category and in the proper period.  

Because this is a chaptered prudential direction, the practical compliance burden is not limited to accounting entries; it also covers **governance, board approval, classification discipline, portfolio operation, and ongoing valuation controls** for all affected investment activities. Any SFB that holds government securities, corporate debt, equity investments, or other portfolio instruments needs to ensure its treasury systems, accounting policies, and MIS reports reflect the RBI classification structure and that staff understand the restrictions and reporting expectations attached to each category. If you want, I can also produce a **section-by-section compliance summary** once you share the remaining text of the directions, so the summary includes all numerical limits, transfer rules, valuation methods, and deadlines from the full document.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks – Interest Rates on Advances) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks – Interest Rates on Advances) Directions, 2025** on **November 28, 2025**, and they take **immediate effect upon issuance**. The Directions apply specifically to **Small Finance Banks (SFBs)** and are framed under the RBI’s powers under **Sections 21 and 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, meaning SFBs must align their lending-rate practices with this new binding framework from the effective date onward. Based on the portion provided, the document begins with a full rewrite/issuance of RBI expectations for how SFBs may set and manage **interest rates on advances**, and it is organized to cover general lending guidelines, benchmark usage, other lending-rate aspects, foreign-currency advances, exemptions, and repeal/savings provisions.

For compliance purposes, the key point from the text supplied is that this is not merely guidance but a formal direction replacing prior RBI treatment of SFB advance-rate requirements. The document expressly states that it applies to all entities classified as **Small Finance Banks**, so any SFB lending book, pricing policy, internal rate-setting process, product approval process, and customer-facing disclosures that depend on advance-rate methodology will need to be checked for conformity as of the issuance date. The excerpt does not yet show the substantive rate formulas, benchmark mechanics, ceilings/floors, or exceptions, but it does make clear that the Directions are intended to govern the entire framework for lending rates, including any special treatment for **foreign currency advances** and any exemptions or transitional provisions that may affect implementation.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks – Securitisation Transactions) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **“Small Finance Banks – Securitisation Transactions) Directions, 2025”** on **November 28, 2025** under **DOR/2025-26/191 / DOR.STR.REC.No.110/21-04-177/2025-26**. These directions specifically govern **securitisation transactions undertaken by Small Finance Banks (SFBs)** and are structured to set out the general prudential, structural, and accounting requirements for securitising assets, as well as additional criteria for **Simple, Transparent and Comparable (STC)** securitisations for regulatory capital treatment.

At a high level, the directions establish which **assets may be securitised**, the **minimum retention requirement (MRR)** that originators must hold, the required **origination standards**, how **payment priorities** and cash-flow observability must be structured, and a **limit on total retained exposures** by originators. They also impose requirements for **issuance and listing**, the conditions that must be met by the **special purpose entity (SPE)**, rules on **representations and warranties**, and the required **accounting treatment**. For transactions claiming **STC** status, the directions set out criteria that must be satisfied for **regulatory capital purposes**, along with related disclosure and prudential obligations.

From a compliance perspective, the key point is that these are not just transaction-design guidelines; they create a framework of mandatory conditions that SFBs must satisfy before, during, and after securitising assets. The document’s listed chapters indicate that compliance teams will need to verify asset eligibility, confirm retention and exposure calculations, ensure originations meet prescribed standards, confirm the SPE structure and issuance mechanics, and validate accounting recognition/derecognition treatment. Because the document is titled as directions from the RBI and is dated in late 2025, compliance teams should treat it as an operative regulatory framework for SFB securitisation activity from its commencement date in the final text, and should review the full chapters for any specific transition, effective-date, or carve-out provisions not visible in the excerpt.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks – Transfer and Distribution of Credit Risk) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on October 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Small Finance Banks – Transfer and Distribution of Credit Risk) Directions, 2025”** (issued **November 28, 2025**, reference **DOR/2025-26/190** and **DOR.STR.REC.109/21.04.048/2025-26**) sets out a comprehensive framework for how **small finance banks (SFBs)** may transfer, distribute, or share credit risk through loan sales and other arrangements. The directions are organized into rules for **transfer of loan exposures** and other lending/risk-transfer structures, and they replace prior RBI guidance on these topics under the repeal and transitional provisions in Part C.

For compliance purposes, the most important point is that the RBI is formalizing when and how SFBs can transfer loans that are **standard (not in default)** and **stressed**. The framework covers general conditions applicable to all loan transfers, separate rules for loans not in default, and distinct requirements for stressed loans, meaning the bank must classify exposures correctly before attempting any transfer and follow the relevant chapter-specific conditions. The document also addresses **consortium or multiple-banking lending, inter-bank participations, and borrower-requested account transfers**, so it applies not just to outright loan sales but also to other arrangements that redistribute credit exposure among lenders.

Although the excerpt provided does not include the detailed operative clauses, the table of contents shows that the RBI has imposed structured requirements that will likely include **preconditions, documentation, due diligence, transfer mechanics, and restrictions by loan type/status** across all loan-transfer activity. Compliance teams should therefore expect to review whether the bank’s existing policies, approval workflows, and transaction documentation for loan sales, participations, consortium exposures, and borrower-led account migrations conform to the new directions, and should treat the issuance date as the effective date unless the body of the directions specifies phased implementation or a later compliance deadline. No specific quantitative thresholds, rates, or carve-outs are visible in the provided text excerpt, so those would need to be checked in the operative chapters and annexes before implementing transaction-level controls.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks - Concentration Risk Management) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on October 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Small Finance Banks (Concentration Risk Management) Directions, 2025”** set out the RBI’s comprehensive prudential framework for **small finance banks (SFBs)** on concentration risk, replacing and consolidating earlier exposure, group exposure, intra-group, country-risk, and inter-bank liability rules. The document is dated **November 28, 2025** and is marked **“Updated as on July 01, 2026,”** so compliance teams should treat it as the operative updated version as of that date. Its core purpose is to limit both **asset-side concentration** (large borrower and group exposures) and **liability-side concentration** (notably inter-bank liabilities), while also prescribing governance, monitoring, and reporting responsibilities.

At a high level, the directions require each SFB’s **board** to approve a formal concentration risk framework, ensure limits and exceptions are monitored, and establish a system for identifying, measuring, managing, and reporting concentrated exposures. The RBI ties these rules to the bank’s **capital funds / eligible capital measures** and prescribes prudential limits for exposures to a single borrower and a borrower group, as well as additional restrictions for connected exposures and intra-group transactions. The document also addresses how SFBs may support **large borrowers through market mechanisms**, indicating that exposure to larger entities should be managed in a way that does not create excessive balance-sheet concentration. Compliance teams should assume that these are not just lending-policy recommendations: they are binding prudential requirements with ongoing board oversight and supervisory review.

The directions specifically cover **exposure norms** for borrowers and borrower groups, meaning the bank must track aggregate commitments to prevent breaching RBI caps when loans, non-fund-based facilities, and other credit exposures are combined. The document also imposes **prudential limits on intra-group transactions and exposures**, which means transactions with entities within the same group need special scrutiny and may be subject to tighter caps or enhanced approval requirements than arm’s-length dealings. In addition, it includes a dedicated chapter on **management of country risk exposure**, requiring SFBs to identify and control exposures arising from cross-border counterparties or foreign jurisdictions, including any country-risk rating or provisioning/limit framework specified by RBI. Another separate chapter sets **prudential limits for inter-bank liabilities (IBL)**, addressing the liability-side concentration risk created when the bank relies too heavily on borrowing from other banks or the inter-bank market.

The document also contains a **repeal and saving / other provisions** chapter, which indicates that prior RBI instructions on these subjects are being superseded or reorganized under this consolidated framework, so firms should map older circulars and directions against the new text to ensure no obsolete policy remains in force. Because the text is titled as an updated version, compliance teams should pay special attention to any changes reflected in the **July 01, 2026** update, especially if the bank maintained legacy limits or reporting formats under earlier RBI instructions. In practice, this means an SFB should review its credit-policy manuals, board-approved concentration limits, exception approval matrix, stress-testing and monitoring reports, treasury funding concentration controls, and related-party/intra-group transaction controls to ensure they align with the new directions and any updated numerical thresholds or reporting expectations contained in the full text and annexes.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks – Credit Risk Management) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on October 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Small Finance Banks – Credit Risk Management Directions, 2025** (issued **November 28, 2025** and **updated as of July 1, 2026**) consolidate and prescribe the credit-risk, lending-control, collateral, reporting, and account-operation requirements that apply specifically to **small finance banks (SFBs)**. The document is structured into multiple mandatory chapters covering board-approved policies, credit risk evaluation, statutory and regulatory lending restrictions, country risk, unhedged foreign currency exposure (UFCE), legal entity identifier (LEI) requirements, valuation of property by approved valuers, filing of security interests with CERSAI, cash credit/current/overdraft account maintenance, and the loan system for delivery of bank credit. It also notes a deleted chapter and includes repeal/transition provisions, meaning compliance teams must treat the document as a comprehensive replacement/updated framework rather than a narrow topic-specific circular.

From a compliance perspective, the core requirement is that each SFB must maintain **board-approved policies** governing credit risk management and lending processes, and these policies must align with the detailed prudential requirements in the directions. The bank must assess credit risk before sanction and during the life of the exposure, and ensure that lending decisions, concentration controls, and collateral practices conform to the RBI’s prescribed restrictions and monitoring expectations. The document also places explicit obligations around **country risk management** for foreign exposures and around **UFCE** monitoring, implying that banks must measure and manage borrower foreign-currency mismatch risk in a way consistent with RBI thresholds and reporting expectations where applicable.

The directions also impose operational compliance requirements on borrower identification and security perfection. Where applicable, borrowers must have a **Legal Entity Identifier (LEI)**, and the bank must ensure LEI capture and validation before extending or continuing covered credit facilities. For secured lending, the bank must comply with the rules on **valuation of properties**, including empanelment/appointment of valuers, and must file security interests relating to **immovable property (other than equitable mortgage), movable assets, and intangible assets** in **CERSAI**, which means the bank must ensure timely and accurate registration of charge/security interest to preserve enforceability and regulatory compliance.

A separate chapter addresses the **maintenance of Cash Credit (CC), Current Account, and Overdraft (OD) accounts by banks**, which is material for treasury, operations, and credit administration teams because it governs how borrower operating accounts are maintained and controlled when exposures are financed by the bank. Another chapter on the **loan system for delivery of bank credit** indicates that certain working-capital facilities must be structured through a loan system rather than being left entirely as revolving drawdowns, affecting sanction documentation, disbursement mechanics, and account monitoring. Because the document is an updated directions set with effective/legal-revision markers, the bank should treat the **July 1, 2026 update date** as the controlling “as updated” version for internal policy mapping and gap analysis, and should confirm chapter-by-chapter whether any transitional or repeal provisions alter existing processes already in place.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks – Credit Information Reporting) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Small Finance Banks – Credit Information Reporting Directions, 2025** apply specifically to **Small Finance Banks (SFBs)** and set out their obligations for **membership in Credit Information Companies (CICs)** and for **reporting, correcting, and using credit information**. The Directions take effect on the commencement date stated in the instrument, and the version provided is **updated as on July 01, 2026**; a compliance team should treat the update date as signaling that the text reflects changes up to that date. The document is organized around mandatory reporting formats, reporting timelines, rectification of rejected records, credit information report corrections, disclosure/display obligations, and the continued applicability of other RBI Department of Regulation instructions.

Substantively, the Directions require SFBs to maintain **CIC membership** and to report customer credit information in the **prescribed data formats** and within the **required timelines** for initial reporting and periodic updation. They also establish rules for how rejected data must be corrected and resubmitted, and they introduce a process for reviewing the institution’s **Data Quality Index (DQI)**, which is used to assess the quality of submitted data. The reporting obligations are not limited to raw credit exposure data: they extend to the way credit information is handled for **credit appraisal**, meaning SFBs must use CIC reports in their underwriting and lending processes in a manner consistent with the Directions.

The document further imposes obligations on the **correction of Credit Information Reports**, so if a customer disputes information or an error is identified, the bank must follow the prescribed correction process rather than leaving inaccuracies unresolved. It also includes requirements on the **display of information**, which indicates some form of customer-facing disclosure or visibility obligation in relation to credit information practices. In addition, the Directions state that **other RBI Department of Regulation instructions remain applicable** unless the new Directions expressly provide otherwise, so compliance teams need to review these Directions alongside any pre-existing RBI credit information, reporting, data quality, and customer grievance requirements.

The table of contents also shows that the document contains a later chapter on a **Technical Working Group** and a chapter on **Customer Se…** (the title is truncated in the excerpt), suggesting the Directions may include additional governance or customer-related provisions beyond the reporting rules listed above. Because the excerpt does not include the detailed chapters and schedules, a compliance team should separately review the full text for any **specific filing deadlines, data fields, error-resolution timelines, DQI thresholds, escalation requirements, or customer communication obligations** that are likely embedded in Chapters III–V and any annexes.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks – Credit Cards and Debit Cards: Issuance and Conduct) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on October 1, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks – Credit Cards and Debit Cards: Issuance and Conduct) Directions, 2025**, effective **immediately on November 28, 2025**, and they apply specifically to **Small Finance Banks**. The directions are issued under **Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and state that they govern the **general and conduct regulations for credit cards and debit cards** issued or managed by those banks.

From the portion provided, the document establishes the framework for how small finance banks must conduct their card businesses, with separate chapters covering **credit card conduct**, **debit card issuance**, **form factor**, **co-branding arrangements**, **general guidelines for both credit and debit cards**, **miscellaneous matters**, and **repeal/transition provisions**. The table of contents indicates that the directions are not limited to issuance alone but also cover ongoing operational, conduct, and compliance requirements for card products and related arrangements.

A compliance team should note that the rules are comprehensive and bank-specific: they are intended to apply to each small finance bank individually, and they appear to regulate both the institution’s own card issuance activities and any related third-party arrangements such as co-branding. Because the document is titled as a conduct-and-issuance framework, the relevant compliance obligations are likely to include product governance, customer treatment, card issuance controls, and adherence to RBI-prescribed standards across card operations.

No specific monetary thresholds, fees, interest rates, operational deadlines, or transition dates beyond the **immediate commencement** are visible in the text provided, so those details would need review of the remaining chapters if a more granular implementation assessment is required. The key takeaway from the excerpt is that RBI has created a dedicated, mandatory regime for **small finance banks’ credit and debit card activities**, and compliance teams at affected banks should treat the directions as effective immediately and review all card-related policies, customer terms, issuance processes, and co-branding structures against the full text.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on October 1, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Small Finance Banks – Credit Facilities” Directions, 2025** (as updated through **July 15, 2026**) are binding directions issued under the RBI Act framework for **small finance banks (SFBs)** and set the compliance standards for how these banks may extend credit, including board governance, digital lending, credit linked to specific payment instruments, and lending against **gold and silver collateral**. The document’s structure indicates that it replaces or consolidates operational expectations into a formal directions framework effective from its stated commencement date, with later amendments reflected in the July 15, 2026 update. Compliance teams at SFBs should treat this as a comprehensive rulebook governing both traditional and digitally enabled lending activities, not just a narrow product-specific circular.

A major focus of the directions is **digital lending**. The document establishes requirements for **bank–LSP (lending service provider) arrangements**, along with conduct and customer protection controls, technology and data safeguards, reporting of credit information and digital lending apps (DLAs), and **loss-sharing arrangements in case of default**. This means SFBs must have documented oversight over third-party partners that source, service, or support loans; ensure customer-facing disclosures and fairness controls are in place; maintain proper governance over data collection, storage, access, and sharing; and ensure that credit reporting obligations are met even when lending is distributed through platforms or intermediaries. The presence of a dedicated section on loss-sharing indicates that any contractual risk-sharing with an LSP or other partner is regulated and must be structured to comply with RBI-prescribed conditions rather than left solely to commercial negotiation.

The directions also specifically address **credit facilities linked to specific payment instruments**, suggesting that SFBs offering loans tied to cards, wallets, UPI-like instruments, or other payment rails must comply with a separate set of rules for those products. While the table of contents does not provide the detailed substance, the existence of a separate chapter signals that compliance officers should identify all credit products connected to payment instruments and verify they are being offered under the RBI’s prescribed terms, rather than under general lending policies alone. This is particularly relevant where a payment product and a credit product are bundled or where repayment, drawdown, or usage occurs through a designated instrument.

Another key area is **lending against gold and silver collateral**, which is treated as a separate chapter with both general provisions and **restrictions and ceilings**. This means SFBs engaging in secured lending against precious metals must comply not only with standard lending controls but also with RBI-specific limits and operational requirements governing acceptance, valuation, safekeeping, and exposure management for gold and silver-backed loans. Because the document expressly includes “restrictions and ceilings,” compliance teams should expect binding quantitative or procedural limits to apply to this line of business and ensure product design, branch operations, valuation practices, and risk controls are aligned accordingly.

Finally, the document includes a chapter on the **Role of the Board**, which indicates that responsibility for oversight, policy approval, and governance is not purely operational but requires board-level engagement. For compliance purposes, this means the board of each small finance bank must ensure appropriate policies, controls, and monitoring mechanisms are approved and periodically reviewed for the covered credit activities. In practice, SFBs should review board mandates, committee reporting, product approvals, outsourcing/LSP governance, digital lending controls, and collateral lending policies to confirm they reflect the RBI’s framework as updated through **July 15, 2026**.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks – Interest Rate on Deposits) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on October 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Small Finance Banks – Interest Rate on Deposits Directions, 2025** applies to **small finance banks** and sets the framework for how they may price and pay interest on domestic rupee deposits. The directions take effect from the date specified by RBI in the instrument (document dated **November 28, 2025**; updated through **August 25, 2026**) and replace/operate as the controlling RBI instructions on deposit interest rates for this class of banks. The document is organized around a general interest-rate framework and then specific rules for domestic rupee deposits, so a compliance team should treat it as governing both policy setting and operational payment of interest across deposit products.

A core requirement is that small finance banks must follow RBI’s prescribed **interest-rate framework** for deposits rather than freely setting rates outside the permitted structure. The directions distinguish between **domestic current accounts, savings deposits, and term deposits**, and require banks to apply the respective rules for each product category. Compliance teams should note that the document specifically addresses not only ordinary interest accrual and payment but also special cases such as **additional interest**, **overdue deposits**, **floating-rate term deposits**, and interest treatment when a **deposit account holder has died**.

For **domestic current accounts**, the document sets the applicable interest-rate treatment under the general framework; for **domestic savings deposits** and **domestic term deposits**, banks must apply the separate rules in Chapter III. The directions also cover the **periodicity of interest payment on savings deposits**, meaning banks must pay interest at the interval required by the RBI framework rather than on an ad hoc basis. For **term deposits**, banks must ensure the rate methodology and payment terms comply with RBI’s specific rules, including any conditions for **floating-rate term deposits**.

The directions further require banks to apply RBI’s rules on **additional interest on domestic deposits** where eligible, and on **interest payable on the domestic deposit account of a deceased depositor**, which is a sensitive operational area for complaint handling and estate processing. They also include provisions on **interest on overdue domestic deposits**, meaning if a term deposit matures and is not renewed or withdrawn on time, the bank must use the RBI-prescribed treatment rather than a discretionary or inconsistent rate. The document additionally mentions the bank’s **discretion to pay interest on the minimum credit balance in a farmer’s composite cash credit account**, indicating a specific optional payment scenario that must still be exercised within RBI’s stated boundaries.

Because this is an RBI directions document for a regulated banking segment, the practical compliance obligations are to ensure product terms, account-opening disclosures, core banking system interest calculation rules, and maturity/renewal workflows align with the RBI prescriptions; any deviation in rate setting, interest compounding, payment timing, or treatment of special accounts would create regulatory risk. If you want, I can also turn this into a **compliance checklist** for product, operations, and legal teams.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks - Resource Raising Norms) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Small Finance Banks - Resource Raising Norms Directions, 2025** apply specifically to **Small Finance Banks (SFBs)** and take effect **on the date they are placed on the RBI’s official website**. They are issued under **Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, so they are mandatory regulatory directions rather than guidance. The document’s main subject is how SFBs may **raise resources by issuing long-term bonds** to finance infrastructure-related activity.

For compliance purposes, the key operative change is that the directions establish a dedicated framework for **issuance of long-term bonds for financing infrastructure sub-sectors** by SFBs, replacing or updating the prior regulatory treatment of this funding route. The text provided does not yet include the detailed issuance conditions, limits, eligibility criteria, lock-in periods, tenor requirements, or reporting obligations, but it clearly signals that SFBs are now governed by a specific RBI framework for this form of resource raising. Because the applicability is limited to SFBs, other banks are not the direct subject of these directions unless they are acting in a transaction chain relevant to an SFB’s bond issuance. The document also contains a **repeal and saving** chapter, which indicates that earlier directions on the same subject are being superseded while preserving anything lawfully done under the old regime, and it states that other applicable laws are not barred and that RBI interpretations will govern where needed.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks – Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on October 7, 2026)
rows.summary:
This RBI directions document lays down the prudential capital adequacy framework specifically for **Small Finance Banks (SFBs)**, and it is the governing direction for how these banks must classify capital, maintain minimum capital levels, and structure certain loss-absorbing instruments under the RBI’s Basel III regime. It is titled **“Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks – Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy) Directions, 2025”** and is shown as **updated as on July 01, 2026**; the document itself is issued on **November 28, 2025**. For compliance purposes, the key point is that these are not general banking guidelines—they are **prudential capital rules for SFBs**, so the affected entities are Small Finance Banks and, where relevant, their board-approved governance and capital instruments.

The document is organized to require SFBs to maintain **board-approved policies** and follow RBI-prescribed criteria for regulatory capital. It covers the **definition and classification of capital**, the **components of regulatory capital**, and the **limits and minima** that apply to capital composition. The table of contents shows detailed treatment of **Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1)** capital, including the **criteria for classifying instruments as common shares (paid-up equity capital)** for regulatory capital purposes, which is critical because only qualifying instruments can be counted as the highest-quality capital.

The directions also separately address **Additional Tier 1 (AT1) capital**, including the criteria for inclusion of **Basel III Preference Non-Convertible Perpetual Shares (PNCPS)** and **Basel III Perpetual Debt Instruments (PDI)** in AT1 capital. This means SFBs must ensure that any AT1 instruments they issue are structured to meet the exact Basel III/RBI conditions for recognition; otherwise, those instruments will not count toward regulatory capital. In practical compliance terms, this requires ongoing validation of instrument terms, loss-absorption features, permanence, and any other eligibility conditions specified by RBI for Tier 1 recognition.

Because the content shown is the document front matter and table of contents rather than the full chapter text, the material compliance takeaway is that **SFBs are subject to a formal RBI capital adequacy regime with detailed eligibility tests for capital instruments and mandatory board oversight**. The document clearly indicates that it includes rules beyond mere minimum ratios, extending to **what qualifies as capital**, **how boards must oversee policies/documents**, and **which capital instruments may be counted in CET1 or AT1**. A compliance team should treat this as the controlling framework for capital planning, issuance, and ongoing monitoring for Small Finance Banks, and should review the operative chapters for the exact thresholds, deductions, and calculation mechanics referenced by the headings.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks – Cash Reserve Ratio and Statutory Liquidity Ratio) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on October 09, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks – Cash Reserve Ratio and Statutory Liquidity Ratio) Directions, 2025** under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 and the RBI Act, 1934, effective from **November 28, 2025**, and the version provided is updated through **August 25, 2026**. The directions apply specifically to **small finance banks (SFBs)** and consolidate the RBI’s requirements on **cash reserve ratio (CRR)** and **statutory liquidity ratio (SLR)**, along with the procedures for computation, reporting, penalties, and repeal/transition provisions.

For compliance purposes, the key requirement is that SFBs must maintain the prescribed **CRR with the RBI** and the prescribed **SLR in approved liquid assets** at all times, subject to the detailed definitions and computation rules in the directions. The document also sets out how banks must calculate the relevant demand and time liabilities, what items are eligible for inclusion or exclusion in reserve computations, and the method by which SLR is to be computed and reported. Because the directions include a full chapter on **reporting**, SFBs have a continuing obligation to submit the prescribed returns and maintain internal records supporting their CRR/SLR calculations and holdings.

The document also contains a **penalties** chapter, indicating that non-compliance with the reserve maintenance, reporting, or related procedural requirements can attract RBI enforcement action under the applicable legal framework. In addition, the **repeal and other provisions** chapter means these directions supersede or modify prior RBI instructions on the same subject for SFBs, so compliance teams should treat this as the controlling updated framework and verify that legacy policies, reserve maintenance processes, and reporting templates have been aligned to the 2025 directions as amended through August 25, 2026.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks - Governance) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on October 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s “Small Finance Banks – Governance) Directions, 2025” are a governance rulebook for small finance banks, issued on November 28, 2025 under DOR/2025-26/180 (DOR.HGG.GOV.No.99/29.67.001/2025-26). The document sets out binding requirements on board constitution, appointment and conduct of directors, roles of the MD&CEO, part-time chairman and whole-time directors, board procedures, committee structures, key control-function appointments, remuneration, and approval/reporting obligations. Its applicability is to small finance banks, and it supersedes or consolidates governance expectations into a formal directions framework effective from the date specified in the opening chapter (the excerpt provided does not show the actual commencement date, so that date should be checked in the full text before implementation planning).

Substantively, the directions require small finance banks to maintain a board and leadership structure that meets RBI-prescribed governance standards, including rules for appointing and managing directors, defining the authority and responsibilities of the MD&CEO, part-time chairman, and whole-time directors, and ensuring the board’s role and each director’s duties are clearly set. The document also establishes expectations for how the board must function in practice, including formalized board structure and practices, and it creates/updates mandatory board committees: the Audit Committee of the Board, the Risk Management Committee, and the Nomination and Remuneration Committee. These committees are not optional; their composition, responsibilities, and reporting lines are part of the governance framework the bank must operate under.

The directions further require specific senior control and support roles to be appointed, including a Chief Risk Officer, a Chief Financial Officer, and a Chief Technical Officer, with the relevant chapters governing their appointment criteria and oversight expectations. Compensation governance is also explicitly regulated: remuneration of non-executive directors, whole-time directors, the MD&CEO, material risk takers, and control function staff is covered in a dedicated chapter, meaning banks must align pay structures with RBI’s governance and risk principles rather than treating compensation as a purely internal HR matter. A final chapter addresses regulatory approvals and reporting, so any covered appointment, governance change, or other item requiring RBI consent or notification must follow the specified approval/reporting process rather than being implemented solely through board approval.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks – Undertaking of Financial Services) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on October 05, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Small Finance Banks – Undertaking of Financial Services Directions, 2025** (issued **November 28, 2025**, and noted as **updated through April 27, 2026**) set out the framework under which **small finance banks (SFBs)** may engage in financial services beyond core banking. The document is structured around board governance, general business restrictions, investment prudential norms, application procedures, and specific permitted ancillary businesses such as **equipment leasing, hire purchase, factoring, primary dealership, underwriting, agency business, and referral arrangements**. For a compliance team, the key takeaway is that these are not open-ended permissions: SFBs can undertake only those activities and structures expressly allowed by the RBI directions, and the board is expected to maintain approved policies and oversight for each relevant line of business.

The directions place substantial responsibility on the **board of directors** to approve the bank’s policies for undertaking financial services and to ensure the bank has controls, governance, and risk-management arrangements appropriate to the permitted activities. The bank must ensure the activities are carried out in compliance with RBI-prescribed conditions, with the board overseeing not only strategy but also ongoing adherence, limits, and due diligence. Compliance officers should treat this as a board-governance requirement, not merely an operational one: the bank must be able to show formal policy approval, monitoring, and accountability for every financial service it offers.

The **general guidelines** section governs the **forms of business** that an SFB may engage in and the **prudential regulation for investments**, which implies limits and safeguards on how the bank may deploy funds in investment activities connected to its permissible services. The directions also include a **procedure for application**, indicating that where RBI permission or approval is required for a particular business line or structure, the bank must follow the prescribed application process rather than commencing the activity independently. Compliance teams should ensure that any proposed activity is checked against the RBI’s permitted forms of business and that no launch occurs until all required internal approvals and RBI permissions are in place.

The document’s financial-services chapter specifically addresses several activity types that may be undertaken by SFBs only within the RBI’s conditions. These include **equipment leasing and hire purchase**, **factoring services**, **primary dealership business**, **underwriting activities**, **agency business**, and **referral arrangements**. For each of these, the compliance obligation is to confirm that the bank’s role, exposure, contractual terms, disclosures, operational controls, and capital/risk treatment match the RBI’s conditions for that activity; the summary provided here does not include the detailed item-by-item thresholds because they are not shown in the excerpt, but the directions clearly indicate that these business lines are regulated and conditional rather than generally available.

Because the document excerpt provided is primarily a table of contents and high-level chapter listing, it does not expose the full operational thresholds, ratios, or procedural specifics that may appear in the chapter text itself. From the visible material, however, the enforceable message is clear: **SFBs may undertake only the financial services expressly covered by these directions, subject to board-approved policies, prudential investment discipline, and RBI-prescribed application and compliance processes**, with the directions being in force from their issuance date and updated as of **April 27, 2026**. If you want, I can also turn this into a **compliance checklist** or review the full chapter text if you provide it.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks – Digital Banking Channels Authorisation) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Small Finance Banks – Digital Banking Channels Authorisation Directions, 2025** apply **only to Small Finance Banks operating in India** and take effect on **January 1, 2026**. The directions are issued under **Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and set out the framework under which small finance banks may offer digital banking services through internet banking, mobile banking, and other customer electronic-device-based channels for financial and banking transactions.

The document establishes **prudential, technological, and general governance requirements** for authorising and operating digital banking channels. While the excerpt provided starts with the definitions and chapter structure, the compliance significance is that affected banks must align their digital banking offerings and controls to RBI’s specific authorization regime rather than treating digital channels as purely operational extensions of branch banking.

For compliance teams, the key immediate point is the **effective date of January 1, 2026**: any small finance bank offering, expanding, or re-authorising digital banking channels should have its approvals, internal controls, technology governance, customer protection measures, and regulatory compliance arrangements ready by then. The directions are mandatory for the covered entities and are framed as binding regulatory instructions, meaning banks should assess existing internet/mobile banking arrangements against the final rules once the full operative chapters are reviewed, particularly any requirements on authorization prerequisites, security, operational resilience, and customer-facing procedures.

Based on the text supplied, the document also defines “digital banking channels” broadly to include **websites (internet banking), mobile phones (mobile banking), and other digital channels through customer electronic devices/equipment** used to execute financial and other banking transactions. No numerical thresholds, fee caps, or rate changes are visible in the excerpt you provided, but the existence of separate chapters on **prudential guidelines, technological issues, and general guidelines** indicates there are likely detailed compliance obligations beyond the definitional section that will govern how these channels may be offered and controlled.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks - Branch Authorisation) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on October 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Small Finance Banks (Branch Authorisation) Directions, 2025** are dated **November 28, 2025** and appear to replace or consolidate the RBI’s operating framework for how small finance banks may open and manage physical access points, including banking outlets, ATMs/CDMs/BNAMs, and digital banking units (DBUs). The directions apply specifically to **small finance banks** and set out both the **regulatory permissions** for establishing outlets and the **internal governance requirements** banks must follow before opening or relocating them.

A key compliance requirement is that each small finance bank must maintain a **Board-approved policy** governing branch authorisation and related outlets, with the Board explicitly responsible for oversight, approvals, and ensuring the bank’s expansion aligns with regulatory expectations. The document places responsibility on the bank’s leadership to implement controls over how outlets are proposed, approved, opened, shifted, and monitored, rather than leaving those decisions to operational teams alone. Compliance teams should therefore expect formal board-level review of expansion plans and documented internal procedures covering outlet authorisation.

For **banking outlets**, the directions regulate when and how a small finance bank may open or authorise locations where banking services are provided. The document also separately covers **off-site/mobile ATMs, Cash Deposit Machines (CDMs), and Bunch Note Acceptor Machines (BNAMs)**, indicating that these are treated as distinct infrastructure categories with their own authorisation rules rather than being automatically covered by standard branch permissions. Banks must ensure any such deployment is consistent with the RBI’s branch-authorisation framework and any conditions attached to the type and location of the machine or outlet.

The directions also include a dedicated chapter on **Digital Banking Units (DBUs)**. Small finance banks are given **general permission to open DBUs**, but only subject to the conditions set out in the directions. Those conditions address **infrastructure and resources**, **cyber security**, and the **products and services** that may be offered through DBUs, which means compliance teams need to verify that any DBU rollout is not just commercially approved but also operationally secure and within the permitted service scope. In practice, this means banks must align DBU deployment with technology controls, security governance, and product-rule boundaries established by the RBI.

Overall, the document is an RBI authorisation and governance framework for small finance banks’ physical and digital distribution footprint. The material compliance obligations are: establish and follow a Board-approved policy; ensure the Board retains responsibility for branch/outlet strategy; comply with RBI conditions for opening banking outlets and deploying off-site/mobile ATM and cash-deposit infrastructure; and treat DBU openings as permitted only within a controlled framework that addresses cyber security, infrastructure readiness, and allowed services.
