No specific numeric thresholds, dates for phased implementation, or transaction limits are visible in the excerpt provided, but the directions are effective as an RBI directive dated **28 November 2025** and should be reviewed in full for any chapter-specific procedural requirements.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks - Voluntary Amalgamation) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Small Finance Banks (Voluntary Amalgamation) Directions, 2025** set out the mandatory process for any **voluntary amalgamation involving a small finance bank**, and they take effect on **November 28, 2025**. The directions apply to **small finance banks** and govern both the internal approvals and the RBI approval process for an amalgamation, as well as related shareholder and promoter protections.

Before an amalgamation can proceed, the **board of directors** of each concerned bank must approve the proposal, and the **shareholders** must also approve it in the manner required under the directions. The document then requires **RBI approval/sanction** before the scheme can be implemented, so the transaction is not effective solely on company-law or shareholder approval. The directions also establish rules for **dissenting shareholders**, meaning shareholders who do not support the amalgamation are given prescribed entitlements rather than being left without a remedy.

In addition, the directions impose **norms on buying and selling shares by promoters** in the context of a voluntary amalgamation, indicating that promoter share transfers are specifically regulated during the transaction process. The final chapter states that prior related provisions are **repealed and saved** to the extent necessary, while also clarifying that the directions do **not bar the application of other laws** where those laws remain applicable. The RBI also retains authority for **interpretation** of the directions, meaning compliance teams should treat the RBI’s reading as controlling if any ambiguity arises.

Because the document excerpt provided is only the cover and table of contents, it does not disclose the detailed procedural thresholds, voting percentages, timelines, valuation rules, or payout formulas; however, it clearly signals that any SFB considering a voluntary merger or amalgamation must build its transaction timetable around **board approval, shareholder approval, and prior RBI sanction**, and must account for separate protections for dissenting shareholders and restrictions on promoter share dealings.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks – Acquisition and Holding of Shares or Voting Rights) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on October 1, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Small Finance Banks – Acquisition and Holding of Shares or Voting Rights) Directions, 2025”** were issued on **November 28, 2025** under reference **DOR/2025-26/176 (DOR.HOL.REC.95/16.13.100/2025-26)**. The document establishes the RBI’s framework governing **who may acquire or continue to hold shares or voting rights in Small Finance Banks (SFBs)**, and it is organized around three operational areas: **prior approval for acquisition, ongoing monitoring, and reporting of violations**, plus standard repeal/savings and interpretation provisions.

The directions apply to **Small Finance Banks and persons/entities seeking to acquire or hold shares or voting rights in them**. A key substantive requirement is that certain acquisitions cannot proceed without **prior RBI approval**, and the document sets out the **fit-and-proper criteria** and the **procedure for obtaining that approval**. This means compliance teams at SFBs must ensure that any proposed change in ownership or voting control is screened in advance against the RBI’s eligibility standards before any transfer or acquisition is completed.

The directions also impose a **continuous monitoring obligation** on SFBs, requiring them to maintain arrangements for **ongoing due diligence** over shareholding and voting-right changes rather than relying only on one-time approval checks. The bank must be able to **detect any violation of Section 12B(1) of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, which is the statutory provision the directions reference for prohibited or non-compliant acquisition/holding of shares or voting rights. This indicates a positive compliance obligation to monitor ownership structures and voting rights on an ongoing basis so that breaches can be identified promptly.

In addition, the directions introduce **reporting requirements** tied to those monitoring efforts: if a violation or suspected breach is identified, the SFB must report it in the manner required by the RBI. The document also notes **repeal and saving provisions**, meaning the new directions supersede prior instructions in this area while preserving actions taken under the earlier framework to the extent specified. It further clarifies that **other applicable laws are not barred**, so compliance with these directions does not remove obligations under company law, banking law, securities law, or other relevant regulatory regimes, and the RBI retains authority to interpret the directions.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks – Licensing) Guidelines, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s 2025 Small Finance Banks (Licensing) Guidelines set out the “on tap” licensing framework for new private sector small finance banks and for certain entities that may convert into such banks. The guidelines apply to applicants seeking registration/licensing as a small finance bank, including eligible promoters such as resident individuals/professionals with at least 10 years of relevant banking/financial experience, resident-owned entities controlled by residents, and corporate groups meeting the RBI’s conditions; the document also contemplates conversions from NBFCs, MFIs, local area banks, and payment banks. The stated objective is to deepen financial inclusion by creating banks that primarily serve underserved and unserved segments, while operating under prudential banking regulation.

A key requirement is the scope of activities: small finance banks are expected to focus on basic banking services, lending to small borrowers and priority sectors, and other permitted banking activities, subject to RBI restrictions and conditions. The guidelines prescribe a minimum paid-up voting equity capital of ₹200 crore for new applicants, and promoters must contribute at least 40% of this paid-up voting equity capital at the time of licensing; this promoter stake is subject to a lock-in period and phased dilution requirements over time under RBI rules. The document also addresses foreign shareholding, voting rights, and share transfer/acquisition limits, meaning any foreign investment or ownership changes must stay within RBI’s permitted caps and approval framework.

For regulatory compliance, the guidelines impose prudential norms and governance expectations from the outset, including requirements around capital adequacy, exposure limits, fit-and-proper standards for owners/managers, and a credible business plan demonstrating viability and public-interest benefits. For NBFCs/MFIs/LABs/payment banks seeking conversion into a small finance bank, the RBI adds specific conditions beyond the general licensing criteria, reflecting the need to transition into full banking regulation and satisfy any additional capital, governance, and operational requirements the RBI may impose. Overall, the document creates an RBI-controlled licensing regime that requires applicants to be financially strong, promoter-backed, governance-ready, and aligned with inclusion-oriented banking objectives before a license is granted and during ongoing operation.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Payments Banks – Prudential Norms on Declaration of Dividend) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Payments Banks – Prudential Norms on Declaration of Dividend Directions, 2026** (RBI/2025-26/388, DOR.ACC.REC.No.429/21.02.067/2025-26) is a new framework dated **March 10, 2026** governing when and how **payments banks** may declare and pay dividends. From a compliance perspective, the document is organized around commencement/applicability, definitions, dividend-declaration controls, reporting, enforcement, and repeal/saving, which signals that the RBI is imposing a formal prudential gatekeeping regime rather than leaving dividend policy to general corporate discretion.

The directions apply specifically to **payments banks** and require **board-level oversight** before any dividend is declared. The board must assess compliance with RBI-prescribed **eligibility criteria** and determine whether the bank meets the conditions for distribution, rather than authorizing dividends solely based on distributable profits under company law. The document also sets out rules on the **quantum of dividend payable**, meaning the amount distributed will be subject to RBI’s prudential limits rather than being entirely at management’s discretion.

A key substantive element is that certain **profits are ineligible for dividend distribution**, so not all accounting profits can be treated as freely distributable for dividend purposes. The directions therefore require the bank to segregate profits eligible for payment from profits that may not be used for dividends, and to follow the RBI’s restrictions before making any distribution decision. The framework also includes a **reporting system**, indicating that payments banks must submit prescribed information to the RBI in connection with proposed or declared dividends, which likely creates a pre- or post-declaration compliance filing obligation.

The directions further impose an explicit **restriction on payment of dividend** where the prudential conditions are not satisfied, and they provide for **penal consequences for non-compliance**, so violations may attract supervisory action in addition to any corporate-law consequences. The final chapter includes **repeal and saving** provisions, which means any earlier RBI dividend instructions covered by this instrument are superseded, while actions already taken or rights accrued under the old framework may be preserved to the extent stated. It also clarifies that **application of other laws is not barred**, so payments banks must comply with these RBI directions in addition to applicable company-law, accounting, and other legal requirements.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Payments Banks – Miscellaneous) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on October 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Payments Banks – Miscellaneous Directions, 2025** (updated through **April 1, 2026**) are a consolidated compliance framework for **payments banks** and cover governance, deposit handling, depositor-protection obligations, and related operational requirements. The document is issued as **DOR/2025-26/221 / DOR.SOG(SPE).REC.No.140/13-04-001/2025-26 dated November 28, 2025**, and applies to entities classified as payments banks under RBI regulation. At a high level, it appears to replace/organize prior instructions into one direction set and is structured into chapters on board oversight, deposit acceptance, and the Depositor Education and Awareness Fund (DEAF), among other topics.

From the portions provided, the **board of a payments bank** must have formally approved policies covering the bank’s key activities and must take responsibility for ongoing oversight and periodic review of those policies and controls. This means compliance is not left to operations alone: the board is expected to set the framework, ensure key responsibilities are assigned, and conduct reviews rather than treating these as optional governance best practices.

The directions also regulate **acceptance of deposits**, which is a core activity for payments banks. Compliance teams should expect prescriptive rules on what kinds of deposits may be accepted, how they must be maintained, and any limitations or safeguards that apply to these products. Because the document is specifically focused on payments banks, these deposit rules are central to whether products, account structures, and customer communications are permissible.

A substantial portion of the document addresses the **Depositor Education and Awareness Fund (DEAF)**. The table of contents shows rules on **definitions, credits to the Fund, refunds and interest, registration guidelines, and related procedures**, indicating that banks must identify in-scope unclaimed/transferable balances and follow RBI-mandated handling requirements. Compliance officers should assume there are operational obligations to move eligible amounts into the fund, process customer claims/refunds correctly, and calculate or account for interest as required by the DEAF rules. The document also includes registration-related guidance, which likely means banks must ensure they are properly registered or recognized for DEAF participation and maintain the procedures needed to comply with fund reporting and transfer obligations.

Because the provided text is only the opening and table of contents, the exact thresholds, timelines, and transaction-level mechanics are not visible here; however, the document clearly signals that payments banks must maintain RBI-compliant governance, deposit-taking controls, and DEAF processing procedures, with the rules effective as of the 2025 issuance and updated through **April 1, 2026**. A compliance team should review the full text for any specific numeric limits, reporting deadlines, eligibility conditions, and workflow requirements that apply to deposits and unclaimed balances.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Payments Banks – Managing Risks in Outsourcing) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Payments Banks – Managing Risks in Outsourcing Directions, 2025** (issued **November 28, 2025**, reference **DOR/2025-26/220 DOR.ORG.REC.No.139/21-04-158/2025-26**) establishes a formal outsourcing-risk framework specifically for **payments banks**. It sets out the regulatory expectations for when and how a payments bank may outsource activities, with a strong emphasis on the bank’s continuing accountability for outsourced functions, board oversight, senior-management governance, and risk controls. The directions apply to **payments banks** and focus on outsourcing arrangements involving **financial services and related operational/support functions**.

At a high level, the document requires each payments bank to have a **board-approved outsourcing policy** and assigns the **board** responsibility for approving the policy, setting risk appetite, ensuring effective oversight, and satisfying itself that the bank retains control over outsourced activities. Senior management is expected to implement the policy, maintain monitoring mechanisms, and ensure outsourcing does not compromise customer interests, confidentiality, service quality, or regulatory compliance. The document also requires a governance framework covering due diligence of service providers, contractual protections, ongoing monitoring, audit/access rights, and contingency/exit planning.

A key substantive requirement is that certain activities **must not be outsourced**; the directions identify categories of core functions that are considered too critical to delegate in a way that would dilute the bank’s responsibility or supervisory control. For any permitted outsourcing, the payments bank remains fully accountable to the Reserve Bank for the outsourced function as if it were performed in-house. The bank must therefore ensure appropriate authorization, documented oversight, and risk mitigation over the entire outsourcing lifecycle, including vendor selection, contract execution, service monitoring, and termination/transition.

The directions also require a structured **risk management** approach for outsourcing arrangements, including assessment of operational, legal, reputational, concentration, and business-continuity risks. Banks must maintain mechanisms to ensure that outsourcing does not create unreasonable dependence on a service provider, impair the bank’s ability to manage customer grievances, or obstruct regulator access to information and records. Where outsourcing affects critical services, the bank is expected to have stronger continuity arrangements and contingency plans so that customer services can be maintained if the provider fails or the arrangement is disrupted.

In practical compliance terms, the document means payments banks need to review all existing and proposed outsourcing arrangements against the new directions, update policies and contracts where needed, and verify that governance, monitoring, audit rights, data protection, and exit provisions meet the RBI’s expectations. Because the table of contents also indicates dedicated provisions on **definitions, board responsibilities, financial-service outsourcing, governance, and risk management**, a compliance team should expect detailed operational requirements rather than just broad principles, and should map each outsourced activity to determine whether it is prohibited, permitted subject to controls, or requires enhancement of oversight.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Payments Banks - Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on October 1, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Payments Banks – Responsible Business Conduct Directions, 2025** (updated as of **April 1, 2026**) are a consolidated regulatory framework for **payments banks** governing governance, customer protection, financial inclusion, payments/remittance services, and deposit-liability handling. The document was issued by the RBI on **November 28, 2025** as **DOR/2025-26/219 / DOR.MCS.REC.No.138/01-01-034/2025-26**, and it replaces prior instructions through a repeal-and-savings structure in Chapter VII. For a compliance team, the key point is that the Directions are not just conduct guidance; they impose ongoing operational obligations across the bank’s institutional controls, customer-facing processes, inclusion/accessibility measures, and account-claim settlement procedures.

At the institutional level, payments banks must maintain a governance and compliance framework that supports “responsible business conduct,” meaning they are expected to embed controls, policies, and oversight mechanisms rather than treat these as isolated customer-service rules. Chapter II’s framework is the compliance backbone for the later chapters, so procedures for board/management oversight, internal responsibility assignment, and policy documentation should be aligned to the Directions as a whole. Because the document is updated as of **April 1, 2026**, compliance teams should treat that date as the operative reference point for the current version of the obligations.

Customer protection requirements are a major component of the Directions, and the bank must have processes for clear customer guidance, fair treatment, and complaint handling. The document’s structure indicates specific RBI expectations for disclosure, communication, and service standards that affect how products are marketed, how terms are explained, and how disputes are handled. Compliance officers should assume that customer-facing materials, complaint workflows, escalation mechanisms, and grievance redress records need to be reviewed against the final Chapter III requirements, since these provisions are intended to prevent mis-selling, confusion, and unfair outcomes.

The Directions also impose obligations around **financial inclusion and accessibility**, meaning payments banks must ensure their services are usable by underserved and differently abled customers, rather than merely available in a technical sense. This would typically require accessible channels, inclusive service design, and operational measures so account opening, transactions, and support are not effectively limited by disability, language, or geography. Any business line relying on digital-only or limited-footprint delivery should check that its service model satisfies the specific inclusion standards in Chapter IV.

For **payment and remittance services**, the Directions govern how payments banks may offer and manage transaction services, which is central to their permitted business model. Compliance teams should expect requirements affecting transaction processing, customer instructions, remittance handling, and related safeguards, with internal controls needed to ensure only authorized activities are offered and that transaction records and customer confirmations are properly maintained. Because Chapter V is a distinct substantive chapter, any product or operations team running payment or remittance rails should map its procedures directly to those rules.

The document also addresses **deposit accounts and other liabilities**, which means compliance must control account opening, ongoing account maintenance, and liability-handling processes in accordance with Chapter VI. The presence of multiple annexes on claims, nominations, affidavits, indemnities, and inventory forms indicates that the Directions include formal procedures for settling claims on account-holder death and for handling situations where nomination or survivorship instructions exist or are absent. The annexes specifically include **claim forms for accounts with and without nominee/survivorship clauses**, a **bond of indemnity/surety**, a **letter of disclaimer/no objection**, a **declaration/affidavit**, and an **inventory form for safe deposit locker contents**, which means the bank must have standardized documentary workflows and staff training for these situations.

Finally, Chapter VII confirms there are **repeal and other provisions**, so compliance cannot rely on older circulars or piecemeal instructions without checking whether they have been superseded by this consolidated direction set. Annex I, titled **“Rates at a Quick Glance,”** indicates that the Directions also contain specific fee/rate or charge references that must be monitored against the official annex rather than inferred from legacy pricing schedules. In practice, the bank should perform a line-by-line gap review of current policies, customer communications, claims processing forms, accessibility measures, and transactional operating procedures to ensure they match the revised 2025 Directions as updated through **April 1, 2026**.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Payments Banks – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on October 1, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Payments Banks – Know Your Customer Directions, 2025** (issued **November 28, 2025** and updated through **December 29, 2025**) set out the KYC/AML framework that **payments banks** must follow for onboarding, identifying, and monitoring customers. The document is structured as binding directions under the RBI’s AML/KYC regime and applies specifically to payments banks and their customer-facing account-opening and ongoing due-diligence processes. It replaces/updates prior KYC instructions for this category and is organized around governance, customer acceptance, risk management, customer identification, customer due diligence, beneficial ownership, and ongoing monitoring.

At a high level, the directions require each payments bank’s **Board of Directors** to approve and oversee a formal KYC policy and related controls, with management responsible for implementation. The bank must maintain a **risk-based approach** to customer due diligence, meaning customers are to be classified and monitored according to assessed money-laundering/terrorist-financing risk rather than treated identically. The document also requires the bank to establish clear internal procedures for **customer acceptance**, **risk categorization**, **CIP (Customer Identification Procedure)**, **CDD (Customer Due Diligence)**, and **ongoing due diligence**, with periodic review and escalation where transactions, identities, or beneficial ownership information do not match expected profiles.

For **individual customers**, the directions specify that the bank must obtain and verify prescribed identification information before opening or continuing the relationship, and it must conduct enhanced checks where risk is higher or where there are inconsistencies or red flags. For **sole proprietorships**, the bank must perform due diligence not only on the proprietor as an individual but also on the business itself, using documents and evidence appropriate to establish the proprietorship’s existence and control. For **legal entities**, the bank must verify the entity’s legal existence, identify and verify authorized signatories and controllers, and determine the **beneficial owner(s)**—that is, the natural person(s) who ultimately own or control the customer—before onboarding and on an ongoing basis. The directions also require ongoing monitoring of transactions against the customer’s stated profile so that unusual, large, complex, or suspicious activity can be reviewed and escalated as needed.

Because the provided excerpt only shows the opening chapters and table of contents, it does **not** expose the detailed operational thresholds, documentary lists, or any specific numerical trigger levels that may appear later in the text. However, compliance teams should assume the directions impose full implementation obligations across the payments bank’s onboarding, periodic review, beneficial-ownership identification, and transaction-monitoring workflows, with the Board-approved policy and internal controls aligned to the RBI’s updated KYC framework as of **December 29, 2025**. If you want, I can also produce a **section-by-section compliance checklist** once you provide the full text beyond the table of contents.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Payments Banks – Financial Statements: Presentation and Disclosures) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on April 1, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Payments Banks – Financial Statements: Presentation and Disclosures Directions, 2025** apply to **payments banks** and set out the mandatory format, presentation rules, and disclosure requirements for their standalone and consolidated financial statements. The directions are identified as **DOR/2025-26/216, DOR.ACC.REC.No.135/21.04.018/2025-26 dated November 28, 2025**, and the version provided is **updated as on April 1, 2026**. For compliance purposes, the key point is that payments banks must prepare financial statements using RBI-prescribed formats for the **Balance Sheet, Profit and Loss Account, notes to accounts, and consolidated financial statements**, and must follow the detailed compilation instructions and accounting guidance attached to those formats rather than relying only on generic statutory financial statement presentation.

The document is structured into multiple mandatory chapters: **Chapter II** prescribes the **format of the Balance Sheet and Profit and Loss Account**, with notes and instructions for compilation and specific guidance on accounting-standard issues; **Chapter III** sets out the **notes to accounts and disclosure requirements**; **Chapter IV** addresses **consolidated financial statements**; and **Chapter V** contains additional operational instructions such as treatment of **inter-branch account net debit balances**, **reconciliation of Nostro accounts and outstanding entries**, and **transfer to or appropriation from reserve funds**. This means compliance teams must verify not only that the primary statements are in the exact RBI format, but also that supporting notes and any group-level reporting are prepared in the prescribed manner and that internal accounting treatments reflect the special RBI directions. The document also includes specific guidance on how certain accounting standards should be applied in the payments-bank context, so accounting policy decisions and disclosures must be checked against those RBI instructions rather than only against general Indian Accounting Standards.

Because the title states the directions are **“Updated as on April 1, 2026,”** the effective compliance version is the April 1, 2026 updated text, and the institution should ensure its reporting templates, financial statement disclosures, and internal closing procedures align with that update for reporting periods governed by it. The document does not provide a single numerical threshold or rate in the excerpt shown, but it clearly imposes a comprehensive reporting and disclosure framework that is mandatory for payments banks. A compliance officer should treat this as a detailed RBI reporting rulebook: confirm the bank is using the prescribed statement formats, verify all required notes and disclosures are included, check group/consolidation reporting obligations, and ensure any special balances or account items are treated exactly as directed in the RBI instructions.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Payments Banks – Asset Liability Management) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **“Reserve Bank of India (Payments Banks – Asset Liability Management) Directions, 2025”** on **November 28, 2025** (DOR/2025-26/215; DOR.LRG.No.134/13-10-003/2025-26). This is a formal directive setting out the asset-liability management and liquidity risk framework applicable to **payments banks**. At the highest level, the document shifts the compliance burden onto the board and senior management of each payments bank to ensure a structured, board-approved governance framework for liquidity risk, supported by policy, limits, monitoring, and reporting arrangements.

The directions require each affected payments bank to have **board oversight** over asset-liability management, including approval of the institution’s relevant policies, risk limits, and periodic reviews. The board is expected to take responsibility for the overall liquidity risk framework rather than leaving it solely to management, and the bank must maintain documented processes that define how liquidity risk is identified, measured, monitored, and controlled. The title and chapter structure show that the RBI is specifically formalizing the management of liquidity risk through a governance framework and measurement methodology, rather than leaving this to internal discretion.

A key compliance implication is that payments banks must implement a **liquidity risk management policy** and an accompanying **strategy for managing liquidity risk**, both of which must be aligned with the bank’s business model and approved by the board. The directions also require the bank to establish processes for **identification** of liquidity risk, followed by **risk measurement using both a flow approach and a stock approach**, indicating that banks must monitor both cash-flow mismatches over time and available liquid assets/stock positions. The document also refers to **risk monitoring**, meaning compliance teams should expect ongoing surveillance of liquidity positions, escalation thresholds, and internal reporting arrangements to management and the board.

Because the excerpt provided includes only the opening structure and table of contents, it does not yet show the detailed thresholds, ratios, internal limits, reporting frequencies, or any specific implementation deadlines beyond the **effective date of November 28, 2025** in the document header. However, the material requirements clearly indicate that payments banks need to ensure their ALM framework, governance, and liquidity measurement practices are formally documented, board-approved, and operationally embedded as of the commencement of these directions. Compliance teams should treat this as a mandatory framework update affecting all payments banks and should review their current policies, board approvals, monitoring reports, and liquidity measurement methodologies against the full text once available.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Payments Banks – Debit Cards: Issuance and Conduct) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on October 1, 2026)

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Payments Banks – Interest Rate on Deposits) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on October 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Payments Banks – Interest Rate on Deposits Directions, 2025** are issued under the RBI Act, 1934 and are intended to govern how **payments banks** may set and pay interest on **domestic rupee deposits**. The directions are dated **November 28, 2025** and are structured to replace the earlier framework by setting a standalone rule set for payments banks’ deposit-rate practices, including a formal interest-rate framework, rules for current and savings accounts, payment of additional interest, periodicity of interest credit, and a list of prohibitions and exemptions.

For compliance purposes, the key affected entities are **payments banks** (and their deposit-taking activities), with the directions applying to **domestic rupee deposits** maintained by such banks. The document expressly covers **domestic current accounts** and **domestic savings deposits**, and it also addresses the payment of **additional interest** on domestic deposits. The directions include general guidelines that shape the interest-rate framework, which means a payments bank’s deposit-rate policy, account product design, customer disclosures, and operational systems must conform to the RBI’s specific instructions in this instrument rather than relying on a purely bank-discretionary pricing model.

The document also sets out **prohibitions and exemptions**, indicating that some deposit-related practices are expressly barred while certain activities may be carved out by the RBI. A compliance team should treat this as a rulemaking that likely requires review of all customer-facing deposit terms, internal product approvals, interest-calculation logic, and exceptions handling to ensure the bank does not apply prohibited rate structures or benefits outside the permitted scope. Because the table of contents identifies a dedicated chapter on **repeal and other provisions**, the directions likely supersede or modify earlier RBI instructions on the same topic, so legacy policies and operating procedures should be checked for consistency and formally updated.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Payments Banks – Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy) Directions, 2025 (updated as on October 7, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Payments Banks – Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy Directions, 2025** sets out the capital adequacy framework that applies specifically to **payments banks** and governs how they must calculate regulatory capital and risk-weighted assets (RWAs) for prudential compliance. The document is structured to cover the scope of application, definitions, the composition and limits of regulatory capital, deductions and adjustments from capital, and the methodology for computing RWAs for credit risk and other exposures. It is an updated 2026 version of the 2025 Directions, and compliance teams should treat the updated text as the controlling version for any requirements reflected in the update date shown in the title.

The directions require payments banks to maintain regulatory capital according to the RBI’s specified framework, broken into **Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1)**, **Additional Tier 1 (AT1)**, and **Tier 2 capital**, with detailed rules on what instruments qualify, what deductions must be made, and what prudential limits/minima apply. The document also specifies how capital charges are to be computed against **risk-weighted assets**, beginning with the credit-risk framework and external credit assessment rules. Because the table of contents shows separate sections for regulatory capital components, limits and minima, and deductions, the substantive obligation is not just to hold capital, but to ensure the instruments counted as capital meet the RBI’s eligibility criteria and that all required regulatory adjustments are applied before assessing compliance.

For a compliance team, the key operational takeaway is that this is a **capital adequacy regime for payments banks**, so institutions in that category must continuously monitor their capital composition and ensure that any instruments or exposures counted toward regulatory capital satisfy the RBI’s definitions and conditions. The directions imply ongoing obligations to classify capital correctly, apply deductions where required, and maintain sufficient capital against calculated RWAs rather than relying on book capital or internal measures alone. The document’s structure also indicates that the RBI has laid out specific rules for **general treatment, components of capital, minimums/limits, and deductions**, meaning compliance should be reviewed both at issuance of capital instruments and during periodic capital reporting and supervisory returns. Since the provided excerpt only shows the table of contents and heading information, it does not reveal the exact numerical capital ratios, thresholds, or detailed instrument conditions; those would need to be checked in the body of the directions for a full control-by-control implementation review.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Payments Banks – Cash Reserve Ratio and Statutory Liquidity Ratio) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on October 09, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Payments Banks – Cash Reserve Ratio and Statutory Liquidity Ratio) Directions, 2025**, updated as of **January 22, 2026**, under its powers in **Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, read with **Section 42 of the RBI Act, 1934** and **Sections 18 and 24 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**. The document is specifically directed at **payments banks** and sets out the framework for their **cash reserve ratio (CRR)** and **statutory liquidity ratio (SLR)** obligations, together with related computation, reporting, and penalty provisions. The material shown indicates the directions are effective from the date specified in the full text and are organized into chapters covering CRR, SLR, computation procedure, reporting, penalties, and repeal/transition provisions.

For a compliance team, the key point is that these directions create binding RBI requirements on **what reserves payments banks must maintain**, **how those reserves are to be computed**, **how they must be reported to the RBI**, and **what penalties can follow non-compliance**. The document also includes **Annexures I and II**, which likely contain operational details, forms, or computation/reporting formats that payments banks must follow. Because the text provided is only the opening portion and table of contents, it does not yet show the actual CRR/SLR percentages, maintenance periods, eligible assets, or filing deadlines; however, the compliance obligation is clearly to align treasury, reserve maintenance, and regulatory reporting processes with the RBI’s updated directions for payments banks.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Payments Banks - Governance) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on October 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Payments Banks (Governance) Directions, 2025** (issued **November 28, 2025**) set out a comprehensive governance framework for **payments banks** and replace the prior governance instructions for that sector. The directions are organized to cover board composition, director and senior management appointments, board and committee responsibilities, meeting and review procedures, remuneration, and regulatory approval/reporting requirements, so compliance teams should treat them as a sector-wide governance rulebook rather than a narrow procedural update.

The document requires payments banks to maintain a board and senior leadership structure that meets RBI’s governance expectations, including rules for the **constitution of the board and appointment of directors**, and specific provisions governing the **Managing Director & CEO (MD&CEO), part-time chairman, and whole-time directors**. It also prescribes the **role of the board and individual directors**, which means the compliance function must ensure the board is not only properly constituted but also performing oversight, review, and accountability duties in the manner RBI expects. A separate chapter on **calendar of reviews and board meeting procedures** indicates that banks must follow RBI-defined periodic review cycles and meeting discipline, so meeting cadence, agenda preparation, minutes, and review tracking become compliance obligations rather than informal governance practices.

The directions also create mandatory board committee and control-function requirements. Payments banks must operate a **Nomination and Remuneration Committee** and an **Audit Committee of the Board**, with the expectation that these committees perform formal governance, appointment, remuneration, and oversight functions. In addition, the document specifically addresses the appointment of a **Chief Risk Officer (CRO)**, **Chief Financial Officer (CFO)**, and **Chief Technical Officer (CTO)**, signaling that these roles are subject to RBI’s governance framework and that banks must ensure appropriate appointment, reporting lines, and control ownership for risk, finance, and technology functions.

Compensation governance is a major component of the directions. RBI establishes requirements for the **remuneration of non-executive directors (NEDs), whole-time directors (WTDs), the MD&CEO, material risk takers, and staff in control functions**, meaning payments banks must align pay practices with governance and risk outcomes, not just internal policy. The presence of a dedicated chapter on **regulatory approvals and reporting** indicates that certain appointments, changes, or governance actions will require RBI approval or notification, and that the bank must maintain reporting discipline for those items. Because the table of contents also includes a **repeal and other** chapter, the directions appear intended to supersede prior governance rules for payments banks; however, the excerpt provided does not include the transition or commencement text, so implementation timing should be verified in the operative provisions before changing policies or board processes.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Payments Banks – Undertaking of Financial Services) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on December 05, 2025)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Payments Banks – Undertaking of Financial Services Directions, 2025** (issued **November 28, 2025**, updated **December 05, 2025**) set the framework for what payments banks may do beyond core deposit and payments activity, and the document is expressly applicable to **payments banks**. It formalizes two permitted non-core business lines: **agency business** and **referral services**, and makes clear that these activities must be conducted within RBI’s prescribed governance and approval framework rather than as unrestricted ancillary businesses.

The directions place responsibility on the **board of the payments bank** to oversee these activities, with board-level governance expected for any financial services the bank undertakes. The “forms of business” and “procedure for application” provisions indicate that a payments bank cannot simply start such services on its own initiative; it must follow the RBI’s application/approval process and satisfy the conditions laid down in the directions before offering these services. In other words, the document is not merely descriptive—it is an operating authorization framework that requires prior compliance steps and continuing oversight.

For **agency business**, the payments bank may act as an agent for third-party financial products/services only as permitted by the RBI directions, which means the bank can distribute or facilitate products rather than underwrite them on its own account. For **referral services**, the bank may refer customers to other service providers, again only within the constraints and procedures specified by RBI. The compliance implication is that any such arrangement must be reviewed for scope, customer disclosures, authorization status, and adherence to the RBI’s prescribed role boundaries so the bank does not cross into unauthorized financial activity.

The document also contains a **repeal and saving** clause, meaning earlier directions on the same subject are superseded to the extent covered by the 2025 framework, while preserving anything lawfully done or rights/obligations that survive under the savings language. It further states that the directions do **not bar the application of other laws**, so payments banks remain subject to all other applicable legal and regulatory requirements in addition to these RBI directions. The “interpretations” section indicates that RBI will control how the directions are read in practice, so compliance teams should treat RBI clarification as authoritative if there is ambiguity in implementation.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Payments Banks – Digital Banking Channels Authorisation) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Payments Banks (Digital Banking Channels Authorisation) Directions, 2025** apply **only to Payments Banks** and take effect **January 1, 2026**. They are issued under **Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and are intended to govern when and how payments banks may offer digital banking services through **websites/internet banking, mobile banking, and other digital channels on customer electronic devices**. For compliance purposes, the key point is that payments banks must ensure any digital banking activity they conduct is authorized and aligned with these Directions from the effective date onward.

Because the excerpt provided ends in the middle of the definitions section, it does not yet disclose the full set of operational conditions, prudential thresholds, approval steps, technology standards, or exemptions that the Directions may impose. However, the document clearly establishes a new regulatory framework specifically for **digital banking channel authorization by payments banks**, so a compliance team should treat this as a formal RBI requirement affecting product approval, channel deployment, and ongoing governance for internet/mobile/other digital banking offerings. If you share the remaining text, I can produce a complete item-by-item compliance summary of all specific obligations and limitations.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Payments Banks - Branch Authorisation) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on October 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Payments Banks (Branch Authorisation) Directions, 2025** (DOR/2025-26/207, DOR.LIC.REC.No.126/22-01-001/2025-26, dated **November 28, 2025**) set out the branch/banking-outlet authorisation framework that applies to **payments banks** and related outlet expansion models. The document is structured as a binding set of directions covering when and how a payments bank may open banking outlets, deploy off-site/mobile ATMs and cash-handling machines, and use business facilitator/business correspondent arrangements and doorstep banking. The directions are intended to govern both the internal governance process and the operational conditions for expansion and customer service delivery.

At a high level, the directions require each payments bank’s **Board of Directors** to approve a formal policy governing branch/banking outlet authorisation and to define the bank’s control framework for opening and managing outlets. The board is assigned responsibility for ensuring the bank follows RBI’s authorisation conditions before opening any banking outlet or using permitted alternate delivery channels. Compliance teams should therefore expect mandatory board-level policy adoption, documented internal approvals, and ongoing oversight of all outlet openings and related outsourced or agency arrangements.

The document specifically addresses **“banking outlet authorisation”** as the core issue and includes separate provisions for **opening banking outlets** and for the placement/use of **off-site or mobile ATMs, Cash Deposit Machines (CDMs), and Bunch Note Acceptor Machines (BNAMs)**. It also separately regulates the **Business Facilitator / Business Correspondent (BF/BC) model**, setting out eligibility and operating guidelines for engaging business facilitators and business correspondents. In addition, the table of contents shows a dedicated chapter on **doorstep banking**, indicating that home-service or customer-premises banking services are also covered and subject to compliance conditions.

Because the excerpt provided is only the cover/table-of-contents portion, the detailed operational thresholds, procedural conditions, and any numerical limits or time-bound deadlines are not visible here. However, a compliance team should treat the directions as a formal RBI framework effective from the stated issuance date unless the text specifies a different commencement date in Chapter I. In practical terms, this means the institution should confirm that any planned outlet expansion, ATM/CDM/BNAM deployment, BF/BC onboarding, or doorstep banking offering is mapped to the final directions’ requirements and supported by a board-approved policy and documented authorisation process before implementation.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Payments Banks – Voluntary Amalgamation) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Payments Banks – Voluntary Amalgamation Directions, 2025** were issued on **November 28, 2025** and establish the framework a payments bank must follow if it seeks to merge voluntarily with **another payments bank or with a small finance bank**. The directions apply to **payments banks organized as companies incorporated under the Companies Act, 2013 or as a body corporate under any other law in force in India**, and they define the scope, terms, and procedures for such amalgamations. They also make clear that the directions are intended to govern the process alongside, and not to override where applicable, other legal requirements.

The document requires **approval by the board of directors and by shareholders** of the participating bank(s) before a voluntary amalgamation can proceed, and then requires **approval or sanction from the RBI** under the prescribed chapter. It also sets out protections for **dissenting shareholders**, specifying that they are entitled to treatment under the prescribed entitlement rules rather than being left without recourse if they do not support the transaction. In addition, the directions contain specific rules for **promoters’ buying and selling of shares** during the process, indicating that promoter share transactions are not unrestricted and must comply with the norms stated in the directions.

The document further includes **repeal and saving provisions**, meaning prior guidance on this subject is superseded to the extent covered by the new directions, while preserving actions already taken or rights accrued where required. It also states that **other applicable laws are not barred**, so compliance teams must continue to observe the Companies Act, RBI approval requirements, and any other relevant corporate, securities, or banking law provisions in parallel. An annex is included, which likely contains operative forms, criteria, or process detail that would need to be reviewed before initiating or approving any amalgamation transaction.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Payments Banks – Acquisition and Holding of Shares or Voting Rights) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on October 1, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Payments Banks – Acquisition and Holding of Shares or Voting Rights Directions, 2025** (issued **November 28, 2025**) set out the approval, monitoring, and reporting framework for acquisitions of shares or voting rights in **payments banks**. The directions apply to **payments banks** and are intended to govern both **prior approval for acquisitions** and the banks’ **ongoing monitoring of shareholding/voting-right compliance**, including detection of breaches of **Section 12B(1) of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**. The document also contains a **repeal-and-saving clause**, meaning it replaces earlier arrangements on this subject while preserving actions already taken or rights accrued under the superseded framework, and it clarifies that other applicable laws are not excluded.

A key requirement is that a person or entity seeking to **acquire shares or voting rights in a payments bank** must obtain **prior RBI approval** before crossing the relevant ownership/voting thresholds. The directions establish a **fit-and-proper test** for proposed acquirers, so the RBI will assess the acquirer’s integrity, financial soundness, and suitability before approving the transaction. They also prescribe a formal **procedure for prior approval**, which means the acquisition cannot be completed first and regularized later; instead, it must be pre-cleared through the RBI process described in the directions.

For compliance purposes, the payments bank itself has continuing obligations to maintain **continuous monitoring arrangements** over its shareholding pattern and voting rights. This includes carrying out **due diligence** on its shareholders and transaction activity so it can identify potential or actual violations of the statutory limits under **Section 12B(1) of the B R Act, 1949**. The bank must also have mechanisms to **detect breaches** and to ensure that any violation is surfaced promptly rather than remaining undetected until a filing or inspection event.

The directions further require **reporting of relevant matters to the RBI** under the specified reporting framework, so the compliance team should expect ongoing regulatory reporting rather than only transaction-by-transaction approval. Because the document is organized into chapters on prior approval, continuous monitoring, and reporting, the practical compliance impact is twofold: first, transaction controls must block any ownership/voting-right acquisition without RBI clearance; second, internal surveillance, shareholder KYC/due diligence, and escalation procedures must be strong enough to identify and report ownership changes that could breach statutory limits. The document’s operative date is its issue date, **November 28, 2025**, unless the chapter on commencement specifies otherwise in the full text.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Prudential Norms on Declaration of Dividend) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s “Local Area Banks – Prudential Norms on Declaration of Dividend” Directions, 2026, issued on March 10, 2026, establish a new prudential framework for when local area banks may declare and pay dividends. The Directions apply specifically to local area banks and govern only dividend declaration/payment, not general capital management. They are intended to ensure dividends are paid only from genuinely distributable profits and only when the bank remains prudentially sound.

Under the new regime, a local area bank’s Board must exercise explicit oversight before any dividend is declared, and dividend payment is permitted only if the bank satisfies the RBI’s eligibility criteria and other prescribed conditions. The Directions also set requirements on the quantum of dividend payable, meaning the amount that can be distributed is subject to RBI’s prudential limits rather than being fully at management’s discretion. In addition, certain profits are ineligible for dividend distribution, so banks must exclude those profits from the pool used to determine distributable surplus. The document also creates a reporting system, requiring banks to submit the prescribed information to the RBI in connection with dividend declaration, and it imposes a restriction on payment of dividend where the conditions are not met.

The Directions further provide for penal consequences for non-compliance, so a bank that declares or pays dividend contrary to the prudential norms may face regulatory action. The document includes a repeal-and-saving clause, meaning any prior dividend-related directions on local area banks are superseded to the extent covered, while actions already taken under the earlier framework are preserved as appropriate. It also states that the new Directions do not bar the application of other laws, so local area banks must comply not only with these RBI requirements but also with any other applicable statutory or regulatory provisions governing dividends.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Miscellaneous) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on October 05, 2026)
rows.summary:
This RBI direction applies to **Local Area Banks** and consolidates their miscellaneous compliance obligations as of **November 28, 2025**, with updates reflected **through April 27, 2026**. It is organized into three main areas: board governance, Depositor Education and Awareness Fund (“DEAF”) requirements, and disclosure/reporting obligations. For a compliance team, the key point is that the document is not a single rule change but a set of binding operating requirements that govern how the board must oversee policy, how unclaimed depositor balances must be transferred and later claimed, and what records/returns/disclosures the bank must maintain.

At the governance level, the directions require the **board of the local area bank** to approve the relevant internal policies and to conduct reviews as specifically mandated by the RBI in the applicable chapters. That means these matters are not left to management discretion: the board must formally own the policy framework and periodic oversight process. Compliance teams should ensure there is evidence of board approval, review cadence, and implementation tracking for all mandated policies.

The most substantive operational requirements relate to the **Depositor Education and Awareness Fund (DEAF)**. The directions set out what amounts must be credited to the fund, how refunds and interest are handled, the registration and procedural steps for transfer/claim, and the returns that must be filed. In practical terms, the bank must identify eligible unclaimed or dormant depositor balances, transfer them to the DEAF in the manner required by RBI, and maintain a process for depositors or rightful claimants to recover amounts with the specified interest treatment. The bank also has to follow RBI’s registration guidance and claim-handling procedure, rather than relying on informal or ad hoc recovery practices.

The document further requires **returns and disclosures** connected to DEAF compliance. This means the bank must submit the prescribed reports to RBI and make the required disclosures in its records/public reporting framework. A compliance officer should therefore verify that operations, finance, and regulatory reporting teams are aligned on: which accounts are reportable, when transfers to the fund must occur, how interest is computed and paid on refunds, what supporting documentation is needed for claims, and what periodic reporting deadlines apply. Because the excerpt provided stops at the table of contents, the exact thresholds, timelines, and procedural details are contained in the listed chapters and should be checked against the full text before implementation.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Managing Risks in Outsourcing) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Local Area Banks – Managing Risks in Outsourcing) Directions, 2025”** set out the RBI’s updated outsourcing-risk requirements specifically for **Local Area Banks (LABs)**. The directions are issued under the RBI’s supervisory authority and are intended to ensure that LABs retain appropriate control, oversight, and accountability when outsourcing activities, with a particular focus on **outsourcing of IT services** and the governance arrangements around such outsourcing.

At a high level, the document requires each affected bank to have a **board-approved outsourcing policy** and a governance structure that clearly assigns responsibility for outsourcing risk. The **board** is expected to approve the policy and oversee compliance, while senior management and the IT function must implement and monitor controls, risk management, vendor oversight, and reporting. The directions emphasize that outsourcing does **not** transfer the bank’s accountability: the LAB remains responsible for outsourced activities, service quality, customer impact, risk mitigation, and regulatory compliance even when a third party performs the work.

A distinct section addresses **outsourcing of information technology (IT) services**, requiring a formal authorization and oversight framework before IT services are outsourced. The bank must maintain a governance framework that covers the outsourcing policy, defined roles for senior management, and specific responsibilities for the IT function, along with a risk management framework for identifying, assessing, monitoring, and controlling outsourcing-related risks. Although the provided excerpt does not include the detailed clauses, the structure shows that the directions are intended to require documented controls over vendor selection, ongoing supervision, and risk management for outsourced IT operations.

The document is dated **November 28, 2025** and identified as **DOR/2025-26/245 / DOR.ORG.REC.No.164/21-04-158/2025-26**. Based on the excerpt provided, no specific quantitative thresholds, monetary limits, or numerical compliance metrics are visible in the text shown, and no explicit implementation deadline is included in the excerpt. The principal compliance takeaway is that **Local Area Banks** need to ensure their outsourcing arrangements—especially IT outsourcing—are governed by a board-approved framework with clear accountability, management oversight, and risk controls aligned to the RBI’s directions.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks - Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on October 1, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Local Area Banks (Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025** are a comprehensive compliance framework for local area banks, with the version provided marked **“Updated as on July 1, 2026.”** Although the excerpt shown is only the title and table of contents, it makes clear that the directions govern the bank’s conduct across the full retail and institutional customer lifecycle: internal governance and institutional framework, branch-level customer service, customer guidance and protection, financial inclusion and accessibility, payment and remittance services, deposit and other liability products, responsible lending conduct, and miscellaneous/repeal provisions.

For compliance purposes, the document’s structure indicates that local area banks must align their policies, procedures, and customer-facing practices with RBI-prescribed responsible business conduct standards in all these areas. The inclusion of dedicated chapters on **financial inclusion and accessibility** and **customer guidance and protection** signals that banks are expected to maintain processes that improve access to services, ensure fair treatment of customers, and provide clear information and safeguards in branch operations and product handling. The presence of a separate chapter on **payment and remittance services** indicates that these services are subject to specific conduct and operational requirements, while **deposit and other liabilities** and **responsible lending conduct** indicate that both liability products and lending practices are regulated at a detailed level and require formal compliance controls.

The annexes listed are also material from a compliance standpoint because they point to prescribed forms and documentary procedures. The document includes forms for **inventory**, **settlement of claims**, **claim forms for accounts with nominee(s) or survivorship clause**, **claim forms for accounts without nominee or survivorship clause**, and **bond/indemnity/surety documentation for deposit accounts**, as well as a **letter of disclaimer / no objection**. That means local area banks will need standardized internal workflows for deceased customer claims, succession-related account settlements, and related indemnity and no-objection documentation, rather than handling such matters ad hoc.

The title and date information show that this is an RBI issued direction dated **November 28, 2025**, but the copy provided is updated through **July 1, 2026**, so compliance teams should treat the July 1, 2026 version as the operative consolidated text reflected here. No specific rates, thresholds, or numeric limits are visible in the excerpt you provided, so those would need to be checked in the substantive chapters for exact operational requirements.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on October 1, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Local Area Banks – Know Your Customer Directions, 2025** are a consolidated KYC/AML framework for **local area banks** and set out the bank-level governance, customer acceptance, risk management, identification, and due diligence standards these institutions must follow. The directions are issued as **DOR/2025-26/243 / DOR.AML.REC.No.162/14.01.008/2025-26 dated November 28, 2025**, and the document is marked **updated as on December 29, 2025**. For compliance purposes, the key point is that local area banks must maintain formal Board-approved policies and operating procedures covering customer onboarding, ongoing monitoring, and customer identification/due diligence, with obligations organized across the general governance chapter, customer acceptance policy, risk management, and detailed CIP/CDD chapters for individuals, sole proprietorships, legal entities, and beneficial ownership.

At a high level, the directions require local area banks to have an explicit **customer acceptance policy** that defines who may be onboarded and under what conditions, and a **risk-management framework** that applies KYC measures proportionately to customer risk. The document also sets out a **Customer Identification Procedure (CIP)** and **Customer Due Diligence (CDD)** regime, meaning banks must identify customers and verify their identity before or during onboarding as prescribed, then apply additional diligence where the customer type or risk profile warrants it. The document specifically signals separate procedures for **individuals**, **sole proprietary firms**, **legal entities**, and the **identification of beneficial owners**, which means compliance teams must ensure onboarding rules and evidence requirements differ by customer category rather than using a one-size-fits-all process.

The directions place responsibility on the **Board of Directors** and related governance functions to approve and oversee KYC policy and implementation, so this is not merely an operational rulebook but a board-governed compliance obligation. Banks will need to ensure their internal policies, staff procedures, and account-opening controls match the RBI’s chapter structure and requirements, and that they can demonstrate customer identification, risk classification, and due diligence records on request. Because the document is a formal RBI direction rather than guidance, failure to align policies and controls could create supervisory and regulatory exposure for local area banks.

The provided excerpt does not include the detailed substantive thresholds, documentary lists, or deadline mechanics from the later chapters, so the safest compliance reading is that the document establishes a comprehensive KYC framework for local area banks and requires immediate internal alignment with RBI-prescribed customer acceptance, identification, due-diligence, and beneficial-ownership procedures as contained in the full directions. If you want, I can also turn the full document into a **compliance checklist** or a **gap-assessment template** for a local area bank.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Financial Statements: Presentation and Disclosures) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on May 18, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Local Area Banks – Financial Statements: Presentation and Disclosures Directions, 2025** set mandatory reporting and disclosure requirements for **local area banks** in India, with the document updated as of **May 18, 2026**. The directions establish the **required format for the Balance Sheet and Profit and Loss Account**, along with detailed instructions for how local area banks must compile financial statements, apply relevant accounting standards, and present notes to accounts. They also contain specific guidance on accounting issues and disclosure treatment for certain items, meaning compliance teams must ensure that the bank’s financial reporting templates, chart of accounts mapping, and note-disclosure processes conform to the RBI-prescribed presentation rather than using only generic statutory formats.

A major compliance focus is the requirement to follow the RBI’s prescribed **presentation, classification, and disclosure rules** in the financial statements and notes, including the chapter on **disclosure in financial statements – notes to accounts**. The directions cover general presentation requirements and detailed item-by-item disclosure obligations, so the bank must be able to produce disclosures consistently and completely at period-end. This is not merely a drafting guidance document: it imposes formal reporting structure and content requirements that likely affect financial reporting controls, review checklists, and sign-off procedures before publication of annual or interim financial statements.

The final chapter sets out additional operational/accounting compliance instructions, including treatment of **inter-branch account net debit balances**, **reconciliation of Nostro accounts and outstanding entries**, **transfer to or appropriation from reserve funds**, and **provisioning for fraud**. For compliance purposes, these items indicate that the bank must maintain robust reconciliation processes, provisioning policies, and documentation trails for unresolved items and inter-branch exposures, as well as ensure that reserve transfers and fraud provisions are booked in line with RBI directions. Any local area bank preparing financial statements after the effective commencement of these directions must therefore align both accounting entries and note disclosures with the RBI-prescribed rules, rather than relying solely on internal accounting practices.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Treatment of Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Treatment of Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters) Directions, 2025** on **November 28, 2025** under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 and the Credit Information Companies (Regulation) Act, 2005. These Directions replace the prior framework for local area banks and are intended to ensure a **non-discriminatory, transparent process** that follows **natural justice** when classifying a borrower as a wilful defaulter, while also creating a system to **share credit information** so lenders can be cautioned against extending further institutional finance to such borrowers.

For compliance purposes, the document applies specifically to **local area banks** and sets out how they must identify, review, report, and manage **wilful defaulters** and **large defaulters**. It establishes the overall regulatory framework, the role of the **board** in governance and oversight, the procedure for determining wilful default, reporting obligations to RBI and credit information systems, and the preventive/internal control measures expected from the bank, including auditor involvement.

The Directions require banks to follow a formal process before classifying any borrower as a wilful defaulter, with safeguards designed to ensure fairness and proper opportunity for the borrower to be heard. They also require banks to maintain systems for **reporting wilful defaulters and large defaulters**, using the prescribed formats in the annexures for submission of the **list of large defaulters** and **data on wilful default cases**. This means local area banks will need to ensure their credit monitoring, delinquency escalation, default classification, and regulatory reporting processes are aligned to the RBI’s mandated formats and timelines once those provisions are applied.

The document also indicates that these Directions include **preventive measures** and assign a role to **auditors**, implying that compliance is not limited to ex-post classification but also includes internal controls to reduce misclassification and ensure appropriate escalation. The table of contents shows separate chapters for the **Board’s function**, **treatment of wilful defaulters**, **reporting**, **preventive measures and auditors**, and **repeal/other provisions**, so compliance teams should expect detailed operational obligations, board-level oversight responsibilities, and transition/repeal provisions that may affect prior guidance. However, the excerpt provided does not include the substantive operative text of those chapters, so specific thresholds, deadlines, or procedural steps beyond the existence of the reporting formats are not visible in the supplied content.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Resolution of Stressed Assets) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on October 1, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Local Area Banks – Resolution of Stressed Assets Directions, 2025** set out a dedicated framework for how **local area banks** must identify, report, disclose, and resolve stressed loan accounts, including restructuring, compromise settlements, technical write-offs, and relief for accounts affected by calamities. The directions are issued under the RBI’s regulatory powers and are **effective from November 28, 2025**, with the text noted as **updated as on July 1, 2026**. They apply specifically to **Local Area Banks**, so compliance teams at such banks need to treat these as binding prudential and operational requirements for all covered credit exposures.

A core requirement is that each bank must maintain **Board-approved policies** governing resolution of stressed assets. Those policies must address how stress is identified early, how accounts are monitored and reported internally, and how restructuring or other resolution measures are approved and implemented. The directions also require **early identification and reporting of stress**, meaning banks cannot wait until an account becomes severely delinquent before classifying or escalating it; they must have processes to detect deterioration promptly and ensure appropriate internal reporting and management action. In addition, the RBI requires **disclosures**, so banks must make the prescribed public or regulatory disclosures regarding stressed assets and resolution actions in the manner required by the directions.

For **restructuring of accounts**, the directions provide general prudential norms that apply when a stressed exposure is modified rather than immediately liquidated or written off. Compliance officers should assume that restructuring is not a discretionary accounting exercise: it is subject to RBI-prescribed conditions and prudential treatment, including governance controls, documentation, and likely recognition/classification consequences. The document also separately addresses **special cases of restructuring**, including **compromise settlements and technical write-offs**, indicating that these are distinct resolution tools with their own rules and do not substitute for formal restructuring requirements.

A separate chapter deals with **resolution of accounts impacted by calamities**. In those situations, the document assigns a role to the **State Level Bankers’ Committee (SLBC)**, **Union Territory Level Bankers’ Committee (UTLBC)**, and **District Consultative Committee (DCC)**, which are expected to coordinate the response framework. Banks must then **implement the resolution plan** according to the direction’s calamity-relief process, rather than handling such cases ad hoc at branch level. The overall compliance implication is that local area banks need documented internal procedures, board-approved policy coverage, and operational readiness for stress recognition, restructuring approvals, settlement/write-off decisions, disclosures, and calamity-related relief actions under the RBI framework.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on October 1, 2026)
rows.summary:
This RBI direction applies to **Local Area Banks** and sets the current framework for **income recognition, asset classification, and provisioning on advances**, with the text noted as **updated through July 1, 2026**. It is issued as **DOR/2025-26/238, DOR.STR.REC.157/21.04.048/2025-26, dated November 28, 2025**, and it replaces/updates the operative prudential rules for how these banks must treat loan accounts for accounting and regulatory purposes.

From the material shown, the Directions are organized into four main compliance areas: **general instructions**, **asset classification**, and **provisioning norms** (with detailed sub-rules for NPAs and upgradation), and they expressly cover **advances** rather than general banking activities. The content indicates the RBI is imposing or restating requirements on the **Board’s role**, **prudence in lending and consumer education**, and **mandatory disclosure requirements**, so banks must ensure these are embedded in governance, credit policy, and customer-facing processes. The asset-classification chapter specifically addresses **when an account becomes a non-performing asset (NPA)**, how to handle **accounts regularised near the balance sheet date**, special treatment for **specific cases of classification**, the **different NPA categories**, and the rules for **upgrading loan accounts once they have been classified as NPAs**.

For a compliance team, the key operational takeaway is that the bank must have policies and systems that correctly track delinquency, NPA triggers, and provisioning consequences, because the Directions are framed as binding prudential norms rather than advisory guidance. The document also suggests there are explicit requirements for **board oversight**, **loan-prudence standards**, and **consumer education/disclosures**, which typically means compliance, credit risk, finance, and operations must align on classification logic, reporting controls, and customer communications. However, the excerpt provided does not include the actual numerical provisioning percentages or the detailed rule text in Chapters III and IV, so those exact thresholds and deadlines cannot be extracted from the supplied content alone.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Asset Liability Management) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Asset Liability Management) Directions, 2025** on **November 28, 2025** under reference **DOR/2025-26/237 / DOR.LRG.No.156/13-10-009/2025-26**.
