The directions apply to **Local Area Banks** and set out a formal framework for **asset-liability management (ALM)** and **liquidity risk management**, with a governance structure that assigns clear oversight responsibility to the **Board of Directors**. The Board is required to approve the bank’s ALM/l liquidity policies, set and periodically review internal limits and risk management standards, and ensure that the bank maintains systems and organizational arrangements capable of measuring, monitoring, and controlling liquidity and balance-sheet mismatches.

The document requires Local Area Banks to maintain an **ALM information system** that can capture relevant balance-sheet and cash-flow data, support timely reporting, and allow management to identify maturity and liquidity gaps. It also requires an **ALM organization/process** with defined internal responsibilities so that risk positions are regularly measured, monitored, and escalated. The operational focus is on ensuring that the bank has procedures to manage **liquidity risk** on an ongoing basis rather than relying on ad hoc management.

A specific reporting/monitoring requirement is the maintenance of a **Structural Liquidity Statement (SLS)**, which is identified as a core liquidity monitoring statement under Chapter IV. While the excerpt provided does not include the detailed tables or thresholds, the title and chapter structure make clear that the direction is intended to impose formal structural liquidity measurement and short-term liquidity monitoring obligations on Local Area Banks. For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that these directions create a binding RBI framework requiring board-level approval, documented internal policies, formal ALM systems, and ongoing liquidity-risk oversight for all affected Local Area Banks.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Classification, Valuation and Operation of Investment Portfolio) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on October 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Local Area Banks – Classification, Valuation and Operation of Investment Portfolio Directions, 2025** set out the prudential framework local area banks must follow for how they classify, value, and manage their investment portfolios. The document is **issued November 28, 2025** and is labeled **“Updated as on May 18, 2026,”** so compliance teams should treat the directions as the operative framework as updated through that date. It applies specifically to **local area banks**, and it is structured to govern both the **board’s oversight responsibilities** and the bank’s **investment policy, portfolio classification, valuation, and operating limits/procedures**.

A key compliance implication is that the directions require a formal **investment policy framework** approved and overseen by the board, rather than ad hoc portfolio management. The document’s chapter structure shows that it specifically addresses the **role of the board**, **general guidelines**, and the **categorization of investments**, indicating that banks must ensure internal policies, accounting treatment, and trading/holding decisions align with RBI-prescribed buckets and related controls. The classification chapter explicitly distinguishes between **Held to Maturity (HTM)**, **Available for Sale (AFS)**, and **Fair Value through Profit and Loss (FVTPL)**, with a further sub-category for **Held for Trading (HFT)** under FVTPL, meaning banks must classify instruments into the correct accounting/valuation bucket and apply the corresponding measurement and operational rules.

The directions also cover **investments in subsidiaries, associates, and joint ventures**, so compliance teams should expect additional restrictions or treatment rules for group exposures and strategic holdings, not just plain-vanilla securities. Although the excerpt provided does not include the detailed thresholds, valuation percentages, or reclassification rules, the document clearly indicates that such items are addressed in the full directions and must be built into internal investment governance, valuation processes, and accounting controls. In practical terms, the bank should ensure that its treasury, finance, risk, and board-level governance processes all reflect the RBI’s prescribed portfolio classification and valuation regime, and that any investment in related entities is reviewed under the specific rules applicable to those holdings.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Interest Rates on Advances) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Interest Rates on Advances) Directions, 2025** on **November 28, 2025**, and they **take effect immediately upon issuance**. The directions apply specifically to **Local Area Banks** (referred to collectively as “banks” and individually as a “bank”) and are issued under the RBI’s powers under **Sections 21 and 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and other enabling provisions. From a compliance standpoint, this means affected banks must implement the new lending-rate framework right away, with no delayed transition date stated in the excerpt.

The document establishes a formal regulatory framework for how Local Area Banks must set and disclose **interest rates on advances**, organized around general lending principles, the **benchmark** to be used, other aspects of lending rates, foreign currency advances, exemptions, and repeal/transitional provisions. The content shown begins the definitions section, indicating that the directions will include specific defined terms that govern how loan pricing rules are interpreted and applied; one definition shown starts with **“advance against own deposit”**, signaling that special treatment may apply to lending secured by a customer’s own deposits. Compliance teams should expect operational rules covering pricing methodology, benchmark linkage, and likely disclosure or documentation standards, since the directions expressly address not only rates themselves but also related lending-rate processes.

Because the excerpt does not yet include the operative rate-setting clauses, no numerical interest-rate cap, spread, floor, benchmark percentage, or deadline other than immediate commencement is visible here. However, the title and chapter structure make clear that these are mandatory RBI directions for Local Area Banks’ advance-pricing practices, so the key compliance task is to review the full text for any required benchmark adoption, rate computation rules, exceptions, foreign-currency lending constraints, and any grandfathering or repeal effects on earlier instructions.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Transfer and Distribution of Credit Risk) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on October 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has issued a new, self-contained framework titled the **Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Transfer and Distribution of Credit Risk) Directions, 2025**, effective **from the date it is placed on the RBI’s official website**. The document states that it is issued under **Sections 21, 35A, and 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, and its purpose is to govern the **transfer and distribution of credit risk** by lending institutions, including for liquidity management, exposure rebalancing, strategic sales, and other loan-exposure transfer arrangements.

For a compliance team, the key point is that RBI is replacing or consolidating prior approach into a **comprehensive regulatory framework** for these activities, rather than leaving them to fragmented instructions. The directions apply specifically to **Local Area Banks** and cover the **transfer of loan exposures** and related credit-risk distribution arrangements. The content indicates that the framework is organized into provisions covering the **scope and definitions**, **general conditions applicable to all loan transfers**, and **special rules for stressed loans**, so compliance will need to distinguish ordinary loan transfers from transfers involving stressed assets.

The document also makes clear that it is not just descriptive guidance: it is a binding set of directions, meaning affected banks must ensure their transfer and distribution practices conform to the RBI’s conditions and any procedural requirements embedded in the later chapters. The introduction signals that RBI expects these directions to serve as the operative regulatory baseline for credit-risk transfer transactions going forward. No specific numeric thresholds, transaction caps, deadlines, or reporting dates are visible in the excerpt provided beyond the effective trigger of publication on the RBI website, so any operational limits or special approval requirements would need to be confirmed from the full text of the later chapters.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Concentration Risk Management) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Local Area Banks (Concentration Risk Management) Directions, 2025** are a prudential framework specifically applicable to **Local Area Banks (LABs)** and are intended to control concentration risk on both the **asset side** and **liability side** of their balance sheets. The document states that RBI has long required limits on exposures to a single borrower or connected borrower group, originally introduced in **March 1989**, and later added liability-side controls through **Prudential Limits for Inter-Bank Liabilities (IBL)** in **2007**; these Directions make those risk-management concepts applicable to LABs in proportionate form.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that LABs must follow RBI’s exposure and inter-bank liability prudential limits as set out in the chapters that follow, under authority of **Sections 21 and 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and other enabling provisions. The document is framed as a formal RBI direction issued on **November 28, 2025** under reference **DOR/2025-26/233** and **DOR.CRE.REC.152/07-03-003/2025-26**. While the excerpt provided does not include the actual numerical thresholds or operational mechanics, it makes clear that the Directions are meant to impose enforceable concentration-risk constraints on LABs, covering both lending/exposure concentration and inter-bank liability concentration, and that the detailed requirements are organized into chapters on **Exposure Norms**, **Prudential Limits for Inter-Bank Liabilities**, and **Repeal and other provisions**.

Because the text provided is only the introduction and table of contents, the specific compliance limits, calculation methods, reporting obligations, implementation dates, and any transitional provisions are not visible here. However, from the introduction alone, a compliance officer should understand that these Directions are a new RBI-issued framework for LABs that formalizes concentration-risk controls as mandatory prudential requirements, and that affected institutions should review the remaining chapters for the exact percentage caps, exceptions, and any procedural obligations tied to borrower/group exposure and inter-bank liability limits.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Credit Risk Management) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
This RBI direction set, issued on November 28, 2025 and updated as of July 1, 2026, consolidates and updates the credit-risk framework applicable to Local Area Banks (LABs). Its core purpose is to require LABs to manage credit risk through formal board-approved policies and operational controls because credit exposures can create broader financial and non-financial risk for the bank if not properly managed. The document is organized into requirements on board-approved lending and risk policies, credit risk evaluation, statutory and regulatory lending restrictions, unhedged foreign currency exposure (UFCE), Legal Entity Identifier (LEI) requirements for borrowers, valuation and empanelment of property valuers, filing of security interests in CERSAI for immovable/movable/intangible assets, maintenance of cash credit/current/overdraft accounts, and repeal/transitional provisions.

From a compliance perspective, the document indicates that LABs must maintain board-approved policies for credit risk management and lending, with specific internal standards governing how credit proposals are assessed and approved. It also imposes statutory and regulatory restrictions on lending exposures that LABs must observe, meaning the bank’s credit operations cannot rely on ad hoc judgment alone and must be checked against RBI-prescribed limits and prohibitions. Although the excerpt provided does not show the detailed thresholds in each chapter, the table of contents makes clear that the directions address potentially material compliance areas such as UFCE measurement/controls, LEI-based borrower identification, property valuation standards, and registration of security interests with CERSAI.

The document also extends beyond underwriting into ongoing account management and collateral/perfection requirements. LABs must ensure appropriate valuation of properties through empanelled valuers, file security interests relating to immovable assets other than equitable mortgages as well as movable and intangible assets in CERSAI, and comply with rules for operating cash credit, current, and overdraft accounts. For a compliance team, the key takeaway is that these are not merely credit-policy guidelines; they are regulatory directions that require documented internal procedures, monitoring, and evidence of compliance across the loan lifecycle, from sanction and documentation through post-disbursement account conduct and security registration.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Credit Information Reporting) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Local Area Banks – Credit Information Reporting Directions, 2025** set out mandatory credit information reporting and related governance requirements for **Local Area Banks (LABs)**, and the updated text is marked **“Updated as on July 01, 2026.”** The directions apply to the entities and activities covered by the RBI’s definition of a Local Area Bank and focus on how those banks must participate in credit information company (CIC) reporting, maintain data quality, and use credit information in lending decisions.

A key structural requirement is that the covered bank must comply with the RBI’s directions on **membership of CICs** and ongoing **reporting/dissemination of borrower credit information**. The document requires the bank to submit credit data in the **prescribed data formats**, follow the RBI’s **reporting timelines and periodic updation rules**, and adhere to the detailed **reporting guidelines** in Chapter III. This means compliance is not limited to sending data, but also includes ensuring the information is complete, accurate, timely, and accepted in the format required by the RBI/CIC ecosystem.

The directions also impose a workflow for **rejected data** and **Data Quality Index (DQI) review**, requiring the bank to rectify data that is rejected and to participate in review of its DQI where applicable. In addition, there are obligations for **correction of Credit Information Reports**, which means the bank must be prepared to resolve inaccuracies in reported credit data and ensure corrections propagate through the credit reporting system. The document further requires the bank to use **credit information reports in credit appraisal**, indicating that such reports are not optional reference materials but part of the bank’s lending assessment process.

The directions also address **display of information**, so the bank must ensure required credit-information-related disclosures or displays are made in the manner prescribed by the RBI. Finally, the document notes the **applicability of other instructions issued by the Department of Regulation**, meaning these directions sit alongside other RBI regulatory instructions and do not override broader compliance duties unless specifically stated. Chapter IV references a **Technical Working Group**, indicating an additional governance or consultative mechanism associated with implementation, but the substantive operational obligations for compliance teams are the reporting, correction, DQI, and credit-appraisal requirements described above.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Debit Cards: Issuance and Conduct) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on October 1, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Local Area Banks – Debit Cards: Issuance and Conduct Directions, 2025** take effect **immediately** and apply specifically to **Local Area Banks**. They govern the **general issuance and conduct rules for debit cards**, explicitly including **co-branded debit cards**, and must be read together with all other applicable **prudential, payment, technology, and cyber security directions** relating to debit and co-branded debit cards.

For compliance purposes, the key point from the excerpt is that RBI is exercising its statutory powers under **Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** to impose binding requirements on Local Area Banks in this area. The document indicates that these Directions are a standalone regulatory framework for how such banks may issue and manage debit cards, rather than a mere guidance note. Although the excerpt cuts off before the substantive chapters are detailed, it clearly signals that compliance teams should expect rules covering **board-approved policy and procedures, issuance of debit cards, card form factors, co-branding arrangements, and general operating/conduct standards** for debit card programs.

Because the document begins with a broad applicability statement, a compliance officer should assume that **all Local Area Banks issuing or planning to issue debit cards, including co-branded variants, are in scope from the commencement date onward**. The excerpt does not yet provide numeric thresholds, fees, limits, or implementation deadlines beyond the **immediate effective date**, so the operative compliance obligation visible here is to ensure the bank’s debit card practices align with these Directions and with the related RBI regimes referenced alongside them.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on April 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
This RBI direction, effective from **November 28, 2025** and updated through **April 1, 2026**, sets out the credit-facility framework applicable to **Local Area Banks (LABs)** and governs both traditional lending and digital-lending arrangements. The document is organized around board-approved policy expectations, digital lending controls, and specific restrictions for lending against **gold and silver collateral**, so compliance teams should treat it as a binding operational rulebook rather than a high-level guidance note.

At a governance level, the directions require the **board of the LAB** to approve and oversee the bank’s lending policies, including the risk appetite, customer-protection framework, outsourcing / third-party engagement controls, and the internal procedures used for digital and collateral-backed lending. This means the bank cannot rely on informal business-line practices for loans or digital channels; the board must own the policy architecture and the bank must be able to evidence that its procedures, monitoring, and control environment are consistent with those approved policies.

The **digital lending** chapter is the most operationally significant. It applies wherever the bank uses a **lending service provider (LSP)** or other digital-lending arrangement, and it imposes requirements on how the bank interacts with the customer, manages consent, and supervises the technology stack. The direction requires the bank to ensure customer-facing disclosures, fair conduct, grievance handling, and data controls are built into the arrangement; it also requires the bank to maintain responsibility for the lending activity rather than treating the LSP as the primary lender in substance. In practice, this means the bank must have procedures for onboarding/monitoring LSPs, protecting customer data, ensuring customers know who the actual lender is, and making sure loan terms, charges, and recovery practices remain within the bank’s own compliance oversight.

The digital-lending framework also includes obligations around **technology and data**: the bank must control what data is collected, how it is stored/shared, and how DLAs (digital lending applications) operate, and it must ensure that the deployment of digital channels does not undermine credit information reporting or customer protections. The document specifically addresses **reporting of credit information and DLAs**, implying that credit data must be properly reported to the relevant credit information system and that the bank must have traceability from the app/LSP interface back to the underlying bank loan. It also addresses **loss-sharing arrangements in case of default**, which indicates that any contractual allocation of losses between the bank and an LSP must be structured so it does not dilute the bank’s primary responsibility to the borrower or weaken compliance with regulatory norms.

The chapter on **lending against gold and silver collateral** introduces separate restrictions and ceilings for these secured loans, meaning LABs that offer such products must apply additional valuation, collateral, and exposure controls beyond ordinary lending rules. Because the document explicitly contains a “Restrictions and Ceilings” section, compliance should expect limits on the types of collateral accepted, eligibility conditions, margins or loan-to-value style limits, and possibly operational requirements for safe custody and valuation of pledged metal. Any LAB engaged in gold or silver-backed lending will need to verify that product design, branch procedures, appraisal methods, and monitoring systems comply with these specific caps and restrictions before origination and throughout the loan life cycle.

Overall, the document requires LABs to formalize board-level policies, tightly supervise any digital-lending partner ecosystem, maintain strong data and reporting controls, and apply special restrictions when lending against precious-metal collateral. A compliance team should review whether current policies, vendor contracts, customer disclosures, reporting processes, and collateral-lending practices already map to these directions, and if not, implement changes before relying on the affected products or channels.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Interest Rate on Deposits) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on October 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
This RBI direction applies to **Local Area Banks (LABs)** and sets the rules for the **interest rate framework on domestic rupee deposits**. The document’s stated objective is to ensure LAB deposit rates are administered within a regulatory framework, and it is organized to govern current accounts, savings accounts, term deposits, additional/overdue interest, floating-rate term deposits, periodic interest payments, and special cases such as deceased depositors and farmer composite cash credit accounts.

For **domestic current accounts**, LABs are directed not to pay interest on balances in current accounts. For **domestic savings deposits**, the directions prescribe how interest is to be calculated and paid, including the periodicity of payment, but the excerpt provided does not include the detailed rate formula or payment frequency text itself. For **domestic term deposits**, the directions govern how interest rates may be set and paid, including rules for floating-rate term deposits, and also address **payment of additional interest**, **interest on overdue domestic deposits**, and **interest payable on the domestic deposit account of a deceased depositor**.

The document also includes a specific provision giving banks discretion to pay interest on the **minimum credit balance in the composite cash credit account of a farmer**, indicating a special case where interest treatment differs from standard current-account treatment. Because the text provided is only the table of contents and heading list, no numerical rates, thresholds, or exact timelines for implementation are visible in the excerpt; however, the full directions are dated **November 28, 2025** and are marked as **updated as on August 25, 2026**, so compliance teams should treat the updated version as the operative one and review the full Chapter II and Chapter III provisions for the precise operational rules, rate formulas, and any compliance mechanics.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Local Area Banks (Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy) Directions, 2025”** are a comprehensive capital-adequacy framework for **Local Area Banks (LABs)**, replacing/setting out the RBI’s current rules on what counts as regulatory capital, how capital must be measured, and how risk-weighted assets (RWAs) are to be calculated. The document is dated **November 28, 2025** and is organized into provisions on **minimum regulatory capital, capital-funds composition, Tier 1 and Tier 2 capital, deductions, limits on Tier 2 instruments, cross-holdings, capital for subsidiaries, and RWA calculations** for the major risk types. For a compliance team, the key point is that it is not just a high-level policy statement: it prescribes detailed eligibility criteria and computational rules that LABs must apply in determining whether they meet RBI capital requirements.

The directions require LABs to maintain **minimum regulatory capital** in accordance with RBI’s prudential standards and to compute capital funds using the specified definitions of **Tier 1 capital** and **Tier 2 capital**, with mandated deductions from capital funds where applicable. The document also imposes **limits on the amount of Tier 2 elements** that can be recognized and includes rules governing **cross-holdings** (to prevent capital being double-counted or artificially inflated through holdings in other entities) as well as the treatment of **capital invested in subsidiaries**. Compliance teams should expect that holdings, instruments, and deductions must be assessed under the RBI’s prescribed classification rules rather than internal accounting treatment alone.

A separate chapter requires LABs to calculate **risk-weighted assets (RWAs)** and apply capital charges for the main risk categories, beginning with **credit risk** and continuing through additional risk charges covered in the directions. This means the bank must classify exposures, apply the correct risk weights and capital charges, and use those RWAs to determine regulatory capital ratios. In practical terms, this document is the authoritative capital adequacy standard for LABs and will affect capital planning, regulatory reporting, treasury/instrument issuance, investment in subsidiaries, and internal controls over exposure classification and prudential computation.

The table of contents also shows that the directions contain multiple detailed subparts under each capital category, so implementation is likely to require line-by-line mapping of existing capital instruments and balance-sheet exposures to RBI’s eligibility, deduction, and limit rules. Because the excerpt does not include the operative commencement clause or specific percentage thresholds, a compliance review should verify the exact effective date and any transition provisions in the full text before relying on it operationally.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Cash Reserve Ratio and Statutory Liquidity Ratio) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on October 09, 2026)
rows.summary:
This RBI direction applies specifically to **Local Area Banks (LABs)** and sets out how they must maintain and report **Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR)** and **Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR)** requirements under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 and the RBI Act, 1934. The document is issued under **Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, read with **Section 42 of the RBI Act, 1934** and **Sections 18 and 24 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, and it is titled the **Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Cash Reserve Ratio and Statutory Liquidity Ratio) Directions, 2025** (updated through **January 22, 2026**). For compliance purposes, the key point is that it consolidates the mandatory reserve-maintenance and liquidity-investment rules LABs must follow, along with the related computation, reporting, and penalty framework.

The directions require LABs to maintain the prescribed **CRR**—that is, a specified percentage of their **Net Demand and Time Liabilities (NDTL)** with the RBI in the form and manner the RBI prescribes—and to maintain the prescribed **SLR** by holding eligible liquid assets at the required level against NDTL. The document’s structure shows that it does more than restate the ratios: it also provides the **procedure for computing SLR**, the **reporting obligations**, and the **consequences for non-compliance**, meaning compliance teams must track not only the end ratios but also the exact computation methodology and reporting cycle. Because the excerpt provided does not include the specific ratio percentages or operative sub-paragraphs of the chapters, a compliance officer should treat the full directions as the controlling source for the applicable CRR/SLR percentages, eligible asset categories, maintenance period, and any operational exceptions or averaging rules.

The directions also establish a formal **reporting regime** under Chapter V, so LABs must submit the required returns/data to the RBI in the prescribed format and timeline, and any failure or inaccuracy may trigger the penalties described in Chapter VI. Chapter VII (“Repeal and Other Provisions”) indicates that the 2025 directions replace or supersede prior instructions in this area, so banks should confirm that legacy circulars or internal policies on LAB CRR/SLR compliance have been updated to match these directions. In practical terms, a LAB compliance team should verify that treasury/reserve-monitoring systems, reserve computation controls, statutory return preparation, and escalation procedures are aligned to the 2025 directions and any updates effective by **January 22, 2026**.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks - Governance) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on October 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Local Area Banks (Governance) Directions, 2025** are a comprehensive governance framework for **all local area banks** and replace prior governance instructions once they take effect. The document is issued on **November 28, 2025** and, based on the title and structure, sets out binding requirements covering board composition, director appointments, management roles, board functioning, committees, remuneration, and RBI approvals/reporting.

The directions require local area banks to maintain a board and leadership structure that satisfies RBI’s governance standards for **constitution of the Board**, **appointment of directors**, and the roles of the **Managing Director & CEO (MD&CEO), part-time chairman, and whole-time directors (WTDs)**. They also define the **role of the Board and individual directors**, prescribe a **calendar of reviews and board meeting procedures**, and establish mandatory board committees, specifically a **Nomination and Remuneration Committee** and an **Audit Committee of the Board**. These provisions mean affected banks must ensure their internal governance documents, appointment processes, and board operating procedures align with the RBI’s specified standards rather than relying on ad hoc or legacy practices.

A significant part of the framework addresses **remuneration**, and it applies not only to **non-executive directors (NEDs)**, **WTDs**, and the **MD&CEO**, but also to **material risk takers** and **control function staff**. This indicates RBI is imposing governance oversight over both board-level pay and compensation for key risk and control personnel, which would require banks to review compensation policies, approval workflows, and any incentive structures to ensure they are consistent with the directions. The document also contains a dedicated chapter on **regulatory approvals and reporting**, meaning certain appointments, governance actions, or remuneration-related matters likely require RBI notification or prior approval, and banks must follow the specified filing/reporting procedures and timelines.

Finally, the directions include a **repeal and other provisions** chapter, which signals that earlier RBI governance instructions for local area banks are being superseded or modified by this instrument. For compliance teams, the practical takeaway is that local area banks should conduct a full gap assessment against these 2025 directions, update board charters and committee terms of reference, verify director/MD&CEO appointment compliance, and map any required RBI approvals and reporting obligations as soon as the effective date and transition provisions in the full text are confirmed.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Digital Banking Channels Authorisation) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Local Area Banks – Digital Banking Channels Authorisation Directions, 2025** are issued under **Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and apply specifically to **Local Area Banks** (referred to in the directions as “banks”). The directions are **effective from January 1, 2026**. At the outset, the document defines **digital banking channels** broadly as bank-provided access through **websites/internet banking, mobile phones/mobile banking, or other digital channels via customers’ electronic devices/equipment** for carrying out financial and other banking transactions as part of digital banking services.

Based on the text provided, this excerpt is primarily the **preliminary portion** of the directions and establishes the scope and legal basis rather than detailed operational requirements. The material compliance point is that, from the effective date, any local area bank offering or seeking to offer digital banking services through these electronic channels must do so under this RBI framework. A compliance team should therefore treat the direction as a sector-specific authorisation regime for **internet banking, mobile banking, and similar digital transaction channels** offered by local area banks, and confirm that internal product, technology, and authorization plans are aligned to the January 1, 2026 commencement date.

The excerpt does **not yet include** the substantive prudential, technology, or general compliance requirements that appear later in the document (for example, approval procedures, security controls, customer protection measures, or reporting obligations). If you want, I can also summarize the remaining chapters once you provide the rest of the text.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks - Branch Authorisation) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on October 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Local Area Banks (Branch Authorisation) Directions, 2025** set out the branch and outlet authorisation framework specifically for **Local Area Banks (LABs)**, replacing earlier/other branch-opening rules with a consolidated regime effective from the date of issuance, **28 November 2025** (DOR/2025-26/224; DOR.LIC.REC.No.143/22-01-001/2025-26). The document is structured around three main compliance areas: **board governance**, **authorisation of banking outlets (including ATMs and similar machines)**, and **use of Business Facilitator/Business Correspondent and doorstep banking models**. For compliance teams, the core point is that LABs must not treat branch expansion or customer-service expansion as an ad hoc business decision; it is governed by an RBI-prescribed authorisation framework with board-approved policy, defined internal controls, and RBI reporting/approval requirements where applicable.

At the governance level, the directions require the **Board of Directors** to approve a formal policy for branch authorisation and related outlet expansion, and to retain responsibility for oversight of the bank’s network expansion strategy. The policy is expected to define how the bank decides where and how to open banking outlets, how it uses alternate delivery channels, and how it ensures regulatory compliance in doing so. This means compliance functions must ensure that any branch/outlet proposal is vetted against the board-approved framework before implementation, rather than relying solely on business-line approval.

The biggest operational requirement concerns **opening of banking outlets**. The directions cover when and how a LAB may open new banking outlets and regulate the use of **off-site ATMs, cash deposit machines (CDMs), and bunch note acceptor machines (BNAMs)**. These machines are treated as part of the bank’s outlet strategy and are not merely technology deployments; compliance teams should assume that deployment, location, and authorisation rules apply to them as distinct banking service points. The document also indicates that these directions govern the bank’s expansion of physical and semi-physical service access points, so any move to expand customer touchpoints must be checked against the RBI’s branch-authorisation regime rather than treated as an ordinary facilities decision.

The directions also address the **Business Facilitator (BF) / Business Correspondent (BC) model** and **doorstep banking**. LABs may engage third parties under these models only within RBI’s prescribed framework, meaning the bank must have documented due diligence, contractual, oversight, and conduct controls before outsourcing customer-facing banking activities. Compliance teams should expect obligations around agent selection, monitoring, customer grievance handling, and service delivery standards, because the RBI is effectively controlling the way LABs extend banking services through intermediaries and at customers’ premises. Any BF/BC arrangement or doorstep service initiative therefore needs to be reviewed as a regulated outsourcing/channel-expansion activity, not just a commercial service enhancement.

From a practical compliance perspective, the document means LABs should inventory all planned and existing **branches, extension counters/outlets, ATMs, CDMs, BNAMs, BC/BF arrangements, and doorstep banking services**, and map each against the board policy and RBI’s authorisation rules. If the bank is planning to open, shift, convert, or expand a banking point, the approval path should be documented and evidence retained that the action fits the RBI framework in force from **28 November 2025**. Because the excerpt provided stops at the chapter headings, it does not disclose the detailed operational thresholds, exceptions, reporting forms, or any geographic/performance conditions; however, the document clearly establishes that LAB branch and outlet expansion is regulated, board-governed, and subject to RBI-compliant controls across both physical outlets and outsourced/digital delivery models.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Voluntary Amalgamation) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Local Area Banks (Voluntary Amalgamation) Directions, 2025** set out the mandatory process for a **local area bank (LAB)** to merge voluntarily with another banking company, including the internal approvals, RBI approval, treatment of dissenting shareholders, and shareholding restrictions for promoters. The directions apply specifically to **local area banks** and govern **voluntary amalgamations**; they do not create a general merger framework for all banks. They became effective on **November 28, 2025**, the date of the circular.

Before any application is made to RBI, the **board of directors** of the LAB(s) involved must approve the proposed amalgamation, and the proposal must then be placed before shareholders for approval. The directions require **shareholder approval by a special resolution** (so the merger cannot proceed on a simple majority), and the board/shareholder process must be completed in the manner prescribed by the RBI before the matter is submitted for regulatory sanction. After corporate approvals, the amalgamation is still not effective unless the **RBI grants approval/sanction**, so the transaction remains contingent on the central bank’s review and consent.

The directions also address the rights of **dissenting shareholders**, requiring a mechanism for their entitlement where they do not agree with the amalgamation. The document further includes **norms for buying and selling shares by promoters**, meaning promoters’ share transactions around a voluntary amalgamation are subject to RBI-prescribed constraints rather than being left entirely to ordinary corporate law. A compliance team should therefore expect transaction documents, board/shareholder resolutions, and promoter share movements to be reviewed for consistency with these specific RBI conditions.

Finally, the directions include a **repeal and saving** provision, meaning any earlier contrary RBI instructions on the same subject are replaced, while actions already taken or rights accrued may be preserved to the extent stated. The document also clarifies that other applicable laws are **not barred**, so companies must still comply with the Companies Act and other relevant legal/regulatory requirements in addition to these RBI directions. A compliance officer should treat this as the controlling RBI framework for any LAB voluntary amalgamation initiated on or after **28 November 2025**, and should ensure the merger timeline is built around the required board approval, shareholder special resolution, RBI sanction, dissenting shareholder handling, and promoter shareholding restrictions.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Acquisition and Holding of Shares or Voting Rights) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on October 1, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s 2025 Directions on **Local Area Banks (LABs) – Acquisition and Holding of Shares or Voting Rights** set out the framework for when prior RBI approval is required before acquiring LAB shares or voting rights, how applicants must establish that they are “fit and proper,” and what ongoing monitoring and reporting obligations LABs must maintain. The document applies specifically to **local area banks** and to **persons seeking to acquire shares or voting rights** in those banks, and it is organized around three core compliance areas: pre-acquisition approval, continuous monitoring, and reporting of breaches of statutory ownership/voting limits. The Directions are issued under the RBI’s regulatory authority and are accompanied by repeal-and-savings provisions, indicating they replace prior direction(s) on the same subject while preserving actions already taken under the earlier framework.

For any acquisition that falls within the scope of the Directions, the proposed acquirer must obtain **prior RBI approval** before completing the transaction. The bank and/or applicant must satisfy the RBI that the acquirer meets the applicable **fit and proper criteria**, and the application process is prescribed by the Directions rather than left to informal correspondence. This means compliance teams at LABs must treat any change in ownership or voting control as a regulated event requiring pre-clearance, not merely a post-closing disclosure.

The Directions also require LABs to implement **continuous monitoring arrangements** so they can identify and track holdings and voting rights on an ongoing basis, rather than only at the time of acquisition. LABs must conduct **due diligence** on relevant shareholders and maintain mechanisms to detect any violation of **Section 12B(1) of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, which governs statutory limits on shareholding/voting rights in the banking context. If an actual or potential breach is identified, the bank has a reporting obligation to the RBI under the procedures and timelines set out in the Directions, so compliance functions must be capable of flagging threshold breaches promptly and escalating them for regulatory reporting.

The effective date is tied to the document’s **November 28, 2025** issuance, and the Directions expressly include a chapter on **commencement** and **applicability**, but the excerpt provided does not specify the exact operative date or any numerical shareholding threshold in the text shown. The document also states that other laws are not barred, meaning compliance with these Directions does not remove the need to comply with any other applicable banking, company, securities, or foreign investment rules. For a compliance team, the key operational takeaway is that any acquisition or holding of LAB shares or voting rights must be screened against RBI approval requirements, fit-and-proper standards, statutory ownership/voting caps, and ongoing monitoring/reporting obligations under the new 2025 framework.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Prudential Norms on Declaration of Dividend) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Prudential Norms on Declaration of Dividend) Directions, 2026** (RBI/2025-26/390, DOR.ACC.REC.No.431/21.02.067/2025-26, dated **March 10, 2026**), which sets out the prudential framework that **Regional Rural Banks (RRBs)** must follow before declaring or paying dividends. The document is organized around eligibility, board oversight, reporting, and consequences for non-compliance, and it applies specifically to **RRBs** rather than to banks generally. From the table of contents, the directions cover a new or updated set of requirements on declaration of dividend, including when dividend may be paid, what profits are not eligible for dividend distribution, the reporting process, restrictions on payment, and penalties for violations.

A key feature of the directions is that **the Board of the RRB must exercise oversight over dividend declaration**, meaning dividend decisions are not purely managerial and must be considered at board level against the prudential conditions laid down by RBI. The document also contains **eligibility criteria** that an RRB must satisfy before any dividend can be declared; although the provided text does not reproduce those criteria in full, the directions clearly indicate that dividend payment is contingent on compliance with RBI-prescribed prudential standards. In addition, the directions identify **profits that are ineligible for dividend payment**, which means not all reported earnings may be used for distribution even if the bank is otherwise profitable.

The framework also introduces a **reporting system**, implying that an RRB must submit prescribed information or returns before or in connection with dividend declaration, so RBI can verify compliance with the eligibility conditions. There is an explicit **restriction on payment of dividend**, indicating that if the required conditions are not met, the bank is prohibited from distributing dividend. The directions further provide for **penal consequences for non-compliance**, signaling that breach of these norms can attract regulatory action beyond simply disallowing the dividend.

Finally, the document includes a **repeal and saving** clause, so earlier provisions on the same subject are replaced to the extent inconsistent with the new directions, while any actions taken under the old framework are preserved as specified by the saving provision. It also states that **other applicable laws are not barred**, meaning compliance with these RBI directions does not remove obligations under company law, banking law, tax law, or any other applicable statute. For compliance purposes, the practical takeaway is that an RRB should treat dividend declaration as a controlled regulatory event, confirm it meets RBI’s prudential eligibility tests, ensure board-level approval, verify that the profits proposed for distribution are eligible, complete any required reporting, and avoid any dividend payment unless all conditions are satisfied.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Miscellaneous) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Regional Rural Banks (Miscellaneous) Directions, 2025** (issued **28 November 2025**) consolidate and formalize governance, depositor-protection, and reporting requirements for **Regional Rural Banks (RRBs)**. The document applies to RRBs and requires them to align internal policies and board oversight with RBI-prescribed rules, with specific provisions focused on the **Depositor Education and Awareness Fund (DEAF)**, including how eligible unclaimed balances are transferred, how claims are handled, and what disclosures and returns must be made. The directions are organized into chapters on applicability, board responsibilities, DEAF treatment, procedural requirements, and reporting/disclosure obligations, indicating that compliance is not optional or informal but must be embedded into board-approved policy and operational practice.

A key compliance requirement is that each RRB must maintain **board-approved policies** governing the covered matters and the board must conduct **reviews** of those policies and processes, making senior governance accountable for implementation rather than leaving it solely to operations. The DEAF chapter sets out the bank’s obligations for **credits to the fund**, **refunds and interest**, and **registration/claim procedures** for customers seeking return of amounts transferred to the fund. It also prescribes **procedural guidelines for transfer and claim**, meaning RRBs must have a documented workflow for identifying eligible balances, transferring them, processing claims, and ensuring amounts are repaid in accordance with RBI rules.

The directions also require **returns** to be submitted and **disclosure in the notes to accounts**, so compliance teams should expect reporting obligations both to the RBI and through financial statement disclosures. Although the excerpt provided does not include the detailed thresholds, timelines, or rate calculations, the structure indicates that the directions are intended to standardize when balances must be moved to DEAF, how interest/refund treatment is to be handled, and what public and regulatory reporting must accompany those activities. For compliance purposes, the practical impact is that RRBs need to confirm their policies, customer claim-handling process, accounting treatment, and statutory reporting are all updated to match the 2025 directions once the operative provisions and commencement dates in the full text are applied.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 1, 2026)
rows.summary:
This Reserve Bank of India direction is a consolidated set of conduct, service, deposit, payment, inclusion, and lending requirements for **regional rural banks (RRBs)**, issued as the **Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025**, with the text updated as of **July 1, 2026**. It replaces and organizes requirements across multiple subject areas into one framework covering branch customer service, customer protection and guidance, financial inclusion and accessibility, payment/remittance services, deposit and liability accounts, and responsible lending conduct. The document’s structure indicates that compliance obligations are not limited to a single policy area; they extend across day-to-day branch operations, product governance, account handling, customer communication, complaints, claims/settlement processes, and lending practices.

For a compliance team, the key point is that the RBI is imposing a **comprehensive conduct standard** on RRBs rather than only prudential rules. The directions require banks to maintain an institutional framework for implementation and oversight, deliver defined service standards in branches, and provide customer guidance and protection measures. They also create obligations around inclusion and accessibility—meaning RRBs must ensure their products and services are usable by intended customer segments, including those requiring special accessibility support—and around payment and remittance services, which suggests operational requirements for transaction processing and customer-facing service delivery. Because the document also contains a chapter on “deposit accounts and other liabilities,” compliance will need to review account-opening, account-operation, nomination/survivorship handling, claim settlement, and related documentation, including the referenced annexed forms and procedures.

The directions also cover **responsible lending conduct**, which means lending policies, underwriting, disclosures, communications with borrowers, and servicing/collection practices must align with the RBI’s conduct expectations. The presence of an annex titled **“Rates at a Quick Glance”** indicates that certain charges, rates, or standard pricing references are likely prescribed or summarized in the instrument and should be checked for any numeric limits or standardized rates that apply to deposits, lending, or service charges. Similarly, the annexes on **comprehensive notice period**, **inventory forms**, and **settlement of claims** indicate that the bank must follow specified notice and documentation procedures, not just internal discretion, when handling customer communications, branch inventories, and claim processing.

The document is relevant to **all regional rural banks** and any internal units that manage branch operations, customer service, deposit operations, payments, lending, complaints, accessibility, or legal/regulatory compliance. Because the document is marked **“Updated as on July 1, 2026,”** the compliance team should treat that date as the operative consolidated version and verify whether any provisions became effective earlier or were amended through that update. A full implementation review should focus on mapping every chapter’s requirements to internal policies, SOPs, branch processes, product terms, customer communication templates, claims forms, and lending controls, with special attention to any specific deadlines, notice periods, service standards, thresholds, or rates contained in the chapters and annexes.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on September 18, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s “Regional Rural Banks – Know Your Customer Directions, 2025” (DOR/2025-26/266, DOR.AML.REC.No.185/14.01.004/2025-26, dated November 28, 2025 and updated as of December 29, 2025) consolidates and updates the KYC/AML obligations that apply to Regional Rural Banks (RRBs). It takes effect from the stated commencement date in the directions and is organized to govern governance, customer acceptance, risk management, customer identification, and customer due diligence, with separate requirements for individuals, sole proprietorships, legal entities, and beneficial ownership identification. For a compliance team, the key point is that these directions are not merely policy guidance: they impose mandatory procedures for onboarding, ongoing monitoring, and periodic updating of customer information, with the bank’s board and senior management responsible for ensuring implementation through approved policies and internal controls.

At the governance level, the directions require the RRB’s board of directors to approve a formal KYC/AML policy framework and to ensure it is aligned with RBI requirements. The bank must maintain a customer acceptance policy that defines which customers can be onboarded, how exceptions are handled, and how enhanced scrutiny is applied where risk is higher. A risk-based approach is required throughout, meaning customers must be categorized by risk level and subjected to corresponding due diligence intensity, monitoring frequency, and periodic review; the document also expects the bank to use internal risk management systems and controls to detect suspicious or unusual activity.

The customer identification procedure and CDD chapter require the bank to establish the identity of every customer before opening an account or entering into a relationship, and to identify and verify the beneficial owner where the customer is a non-individual. The directions distinguish between individuals, sole proprietorship firms, and legal entities, requiring different evidence and verification methods appropriate to the customer type. The bank must collect prescribed KYC information, verify it through acceptable documents or electronic means permitted by RBI, and ensure that the relationship is not established if identity cannot be satisfactorily verified or if the customer is unwilling to provide the required information.

The document also requires ongoing due diligence after account opening, including monitoring transactions against the customer’s declared profile and expected activity, and updating KYC records periodically based on risk classification. Where higher risk is identified, the bank must apply enhanced due diligence rather than routine onboarding checks, and it must be prepared to refuse, freeze, or discontinue a relationship where compliance requirements are not met or where suspicious indicators arise. The updated directions also imply specific operational obligations around recordkeeping, employee training, internal accountability, and escalation/reporting of suspicious transactions in line with India’s AML framework, so compliance officers should ensure that branch processes, digital onboarding workflows, and periodic KYC refresh cycles are all mapped to the new RBI-issued directions.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Financial Statements: Presentation and Disclosures) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on April 1, 2026)
rows.summary:
This RBI direction, issued on November 28, 2025 and updated as of April 1, 2026, governs how Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) must prepare and disclose their financial statements. It replaces or consolidates the RBI’s prescribed presentation/disclosure framework for RRBs by setting mandatory formats for the Balance Sheet and Profit and Loss Account, along with detailed notes, instructions for compilation, and guidance on specific accounting-standard issues. It applies to Regional Rural Banks covered by RBI supervision, so compliance teams at affected RRBs should treat this as the controlling statement-format and disclosure rulebook for financial reporting.

The document is organized into four chapters: preliminary provisions, the required balance sheet and P&L presentation, disclosure requirements in notes to accounts, and other operational instructions. Chapter II requires RRBs to use the RBI-prescribed formats for the Balance Sheet and Profit and Loss Account and follow the accompanying compilation instructions; it also provides guidance on how to apply certain Accounting Standards in the RRB context. Chapter III sets the mandatory notes-to-accounts presentation and disclosure framework, including general presentation rules and specific disclosures that must appear in the financial statements.

Chapter IV adds separate compliance instructions on several accounting and provisioning topics that affect year-end close and audit readiness. It specifically covers provisioning for net debit balances in inter-branch accounts, reconciliation of Nostro accounts and treatment of outstanding entries, transfers to or appropriations from reserve funds, and provisioning for fraud. For compliance purposes, these areas require banks to have reconciled balances, documented treatment of unreconciled items, and appropriate provisions/transfers recorded in accordance with RBI direction rather than leaving them as purely internal accounting judgments.

Because the title states “Updated as on April 1, 2026,” compliance teams should verify that the version in use reflects all updates effective through that date and that reporting templates, accounting policies, and disclosure checklists have been aligned to the revised RBI directions before financial statements are finalized. The document excerpt provided does not include the detailed thresholds, percentages, or line-item disclosure text, so the key compliance takeaway is the mandatory adoption of RBI’s prescribed formats and disclosures for RRB statutory financial statements, together with the specified special treatments for inter-branch balances, Nostro reconciling items, reserve transfers, and fraud provisioning.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Treatment of Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Treatment of Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters) Directions, 2025** on **November 28, 2025** under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 and the Credit Information Companies (Regulation) Act, 2005. The stated purpose is to create a **non-discriminatory, transparent, natural-justice-based process** for classifying borrowers as wilful defaulters and to ensure that information on such defaulters is shared so that **further institutional finance is not extended to them**. These Directions are specifically aimed at **regional rural banks (RRBs)** and replace the prior framework on the same subject.

For compliance purposes, the key requirement is that RRBs must follow a formal process before classifying any borrower as a **wilful defaulter**, with the process designed to ensure fairness, notice, and an opportunity to be heard. The document also introduces obligations to identify and report **large defaulters** in a prescribed format, alongside separate reporting for wilful default cases, so compliance teams should expect new or updated internal controls around borrower classification, documentation, escalation, and credit-information reporting. The Directions place emphasis on **board-level responsibility**, meaning the bank’s board must oversee the framework and related policies rather than leaving classification decisions purely to business units.

The document further requires **preventive measures** and assigns a role to **auditors**, indicating that compliance is not limited to post-default classification but also includes controls intended to detect or prevent wilful default and ensure proper audit scrutiny of relevant cases. It contains separate chapters on the **treatment of wilful defaulters**, **reporting of wilful defaulters and large defaulters**, and **repeal and other provisions**, which means institutions must align existing policies and reporting templates to the new RBI-prescribed structure and transition away from any superseded directions. The annexures provide the required **submission formats** for the list of large defaulters and the data on wilful default cases, so operational teams will need to use those exact formats when reporting to the RBI or other relevant channels.

Because the excerpt provided stops at the opening of Chapter I, the specific commencement date, thresholds for “large defaulter,” procedural timelines, and detailed reporting deadlines are not visible in the text shown here. However, even from the introductory material, the compliance impact is clear: RRBs should treat this as a formal RBI directive requiring a documented internal process, board oversight, audit involvement, and structured reporting for borrower default classification and dissemination of defaulter information.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Resolution of Stressed Assets) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on October 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s “Regional Rural Banks – Resolution of Stressed Assets” Directions, 2025, as updated through July 1, 2026, set out the framework Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) must follow for identifying, reporting, disclosing, and resolving stressed assets, including restructuring, compromise settlements, technical write-offs, and special treatment for accounts affected by natural calamities. The document applies to RRBs and establishes mandatory board-approved policies, so compliance teams should ensure the bank has an updated policy framework covering early stress recognition, resolution options, prudential treatment, and reporting/disclosure obligations. The directions are organized to require early identification and reporting of stress, formal disclosures, and prudential norms for restructuring, with separate rules for special cases such as compromise settlements and technical write-offs, plus a dedicated chapter for accounts impacted by natural calamities.

For restructuring, the directions prescribe general instructions that must be followed when an account is to be restructured, and these prudential requirements govern how such accounts are to be classified and treated for regulatory purposes. The document also creates a specific process for natural calamity-affected accounts, involving the State Level Bankers’ Committee (SLBC), Union Territory Level Bankers’ Committee (UTLBC), and District Consultative Committee (DCC), indicating that resolution in such cases is coordinated through those local banking committees rather than handled solely at the branch level. Because the table of contents shows a distinct chapter for compromise settlements and technical write-offs, compliance teams should expect mandatory internal procedures for approving such actions and for ensuring proper accounting and regulatory recognition.

The title page and update note indicate the directions were issued on November 28, 2025 and are consolidated as updated on July 1, 2026, so that date should be treated as the current operative version for compliance purposes unless superseded later. The document’s structure suggests that the key obligations are not limited to one-time remediation; they include ongoing governance, timely identification of stress, and periodic disclosures to the RBI and/or in financial statements as required by the relevant chapters. Since the content excerpt provided does not include the full operative text of each chapter, a compliance officer should review the full directions for the exact timelines, reporting formats, approval authorities, asset-classification consequences, and any quantitative thresholds or exceptions that may apply to specific restructuring or settlement actions.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on October 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
This RBI direction sets the income recognition, asset classification, and provisioning framework for **regional rural banks (RRBs)**, and it is issued as **DOR/2025-26/262** under **DOR.STR.REC.181/21.04.048/2025-26** dated **November 28, 2025**, with the text updated as of **July 1, 2026**. For a compliance team, the key point is that this is a consolidated prudential framework governing when RRBs may recognize income, how they must classify exposures and NPAs, what disclosures they must make, how security must be valued, how upgrades from NPA status are handled, and how IRAC processes are to be automated. The document is organized into chapters on preliminary matters, general instructions and disclosure requirements, asset classification, and provisioning norms, indicating that it is meant to be the operative supervisory rulebook rather than guidance only.

The applicability is to **regional rural banks**, and the directions appear designed to replace or update prior IRAC-related instructions by imposing a uniform classification/provisioning regime. The asset-classification chapter specifically covers the core classification norms, special treatment for particular cases of classification, valuation of security, the categories of non-performing assets, and the conditions for upgrading loan accounts once they have been classified as NPAs. It also contains a dedicated section on **automation of income recognition, asset classification, and provisioning processes**, which signals that banks must have systems capable of applying the rules consistently and electronically rather than relying only on manual review.

The general-instructions and disclosure chapters mean RRBs are expected not only to apply the prudential rules internally but also to make the required external disclosures in their financial reporting. The provisioning chapter indicates that the directions prescribe mandatory provisioning requirements tied to asset classification outcomes, so compliance teams should expect the rules to affect balance-sheet provisioning, capital planning, and loan monitoring workflows. Because the table of contents lists separate treatment for **specific cases**, **NPAs**, and **upgradation**, the document likely contains detailed trigger-based requirements that must be applied loan-by-loan and not merely at portfolio level.

From a compliance perspective, the operational impact is that RRBs should ensure their loan systems can: identify when income recognition must stop, classify assets in line with RBI’s prescribed norms, value security according to the stated rules, determine NPA categories correctly, apply the upgrade criteria only when permitted, and generate the mandated disclosures. The effective framework date is the issuance date (**November 28, 2025**), while the version cited is the **updated text as of July 1, 2026**; any compliance review should therefore confirm whether the bank is working from the updated consolidated version rather than the original issuance alone. Since the provided excerpt contains only the heading structure and not the substantive clause text, the exact thresholds, day-count triggers, provisioning percentages, or special carve-outs are not visible here and would need the full body of the directions to summarize precisely.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Asset Liability Management) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Regional Rural Banks – Asset Liability Management Directions, 2025** (issued **November 28, 2025** as **DOR/2025-26/261**, **DOR.LRG.REC.No.180/13-10-008/2025-26**) set out the RBI’s framework for how **regional rural banks (RRBs)** must govern, measure, monitor, and control **asset-liability management (ALM)** and **liquidity risk**. The document is structured as binding directions covering: when it takes effect, which institutions it applies to, how boards must oversee ALM, how ALM systems and organization must be designed, and how liquidity risk must be tracked through maturity-ladder monitoring.

A compliance team should note that these directions are intended to impose a formal **board-level governance framework** over ALM, rather than leaving it as a purely treasury function. The board is expected to approve the bank’s ALM-related policies, set and review risk limits, and oversee periodic review of ALM positions and liquidity risk management practices. The directions also require a dedicated ALM information system and organizational structure, implying that RRBs must have reliable internal data, reporting lines, and processes for analyzing maturity mismatches and liquidity needs.

The document specifically addresses **liquidity risk management** and introduces **maturity ladder-based monitoring** as the core mechanism for tracking cash inflows and outflows across time buckets. That means RRBs must maintain a structured view of their funding profile and asset maturities, identify mismatches, and ensure management action is taken where short-term liabilities exceed available liquid resources or where future cash outflows could exceed inflows. The substance of the directions indicates that compliance is not limited to reporting; banks must establish operational processes, controls, and escalation mechanisms to actively manage liquidity stress.

From the content provided, the directions clearly cover: **Chapter I** (preliminary matters such as short title, commencement, applicability, and definitions), **Chapter II** (board responsibilities and approval/review obligations), **Chapter III** (ALM governance, including information systems, organization, and process), and **Chapter IV** (liquidity risk management and maturity-ladder monitoring). However, the excerpt does **not** include the detailed operative clauses, so the exact commencement date, any quantitative thresholds, time-bucket requirements, reporting frequencies, or specific limits are not visible in the provided text. For compliance purposes, the key takeaway from the available material is that **all RRBs subject to these directions must have a formal, board-approved ALM and liquidity risk framework in place and must use maturity-ladder monitoring to control funding mismatches under RBI supervision**.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Classification, Valuation and Operation of Investment Portfolio) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on May 18, 2026)
rows.summary:
The RBI’s **“Regional Rural Banks – Classification, Valuation and Operation of Investment Portfolio) Directions, 2025”** apply to **all Regional Rural Banks (RRBs)** and lay out a comprehensive framework for how RRBs must set policy, classify securities, value them, transfer them between buckets, and report/operate their investment books. The directions are effective from **November 28, 2025** (with the document shown as updated through **May 18, 2026**), and they replace/standardize the investment-portfolio treatment for RRBs under RBI supervision.

At the governance level, the **Board of the RRB** is made responsible for approving and overseeing an investment policy that covers the bank’s overall investment objectives, risk appetite, prudential limits, internal controls, valuation approach, and delegation of operational authority. The policy must be robust enough to govern the entire investment portfolio and is not just a back-office treasury document; the Board is expected to ensure proper oversight, including regular review of compliance, limits, and exceptions. The directions also require a clear operational role for the **Sponsor Bank**, which must provide support and guidance as prescribed by the RBI, particularly where the RRB lacks infrastructure or expertise.

For **classification**, the directions require RRBs to categorize investments into the standard RBI buckets: **Held to Maturity (HTM)**, **Held for Trading (HFT)**, and **Available for Sale (AFS)**. The rules specify when an instrument can be held in each category and restrict arbitrary switching, so the initial intent and ongoing management of each security matter for accounting and prudential treatment. RRBs must follow the RBI’s instructions on **shifting securities between HTM, HFT, and AFS**, including the conditions under which transfers are permitted and the documentation/approval expectations for such moves.

On **valuation**, the directions require investment securities to be marked and carried according to their category, with valuation norms aligned to the RBI framework for market-linked instruments. The document covers the treatment of **depreciation and appreciation**, the recognition of valuation changes, and the operational procedures for periodic revaluation. Compliance teams should note that the classification bucket chosen directly affects valuation and profit-and-loss recognition, so controls around booking, reclassification, and period-end marking are material compliance points.

The directions also include instructions on the **operation of the investment portfolio**, meaning RRBs must ensure investments are acquired, held, transferred, and reported through controlled processes with proper authority, documentation, and internal checks. Where the document specifies special treatment or exceptions—such as transfers into or out of HTM, or investment actions requiring Board approval—those rules are mandatory and should be reflected in treasury SOPs, internal accounting policies, and management reporting. Overall, the compliance burden is to ensure the RRB’s investment book is managed under an RBI-consistent framework with Board-approved policy, accurate classification, proper valuation, and tightly controlled transfers and operations.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Interest Rates on Advances) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Regional Rural Banks (Interest Rates on Advances) Directions, 2025** apply specifically to **Regional Rural Banks (RRBs)** and take effect **immediately upon issuance** on **November 28, 2025**. The directions are issued under the RBI’s powers under **Sections 21 and 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, and they set the governing framework for how RRBs may charge interest on advances.

The document defines **“microfinance loan”** by reference to the definition in the RBI’s **Regional Rural Banks – Credit Facilities – Directions, 2025**, and defines **“rests”** as the periodicity with which interest is charged to borrowers. Any other undefined terms take their meanings from the **Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, the **Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934**, or their ordinary commercial meaning. From the excerpt provided, the substantive operative content shown is the issuance of a general interest-rate framework chapter, but the detailed rate-setting rules are not included in the text supplied.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that **RRBs must align their advance-interest policies and charging practices with these new RBI directions as of the effective date**, rather than waiting for any future implementation window. Because the directions are mandatory RBI directions, affected institutions should treat them as a binding regulatory requirement for all applicable lending/advance products, including any products that meet the definition of microfinance loan under the linked RBI credit-facilities directions.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Transfer and Distribution of Credit Risk) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Transfer and Distribution of Credit Risk) Directions, 2025** on **November 28, 2025**, creating a **comprehensive, self-contained framework** for how **Regional Rural Banks (RRBs)** may transfer or distribute credit risk. The stated purpose is to govern credit-risk transfer and distribution mechanisms used for **liquidity management, rebalancing exposures, strategic sales, and related lending arrangements**, replacing or consolidating prior RBI guidance in this area. The document is issued under the RBI’s powers under **sections 21 and 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**.
