The excerpt provided does not yet include the substantive rate-setting clauses, but it establishes that the directions are binding on all affected UCBs from the date of issue and that they are meant to govern the interest-rate framework for loans/advances, including the treatment of interest “rests.” The document also signals that these directions are part of a broader 2025 RBI overhaul for UCB credit regulation, so compliance teams should align this instrument with the linked **Credit Facilities Directions, 2025** when reviewing loan pricing, interest computation, and borrower disclosures.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Transfer and Distribution of Credit Risk) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has issued a new consolidated framework for urban co-operative banks on **transfer and distribution of credit risk**, titled **“Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Transfer and Distribution of Credit Risk) Directions, 2025”** (issued **November 28, 2025**). The document is intended to replace and unify earlier RBI guidance covering **loan transfers, stressed-loan transfers, consortium lending, multiple banking arrangements, and other credit-risk transfer arrangements**, creating a self-contained regulatory regime for urban co-operative banks (UCBs). From a compliance perspective, the key change is not a single isolated rule but the creation of an overarching framework governing how UCBs may sell, transfer, participate in, or otherwise redistribute loan exposures and associated credit risk.

The directions are structured in three substantive parts: **Part A covers transfer of loan exposures**, including both general rules for all loan transfers and specific rules for **transfer of stressed loans**; **Part B covers other lending and risk-transfer arrangements**, specifically **lending under consortium and multiple banking arrangements**; and **Part C addresses repeal and related transitional provisions**. This means compliance teams should expect the directions to apply across the full lifecycle of loan exposure management, not just to sale transactions. The document signals that RBI is formalizing and tightening the regulatory treatment of credit-risk transfer activity by UCBs, so institutions engaged in loan sales, participation arrangements, syndications, or similar exposure-sharing structures will need to align internal policies, approval processes, documentation, reporting, and portfolio controls to the new framework.

The table of contents shows that the rules are organized into: **Chapter I – Preliminary**, followed by **Part A – Transfer of Loan Exposures** with separate chapters for **Scope and Definitions**, **General Conditions applicable for all loan transfers**, and **Transfer of stressed loans**; then **Part B – Other Types of Lending and Risk Transfer Arrangements**, consisting of **Lending under Consortium / Multiple Banking Arrangements**; and finally **Part C – Repeal and Other Provisions**. Even from the introductory material alone, the compliance implication is that UCBs must assess whether any of their lending or credit-risk sharing practices fall within the new definitions and conditions, because the framework is designed to govern “different avenues of credit risk transfer and distribution.” Where a bank uses loan transfer as a liquidity-management tool, to rebalance exposures, or to make strategic sales, those activities are now expressly within the RBI’s consolidated supervisory framework.

Because the excerpt provided does not include the detailed operative clauses, specific thresholds, procedural steps, or transitional deadlines from the chapters and annexes, the safest compliance takeaway is that this is a **new RBI directions circular dated November 28, 2025** that likely **supersedes prior fragmented guidance** and requires UCBs to review all existing loan-transfer, stressed-loan transfer, consortium, and multiple-banking arrangements for conformity with the new directions. A compliance officer should treat this as a prompt to update internal policies, transaction approvals, legal documentation, and monitoring controls for any credit-risk transfer activity, and to verify the repeal/transitional section for any grandfathering, effective-date, or reporting obligations once the full text is reviewed.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks - Concentration Risk Management) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on October 1, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has issued the **“Urban Co-operative Banks (Concentration Risk Management) Directions, 2025”** on **November 28, 2025** to consolidate and update prudential rules meant to reduce concentration risk in Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs). The document explains that RBI has long regulated UCB exposures because excessive lending to a single borrower or connected group can create asset-side concentration risk; these rules were originally introduced in **May 1994** using demand and time liabilities (DTL), then revised in **January 1996** to use **Capital Funds** as the reference base. The new Directions bring together the existing exposure limits on **individual borrowers**, **groups of interconnected borrowers**, **unsecured advances**, **inter-bank exposures**, and **small-value loans** into one consolidated framework.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that the Directions apply specifically to **Urban Co-operative Banks** and are issued under RBI’s powers under the **Banking Regulation Act, 1949** (including **Sections 21 and 35A read with Section 56**). The document signals that UCBs must continue to operate within prudential exposure limits designed to keep their loan book granular and prevent outsized exposure to very large borrowers. Although the excerpt provided does not yet state the detailed numerical caps, implementation mechanics, or reporting formats, it confirms that the new Directions are intended to govern how UCBs measure and manage concentration risk across all of the above exposure categories.

Because this is a consolidated directions circular, a compliance team should treat it as a potentially comprehensive replacement or restatement of prior RBI instructions on UCB exposure concentration, and should verify the full operative chapters for any revised definitions, limits, exceptions, and transitional provisions. The document’s structure indicates three parts: **Chapter I – Preliminary**, **Chapter II – Exposure Norms**, and **Chapter III – Repeal and other provisions**, which suggests that the final chapter likely identifies prior instruments being repealed or superseded and any savings/transitional treatment. Based on the excerpt, the immediate compliance takeaway is that UCBs remain subject to RBI prudential exposure controls, and any internal lending, risk, or treasury policies should be checked against the finalized norms in the complete text.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Credit Risk Management) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
This Reserve Bank of India direction, issued on 28 November 2025 and updated as on 1 July 2026, sets out the credit risk management framework for Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs). It replaces and consolidates prior RBI instructions on credit exposure, credit administration, borrower identification, security-interest filing, account conduct, and related lending controls for UCBs. The document is structured into board-approved policies, credit risk evaluation, statutory and regulatory restrictions, loan administration, LEI requirements, property valuation, CERSAI filing, cash credit/current/overdraft account maintenance, and the loan system for bank credit.

The core compliance message is that UCBs must manage credit risk through formal board-approved policies and operational controls that govern how loans are originated, evaluated, documented, monitored, secured, and recovered. The directions impose specific obligations on the bank’s board and management to define credit policies, delegate powers, ensure proper appraisal of borrower creditworthiness, and maintain adequate documentation and security creation processes. Where the document refers to statutory or regulatory restrictions, UCBs must observe RBI-prescribed limits and prohibitions on lending concentration, connected lending, exposure norms, and other restrictions that apply to specific borrower categories or credit products.

The directions also require stronger borrower and security identification and tracking mechanisms. UCBs must require Legal Entity Identifiers (LEIs) for specified borrowers/exposures as prescribed, use approved valuation practices and empanelled valuers for property collateral, and file security interests in CERSAI for immovable assets (other than equitable mortgages), movable assets, and intangible assets where applicable. These filings are not optional administrative steps; they are part of the bank’s enforceable credit administration and security perfection obligations.

In addition, the document covers operating discipline for working-capital and overdraft lending, including maintenance of cash credit, current, and overdraft accounts by banks, and the “loan system” for delivery of bank credit. UCBs must comply with RBI’s requirements on how credit is disbursed and monitored, which may include segregation or structuring of working-capital limits, periodic review, and account conduct requirements designed to prevent misuse or diversion of funds. The updated directions therefore create a comprehensive compliance framework affecting virtually all lending activities of UCBs, and the operative date to follow for the consolidated directions is the updated version as of 1 July 2026, subject to any specific chapter-level timelines or exceptions contained in the full text.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Credit Information Reporting) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Urban Co-operative Banks – Credit Information Reporting” Directions, 2025** (issued **November 28, 2025**, and shown as **updated through July 01, 2026**) impose a formal framework for how **urban co-operative banks (UCBs)** participate in the credit information ecosystem and report borrower data to credit information companies (CICs). The directions cover UCBs’ membership obligations with CICs, the data formats and reporting timelines they must follow, how reported data must be updated and corrected, and how credit information is to be used in credit appraisal and displayed in bank systems or customer-facing processes. They are intended to ensure that UCBs submit complete, timely, and accurate credit data and then promptly fix rejected or incorrect records when problems are identified.

For compliance purposes, the most important point is that the document creates **mandatory credit information reporting and maintenance obligations** for the affected institutions, rather than leaving reporting practices to internal discretion. UCBs are expected to adhere to RBI-prescribed reporting standards, including the specified data structures/formats, regular updation cycles, and any reporting rules on borrower records, account statuses, and other credit-related data fields that must be shared with CICs. The directions also establish a process for handling **rejected data**, requiring UCBs to rectify and resubmit such records, and they introduce oversight around the **Data Quality Index (DQI)** so that banks must review the quality of their reporting and address deficiencies where data quality is weak.

The directions also address the downstream use of credit bureau information in lending. UCBs must use credit information reports in **credit appraisal**, meaning lending decisions and underwriting processes are expected to incorporate CIC data rather than relying solely on internal records. In addition, there are instructions on the **display of information**, which means banks may need to ensure that relevant credit-information-related details are made available in the prescribed manner within their systems or to customers, consistent with RBI requirements. The document further states that other instructions issued by the Department of Regulation remain applicable where relevant, so this framework operates alongside existing RBI directions rather than replacing them wholesale.

Because the excerpt provided is only the heading, table of contents, and document metadata, it does **not** disclose the specific numeric deadlines, thresholds, form identifiers, submission frequencies, or exact technical file specifications; those details would need to be reviewed in the substantive chapters. For a compliance team, the immediate takeaway is that any UCB within scope must verify its CIC membership status, confirm its reporting processes against the RBI-prescribed formats and timelines, ensure a procedure for rejected-data remediation and DQI monitoring, and make sure credit bureau information is embedded in lending and disclosure workflows by the effective date of the operative provisions in the full directions.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Credit Cards and Debit Cards: Issuance and Conduct) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Credit Cards and Debit Cards: Issuance and Conduct) Directions, 2025** on **November 28, 2025**, and they take **immediate effect**. They apply to **all Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs)**, whether referred to individually as a bank/UCB or collectively as banks/UCBs. The directions are issued under **Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, read with **Section 56** and other enabling provisions, and replace prior RBI instructions on these topics under the repeal and savings framework set out in Chapter VIII.

At a high level, the document consolidates and governs how UCBs may **issue, manage, and conduct credit card and debit card businesses**, including the conditions for issuance, customer conduct, and operational controls. It also addresses **debit card issuance**, **form factor requirements**, **co-branding arrangements**, and broader **general compliance rules** applicable to both credit and debit cards. For compliance teams, the key takeaway is that these directions create a single binding framework for card lifecycle management by UCBs, rather than leaving such matters to ad hoc internal policy.

Because the excerpt provided stops at the beginning of the applicability section, it does not include the detailed operational rules, thresholds, prohibitions, customer disclosures, reporting obligations, or timelines that appear in later chapters. However, the document structure shows that the RBI intends the directions to cover: credit card business conduct, debit card issuance, acceptable card form factors, permissible co-branding, and general standards for both card types, followed by miscellaneous and repeal provisions. A compliance team should therefore treat this as a **new mandatory RBI framework effective immediately** and review the full text of all chapters to identify any required changes to product approvals, issuance controls, outsourcing/co-branding arrangements, customer onboarding disclosures, and internal governance procedures.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on October 1, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs) – Credit Facilities Directions, 2025** (dated **November 28, 2025** and shown as **updated through July 15, 2026**) consolidates RBI requirements governing how UCBs may extend credit, with emphasis on board-approved lending policy, digital lending controls, and lending against **gold and silver collateral**. For a compliance team, the key takeaway is that these are **mandatory prudential and conduct requirements** for covered urban co-operative banks, and they impose ongoing governance, customer-protection, technology, reporting, and collateral-management obligations rather than optional guidance.

The document begins by defining its scope, commencement, and applicability, then requires the **Board** to approve and oversee lending-related policies. In practical terms, this means the bank’s board must formally set the institution’s approach to credit facilities and ensure that lending practices align with RBI requirements; compliance should expect board-level accountability rather than reliance on management discretion alone. The direction’s structure indicates that the rules are intended to govern both traditional lending and newer credit channels, especially where third parties or digital interfaces are involved.

A major component is **Chapter III on Digital Lending**, which imposes requirements on **bank–LSP arrangements** (where “LSP” refers to lending service providers), customer conduct protections, technology and data controls, reporting of credit information and digital lending apps, and default-related loss-sharing arrangements. The document specifically requires banks engaged in digital lending to maintain controls over how lending is originated and serviced through digital platforms, and to ensure that customer protection, data handling, and reporting processes are compliant. For compliance purposes, this means the bank must review all outsourced or partner-led digital lending models to confirm that responsibilities, disclosures, data access, reporting, and default-risk allocation are documented and operationalized in line with RBI standards.

The directions also include **technology and data requirements**, which signals that banks must have governance over data use, data security, and system controls in digital lending operations. In addition, there is a specific section on **reporting credit information and Digital Lending Apps (DLAs)**, so the bank must ensure the timely and accurate submission of required credit data and that any apps used in lending are handled according to RBI’s reporting and oversight expectations. The presence of a separate section on **loss sharing in case of default** means banks using third-party digital lending structures must have clear contractual allocation of default losses and related responsibilities, which should be reviewed carefully for regulatory alignment and consumer-risk implications.

Chapter IV addresses **lending against gold and silver collateral**, which is a significant area for UCBs. The title indicates that the directions contain both **general provisions** and **restrictions and ceilings**, meaning banks that offer gold- or silver-backed loans must comply with RBI’s limits on such lending and any operational controls governing valuation, lending amount, and collateral management. Because the table of contents specifically flags “Restrictions and Ceilings,” compliance should assume there are quantitative or procedural constraints that must be monitored closely, even where the excerpt does not reproduce the exact figures.

For a compliance officer, the practical action items are to verify that: the board-approved credit policy has been updated to reflect the 2025 directions; all digital lending partnerships, app-based lending processes, and credit reporting workflows comply with RBI’s conduct, technology, and loss-sharing requirements; and the bank’s gold/silver loan products are checked against the applicable restriction and ceiling provisions in Chapter IV. The document’s **effective regime is anchored in the 2025 issuance, with updates through July 15, 2026**, so the compliance program should be assessed against the latest consolidated version rather than the original text alone.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Interest Rate on Deposits) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on October 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
This RBI direction sets the interest-rate framework for **urban co-operative banks (UCBs)** on **domestic rupee deposits** and related deposit-account practices, and it applies to the entities and activities covered under the document’s applicability section (i.e., UCB deposit-taking operations in India). The core compliance message is that UCBs must determine deposit interest rates in line with RBI’s prescribed framework rather than ad hoc or discriminatory pricing, and they must apply the specific rules for current accounts, savings deposits, term deposits, additional interest, overdue deposits, floating-rate term deposits, deceased depositor accounts, and premature withdrawals.

For **domestic savings deposits**, the direction requires a defined interest-rate method and periodic crediting of interest (the document’s chapter headings indicate that the periodicity requirement is separately addressed). For **domestic term deposits**, UCBs must follow RBI’s rules on the rate-setting framework, payment of interest, and treatment of premature withdrawal, including any penalty structure allowed by the directions. The document also specifically addresses **additional interest** on domestic deposits, meaning banks may need to identify depositors or circumstances that qualify for extra interest and ensure the correct calculation and crediting of such amounts.

The directions also require banks to handle **overdue term deposits** and **floating-rate domestic term deposits** under RBI-prescribed rules, which affects both operational systems and customer communications when deposits mature, are renewed, or reprice. In addition, banks must apply the RBI’s rules for interest payable on the **deposit account of a deceased depositor**, which typically governs how interest is calculated up to the date of settlement and the handling of balances pending transmission to legal heirs/nominees.

The document is dated **November 28, 2025** and is shown as **updated through August 25, 2026**; however, the text provided does not include the operative paragraphs, so exact rate caps, thresholds, calculation formulas, or implementation deadlines cannot be extracted from the excerpt alone. A compliance team should therefore treat this as the controlling framework for UCB deposit interest administration and verify the full operative chapters for the precise numerical rates, exceptions, and effective-date mechanics before updating product terms, core banking systems, and customer-facing disclosures.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks - Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on June 16, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs) – Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy Directions, 2025** (updated through **June 16, 2026**) set out the capital adequacy framework that applies to urban co-operative banks, including how they must define regulatory capital, calculate risk-weighted assets, and meet minimum capital standards. The directions are issued under RBI’s prudential powers and are effective from the date specified in the instrument (**November 28, 2025**, subject to any chapter-wise implementation dates that may appear in the full text). For compliance purposes, the key point is that UCBs must determine their capital position under RBI’s prescribed definitions of **net worth, statutory capital requirements, minimum regulatory capital, and the composition of Tier 1 and Tier 2 capital**, rather than relying on local accounting or legacy supervisory approaches.

The document is organized around three substantive compliance areas: **regulatory capital**, **computation of risk-weighted assets (RWA)**, and **other instructions**. Under the capital rules, banks must distinguish between **Tier 1 capital** and **Tier 2 capital** and apply RBI’s eligibility and deduction rules to each; this affects what instruments, reserves, and exposures can be counted for prudential purposes. The directions also specify the capital charge methodology for **credit risk** and **market risk**, meaning UCBs must assign prescribed risk weights to on- and off-balance-sheet exposures and hold capital against market-related positions using RBI’s framework. Compliance officers should therefore expect requirements not only on the amount of capital to be maintained, but also on the exact method used to compute the denominator of the capital ratio through RWA.

Because the table of contents shows dedicated sections on **net worth**, **statutory requirements**, **minimum regulatory capital**, and capital composition, the document is likely intended to align UCB prudential capital with a structured RBI formula rather than a discretionary or purely accounting-based measure. The updated version date (**June 16, 2026**) is important for monitoring whether any amendments, clarifications, or phased-in changes were incorporated after the original issuance. A corporate compliance team should treat this as a primary capital adequacy manual for UCBs: it governs which entities are in scope, how capital is classified, what exposures attract capital charges, and the ongoing obligation to monitor and report capital adequacy in RBI-prescribed form. If you want, I can also turn this into a **controls checklist** or a **“what changed / who must comply / action items”** briefing format for internal use.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Cash Reserve Ratio and Statutory Liquidity Ratio) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on October 09, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Cash Reserve Ratio and Statutory Liquidity Ratio) Directions, 2025**, updated as of **August 25, 2026**, under its powers in the **Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and the **RBI Act, 1934**. This document is specifically directed at **urban co-operative banks (UCBs)** and consolidates RBI requirements on **cash reserve ratio (CRR)**, **statutory liquidity ratio (SLR)**, related computation and reporting procedures, and penalties for non-compliance, while also repealing or superseding prior directions to the extent stated in the final chapter.

The substantive requirements cover how UCBs must maintain reserve balances and approved liquid assets, including the framework for **CRR maintenance**, **SLR maintenance**, and the **procedure for computing SLR**. The document also sets out **reporting obligations** that UCBs must follow to evidence compliance with reserve requirements, as well as the consequences of failure, including **penalty provisions**. Because the directions are issued under the RBI’s statutory authority, they are mandatory for the covered entities and operate as binding compliance instructions rather than guidance.

The table of contents shows that the document is organized into separate chapters for **preliminary matters**, **CRR**, **SLR**, **SLR computation**, **reporting**, **penalties**, and **repeal/other provisions**, with three annexes that likely contain detailed formats, operational instructions, or illustrative material. Based on the text provided, the document is a comprehensive replacement-style regulatory instrument intended to govern how UCBs calculate, maintain, and report statutory reserve requirements, and compliance teams should treat it as the controlling RBI framework for those obligations as of the stated update date.

If you want, I can also produce a **section-by-section compliance memo** once you share the full text beyond the opening pages, including the exact **CRR/SLR percentages, maintenance periods, exemptions, reporting forms, and penalty triggers**.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks - Governance) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on May 25, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs) – Governance Directions, 2025** are a comprehensive governance framework for urban co-operative banks, issued under the RBI’s supervisory powers and **effective from November 28, 2025** as the base instrument, with the version provided noting it is **updated as of May 25, 2026**. The directions apply to **urban co-operative banks**, and the document reorganizes and standardizes requirements around board composition, director responsibilities, periodic board reviews, board committees, a board of management, and the appointment of senior officers. From a compliance perspective, this is not just guidance: it imposes mandatory governance structure, review, and appointment requirements that UCBs must align with going forward.

The document first sets out **how the board must be constituted and how directors are appointed**, indicating that banks must follow RBI-prescribed governance norms rather than ad hoc internal practices. It then defines the **role of the board and of individual directors**, making clear that governance accountability is both collective and personal: the board is expected to oversee strategic direction, control, compliance, and risk, while individual directors carry duties tied to attendance, participation, fitness, and the discharge of fiduciary responsibilities. The directions also include a **calendar of reviews**, meaning UCBs must complete recurring governance/oversight reviews on a scheduled basis rather than only when issues arise; a compliance team should treat these as mandatory recurring control points and ensure the bank has documented tracking, minutes, and follow-up for each required review.

A separate chapter governs **committees of the board**, specifically the **Audit Committee of the Board** and the **Risk Management Committee**. These committees are meant to provide structured oversight of financial reporting, audit findings, internal controls, and risk oversight, so the bank must ensure proper constitution, terms of reference, and functioning of each committee. In addition, the directions introduce a **Board of Management** chapter, indicating that certain UCBs must have an additional management-layer governance body to assist the board in supervising operations and implementing strategy; compliance teams should verify whether their institution falls within the scope of the Board of Management requirements and whether the body has been constituted in the prescribed manner.

The document also contains requirements for the **appointment of key officers**, including the **Chief Executive Officer/Managing Director** and the **Chief Risk Officer**. These provisions are important because they tie senior appointments to formal board/RBI governance expectations rather than purely internal hiring decisions. While the excerpt provided does not state the detailed eligibility criteria or thresholds, the structure makes clear that appointments, roles, reporting lines, and oversight of these officers are regulatory matters that must be documented and aligned with the directions. Finally, Chapter VIII indicates there are **repeal and transitional/other provisions**, which means earlier governance instructions for UCBs may be superseded or harmonized, so compliance teams should check this instrument against prior RBI governance circulars to identify any replaced requirements and transition obligations.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Undertaking of Financial Services) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on October 05, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Undertaking of Financial Services) Directions, 2025** on **November 28, 2025**, with the text noted as **updated through April 27, 2026**. These Directions govern when and how **Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs)** may undertake specified financial services beyond core banking, and they are organized around general governance requirements, investment restrictions, and specific activity-wise permissions. The document is explicitly aimed at UCBs and their boards, and it is intended to control both the approval process and the operational conditions for engaging in these ancillary financial services.

From the portion of the document provided, the Directions require UCBs to follow **general board-level oversight** for such activities and set rules on **investments in Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs)**. The substance of the financial-services chapters shows that UCBs may act as **mutual fund distributors**, serve as **insurance corporate agents without assuming risk**, and act as **insurance referral agents without risk participation**, including where services are provided by **sharing physical space**. The Directions also cover **foreign exchange business**, allow UCBs to offer an **online trading facility to demat account holders**, and permit **Point of Presence (PoP) services under the Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority (PFRDA)** framework. Based on the document structure, these permissions are not blanket authorizations; they are regulated activities subject to RBI conditions, board responsibility, and the specific chapter-by-chapter requirements laid out in the Directions.

Because the excerpt ends at the table of contents, it does not yet show the detailed operational thresholds, reporting procedures, documentary requirements, caps, or any separate effective-date clause beyond the document date and update date. For compliance purposes, however, the key takeaway is that the RBI has consolidated and formalized the conditions under which UCBs may engage in these ancillary financial services, and a UCB should review the full text before commencing or continuing any of the listed activities to confirm the exact approval, governance, and conduct obligations attached to each permission.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Digital Banking Channels Authorisation) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Urban Co-operative Banks (Digital Banking Channels Authorisation) Directions, 2025** were issued under **Section 35A read with Section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and are intended to govern when and how urban co-operative banks may offer digital banking services. The directions **take effect on January 1, 2026** and apply to **urban co-operative banks operating in India**, specifically the **primary co-operative banks** covered under **Section 5(cc) read with Section 56** of the Act.

At a high level, the document establishes a formal RBI authorization framework for **digital banking channels**, meaning banks cannot assume unrestricted freedom to launch or expand such channels without satisfying the prudential, technology, governance, and operational conditions laid out in the directions. The beginning of the document indicates that “digital banking channels” are being defined as bank-provided modes delivered over **websites** and, by implication from the title and structure, other digital access channels subject to the RBI’s authorization and control requirements.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that these directions create a **mandatory regime specific to UCBs** rather than a general banking advisory. Any affected bank will need to review its current and planned digital delivery model against the RBI’s authorization conditions once the full operational requirements in the later chapters are applied, including prudential standards, technology controls, and general compliance obligations. There are **no monetary thresholds, rate changes, or immediate deadlines beyond the effective date shown in the excerpt**.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Voluntary Amalgamation) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **“Urban Co-operative Banks – Voluntary Amalgamation) Directions, 2025”** on **28 November 2025** (RBI/DoR/2025-26/270; DoR.HOL.REC.189/16-13-100/2025-26). These directions set out the RBI’s framework for **voluntary amalgamation of urban co-operative banks (UCBs)**, replacing prior guidance on the same subject, and are intended to govern the entire approval process from the initiating boards through RBI sanction and post-sanction shareholder rights.

At a high level, the directions require any UCB proposing voluntary amalgamation to follow a formal sequence: **approval by the board of directors**, then **approval by shareholders**, then **RBI approval/sanction of the amalgamation scheme**, and finally implementation in accordance with the sanctioned scheme. The document also includes provisions on **the entitlement of dissenting shareholders**, meaning shareholders who do not agree with the amalgamation are given specified rights under the scheme and the RBI framework rather than being left solely to the merging institutions’ discretion.

The directions apply specifically to **urban co-operative banks** involved in a **voluntary amalgamation**; the table of contents indicates that the scope and applicability are defined in Chapter I, and the process is organized into distinct compliance stages across Chapters II through V. The issuance also states there is a **repeal and saving** chapter, along with clarifications that other laws are not barred and that interpretations are addressed, which means compliance teams should treat this as a standalone RBI framework but still check how it interacts with the Banking Regulation Act, co-operative society law, and any applicable state-specific co-operative laws.

For compliance purposes, the key operational implication is that an amalgamation cannot proceed merely by mutual agreement between institutions: it must be documented, approved internally, approved by shareholders, and then submitted to and sanctioned by the RBI under the prescribed framework. Because the text provided here is only the front matter and table of contents, the specific procedural thresholds, voting requirements, filing contents, timelines, dissenting shareholder compensation mechanics, and any effective-date/transitional provisions would need to be read from the body and annexures of the Directions to determine exact filing and governance obligations.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Licensing, Scheduling and Regulatory Classification) Guidelines, 2025
rows.summary:
The RBI’s 2025 UCB Guidelines state that **no new licensing proposals will be entertained** for either the formation of new urban co-operative banks or the conversion of co-operative credit societies into UCBs. For these purposes, “urban co-operative banks” are defined as **Primary Co-operative Banks** under **section 5(ccv) read with section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**.

For regulatory classification, RBI has adopted a **four-tier framework** for UCBs based on deposits and nature of operation. **Tier 1** includes all **unit UCBs and salary earners’ UCBs, regardless of deposit size**, plus all other UCBs with deposits **up to ₹100 crore**; **Tier 2** covers deposits of **more than ₹100 crore up to ₹1,000 crore**; **Tier 3** covers deposits of **more than ₹1,000 crore up to ₹10,000 crore**; and **Tier 4** covers deposits of **more than ₹10,000 crore**. The deposit amount for classification is to be determined from the **audited balance sheet as of 31 March of the immediately preceding financial year**.

The guidelines also provide a **transition relief (“glide path”) of up to two years** for a UCB that moves into a higher tier because its deposits cross a threshold: it may use the financial year in which the threshold is crossed and the **next financial year** to comply with the higher tier’s regulatory requirements, where applicable. This means compliance teams should monitor annual audited deposit figures carefully, as a tier change can trigger new regulatory obligations, but implementation of those higher-tier requirements may be deferred for up to two financial years under the glide path.

The document excerpt then begins a section on **inclusion in the Second Schedule to the RBI Act, 1934**, indicating that further norms follow for whether a UCB may be scheduled, but the substantive criteria are not included in the provided text. The explicit effective date shown on the circular is **December 04, 2025** under reference **DOR/2025-26/269**.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks - Branch Authorisation) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Urban Co-operative Banks (Branch Authorisation) Directions, 2025** (issued **December 4, 2025**) set out the rules urban co-operative banks (UCBs) must follow when opening and operating branches and other places of business. The directions apply to UCBs and are structured around board governance, eligibility for branch expansion, limits tied to the bank’s area of operation, and the procedures for opening new places of business, branches, extension counters, and ATM/CDM-related facilities. For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that branch expansion is no longer just an operational decision: it is governed by RBI-prescribed eligibility criteria, route-based approval requirements, and additional conditions depending on the bank’s category and business model.

At the governance level, the RBI requires the **Board of Directors** to approve the relevant policies and to carry out specific responsibilities before expansion decisions are implemented. This means a UCB cannot treat branch authorisation as a purely management-level function; the board must formally oversee and sanction the policy framework governing branch opening, and ensure compliance with the directions as part of its supervisory role.

The directions then lay down the framework for **Branch Authorisation**, including **Eligibility Criteria for Business Authorization (ECBA)** and the rules on the **area of operation of UCBs**, which determine where a bank may open business outlets. The document also distinguishes between a **new place of business**, a **branch under the automatic route**, and a **branch under the prior approval route**, indicating that not all openings can proceed on the same basis. Compliance teams will need to verify, for each proposed outlet, whether the bank is within the permitted area, whether the outlet qualifies for automatic opening or requires prior RBI approval, and whether any additional conditions apply before launch.

The directions also include specific treatment for **Salary Earners’ Banks** when opening branches, implying that such banks face extra conditions beyond the standard branch-authorisation framework. In addition, the document addresses the opening of an **Extension Counter (EC)** and the operationalisation of **ATMs/CDMs** (the title shown is truncated after “ATM / CDMs / …”), which indicates that non-traditional delivery points and cash-handling devices are covered by the authorisation regime as well. A compliance officer should therefore treat branch rollout, extension counters, and ATM/CDM deployment as regulated events requiring route-based review, board oversight where applicable, and confirmation that the bank satisfies the RBI’s eligibility and location rules before implementation.

Because the excerpt provided is only the table of contents and opening metadata, it does not show the detailed numerical thresholds, specific procedural steps, or any transition provisions that may appear in the body of the directions. However, from the content shown, the material compliance obligation is clear: **UCBs must follow RBI’s 2025 branch-authorisation framework for every new business location or delivery channel, with board-approved policies, eligibility checks, and the correct approval route applied before opening**.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks - Branch Authorisation) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Rural Co-operative Banks – Branch Authorisation Directions, 2025** (DOR/2025-26/296, issued **December 04, 2025**) replace and consolidate the rules governing how rural co-operative banks can open, shift, close, or otherwise authorise places of business. The directions apply to **State Co-operative Banks (StCBs)** and **District Central Co-operative Banks (DCCBs)**, and set out the criteria they must satisfy before authorising new branches, extension counters, ATMs/CDMs/CRMs, or other business locations, as well as the process for shifting or closing existing premises. Compliance teams should treat this as the operative RBI framework for branch expansion and changes in branch footprint for these institutions.

A key requirement is the continued use of RBI’s **Eligibility Criteria for Business Authorization (ECBA)** framework before a branch or other place of business can be opened. The directions also specifically address the **area of operation of DCCBs**, meaning the geographic scope within which a DCCB may conduct branch activity is regulated and cannot be expanded informally. The document distinguishes between **automatic route** and **prior approval route** openings, so some branch openings may proceed only if the bank satisfies predefined conditions, while others require advance RBI approval; the exact route depends on the category of institution and the activity being undertaken.

The directions further regulate **extension counters (ECs)** and the **operationalisation of ATMs, cash deposit machines (CDMs), and cash recycler machines (CRMs)**, indicating that these facilities are subject to authorisation controls and not merely operational decisions. There are also separate rules for **shifting a place of business** and for **closure of a place of business**, which means a bank must follow prescribed RBI procedures before relocating or shutting any branch or other authorised location. In addition, the table of contents shows a distinct chapter on **doorstep banking services**, so banks offering such services should expect explicit compliance conditions tied to their branch-authorisation framework.

Because the excerpt provided is only the table of contents and headings, it does **not** show the detailed thresholds, numeric limits, deadlines, or exact procedural steps that likely appear in the substantive chapters. However, for compliance purposes, the document clearly signals that rural co-operative banks must align their branch planning, location changes, and service-delivery points with RBI authorisation requirements under the 2025 directions, and should review the full text for any institution-specific eligibility tests, filing requirements, or approval timelines before making operational changes.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Miscellaneous) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Miscellaneous) Directions, 2025** on **December 04, 2025** under reference **DOR/2025-26/319** and **DOR.SOG(SPE).REC.No.332/13-04-001/2025-26**. The document is structured as a set of compliance directions for **rural co-operative banks**, with the first chapters covering **preliminary matters, board responsibilities, and Depositor Education and Awareness Fund (DEAF)** requirements. Because the provided excerpt shows the table of contents but not the operative clauses, the summary can identify the subject areas and the compliance framework introduced, but not the exact detailed text of each rule beyond what is named in the contents.

From the table of contents, the directions expressly establish: **the short title and commencement date**, **applicability**, and **definitions** in Chapter I; then in Chapter II they require the **board of a rural co-operative bank to approve policies** and conduct **board-level reviews** of those policies and related matters. This indicates a governance requirement that compliance-sensitive policies are not merely operational documents but must be formally approved and periodically reviewed by the board itself. Any rural co-operative bank subject to these directions should expect that board minutes, policy approvals, and review cycles will need to be documented for regulatory inspection.

Chapter III addresses the **Depositor Education and Awareness Fund**, which is a key compliance area for customer balances that have remained unclaimed or otherwise have to be transferred under RBI rules. The chapter specifically signals rules on **definitions**, **credits to the Fund**, **refunds and interest**, **registration guidelines**, **procedural guidelines for transfer and claim**, and **returns**. For compliance purposes, that means affected institutions must be prepared to identify balances or amounts that must be moved into the Fund, calculate and pay any interest or refunds as required, follow RBI-prescribed registration and claim procedures, and file the required periodic returns.

No specific thresholds, interest rates, timelines, or operational deadlines are visible in the excerpt beyond the publication date of **December 04, 2025** and the indication that commencement is addressed in Chapter I. A compliance team should therefore treat this as a formal RBI update affecting rural co-operative banks’ governance and DEAF handling processes, and review the full operative text to confirm the exact effective date, reporting cadence, transfer triggers, claim documentation, and any numerical limits or interest calculations once the body of the directions is available.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Managing Risks in Outsourcing) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Rural Co-operative Banks – Managing Risks in Outsourcing Directions, 2025** set a formal outsourcing-risk framework for **rural co-operative banks** and became part of the RBI’s regulatory expectations from **November 28, 2025** (the issue date shown on the document). The directions require each covered bank’s **board** to approve a written outsourcing policy and to remain ultimately accountable for outsourced activities; outsourcing does **not** transfer the bank’s regulatory responsibility, and the board/senior management must ensure appropriate oversight, risk controls, and governance over any third-party arrangements. The document also establishes a structured governance model for outsourcing financial services, including the need for the bank to define permissible outsourcing, maintain internal oversight, and manage vendor-related risk rather than treating outsourcing as a hands-off arrangement.

A key substantive restriction is that certain activities **cannot be outsourced**; the directions expressly identify a category of financial services that must remain under the bank’s own control and cannot be delegated to third parties. For any outsourcing that is permitted, the bank must still retain clear accountability, establish authorisation and monitoring processes, and ensure the outsourced service provider operates within the bank’s prescribed risk and control framework. The document places specific emphasis on **board-approved policy**, **senior management responsibility**, and **ongoing evaluation of outsourcing risk**, indicating that the bank must have documented procedures before entering outsourcing arrangements and must continually monitor them afterward.

Because the text provided here only includes the heading, table of contents, and the opening structural sections, the substantive numerical thresholds, specific prohibited activities, detailed vendor due-diligence steps, contract clauses, reporting triggers, and any transition/deadline provisions are **not visible in the excerpt**. If you want, I can also produce a compliance-focused checklist once the full body of the directions is provided, so the summary can capture the exact prohibited functions, required controls, and any timelines or documentation obligations.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 1, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Rural Co-operative Banks – Responsible Business Conduct Directions, 2025** (dated **November 28, 2025**, and shown as **updated through July 1, 2026**) consolidate and replace the RBI’s operating requirements for rural co-operative banks across customer service, inclusion, deposits, payments, and lending. The document is organized into chapters covering institutional governance, branch-level customer service, customer protection, financial inclusion, payment/remittance services, deposit and liability handling, responsible lending, and miscellaneous/repeal provisions, with detailed annexes providing the standard notice-board format, quick-reference rates, and claim-settlement forms. For compliance purposes, the key point is that these are not merely guidance notes: they set mandatory conduct standards and procedures for all covered rural co-operative banks and their branches, with the later chapters imposing day-to-day operational obligations on how products are offered, disclosed, serviced, and documented.

The directions require banks to maintain an institutional framework for responsible conduct, including branch and back-office controls, customer-facing disclosures, grievance handling, and oversight processes that ensure consistent compliance across branch operations. Branches must follow prescribed customer-service standards, display the required information in the prescribed notice-board format, and provide clear guidance on accounts, deposits, payments, and service charges. The customer-protection chapter imposes obligations on transparency, fair treatment, complaint handling, and communication of bank policies so customers can understand the terms, charges, and procedures affecting their accounts and transactions. The financial inclusion chapter adds access-related obligations, meaning banks must not limit service delivery to conventional channels and must support inclusive access for underserved customers in the manner required by the directions.

In payment and remittance services, rural co-operative banks must comply with RBI-prescribed operating standards for funds transfers and related customer transactions, including the disclosures and process controls applicable to such services. The deposit-liability chapter governs how banks may open and operate deposit accounts and handle other liabilities, including the official handling of nominee, joint-holder, deceased-customer, and related claim situations through the prescribed claim-settlement procedures and forms. The annexes indicate that RBI has standardized supporting materials, including a “quick glance” sheet of rates and detailed forms for inventory and settlement of claims, so compliance teams should ensure branches use only the prescribed formats and follow the updated instructions rather than local variations.

The responsible lending chapter is material for credit operations: it sets the conduct rules for lending decisions, borrower communications, and loan servicing practices, and would require lending staff to follow the RBI’s mandated process rather than informal or ad hoc credit practices. Because the document is presented as an updated 2026 version of 2025 directions, compliance teams should treat the **July 1, 2026 update date** as the operative point for any amended provisions or revised forms/rates reflected in the text and annexes. No numeric prudential ratios, interest-rate caps, or monetary thresholds are visible in the excerpt provided, but the document explicitly references a rate appendix, so any branch or product team should verify the annexes for exact charges, interest calculations, or service fees that apply under the updated directions.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on September 18, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s “Rural Co-operative Banks – Know Your Customer” Directions, 2025 impose a consolidated KYC/AML framework for rural co-operative banks, with the document updated as of December 29, 2025 and issued under reference DOR/2025-26/316 and DOR.AML.REC.No.235/14.01.005/2025-26 dated November 28, 2025. For compliance purposes, the key point is that these directions set out mandatory requirements for customer acceptance, customer identification, customer due diligence, risk management, beneficial ownership identification, and related governance expectations that affected banks must implement and maintain through board-approved policies and procedures. The document’s structure indicates detailed obligations across multiple chapters, including specific requirements for how banks must frame and operate their KYC program, rather than leaving implementation discretion entirely to the institution.

The directions apply to rural co-operative banks, and the table of contents shows that they cover both governance-level obligations and operational procedures. In particular, the bank’s Board of Directors is required to approve policies and related guidelines under Chapter II, and the institution must have formal customer acceptance policy, risk management controls, and customer identification procedures under Chapters III through V. Chapter VI then spells out due diligence requirements for individuals, sole proprietorships, legal entities, and beneficial owners, indicating that compliance teams must ensure distinct onboarding and verification workflows depending on the customer type rather than using a one-size-fits-all process.

Although the excerpt provided does not include the body text of the chapters, the document clearly signals that compliance obligations extend to the full customer lifecycle: onboarding, identification, and ongoing due diligence. The inclusion of separate sections for individuals, sole proprietary firms, legal entities, and beneficial ownership means the bank must be able to collect and verify identity and control information appropriate to each category, and must maintain procedures that are risk-based and aligned to the Board-approved KYC framework. The updated-as-of date of December 29, 2025 indicates that the version quoted may reflect later amendments or clarifications through that date, so compliance teams should rely on the complete updated text rather than only the original issuance date.

From the material shown, there are no numeric thresholds, rates, or specific deadlines stated in the excerpt itself beyond the issuance date and update date. A compliance officer reviewing this document should therefore treat the table of contents as a roadmap to mandatory controls and verify the detailed chapter text for any operational triggers, customer categories, periodic review intervals, recordkeeping requirements, or exception handling standards that are not visible in the excerpt.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Prudential Norms on Declaration of Dividends) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Prudential Norms on Declaration of Dividends) Directions, 2025** under **section 35A read with section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and other enabling powers, and these Directions take effect **immediately upon issuance** on **November 28, 2025**. The document applies specifically to **Rural Co-operative Banks (RCBs)**, so compliance teams for such institutions should treat this as a direct dividend-governance requirement rather than a general banking advisory.

On the substance, the Directions establish RBI’s prudential framework for when an RCB may declare dividends, meaning dividend payments are no longer simply a board/shareholder decision but are subject to RBI’s prescribed conditions. The excerpt provided does not include the detailed conditions in Chapter II, but the title and structure make clear that the operative requirement is a prudential control on dividend declaration by RCBs, likely tied to financial soundness and regulatory compliance criteria that must be satisfied before any dividend can be recommended or paid.

The Directions also contain standard legal architecture in Chapter III addressing **repeal and saving**, the fact that **application of other laws is not barred**, and **interpretation provisions**, which means the new Directions supersede any inconsistent earlier RBI dividend norms while preserving actions already taken under prior rules unless expressly affected. For compliance purposes, the key immediate action is to confirm whether the institution is an RCB covered by the Directions, then review dividend policies, board approval processes, and any internal conditions precedent for dividend recommendation to ensure no declaration is made unless it complies with the RBI’s prudential framework effective from the issuance date.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Financial Statements: Presentation and Disclosures) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on April 1, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **“Rural Co-operative Banks – Financial Statements: Presentation and Disclosures) Directions, 2025”** on **November 28, 2025**, with the text noted as **updated as on April 1, 2026**. These directions apply to **rural co-operative banks** and govern how they must **prepare, present, and disclose financial statements**, including the **format of the balance sheet and profit and loss account**, the **notes and instructions for compilation**, and specific guidance tied to certain **Accounting Standards**. In practical terms, the document is not just a high-level reporting framework; it is a detailed prescriptive compliance manual that standardizes statement presentation, disclosure content, and treatment of particular accounting and operational items.

The directions also require compliance with a set of specific disclosure and accounting instructions in the notes to accounts, covering **general presentation rules** and **mandatory disclosures** in financial statements. The table of contents shows that the RBI further addresses operational and financial-control items in the final chapter, including **provisioning for net debit balances in inter-branch accounts**, **reconciliation of Nostro accounts and the treatment of outstanding entries**, **transfers to or appropriations from reserve funds**, and **provisioning for fraud**. For a compliance team, this means the bank must ensure its year-end and interim reporting processes are aligned with RBI’s prescribed formats and accounting treatments, and that internal controls are in place to identify, reconcile, and disclose items that could affect reported assets, liabilities, reserves, or losses.

Because the text provided is only the document header and table of contents, it does not show the detailed thresholds, percentages, line-item wording, or any specific deadlines beyond the issue date and updated-as-of date. However, the scope is clear: the directions create binding reporting and disclosure obligations for rural co-operative banks, and the key compliance risk areas explicitly flagged by the RBI are balance-sheet/profit-and-loss presentation, note disclosures, inter-branch and Nostro reconciliation, reserve fund movements, and fraud provisioning.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Treatment of Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Rural Co-operative Banks – Treatment of Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters) Directions, 2025”** take **immediate effect** and apply to all **Rural Co-operative Banks (RCBs)**, meaning **State Co-operative Banks and Central Co-operative Banks** as defined under the National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development framework. The stated purpose is to create a system for **disseminating credit information on wilful defaulters** so lenders can be cautioned and **further institutional finance can be prevented** from being extended to them. The RBI issues the directions under **Sections 21 and 35A read with Section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, and **Section 11 of the Credit Information Companies (Regulation) Act, 2005**.

A compliance team should note that the directions are focused on two groups: **wilful defaulters** and **large defaulters**. While the excerpt provided does not yet show the detailed operative tests or reporting thresholds in the later chapters, it is clear that the regime requires RCBs to maintain and disseminate information so that such borrowers are identified and flagged for caution across the banking system. This means the bank will need internal controls to detect, classify, and report relevant borrower defaults in line with the RBI’s prescribed framework, rather than handling such cases only as ordinary credit delinquencies.

The document also has a dedicated chapter on **reporting of wilful defaulters and large defaulters**, indicating that RCBs will have specific reporting obligations beyond mere internal labeling. An **Annex I** provides the **format for submission of the list of large defaulters**, which means the bank must be prepared to compile and submit borrower data in a prescribed RBI format, not just ad hoc narrative reports. Because the directions are issued as binding RBI directions, non-compliance would be a supervisory issue, so compliance and credit teams should ensure their borrower monitoring, default classification, and reporting workflows are aligned to the final chapter requirements and the annexed template.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Resolution of Stressed Assets) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on October 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The RBI’s **“Rural Co-operative Banks – Resolution of Stressed Assets” Directions, 2025** (issued **November 28, 2025** and updated through **July 1, 2026**) establish the framework rural co-operative banks must follow for identifying, reporting, restructuring, and resolving stressed borrower accounts. The directions apply to **rural co-operative banks** and govern the treatment of stressed assets, with specific chapters covering general governance requirements, restructuring prudential norms, special resolution mechanisms such as compromise settlements and technical write-offs, and a dedicated process for **accounts impacted by calamities**. The document is organized as a binding supervisory framework, so compliance teams should treat it as a mandatory policy and procedure update rather than guidance.

A key requirement is that each bank must have **board-approved policies** for stressed-asset resolution and restructuring, indicating the RBI expects formal internal governance rather than ad hoc case handling. Banks must implement **early identification and reporting of stress**, meaning signs of borrower distress must be detected and escalated promptly rather than waiting until an account becomes severely delinquent. The directions also require **disclosures**, so the institution must ensure its reporting and external/internal disclosure framework captures stressed-asset actions taken under these rules.

The directions set prudential rules for **restructuring of accounts**, meaning any modification of repayment terms or resolution plan must comply with RBI’s restructuring standards and cannot be used to mask asset quality problems. They also address **special cases of restructuring**, including **compromise settlements** and **technical write-offs**, which implies banks may settle dues for less than the full outstanding amount or remove amounts from the books under specific conditions, but only within the RBI-prescribed framework. Because these are special-case tools, compliance teams should assume they require clear documentation, approval authority, and consistent accounting/classification treatment.

Chapter IV-A introduces a separate process for **resolution of accounts impacted by calamities**, signaling that borrowers affected by natural disasters or similar events may receive tailored relief or restructuring treatment. The document specifically assigns a role to the **State Level Bankers’ Committee (SLBC)**, **Union Territory Level Bankers’ Committee (UTLBC)**, and **District Consultative Committee (DCC)**, meaning resolution in calamity situations is not only bank-level but also coordinated through local banking committees. Compliance teams should ensure branch and regional staff know when to escalate such accounts into the SLBC/UTLBC/DCC channel and that any calamity-related relief is granted only through the prescribed committee-backed process.

No explicit numerical thresholds, interest rates, haircut percentages, or deadline dates for implementation are visible in the excerpt provided beyond the issuance date and the update date of **July 1, 2026**. Based on the table of contents alone, the most material compliance impact is the need to align internal policy, approval matrices, borrower monitoring, accounting treatment, and disclosure controls with RBI’s formal resolution framework for rural co-operative banks.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on October 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
This RBI direction applies to **rural co-operative banks** and sets out the income recognition, asset classification, and provisioning framework they must follow, with the document labeled **“Updated as on July 01, 2026.”** The circular is identified as **DOR/2025-26/311 / DOR.STR.REC.230./21.04.048/2025-26** and was issued on **November 28, 2025**. It establishes the mandatory rules for when income may be recognized, how loans and other assets must be classified, what counts as non-performing assets (NPAs), and how provisions must be made; it also contains separate disclosure obligations. The table of contents shows that the directions cover general instructions and disclosures, detailed asset classification norms, special classification rules for particular cases, NPA categories, treatment where the value of security has eroded, upgrading of NPA accounts, and provisioning requirements, including additional specific provisioning where a resolution plan is implemented.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that the directions replace or consolidate the RBI’s required prudential framework for these banks, so affected entities must ensure their accounting, credit monitoring, and provisioning policies are aligned to the specific rules in the full text. The document expressly contemplates **asset classification norms** that determine when an exposure must be treated as standard, sub-standard, doubtful, or loss, and separate rules for **specific cases of asset classification** and **NPA categorization**. It also imposes requirements where **security value has eroded**, meaning banks must assess and classify such accounts according to the RBI’s specified treatment rather than relying solely on repayment performance. In addition, it contains rules for **upgradation of loan accounts previously classified as NPAs**, indicating that reclassification is not discretionary and must follow the prescribed conditions.

The document also requires **provisioning** in accordance with RBI-prescribed percentages and triggers, including a dedicated section on **additional specific provisioning when a resolution plan is implemented**. That means compliance teams need to track not only ordinary asset-quality movements but also restructuring/resolution events that may create extra provisioning obligations. Although the excerpt provided does not include the substantive numerical provisioning rates or classification thresholds, the document clearly indicates that those numbers and triggers are integral to the directions and must be implemented by rural co-operative banks in their prudential systems, financial statements, and regulatory reporting. Finally, because the title states “Updated as on July 01, 2026,” compliance should treat that date as the latest incorporated update date and verify that all internal policies, loan review procedures, and disclosures reflect the July 1, 2026 version of the directions.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Asset Liability Management) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued these Directions on **November 28, 2025** to establish the asset-liability management (“ALM”) framework for **rural co-operative banks**. The document applies to the institutions covered by the RBI’s rural co-operative bank category and is intended to govern how they manage liquidity risk, cash-flow mismatches, board oversight, and internal ALM systems and processes. Because the excerpt provided is only the front matter/table of contents, it does **not** state the substantive numerical limits, reporting deadlines, or detailed operational procedures; it does, however, show that the directions are organized into mandatory requirements for board responsibilities, board-approved policies and limit-setting, ALM governance, ALM information systems, ALM organization, the ALM process, and liquidity risk management.

From the contents, the key compliance impact is that affected banks must have a board-level ALM framework rather than an informal treasury practice. The Board is expected to take responsibility for ALM oversight, approve policies and risk limits, and conduct periodic reviews of the bank’s ALM position and controls. The ALM governance chapter indicates that banks must maintain information systems capable of capturing the data needed for liquidity and maturity analysis, establish an internal organizational structure for ALM, and operate a formal ALM process rather than ad hoc monitoring.

The liquidity risk management chapter specifically indicates that RBI requires banks to manage **maturity and cash-flow mismatches** as part of liquidity control, implying monitoring of gaps across time buckets and corrective action when mismatches arise. However, this excerpt does not include the actual threshold amounts, time bands, measurement standards, reporting formats, or implementation timelines that would normally define the precise compliance burden. For a compliance team, the practical takeaway from the text provided is that the directions introduce a structured, board-supervised ALM regime for rural co-operative banks and will require formal policies, systems, governance, and ongoing mismatch monitoring once the substantive chapters are reviewed in full.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Classification, Valuation and Operation of Investment Portfolio) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on May 18, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Rural Co-operative Banks – Classification, Valuation and Operation of Investment Portfolio) Directions, 2025”** (issued **November 28, 2025** and updated as of **May 18, 2026**) sets the mandatory framework rural co-operative banks must follow for how they **classify, value, manage, and move investments between portfolio buckets**. It applies to **rural co-operative banks**, and the document makes the **board** responsible for approving and overseeing a formal **investment policy** and ensuring the bank’s investment activities are conducted within the RBI-prescribed framework. Compliance teams should treat this as a full operational rulebook for the investment book rather than a guidance note: it covers the permitted portfolio structure, the board’s governance obligations, general handling rules, valuation methodology, and the process for shifting instruments between categories.

At a high level, the directions require banks to maintain investments in designated categories, with a distinction between **permanent investments** and **current investments**, and to apply the RBI’s rules consistently to each category. The bank must have an approved investment policy and follow general instructions on how investments are to be operated, monitored, and reported internally. The directions also address **classification of investments**, including the initial categorization of securities and the conditions under which instruments may be reclassified or shifted from one category to another. Because the document is specifically about “classification, valuation and operation,” compliance officers should expect obligations around correct bucket assignment, periodic review of portfolio status, and documentation/authorization for any movement between categories.

The document further requires **valuation** of investments in line with the applicable category, meaning the carrying value and recognition treatment will depend on whether the security is held as permanent or current. That implies ongoing compliance obligations for market valuation, any amortization or transfer treatment, and internal controls to ensure books and financial statements reflect the correct RBI-mandated valuation basis. The directions are not limited to accounting entries; they also govern **how the investment portfolio may be operated**, which means trading, reclassification, and portfolio management actions must align with the RBI framework and the bank’s approved policy.

From a compliance perspective, the key practical issue is that the directions create enforceable requirements on **governance, classification discipline, valuation controls, and portfolio movement approvals** for rural co-operative banks. Any bank with an investment portfolio should verify that its board-approved investment policy is updated to match the directions, that staff are using the correct classification and valuation rules, and that any transfer between categories is supported by the procedures and conditions specified in the RBI text. If you want, I can also produce a **section-by-section compliance checklist** from the full directions.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Interest Rates on Advances) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Rural Co-operative Banks (Interest Rates on Advances) Directions, 2025** apply to **Rural Co-operative Banks (RCBs)**, meaning **State Co-operative Banks and Central Co-operative Banks** as defined under the **NABARD Act, 1981**. It specifically defines **“microfinance loan”** by reference to the **RBI (Rural Co-operative Banks – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025**, and clarifies that **“rests”** means the **periodicity at which interest is charged to borrowers**. For compliance purposes, the immediate operational takeaway from the portion provided is that RCBs must align their lending and interest-charging practices with this new 2025 direction **from the date of issuance**, and ensure internal policy documents, loan product terms, and system configurations reflect the new RBI framework for advances to the extent covered in the complete directions. rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Transfer and Distribution of Credit Risk) Directions, 2025

The document says it is intended to govern the various ways banks **transfer and distribute credit risk**, including transactions used for **liquidity management, rebalancing exposures, and strategic sales**. RBI says it is exercising its powers under **sections 21, 35A, read with section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** to create a comprehensive regulatory framework covering these activities.
