For a compliance function, the practical implication is that these institutions must review all loan-transfer and credit-risk-transfer arrangements against this RBI framework, because it is meant to regulate “different avenues” of such transfers rather than only one transaction type.

The table of contents shows the directions are organized into: **preliminary matters, scope and definitions, general conditions for all loan transfers, a dedicated chapter on transfer of stressed loans, and repeal/other provisions**. Based on the introduction, the key compliance point is that RBI is not issuing an advisory but a **binding regulatory direction** that will govern both ordinary loan transfers and stressed-loan transfer arrangements, so affected banks should expect obligations around transaction structure, eligibility, and procedural compliance once the operative chapters are reviewed in full.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Concentration Risk Management) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Concentration Risk Management) Directions, 2025** on **November 28, 2025**, and they **take effect immediately upon issuance**. The Directions apply to **Rural Co-operative Banks** and are intended to strengthen prudential management of **concentration risk** arising from exposures to counterparties and sectors of the economy. RBI states that the framework is issued under its powers in the **Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, including **Sections 21, 27, and 35A read with Section 56**.

Substantively, the document establishes a regulatory framework for how Rural Co-operative Banks must manage exposure concentration risk, replacing or supplementing earlier prudential norms issued through **Credit Monitoring Arrangements (CMA)** and other RBI instructions. It is not a generic policy statement: it is a binding direction requiring these banks to follow RBI-prescribed exposure norms and related controls for managing concentration in lending and other exposures. The introduction makes clear that the purpose is to reduce systemic and institution-specific risk from overexposure to particular borrowers/counterparties or sectors.

The table of contents shows the Directions are organized into **Chapter I – Preliminary**, **Chapter II – Exposure Norms**, and **Chapter III – Repeal and other provisions**, with **Annex I** and **Annex II** supporting the exposure framework. Although the excerpt provided does not include the detailed exposure thresholds, the structure indicates that the core compliance obligations are set out in Chapter II and likely include specific caps, measurement rules, and reporting/monitoring requirements that Rural Co-operative Banks must apply in practice.

For a compliance team, the key immediate takeaway from the excerpt is that this is a **new RBI binding direction with immediate effect** for the rural co-operative banking sector, focused on concentration risk governance and exposure management. Any compliance review should check the full Chapter II text and annexes for the exact exposure limits, methodology, exceptions, transitional treatment, and any repeal or grandfathering provisions contained in Chapter III.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Credit Risk Management) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
This RBI direction updates the credit-risk framework for Rural Co-operative Banks (RCBs) and consolidates both prudential expectations and hard limits on lending and account conduct. It applies to RCBs and is issued as the “Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Credit Risk Management) Directions, 2025,” updated as of July 1, 2026; the text provided here is only the opening portion and states the regulatory purpose but does not yet contain the substantive chapter-by-chapter requirements.

From the introduction, RBI explains that RCBs face significant credit risk because their exposures span multiple sectors, borrower types, and products, and because interconnectedness can create broader systemic effects. The document signals that credit-risk control for RCBs will rely on a combination of board-approved policies, credit-risk evaluation requirements, statutory restrictions, regulatory restrictions, property valuation rules, CERSAI filing requirements for security interests, and rules for maintaining cash credit, current, and overdraft accounts. The table of contents shows the main compliance areas: Chapter II on board-approved policies; Chapter II-A on credit risk evaluation; Chapter III on statutory restrictions; Chapter IV on regulatory restrictions; Chapter V on valuation of properties and empanelment of valuers; Chapter VI on filing security interests in CERSAI for immovable, movable, and intangible assets; Chapter VIA on maintenance of cash credit/current/overdraft accounts by banks; and Chapter VII on repeal and other provisions.

Because the excerpt stops at the introduction, it does not yet provide the actual thresholds, prohibited activities, reporting deadlines, valuation rules, CERSAI filing timelines, or account-maintenance procedures that compliance teams would need for implementation. On the basis of the portion supplied, the key takeaway is that RBI is treating rural co-operative bank credit risk as a governance and operations issue requiring formal policies and multiple control mechanisms, and a full compliance review would need the remaining chapters to identify the exact obligations and effective dates attached to each rule.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Credit Information Reporting) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Rural Co-operative Banks – Credit Information Reporting Directions, 2025** set out a mandatory framework for how **rural co-operative banks** must participate in and use India’s **Credit Information Companies (CICs)** system. The document applies to the covered rural co-operative banks and governs both their **membership obligations with CICs** and their ongoing responsibilities for **reporting, updating, correcting, and using credit information**. It is issued as RBI circular **DOR/2025-26/304, DOR.FIN.REC.No.223/20.06.056/2025-26, dated November 28, 2025**, and the text provided is the version **updated as on July 01, 2026**.

The directions require affected banks to provide credit information in the **prescribed RBI/CIC data formats** and to do so within specified **reporting timelines**, with continuing **updation obligations** for changes in borrower account status. The document also lays down **reporting guidelines** intended to ensure data accuracy and consistency, including procedures for handling **rejected data**, required remediation, and review of the institution’s **Data Quality Index (DQI)**. Where credit information reports contain errors, the directions require the bank to follow a defined process for **correction of the Credit Information Report**, rather than leaving inaccuracies unresolved.

A key compliance requirement is that rural co-operative banks must use credit information reports in their **credit appraisal process**, meaning loan decisions should incorporate bureau/CIC data rather than relying only on internal records. The directions also require **display/disclosure of information** in the manner specified by RBI, so compliance teams should expect obligations that affect what customer-facing or internal information must be shown or made available. In addition, the document states that other applicable instructions issued by the **Department of Regulation** continue to apply, so these directions are not a standalone regime but operate alongside other RBI requirements.

The structure of the document shows that it also covers **technical coordination** through a **Technical Working Group** and includes further custom provisions in later chapters. Because the content provided is only the table of contents and not the full operative text, no specific numeric thresholds, filing dates, or exact technical parameters can be extracted here beyond the document’s issue date and the July 1, 2026 update date. For a compliance team, the practical takeaway is that rural co-operative banks must ensure they are registered/operational with CICs, maintain accurate and timely borrower reporting, actively fix rejected or inaccurate data, and integrate credit bureau information into lending decisions and required disclosures.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Debit Cards: Issuance and Conduct) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Rural Co-operative Banks – Debit Cards: Issuance and Conduct Directions, 2025** take **immediate effect** and apply to **all Rural Co-operative Banks (RCBs)**, specifically **State Co-operative Banks and Central Co-operative Banks** as defined under the **NABARD Act**. The directions are issued under **Section 35A and Section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, and they replace prior RBI instructions on this subject once the repeal provisions operate.

For compliance purposes, the document is a comprehensive framework governing how RCBs may **issue, manage, and conduct debit card operations**. It requires each bank to have a **Board-approved policy and procedures** covering issuance, customer onboarding, risk controls, operational processes, and ongoing conduct around debit cards. The directions also regulate the **form factor** of debit cards, meaning the bank must ensure the card design and format comply with RBI requirements, and they set rules for any **co-branding arrangements**, so banks cannot freely partner or brand cards without meeting the specified regulatory conditions.

The directions additionally lay down **general operating guidelines** for debit cards, which means RCBs must follow RBI-mandated rules for issuance and use, and implement the relevant controls and customer-facing processes prescribed in the document. Compliance teams should treat this as a mandatory update to product governance, card operations, and vendor/co-brand oversight, with responsibility likely extending to policy revision, approval workflows, and monitoring to ensure all debit card activity is aligned with the new directions.

The document’s structure also indicates a **Chapter VII repeal and savings framework**, so compliance officers should verify which earlier RBI circulars or directions are superseded and whether any transitional obligations continue to apply. Since the text provided does not include the later chapter details, a full implementation review should confirm any specific operational thresholds, card issuance conditions, security requirements, customer disclosures, or exception handling provisions contained in the remaining chapters and annexed provisions.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on April 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Rural Co-operative Banks – Credit Facilities Directions, 2025** (updated **as on April 1, 2026**) set out the RBI’s binding framework for how rural co-operative banks may extend credit, with special emphasis on governance, digital lending, and lending against gold/silver collateral. The document is issued under RBI authority on **November 28, 2025** and applies to the covered rural co-operative banking entities identified in the directions; compliance teams should treat it as a consolidated operating rulebook rather than a narrow advisory circular.

A major portion of the directions governs **board-approved policies** and requires covered banks to have formal, approved internal frameworks for credit-related activities rather than ad hoc practices. The document then sets detailed requirements for **digital lending**, including rules for bank–LSP (lending service provider) arrangements, conduct and customer-protection controls, technology and data safeguards, credit-information reporting for digital lending applications (DLAs), and loss-sharing arrangements when borrowers default. Compliance teams should expect obligations around how digital products are designed and delivered, how customers are informed and treated, how data is handled, and how outsourcing/LSP relationships are monitored and documented.

The directions also contain a separate chapter on **lending against gold and silver collateral**, indicating that rural co-operative banks may do so only within RBI-prescribed controls. That chapter includes general provisions plus specific **restrictions and ceilings**, and it addresses **valuation and assaying** of gold and silver, meaning the bank must follow standardized procedures for testing, appraisal, and loan sizing against precious-metal collateral. For compliance purposes, this is important because it implies not just product authorization but also operational requirements around collateral acceptance, valuation integrity, and limits on exposure.

Because the text provided is only the table of contents and cover portion, the exact numerical ceilings, operational deadlines, and any specific thresholds are not visible here; however, the document clearly signals that those details are embedded in the substantive chapters and are binding on the affected banks. A compliance officer should therefore review the full directions for the precise approval, disclosure, reporting, and collateral-handling obligations that apply from the effective/updated date, and should verify whether current policy, customer documentation, digital-lending controls, and gold/silver loan processes already match RBI’s requirements or need to be revised.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Interest Rate on Deposits) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on August 25, 2026)
rows.summary:
This RBI direction sets the interest-rate framework for **rural co-operative banks’ deposit products** and applies to the **rural co-operative bank category** covered by the RBI’s regulatory framework (the document is titled “Rural Co-operative Banks – Interest Rate on Deposits”), with the updated version noted as **effective/updated through August 25, 2026** and originally issued on **November 28, 2025**. It governs how these banks may set and pay interest on **domestic rupee deposits**, and the table of contents shows it also extends to **rupee deposits of non-resident depositors** in a later chapter, so compliance teams should treat it as a comprehensive deposit-rate and deposit-interest compliance instrument rather than a narrow pricing note.

For **domestic current accounts, savings deposits, and term deposits**, the direction prescribes the general framework banks must follow in setting interest rates, including how interest is to be applied to these products and how payment timing is handled. It also specifically addresses **additional interest on domestic deposits**, **interest on overdue domestic deposits**, **floating-rate domestic term deposits**, the **periodicity of interest payment on savings deposits**, and **interest payable to the domestic deposit account of a deceased depositor**, which means banks need procedures covering rate calculation, accrual, payment timing, and account handling in death-settlement situations. The document further includes rules on **penalties for premature withdrawal of domestic term deposits**, so product terms and system controls need to reflect whatever penalty structure the directions require.

The table of contents also shows a dedicated chapter on **rupee deposits of non-residents**, which indicates the directions are not limited to resident customers and likely impose separate conditions for those accounts as well. Because the excerpt provided is only the opening portion and does not include the operative provisions, the compliance-critical takeaway is that rural co-operative banks should review the full text for the exact rate-setting permissions, any prohibited practices, and any operational deadlines or recordkeeping requirements, then ensure all deposit-rate policies, customer disclosures, and core-banking system rules are aligned to the RBI’s 2025 directions as updated on **August 25, 2026**.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on May 15, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Rural Co-operative Banks – Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy” Directions, 2025** set the capital adequacy framework for **rural co-operative banks** and replace the prior regime for these entities, with the text updated as of **May 15, 2026**. The document establishes the rules for what counts as **regulatory capital**, how banks must compute **risk-weighted assets (RWA)**, and the reporting and governance requirements tied to capital adequacy. It is organized to cover: applicability and definitions; capital requirements and the composition of **Tier 1** and **Tier 2** capital; RWA calculation; special instructions on refund of share capital, investor protection in regulatory capital instruments, and reporting; and repeal/saving provisions.  

For compliance purposes, the key obligation is that covered rural co-operative banks must maintain capital under RBI’s prescribed prudential norms rather than legacy capital treatment. The directions specify the regulatory treatment of capital instruments in detail: what can be recognized as Tier 1 capital, what may qualify as Tier 2 capital, and how those amounts feed into the overall capital adequacy calculation against RWAs. The document also lays out the methodology for determining RWAs, which is critical because it directly affects the capital ratio a bank must hold and therefore impacts balance-sheet composition, lending capacity, and supervisory compliance status.  

The directions further impose additional operational and investor-protection rules in connection with **regulatory capital instruments** and **share capital refunds**, indicating that banks cannot treat these instruments purely as ordinary equity/funding arrangements without observing RBI’s prescribed conditions. In practical terms, the compliance team should expect requirements around issuance, recognition, redemption/refund, and treatment of such capital instruments to be tightly controlled, with reporting to RBI required under the chapter on reporting. The repeal and saving provisions mean the new directions supersede earlier capital adequacy instructions for rural co-operative banks, while preserving any actions already taken or rights accrued under the old framework to the extent specified in the text.  

I don’t have the full body of the document here, so I can’t reliably state the exact capital ratios, thresholds, instrument eligibility tests, or reporting timelines if they are contained in the omitted chapters. If you share the full text, I can produce a much more exact compliance summary with all numerical requirements, deadlines, and affected categories of banks/instruments.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Cash Reserve Ratio and Statutory Liquidity Ratio) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on October 09, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s 2025 Directions on **Rural Co-operative Banks’ Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) and Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR)** formally govern how **rural co-operative banks** must maintain mandatory reserves and report compliance, and they are issued under RBI’s powers under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 and the RBI Act, 1934. The document is a consolidated instrument, **updated as of August 25, 2026**, and its operative chapters cover CRR, SLR, the method for computing SLR, reporting, penalties, and repeal/transition provisions. It applies specifically to the class of institutions covered by the title—rural co-operative banks—rather than to commercial banks generally.

At a high level, the directions require affected banks to maintain prescribed minimum balances with the RBI and/or maintain approved liquid assets in the manner the RBI specifies, and to compute and report those requirements according to the procedures in the directions. The document indicates that the RBI may enforce compliance through the penalties framework in the Banking Regulation Act and its own directions, so failure to maintain the required CRR/SLR or to follow the reporting/computation rules can have regulatory consequences. Because the table of contents separately includes a chapter on the **procedure for computation of SLR**, the directions are not only substantive but also operational: banks must use the RBI-prescribed method for determining eligible assets, calculating the ratio, and evidencing compliance in periodic returns.

The document also appears to include detailed annexures and a dedicated reporting chapter, which means compliance officers should expect specific forms, statement formats, or operational definitions to control how holdings are classified and disclosed. The inclusion of a repeal/other provisions chapter suggests these directions may supersede prior RBI instructions on the same subject and contain transitional or saving clauses for existing arrangements. Since the excerpt provided does not show the actual numerical CRR/SLR percentages, reporting deadlines, or asset eligibility rules, a compliance team should treat this as the controlling framework and then review the body of the directions and annexures for the exact ratios, calculation base, maintenance periods, submission dates, and any exemptions or special treatment for particular categories of rural co-operative banks.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks - Governance) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on May 25, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Rural Co-operative Banks (Governance) Directions, 2025** (dated **November 28, 2025** and updated through **May 25, 2026**) establish a consolidated governance framework for rural co-operative banks, covering board constitution, appointment and conduct of the CEO/MD, board meeting discipline, and board committees. The document applies to **rural co-operative banks** and sets out mandatory governance standards that replace earlier scattered provisions; the repeal/transition provisions are referenced in Chapter VI, so compliance teams should treat this as the operative governance rulebook unless a specific grandfathering or savings clause preserves an earlier requirement.

A major area of the directions is the **constitution of the board and appointment of the CEO/MD**. The RBI prescribes how the board is to be formed and governs the process for selecting and appointing the bank’s chief executive function, indicating that board composition and leadership appointments are not merely internal matters but subject to RBI governance standards. Compliance teams should expect these provisions to require documented appointment processes, fit-and-proper style vetting, and adherence to any RBI-prescribed eligibility or tenure rules in the full text.

The directions also impose formal duties on the **board as a collective** and on **individual directors**. Chapter III requires the board to carry out oversight and governance responsibilities directly, and it includes a **code of conduct** for directors, meaning directors must comply with explicit behavioral, independence, confidentiality, and conflict-management expectations rather than informal local practices. For compliance purposes, this typically requires maintaining director declarations, training, attendance/participation records, and processes to address conflicts, recusals, and breaches of conduct.

The document further standardizes **board meeting procedures**. It includes a **model agenda** for board meetings and a **calendar of reviews**, which means boards are expected to conduct recurring oversight of specified control, risk, finance, and compliance matters at defined intervals instead of ad hoc. Compliance officers should ensure the board calendar is aligned to the RBI’s required review cycle, that agenda items are actually placed before the board on schedule, and that minutes evidence review, challenge, and closure of action items.

Finally, the directions establish governance expectations for key **board committees**, specifically the **Audit Committee of the Board** and the **Risk Management Committee**. These committees are intended to formalize oversight of financial reporting, internal controls, audit findings, risk identification, measurement, monitoring, and mitigation, and they must function within the RBI’s governance framework rather than as purely advisory bodies. For compliance teams, the practical obligation is to verify that committee charters, membership, meeting frequency, reporting lines, and issue-tracking processes satisfy the RBI’s directions and that committee decisions are documented and escalated appropriately.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Undertaking of Financial Services) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on October 05, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s “Rural Co-operative Banks – Undertaking of Financial Services) Directions, 2025” (issued November 28, 2025 and updated through April 27, 2026) set out the RBI’s framework for what rural co-operative banks may do when offering selected financial services beyond core banking. The directions apply to rural co-operative banks and cover four main areas: governance and board oversight, investments in Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs), insurance distribution, merchant acquisition services, and issuance of prepaid payment instruments. The document is structured as operative directions, with Chapter I establishing short title/commencement, applicability, and definitions; Chapter II laying out general governance rules; Chapter III setting the service-specific permissions and restrictions; and Chapter IV addressing repeal, saving, and application of the new framework.

A key compliance point is that the board is expressly given a central supervisory role, meaning the bank must ensure board-level control and oversight over any permitted financial-services activity rather than treating these as informal add-ons. The AIF section indicates that rural co-operative banks are subject to RBI’s policy on investments in Alternative Investment Funds, which is typically an area requiring close monitoring because of concentration, exposure, and regulatory restriction risks. Compliance teams should assume any AIF-related investment or exposure must be checked against the specific RBI constraints in the operative text and be approved and tracked at board or equivalent governance level.

On insurance, the directions distinguish two different models. First, a rural co-operative bank may act as a corporate agent for insurance business, but only without taking on risk participation, meaning it can distribute insurance products but cannot underwrite or share insurance risk. Second, the bank may do insurance referral business on a referral basis without risk participation, including by sharing physical space; this means the bank can facilitate customer referrals to an insurer while staying out of insurance underwriting and risk-bearing functions. These permissions are limited and compliance-sensitive: the bank must keep the activity clearly segregated from core banking, ensure the arrangement remains referral/corporate-agency only, and avoid any structure that implies risk participation or unauthorized insurance intermediation.

The directions also allow merchant acquisition business, which means the bank may support merchant payment acceptance activities, and they specifically permit the issue of prepaid payment instruments (PPIs), subject to the RBI’s conditions in the operative provisions. Because PPIs and merchant-acquiring are payments activities with AML/KYC, customer onboarding, settlement, and operational-risk implications, the bank will need documented policies, approved processes, and controls to ensure it stays within the permitted scope. The final chapter repeals earlier provisions covered by the new directions while preserving actions already validly taken under the prior framework to the extent stated in the savings clause, and the document’s updated-as-of date indicates later amendments through April 27, 2026 should be read into the operative requirements.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Digital Banking Channels Authorisation) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Digital Banking Channels Authorisation) Directions, 2025** on **November 28, 2025**, and they take effect on **January 01, 2026**. The directions apply to **rural co-operative banks operating in India**, specifically **State Co-operative Banks and Central Co-operative Banks** as defined under the **National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development Act, 1981**. The document is issued under **Section 35A read with Section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, so it is a binding RBI direction for the covered institutions.

Based on the material provided, the document is structured to set out the framework for **authorising digital banking channels** for these banks, beginning with preliminary scope and definitions and then moving into **prudential requirements, technological guidelines, general guidelines, and exemptions/repeal provisions**.
