rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Fraud Risk Management) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
This RBI direction, issued on **31 July 2026** as **RBI/DoS/2026-27/454** and titled **“Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Fraud Risk Management) Directions, 2026,”** establishes a dedicated fraud-risk framework for **Regional Rural Banks (RRBs)**. It is intended to govern how RRBs prevent, detect, escalate, and report fraud-risk events, with an emphasis on formal governance, early-warning systems, and red-flagging of accounts.

The document requires RRBs to maintain a **board-approved governance structure for fraud risk management**, with clear oversight responsibility and internal accountability for identifying and managing fraud risk. It also introduces a structured **Early Warning Signal (EWS) and Red Flag Account (RFA)** framework for **credit facilities/loan accounts**, under which accounts showing suspicious indicators must be monitored, escalated, and, where warranted, marked as red-flagged rather than left to ad hoc branch-level judgment. The framework is not limited to lending: it also covers **other banking/non-credit related transactions**, meaning compliance teams must ensure fraud-monitoring controls extend beyond loan books to operational and transactional activity as well.

A material compliance obligation is the requirement that once a **credit facility/loan account is classified as a Red-Flagged Account**, the RRB must follow the specified reporting and fraud-classification process under Chapter IV, rather than delaying action until loss is fully crystallized. The directions also require **independent confirmation from third-party service providers, including professionals**, where such external parties are involved in the transaction or account activity, which means banks cannot rely solely on internal records when validating potentially fraudulent activity. This creates a direct need for documented verification procedures, third-party corroboration, and escalation workflows that can stand up to supervisory review.

Although the excerpt provided does not include the full operational thresholds or every procedural step, the table of contents shows that the directions are comprehensive and organized into: **preliminary provisions, governance and oversight, early detection/EWS-RFA controls, and general instructions on red-flagging and fraud reporting**. For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that the RBI is moving RRBs toward a more formal, system-driven fraud-risk regime with mandatory governance oversight, account-level warning signals, broader transaction monitoring, and stronger evidentiary requirements before concluding or closing out suspected fraud matters.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks - Miscellaneous) Supervisory Directions, 2026

For compliance purposes, the most material operational requirement referenced in the table of contents is the mandate on **Core Banking Solution (CBS) implementation**, which signals that covered UCBs must meet RBI-prescribed CBS-related standards and timelines. The document also includes a dedicated **Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) framework** chapter, meaning banks will be subject to RBI’s risk-based supervisory triggers and restrictions when financial/operational thresholds are breached; compliance teams should expect explicit monitoring obligations, escalation processes, and potential business constraints once PCA conditions are met. Because the actual chapter text is not fully included here, the summary cannot state the specific PCA ratios or cutoffs, but the direction clearly establishes that UCBs must maintain internal surveillance and reporting to detect breach conditions early.

The directions also address **Fair Practices Code requirements relating to charging of interest**, which indicates that UCBs must follow RBI rules on interest computation/disclosure and customer communication, and that any deviations or opaque interest practices may be a compliance issue. The **Nomination Facility** chapter indicates obligations for banks to provide and administer nomination for customer accounts/deposits in accordance with RBI procedures, including the operational processes needed to accept, record, and honor nominations. These are standard customer-facing compliance obligations, but the document’s inclusion as a separate chapter means RBI is treating them as enforceable supervisory requirements rather than optional best practices.

A substantial portion of the document is devoted to **Fraud Prevention Measures**, with subparts covering **coordination among agencies, legal and administrative measures, and precautions/safeguards**. The visible contents show detailed operational controls for safeguarding **cash and valuables, negotiable instruments, and books of account**, implying that UCBs must maintain internal controls, custody procedures, and escalation/reporting mechanisms to reduce theft, misappropriation, or fraud risk. Compliance officers should treat this as a requirement for both preventive controls and incident response: the bank is expected to coordinate internally and externally where fraud risk arises, maintain proper records, and implement physical and documentary safeguards over assets and records.

Because the excerpt provided is only the front matter and table of contents, it does **not** reveal the specific effective-date provisions, thresholds, numerical limits, or procedural deadlines that may appear in the chapter text. However, as a July 31, 2026 supervisory direction from RBI’s Department of Supervision, it is clearly intended to be binding on the UCBs within its scope, and compliance teams should review the full chapter text for any implementation dates, reporting timelines, or quantitative trigger points tied to CBS, PCA, interest charging, nomination processing, and fraud-control controls.

rows.summary:
This Master Circular, issued by the RBI on 1 October 2026 to all Scheduled Commercial Banks, including Small Finance Banks, consolidates the RBI’s existing instructions on credit facilities to Scheduled Castes (SCs) and Scheduled Tribes (STs) and requires banks to continue implementing measures to increase advances to these borrower groups. It does not announce a brand-new standalone scheme, but it restates and brings together all prior RBI directions on the subject listed in the appendix, so compliance teams should treat it as the operative consolidated reference for SC/ST credit-related obligations.

On planning and coordination, banks must use the District Level Consultative Committees under the Lead Bank Scheme as the main coordination forum with development agencies, and district credit plans prepared by Lead Banks must explicitly show how credit links to employment and development schemes. Banks are also expected to maintain closer coordination with District Industries Centres, which are specifically identified as a support structure for promoting self-employment. At the block level, the planning process must give SCs/STs a defined weightage, meaning credit planning should be adjusted to reflect these groups’ needs rather than treated neutrally.

The circular further requires banks to step up their lending efforts toward SC/ST borrowers, with the overarching compliance expectation that branch, district, and Lead Bank planning processes actively translate into increased credit access for these communities. While the excerpt provided does not yet include detailed numerical targets, reporting formats, interest concessions, guarantees, or timeline-specific implementation steps beyond the circular’s issuance date, the operative requirement is clear: banks must ensure their internal credit planning, coordination with local institutions, and loan allocation practices support SC/ST credit outreach in a measurable and deliberate way.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has issued draft consolidated Priority Sector Lending (PSL) Directions, 2026 for public comment as part of a broader effort to consolidate PSL instructions that have been issued over time. The draft directions are being proposed separately for five types of regulated entities: commercial banks, small finance banks, local area banks, regional rural banks, and urban co-operative banks, each under its own “Priority Sector Lending – Targets and Classification” Directions, 2026 framework. The notice indicates that any existing instructions not carried forward into the consolidated draft directions will be repealed once the new directions are issued, and RBI says those repeals will be notified separately.

For compliance teams, the immediate action is to review the draft directions relevant to the institution’s regulated-entity category and provide feedback by **November 26, 2026**. Comments can be submitted either through the RBI website’s **“Connect 2 Regulate”** section using the hyperlink provided for each draft document, or by email using the subject line format **“Feedback on [full name of the draft Direction / (including the type of Regulated Entity)]”**. No new PSL target percentages, classification thresholds, or lending ratios are specified in this press release itself; the document is a consultation notice about future binding directions and the potential repeal of superseded instructions.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has issued draft **“Reserve Bank of India (Know Your Customer) Amendment Directions, 2026”** for public comment, following its existing **KYC Directions, 2025** provisions on **Operations of Bank Accounts and Money Mules** and in response to the **Hon’ble Supreme Court’s order dated August 4, 2026**. The Supreme Court directed RBI to adopt and circulate a **Standard Operating Procedure (SOP)** setting out what banks must do when placing **temporary debit holds** on amounts or accounts linked to **money-mule activity** and **cyber-enabled fraud**.  

The draft amendment is intended to update the current instructions on bank account operations and money-mule controls and to advise banks on the procedure for imposing these temporary debit holds in cases connected to money-mule activity and cyber-enabled financial fraud. RBI is issuing this as a **consolidated draft** for consultation, and it is stated to be applicable to **all Commercial Banks, including Small Finance Banks, Payments Banks, Regional Rural Banks, and Local Area Banks, as well as Urban Cooperative Banks**. RBI notes that, after reviewing feedback, it will issue **final directions separately for the relevant regulated entity types**.  

Comments and feedback from regulated entities, stakeholders, and members of the public must be submitted **on or before October 2, 2026**. Submissions can be made either through the RBI website’s **“Connect 2 Regulate”** section or by email using the subject line **“Feedback on Draft Reserve Bank of India (Know Your Customer) Amendment Directions, 2026”**.

rows.summary:
On August 12, 2026, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) issued for public comment the draft **“Reserve Bank of India (Interest Rates on Loans and Advances) Directions, 2026”**, following the announcement in the RBI’s **Statement on Developmental and Regulatory Policies dated August 05, 2026**. The draft is intended to replace the current patchwork of interest-rate instructions with a **harmonized, principles-based framework for all regulated entities (REs)** covering both **fixed-rate and floating-rate loans and advances**, with the framework to be calibrated to the **nature, complexity, and scale** of each RE’s operations.

The RBI says the existing regime is uneven: for **Commercial Banks** (including **Small Finance Banks** and **Local Area Banks**), there are detailed rules already in place for **internal and external benchmark-based lending**, including the setting of **spreads over benchmarks**; by contrast, the rules for **NBFCs, All India Financial Institutions, Regional Rural Banks, Urban Cooperative Banks, and Rural Cooperative Banks** are mostly limited to conduct-related requirements. The RBI also notes that among commercial banks it has observed **divergent practices in determining the MCLR (internal benchmark) and its components**, and that current guidance on **fixed-rate loans** is very limited. The proposed directions are meant to address these gaps and align interest-rate setting practices more consistently across REs.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that this is still a **draft consultation document**, so the immediate obligation is to **review and submit comments/feedback** rather than to implement final rule changes yet. However, the substance of the proposal signals that, once finalized, it may impose a more uniform supervisory standard on all REs for how loan and advance interest rates are determined, including both benchmark-linked floating-rate structures and fixed-rate lending. The document excerpt provided does not yet give a final effective date, transition period, or operative thresholds/rates; those would need to be checked in the final directions once issued.

rows.title: RBI invites public comments on the draft Directions on ‘Credit Valuation Adjustment (CVA) Framework’
rows.desc: August 7, 2026 RBI invites public comments on the draft Directions on ‘Credit Valuation Adjustment (CVA) Framework’ Credit Valuation Adjustment (CVA) reflects the adjustment to the default risk-free prices of derivatives to account for potential counterparty default. CVA risk refers to losses resulting from changes in CVA values, driven by shifts in counterparty credit spreads and market risk factors. The CVA capital charge ensures banks hold sufficient capital to cover these risks. 2. The extant CVA framework was issued by the Reserve Bank in 2011, which was based on the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS) standards issued in 2010. The BCBS has, since, issued revised CVA guidelines under the final Basel III framework. Accordingly, it has been decided to issue revised instructions on CVA framework permitting banks in India to adopt the basic approach (BA-CVA). Banks may choose to implement either the full or reduced version of BA-CVA. Alternatively, in line with BCBS guidelines, banks with an insignificant volume of non-centrally cleared derivatives may calculate their CVA capital charge as 100 per cent of their counterparty credit risk (CCR) capital charge. 3. The revised instructions: (a) allow eligible banks to choose a simpler approach; (b) clarify the eligibility and recognition of CVA hedges; (c) increase the sensitivity of supervisory risk weights for counterparties by sector and credit quality; and (d) separate systematic and idiosyncratic CVA risk components in the full BA-CVA calculation, addressing imperfect alignment of indirect CVA hedges. These revisions enhance risk sensitivity and improve consistency in the CVA framework. 4. Accordingly, the Reserve Bank has released today the Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Credit Valuation Adjustment Framework) Directions, 2026. 5. rows.summary:
On August 7, 2026, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) issued draft revised Directions on the Credit Valuation Adjustment (CVA) Framework and invited public comments by August 28, 2026. The draft replaces the RBI’s existing CVA framework issued in 2011, which had been based on the 2010 Basel Committee standards, and is intended to align Indian rules with the Basel III revisions to CVA treatment.

Substantively, the RBI is proposing to allow Indian banks to use the Basel “basic approach” for CVA capital calculation (BA-CVA), with banks permitted to adopt either the full or reduced version of BA-CVA. In addition, banks with an insignificant volume of non-centrally cleared derivatives may, consistent with BCBS guidance, calculate their CVA capital charge at 100% of their counterparty credit risk (CCR) capital charge instead of using the BA-CVA methodology. The draft also clarifies when CVA hedges are eligible for recognition, increases the sensitivity of supervisory risk weights for counterparties based on sector and credit quality, and separates systematic and idiosyncratic CVA risk components in the full BA-CVA calculation to better reflect indirect CVA hedges.

The RBI states that these changes are meant to make the framework more risk-sensitive and more consistent with current international standards. The new draft Directions, titled the **Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Credit Valuation Adjustment Framework) Directions, 2026**, apply to commercial banks in India that are subject to RBI regulation and to their CVA capital computation for derivative exposures. The consultation is open to regulated entities, market participants, and other interested parties, who may submit comments up to the August 28, 2026 deadline.

rows.title: Review of Guidelines on Concentration Risk Management - Rural Co-operative Banks
rows.desc: August 06, 2026 Review of Guidelines on Concentration Risk Management - Rural Co- operative Banks In pursuance of the announcement made with regard to the captioned subject in the Statement on Developmental and Regulatory Policies dated August 5, 2026, the Reserve Bank of India has today issued the following draft Directions for public comments: (i) Draft Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Concentration Risk Management) – Directions, 2026 to replace Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Concentration Risk Management) – Directions, 2025 (ii) Draft Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Credit Facilities) – Amendment Directions, 2026 to amend certain provisions of Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025 2. The above draft Directions prescribe, inter alia, prudential exposure limits for single/group counterparty, enhanced housing loan limits, and prudential exposure limits on unsecured advances. Additionally, it is proposed to allow flexibility to larger Rural Co-operative Banks (RCBs) with deposits above ₹1,000 crore in deciding the tenor and moratorium requirements for housing loans, while increasing the ceilings for these parameters in cases of other RCBs. Further, the prescribed prudential sectoral exposure limits, except for real estate sector, are proposed to be withdrawn. 3. The comments / feedback on the draft Directions may be submitted by the regulated entities and other stakeholders / members of public on or before August 28, 2026 through the following channels: (i) The ‘Connect 2 Regulate’ section on the website by following the corresponding hyperlink provided against each document in the page where they are hosted; or (ii) by email with the subject line ‘Feedback on (full name of the draft Directions)’. rows.summary:
On August 6, 2026, the Reserve Bank of India released draft directions for public comment to update the concentration risk framework applicable to rural co-operative banks (RCBs). The package consists of two instruments: a new **Draft RBI (Rural Co-operative Banks – Concentration Risk Management) Directions, 2026**, which would replace the existing **2025** concentration risk directions, and a **Draft RBI (Rural Co-operative Banks – Credit Facilities) Amendment Directions, 2026**, which would amend certain provisions of the **2025 Credit Facilities Directions**.

The draft changes are intended to set out prudential exposure limits for **single and group counterparties**, raise **housing loan limits**, and specify prudential limits for **unsecured advances**. RBI also proposes to give **larger RCBs with deposits above ₹1,000 crore** more flexibility to determine the **tenor and moratorium** for housing loans, while for **other RCBs** it proposes to **increase the ceilings** for those housing-loan parameters. In addition, RBI proposes to **withdraw the general prudential sectoral exposure limits**, with the stated exception that the **real estate sector** exposure limit would remain in place.

For compliance purposes, the key operational point is that these are **draft directions** open for consultation, not yet final rules. RBI has set **August 28, 2026** as the deadline for comments/feedback from regulated entities and other stakeholders, which may be submitted either through the **“Connect 2 Regulate”** portal on the RBI website or by email using the subject line **“Feedback on (full name of the draft Directions)”**. Compliance teams at RCBs should review the draft closely for any changes to counterparty exposure, unsecured lending, and housing finance policies, especially where deposits exceed the **₹1,000 crore** threshold.

The consultation period runs **from August 05, 2026 through September 05, 2026**, and comments can be submitted either through the RBI website via the **“Connect 2 Regulate”** section or sent directly to the RBI’s **Department of Regulation, Registration and Licensing Section (Co-operative Banks)** at its Mumbai office; email submissions must use the subject line **“Feedback on Draft Guidelines for ‘on tap’ Licensing of Urban Co-operative Banks”**.

No implementation date for the final guidelines is given in this press release, and no immediate compliance action is mandated other than the opportunity to comment by **September 05, 2026**.

rows.title: Rationalisation of Foreign Exchange Management (Non-Debt Instruments) Rules, 2019 – Draft Rules for Comments
rows.desc: July 21, 2026 Rationalisation of Foreign Exchange Management (Non-Debt Instruments) Rules, 2019 – Draft Rules for Comments Foreign investment into India is presently governed by the Foreign Exchange Management (Non-Debt Instruments) Rules, 2019 ('NDI Rules'). The Union Budget 2026- 27 announced a comprehensive review of the NDI Rules to create a more contemporary, user-friendly framework for foreign investments, consistent with India's evolving economic priorities. Pursuant thereto, a committee was constituted by the Central Government to undertake a comprehensive review of the extant regulatory framework. Based on the recommendations of the Committee, and in consultation with the Central Government and other stakeholders, the Reserve Bank of India has prepared a draft of the rationalized Rules. The salient features of the proposed draft Rules, inter alia, are as under: a) Simplified and principle-based framework: Rationalization of provisions, harmonization of definitions and a simplified regulatory architecture to enhance clarity and reduce regulatory complexity. b) Alignment with the FDI Policy: Clear demarcation of procedural FEMA provisions from policy and sector-specific requirements, improving regulatory coherence and facilitating timely policy changes. c) Enhanced ease of doing business: Streamlined procedures, reduced compliance burden and greater operational flexibility through a transparent and investor-friendly regulatory framework. d) Future-ready regulatory framework: Adoption of principle-based, investee-neutral and investor-neutral provisions aligned with evolving business practices, while preserving necessary regulatory safeguards. � � PRESS RELEASE � � RESERVE BANK OF INDIA : www.rbi.org.in/hindi , �� , � , , - 400 001 Website : www.rbi.org.in Department of Communication, Central Office, Shahid Bhagat Singh Marg, Fort, - /email : helpdoc@rbi.org.in Mumbai - 400 001 /Phone: 022 - 2266 0502 The Rules will be finalized after wider public consultations
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has issued **draft rationalised Foreign Exchange Management (Non-Debt Instruments) Rules, 2019 (NDI Rules)** for public comments on **July 21, 2026**, following the Union Budget 2026–27 announcement of a comprehensive review of the foreign investment framework. The draft is intended to update and simplify the existing foreign investment rules in India by creating a more contemporary, user-friendly structure that better aligns with India’s current economic priorities and the evolving foreign investment environment.

For compliance teams, the key substantive change is that the RBI, based on a committee review and in consultation with the Central Government and other stakeholders, is proposing a **simplified, principle-based framework** with **harmonized definitions** and a more coherent regulatory architecture. The draft also aims to **separate FEMA procedural requirements from FDI policy and sector-specific requirements**, which should make it clearer which obligations arise under FEMA rules versus sectoral policy conditions and may allow policy changes to be implemented more efficiently. The document also emphasizes **reduced compliance burden, streamlined procedures, and greater operational flexibility**, with the stated goal of improving ease of doing business and making the regime more investor-friendly while retaining necessary safeguards.

No specific numeric thresholds, ownership caps, rates, deadlines, or sector-specific eligibility changes are stated in the press release itself. The only procedural deadline mentioned is that the draft will be **finalized after wider public consultations**, meaning the current publication is a consultation stage rather than an immediately effective rule change. Compliance officers should therefore treat this as a signal that the NDI Rules are likely to be materially reworked, but should wait for the final notified text to identify any actual legal obligations, transition requirements, or date-specific implementation steps.

rows.summary:
On July 15, 2026, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) released a draft **“Guidance on Regulatory Expectations for Data Governance”** for public comment. The draft is aimed at a broad set of RBI-regulated entities: **commercial banks, small finance banks, payments banks, local area banks, regional rural banks, urban co-operative banks, rural co-operative banks, all India financial institutions, non-banking financial companies (NBFCs), asset reconstruction companies, and credit information companies**. Compliance teams at any of these entities should treat the draft as potentially applicable to their data governance frameworks and control environment.

The RBI’s stated objective is to respond to the increasing digitalisation of financial services and the growing dependence on technology-driven business models, where data has become a critical asset. The draft explains that as data volume, variety, and velocity increase, regulated entities need stronger governance so that data remains **accurate, consistent, secure, and fit for purpose** across business functions and systems. The RBI also highlights that weak data governance can create **financial, operational, compliance, and reputational risks**, indicating that the guidance is intended to support broader risk management and supervisory expectations, not just IT controls.

The RBI is seeking comments from regulated entities, members of the public, and other stakeholders **by August 17, 2026**. Feedback may be submitted via the **“Connect 2 Regulate”** section on the RBI website, or sent to the **Chief General Manager, Operational Risk Group, Department of Regulation, Central Office, Reserve Bank of India, Shahid Bhagat Singh Marg, Fort, Mumbai – 400 001**, or by email using the subject line **“Feedback on Guidance on Regulatory Expectations for Data Governance.”** No final compliance obligations are imposed yet in this press release, but the issuance of the draft signals that regulated entities should review their data governance practices and be prepared for future final guidance once the consultation closes.

On July 14, 2026, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) released draft amendment directions for public comment to simplify the approval process for **subsequent acquisitions of major shareholding in banking companies** by **mutual funds, insurance companies, and pension funds**, in response to representations from Asset Management Companies (AMCs). The draft package covers four separate instruments: the **Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Acquisition and Holding of Shares or Voting Rights) Amendment Directions, 2026**, the equivalent draft amendment directions for **Small Finance Banks**, **Payments Banks**, and **Local Area Banks**.

The practical compliance implication is that RBI is proposing changes to the rules governing acquisition and holding of shares or voting rights in these categories of regulated banks, specifically for the investor types identified above, with the stated policy objective of making repeat or later-stage major shareholding approvals less cumbersome. The notice does not itself set out the detailed text of the amendments, but it confirms that the revisions are intended to affect the approval framework for these institutions and investors.

RBI is accepting comments and feedback from **regulated entities and members of the public / other stakeholders**. The deadline for submission is **August 4, 2026**.

Feedback may be submitted through either of two channels: via the RBI website’s **“Connect 2 Regulate”** section using the hyperlink provided for each draft document, or by email with the subject line **“Feedback on (full name of the draft Amendment Directions (including the type of Regulated Entity))”**. rows.summary:
On June 24, 2026, the Reserve Bank of India released for public comment a draft **“Guidance on Regulatory Principles for Model Risk Management”**. The draft is intended to broaden and update RBI’s earlier August 5, 2024 draft **“Regulatory Principles for Management of Model Risks in Credit,”** reflecting the fact that model use has expanded significantly across regulated entities and that entities are increasingly using models, including those based on **Artificial Intelligence / Machine Learning**. The stated policy objective is to strengthen governance and risk-management practices for the use of models, and the draft appears to shift the focus from only credit-related model risk to a wider model-risk framework.

The draft Guidance would apply to a wide set of RBI-regulated entities: **Commercial Banks, Small Finance Banks, Payments Banks, Local Area Banks, Regional Rural Banks, Urban Co-operative Banks, Rural Co-operative Banks, All India Financial Institutions, Non-Banking Financial Companies, Asset Reconstruction Companies, and Credit Information Companies**. Compliance teams at any of these entities should treat the draft as relevant to their model governance, validation, oversight, and risk-control frameworks, particularly where models are used in credit, decisioning, or AI/ML-enabled processes. The press release does not state final requirements yet, but it clearly signals that RBI is moving toward formal principles for identifying, governing, and managing model risk across these institutions.

RBI is seeking comments from **regulated entities, members of the public, and other stakeholders** by **July 24, 2026**. Feedback may be submitted through the **“Connect 2 Regulate”** section on the RBI website, or sent to the **Chief General Manager, Operational Risk Group, Department of Regulation, Central Office, Reserve Bank of India, Shahid Bhagat Singh Marg, Fort, Mumbai – 400 001**, or by email with the subject line **“Feedback on Guidance on Regulatory Principles for Model Risk Management.”** There are no monetary thresholds, rates, or implementation dates stated in the press release itself beyond the comment deadline; the immediate compliance action is to review the draft, assess whether the institution falls within the listed regulated entities, and determine whether to submit feedback before the deadline.

rows.title: RBI invites public comments on the draft Amendment Directions on ‘Standardised Approach for Counterparty Credit Risk (SA-CCR)’
rows.desc: June 10, 2026 RBI invites public comments on the draft Amendment Directions on ‘Standardised Approach for Counterparty Credit Risk (SA-CCR)’ The extant guidelines require the use of the Current Exposure Method (CEM) for the computation of Counterparty Credit Risk (CCR) exposure. In 2016, RBI issued final ‘Guidelines for Computing Exposure for Counterparty Credit Risk arising from Derivative Transactions’ and ‘Guidelines on Capital Requirements for Bank Exposures to Central Counterparties’, both based on the Standardised Approach for Counterparty Credit Risk (SA-CCR), with an intended implementation date of April 1, 2018. However, the implementation of these guidelines was subsequently deferred. 2. Since then, the Bilateral Netting of Qualified Financial Contracts Act, 2020, has been enacted, while the margining framework has been implemented under the Reserve Bank of India (Margining for Non-Centrally Cleared OTC Derivatives) Directions, 2024. The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS) has also, over time, issued various FAQs providing further clarity on the SA-CCR guidelines. 3. Considering the time elapsed and the recent legal and regulatory developments, the guidelines have been comprehensively reviewed. The key changes between the 2016 guidelines (currently part of the Commercial Banks – Forthcoming Instructions, Directions, 2025) and the proposed draft Directions include, inter alia, (i) clarification on the scope of CCR across both banking and trading book exposures, (ii) treatment of multiple margin agreements and multiple netting sets elaborated in view of the legal / regulatory developments in netting and margining guidelines, (iii) guidance on the treatment of transactions where a bank acts as a clearing member of SEBI- recognised stock exchanges in the equity derivatives and commodity derivatives segments, (iv) treatment for deferment of option premium, (v) guidance on computation of effective notional for options, and (vi) inclusion of disclosure
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI), on June 10, 2026, issued a public consultation on draft Amendment Directions for the Standardised Approach for Counterparty Credit Risk (SA-CCR). The document explains that the current framework still requires banks to compute counterparty credit risk (CCR) exposure using the Current Exposure Method (CEM), even though RBI had already issued final SA-CCR-based guidelines in 2016 for “Guidelines for Computing Exposure for Counterparty Credit Risk arising from Derivative Transactions” and “Guidelines on Capital Requirements for Bank Exposures to Central Counterparties,” originally intended to apply from April 1, 2018 but later deferred.

RBI says the earlier SA-CCR framework has now been comprehensively reviewed because of major legal and regulatory changes since 2016, including the enactment of the Bilateral Netting of Qualified Financial Contracts Act, 2020 and the implementation of the margining framework under the RBI’s “Margining for Non-Centrally Cleared OTC Derivatives” Directions, 2024. The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS) has also issued multiple FAQs over time to clarify SA-CCR application, and the draft amendments are intended to align the directions with those developments.

The draft directions are described as making several substantive changes to the 2016 version currently reflected in the “Commercial Banks – Forthcoming Instructions, Directions, 2025.” These include clarifying the scope of CCR across both banking book and trading book exposures; setting out how multiple margin agreements and multiple netting sets should be treated in light of the new netting and margining framework; and giving specific treatment for transactions where a bank acts as a clearing member of SEBI-recognised stock exchanges in the equity derivatives and commodity derivatives segments. The draft also adds guidance on deferment of option premium, how to compute the effective notional amount for options, and begins incorporating disclosure-related requirements, though the excerpt cuts off before the full disclosure provisions are listed.

For compliance teams, the practical implication is that RBI is preparing to replace or materially update the deferred SA-CCR framework and is seeking comments before finalizing the rules. Banks and other affected institutions should review their derivative exposure measurement, netting set documentation, margining processes, clearing-member activity on SEBI-recognised exchanges, and option valuation/exposure calculations to assess whether systems and policies need to change once the amended directions are finalized and brought into force.

Substantial feedback has been received from stakeholders on the draft Amendment Directions, which has resulted in changes in many key draft provisions. The published draft Amendment Directions have been suitably amended to incorporate the accepted feedback. rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has issued **revised draft Amendment Directions** for public consultation on the **conduct of regulated entities in recovery of loans and engagement of recovery agents**, following an earlier draft released on **February 12, 2026**. These revised drafts are being issued because RBI received **substantial stakeholder feedback** that led to changes in many key provisions, including feedback on whether lenders should be allowed to use **technology-based mechanisms** to restrict or disable certain functions of a financed device—such as a **mobile phone or tablet**—as a means of recovering dues when a borrower defaults. RBI says the accepted feedback has been incorporated into the revised drafts, and that this is being circulated for **another round of public comments** rather than being finalized immediately.

The revised draft package covers multiple categories of regulated entities, including **commercial banks, small finance banks, local area banks, regional rural banks, urban co-operative banks, rural co-operative banks, and all India financial institutions** (the list is introduced as individual amendment directions for each entity type). The document is therefore relevant to compliance teams at any regulated lender within those classes, especially where the institution uses, or is considering using, recovery practices involving **recovery agents** or **device-level technology controls** on financed consumer electronics.

From a compliance perspective, the key point is that this is **not yet an operative final rule**; it is a revised draft for consultation. No implementation deadline, transition period, numerical threshold, or effective date for binding compliance is provided in the text excerpt. Compliance teams should therefore treat this as an early-warning regulatory consultation, review the proposed changes carefully, and assess whether their current recovery policies, agent management controls, borrower communication practices, and any contemplated device-restriction technologies would need to be modified once the directions are finalized.

rows.summary:
On May 19, 2026, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) issued draft amendment directions to align capital adequacy disclosure rules more closely with Basel Pillar 3 disclosure requirements. The draft package consists of two separate instruments: the **Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy) Seventh Amendment Directions, 2026** and the **Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks – Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy) Fifth Amendment Directions, 2026**. The notice does not state any substantive capital ratio change, threshold, or new quantitative disclosure item in the press release itself; it indicates only that the amendments relate to **Pillar 3 disclosure requirements** and are being issued after a review for consistency with Basel standards.

For compliance purposes, the key immediate obligation is the **consultation deadline**: comments on the draft directions are invited **until June 2, 2026**. Feedback may be submitted through the **“Connect2Regulate”** section on the RBI website, or sent directly to the **Chief General Manager, Balance Sheet Group, Department of Regulation, Central Office, Reserve Bank of India, 12th Floor, Central Office Building, Shahid Bhagat Singh Marg, Fort, Mumbai – 400001**. The RBI also permits submission by email, and requires the subject line to read **“Feedback on (full name of the draft Amendment Directions)”**.

The draft is specifically relevant to **commercial banks** and **small finance banks**, because those are the two categories for which amendment directions have been released. Compliance teams at such institutions should review the draft once available, assess whether any disclosure templates, governance processes, reporting timelines, or Pillar 3 publication controls need updating, and determine whether internal reporting and board/management approval processes must be adjusted before the final directions are issued. The press release itself is limited to the consultation notice and does not yet set an implementation date for the final amendments.

Accordingly, companies are required to submit applications for in-principle approval, post-allotment approval, and trading approval to the Stock Exchange(s). Over a period of time, Stock Exchanges, in a phased manner, have undertaken initiatives to migrate filings made under the SEBI Act, Regulations and circulars from document-based formats to XBRL- based reporting, with an objective to standardize securities market data and enhance regulatory efficiency. No: NSE/CML/2025/04 Date: February 07, 2025 To All Listed Entities, Subject: Clarification on fixing the record date under Regulation 42 of SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 This is with reference to the recent amendment made by the Securities and Exchange Board of India to regulation 42 of the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements), Regulations, 2015 vide notification dated December 12, 2024. It is clarified that listed entities shall ensure a minimum gap of at least three working days between the date of board/shareholders’ approval, as applicable to the specific corporate action mentioned in Regulation 42 (1), and the Record Date fixed for such purpose. The minimum gap shall be exclusive of the date of board/shareholder's approval and the actual record date. Further, as per latest amendment, sub-regulation 5 of Regulation 42 of SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements), Regulations, 2015 has been omitted. Hence the listed entities are not required to announce dates of closure of their transfer books for any purpose. All Listed entities are requested to take note of the same and comply accordingly. For and on behalf of National Stock Exchange of India Limited Senior Manager Harshad Dharod

rows.desc: Non-Confidential Circular Department: Listing Circular Ref No: NSE/CML/2025/02 Date: January 02, 2025 To, The Company Secretaries, All Listed Entities Subject: Implementation of recommendations of the Expert Committee for facilitating ease of doing business for listed entities This has reference to the amendments to the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 (“SEBI LODR”) which have been published in the Gazette of India on December 13, 2024 and to give effect to certain recommendations of the Expert Committee and carry out consequential changes to the provisions of SEBI Master Circular dated November 11, 2024, on compliance with the SEBI LODR by listed entities, SEBI has issued a circular SEBI/HO/CFD/CFD-PoD-2/CIR/P/2024/185 dated December 31, 2024 (‘SEBI Circular’). In this regard a copy of SEBI Circular dated December 31, 2024, is enclosed for your reference and for necessary action at your end. The copy of the circular will also be made available on the NSE website at https://www.nseindia.com/companies- listing/circular-for-listed-companies-equity-market Based on the above, the Integrated Filing shall be applicable for the filings to be done for the quarter ending December 31, 2024, and thereafter. The timelines for Integrated Filing shall be as follows: a. Integrated Filing (Governance): within 30 days from the end of the quarter; b. Integrated Filing (Financial): within 45 days from the end of the quarter, other than the last quarter, and 60 days from the end of the last quarter and the financial year In this regard, the first quarterly Integrated Filing i.e. Integrated Filing (Governance) and Integrated Filing (Financial) which is applicable for the quarter ending December 31, 2024, may be filed within a period of 45 days from the end of the quarter. However, for subsequent quarterly filings, the companies shall follow the timelines as mentioned under point a & b above. Note: Basis the above

rows.title: Update on single filing system through API-based integration between Stock Exchanges- Voting Results
rows.desc: Circular Department: Listing Circular Ref No: NSE/CML/2024/43 Date: December 27, 2024 To, The Company Secretaries, All Listed Entities Subject: Update on single filing system through API-based integration between Stock Exchanges This has reference to Exchange Circular No. NSE/CML/2024/28 dated September 30, 2024, with respect to single filing system through API-based integration between Stock Exchanges. In this connection, we are pleased to inform you that the single filing system has been extended for the filings of disclosures pertaining to Voting Results of Shareholders Meeting with effect from December 28, 2024. With this, the Single filing system through API-based integration shall now be available for below mentioned disclosures: - Particulars Regulation as per SEBI LODR 2015/Depository Regulation Type of Listed Companies Only Equity Equity+ Debt Exclusively Debt REIT's and INVITs Corporate Governance Report 27(2) √ √ Shall be communicated later Shall be communicated later Investor Grievance Report 13 (3) √ √ √ Shall be communicated later Reconciliation of Share Capital Audit Report 76 √ √ - - Meetings of shareholders and voting 44 (3) √ √ - - Since the aforesaid implementation is being aimed at enabling single filing system, the Listed Entities are requested to avoid multiple filings of the same disclosure on both the Exchanges. In case any Exchange seeks any clarification post submission, for any queries/clarifications, the company shall be required to respond to the Exchange which has sought the clarification. In case any queries concerning the captioned subject, please reach out to the respective team members on the contact details available in the NEAPS platform at path NEAPS > Help > Contact Us > Listing Compliance or send an email to takeover@nse.co.in Yours faithfully, For National Stock Exchange of India Limited Yukti Sharma Head - Listing

This Gazette notification of the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI), dated **10 September 2026** and published in **The Gazette of India on 14 September 2026**, is a formal **delegation of powers** issued under **section 23(1) of the IRDAI Act, 1999 (41 of 1999)**. It states that IRDAI has delegated authority relating to **imposition of penalties and issuance of directions** under the **Insurance Act, 1938**, as well as under applicable **regulations and guidelines**, with the delegation taking effect through the notification itself; no separate implementation date is stated beyond the notification/publication date.

The delegation covers specific enforcement powers under the Insurance Act and certain 2015 regulations. Under **section 34 of the Insurance Act, 1938**, the power to issue **directions to any insurer or insurance intermediary** in an enforcement proceeding for identified violations is delegated to the **Chairperson**. Under **section 102 of the Insurance Act, 1938**, the power to impose penalties on any person who fails to: **(a)** furnish any document, statement, account, return, or report to the Authority, **(b)** comply with directions, **(c)** maintain the solvency margin, or **(d)** comply with directions on insurance treaties, is delegated to a **Whole Time Member**, a **panel of the Chairperson and one Whole Time Member**, or a **panel of two Whole Time Members**, with the specific forum to be chosen by the Chairperson.

The notification also delegates the power under **section 104** to impose penalty for failure to comply with the relevant statutory requirements, and under **section 105(2)** it delegates the power to impose the specified penalty for non-compliance with that provision. In addition, for the **IRDAI (Issuance of Captive Insurance Companies) Regulations, 2015**, the notification delegates the power under **regulation 22(6)** to the competent authority specified in the same framework, and for the **IRDAI (Registration of Indian Insurance Companies) Regulations, 2015**, it delegates powers under **regulations 48 to 53** and **section 34 of the Insurance Act, 1938** in relation to the relevant compliance/enforcement actions.

For a compliance team, the practical significance is that **enforcement actions, directions, and penalty proceedings no longer necessarily need to go to the full Authority**; they may be exercised by the Chairperson, a Whole Time Member, or specified panels, depending on the provision. This means compliance failures involving **document/reporting obligations, solvency margin maintenance, insurance treaty directions, or violations identified in enforcement proceedings** can now result in action from these delegated decision-makers, so escalation, response, and legal review processes should be aligned to receive and handle orders issued by those officials as valid IRDAI action.

It applies to **Indian re-insurers and other applicable insurers** covered by Section 101A, and it requires that, for **general insurance policies attaching between 1 April 2023 and 31 March 2024**, a **4% cession of the sum insured on each policy** must be reinsured with the Indian reinsurer(s). For compliance purposes, the key point is that this is a mandatory annual cession requirement for the specified policy period, and insurers subject to Section 101A must ensure their reinsurance arrangements, premium treatment, and placement workflow reflect the **4% compulsory cession** and the stated **NIL treatment** for terrorism and nuclear pool premiums.

rows.summary:
The IRDAI (Other Forms of Capital) Regulations, 2022 were notified on 5 December 2022 and are intended to replace and standardize the framework under which insurers can raise capital through instruments other than ordinary share capital. The regulations apply to insurers regulated under the Insurance Act, 1938 and the IRDA Act, 1999, and they sit within the broader IRDAI regulatory framework governing capital raising and solvency. They define key terms such as “equity share capital,” “other forms of capital,” “preferential issue,” “private placement,” “promoter,” “controlled,” and related expressions, so companies using or issuing non-equity capital must align their instrument structures and disclosures with these regulatory meanings.

A major substantive requirement is the creation of a regulatory framework for issuance, treatment, and monitoring of “other forms of capital,” including instruments that are not pure equity but are intended to count toward an insurer’s capital base subject to conditions. The regulations provide for classification and treatment of instruments based on their features, including terms around priority, redemption, maturity, and loss absorption, and they require insurers to ensure that these instruments are structured so they do not undermine policyholder protection or solvency. Where instruments are held by promoters or related parties, or are issued through private placement or preferential issue, the regulations impose additional scrutiny and compliance conditions. The document also sets out the regulatory expectations for disclosures, approval processes, and ongoing compliance in relation to these instruments.

The regulations appear to include an explicit quantitative treatment for a particular category of capital instruments, showing a phased recognition or crediting of capital value over time. The text references a table in which the recognized value declines in steps from 100% to 80%, 60%, 40%, 20%, and then 0% as maturity approaches, with the example indicating a value of 1.50 plus 20% = 1.80 at one stage, which suggests the instrument’s regulatory value is amortized or progressively reduced before maturity. Compliance teams should treat this as a key capital-adequacy feature: instruments may not retain full regulatory capital recognition throughout their life, and the insurer must monitor residual tenor and the corresponding amount eligible for capital credit.

The regulations also specify conditions around the number and type of investors and the mechanics of issuance. The text references a threshold of 50 and mentions private placement/procedural requirements, suggesting limits or gating conditions for certain offers or placements, and it also refers to a 15-day timeline in at least one procedural context. In addition, the instrument documentation must contain prescribed features and cannot conflict with the regulatory definition of capital; the regulations appear to require careful drafting of offering documents and issuer resolutions before issuance. Where instruments are to be issued or transferred, the insurer must ensure the transaction is approved and documented in the manner prescribed by IRDAI.

Finally, the regulations include amendments or references to prior IRDAI regulations dated 2022 and 2015, indicating that this notification integrates with or modifies existing capital and insurer governance rules rather than operating in isolation. The practical compliance impact is that insurers planning to raise capital through hybrid, subordinated, or otherwise non-equity instruments must review the new definitions, valuation/recognition rules, issuance procedures, and ongoing reporting requirements before launching any transaction. In short, the document does not merely permit alternative capital forms; it imposes a structured legal and prudential framework that controls what can be issued, how it is recognized in capital calculations, and what approvals/disclosures are required.

It also includes representatives from key industry and technical institutions: the Director of the National Insurance Academy; the President of the Institute of Actuaries of India; the Secretary General of the Insurance Institute of India; the President of the Insurance Brokers’ Association of India; and the President of the Indian Institute of Insurance Surveyors & Loss Assessors. The document continues with additional committee membership beyond the excerpt shown, including the Insurance Ombudsman, but the core compliance point is that the committee’s constitution has been formally reset and becomes operative on the stated effective date.

For a compliance team, the practical obligation is to ensure internal governance materials, committee references, and any stakeholder engagement or regulatory communication involving the Insurance Advisory Committee are aligned to this 10 August 2021 reconstitution, rather than any prior composition. No monetary thresholds, filing deadlines, or substantive operational rules are introduced in this notification beyond the change in committee membership and effective date.

The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) issued the **IRDAI (Indian Insurance Companies) (Amendment) Regulations, 2021** on **7 July 2021**, and the amending text appears to take effect from the date of publication unless a specific provision in the underlying regulations says otherwise. The amendments revise several provisions of the **IRDAI (Indian Insurance Companies) Regulations, 2015**, and also make related changes to the **Indian Insurance Companies (Foreign Investment) Regulations, 2015** and the **Indian Insurance Companies (Indian Owned and Controlled) Regulations, 2015**.  

A key change is the insertion of a new **regulation 31** in the 2015 Indian Insurance Companies Regulations, stating that an insurer must comply with **regulation 5** of the 2021 amendment framework, which appears to introduce updated requirements tied to the insurer’s structure and governance. The document also amends **regulation 5(2)(vi)** of the 2015 regulations to update the cross-reference language, replacing earlier references so that the provision now points to the relevant clause(s) under the amended framework; similarly, **regulation 7** is amended to change the wording around **promoter/promoter group ownership and control** and the related cross-references to the 2000 and 2015 rules.  

The amendment makes conforming edits to **regulations 16 and 17** of the 2015 regulations by replacing the prior cross-references with references to **regulation 5(2)** of the amended 2021 framework, indicating that compliance obligations under those provisions now track the updated ownership/control standard. It also deletes or updates references in **regulations 29, 30 and 31** to align them with the new 2021 rule set, and amends the textual reference in the older rules so that the compliance regime is read together with the **2015** and **2021** amendments.  

In the **Indian Insurance Companies (Foreign Investment) Regulations, 2015**, the amendment substitutes the cross-reference in **regulation 5(2)(vi)** and updates **regulation 7** and **regulation 13** to reflect the revised 2021 wording and the applicable ownership/control concepts. The same type of conforming changes are made in the **Indian Insurance Companies (Indian Owned and Controlled) Regulations, 2015**, again updating **regulation 5(2)(vi)**, **regulation 7**, and **regulation 13** so that those provisions refer to the amended regime rather than the superseded language.  

For compliance purposes, the practical effect is that insurers, and especially those affected by **foreign investment**, **Indian ownership and control**, and the linked **promoter/promoter group** provisions, must apply the updated cross-references and the new/modified compliance standard introduced by the 2021 amendment. The document does not set out a monetary threshold or percentage in the extracted text provided here, but it clearly requires regulated entities to realign their internal compliance, ownership-control assessments, and regulatory filings/interpretations to the amended regulatory structure immediately upon the amendment’s commencement.

The Ministry of Finance (Department of Financial Services) issued the **Indian Insurance Companies (Foreign Investment) Amendment Rules, 2021** on **19 May 2021** (G.S.R. 337(E)), after publishing draft rules on **15 April 2021** and inviting public comments for **15 days** from publication. The amendments were made under **section 114(2)(aaa)** read with **section 2(7A)(b)** of the **Insurance Act, 1938**, and they amend the **Indian Insurance Companies (Foreign Investment) Rules, 2015**.

The most significant substantive change is a revised definition of **“foreign investment”** in the 2015 rules. The amendment also revises related definitions and references in the rules (including terms used in rule 2 and rule 5, and an updated statutory citation in rule 8), so compliance teams should treat this as a definitional and cross-reference update rather than a stand-alone licensing regime. The document specifically changes rule 4 to state that **foreign investment up to 74%** of the paid-up equity share capital is permitted in an Indian insurance company, subject to the conditions in the rule and the broader insurance-law framework. In practical terms, the rule change reflects the increase in the foreign investment ceiling for Indian insurance companies from the earlier level to **74%**, and compliance teams should ensure ownership tracking, board/governance checks, and foreign investor reporting are aligned with that cap.

The amendment applies to **Indian insurance companies** and the foreign investment they receive, so any insurer with existing or proposed foreign shareholding must review whether its capital structure, approvals, and internal compliance procedures now fit within the revised **74%** limit and the conditions attached to rule 4. Because the document is an amendment notification rather than a full restatement of the rulebook, affected firms should read it together with the **2015 Foreign Investment Rules** and the **Insurance Act, 1938** to identify every updated definition and cross-reference that may affect filings, ownership monitoring, and regulatory correspondence. The notification does not set a separate operational deadline beyond its issuance date, but it became effective upon publication on **19 May 2021**.

IRDAI has issued a circular dated **2 November 2026** to **all general insurers other than stand-alone health insurers and specialised insurers** directing implementation of the Hon’ble Supreme Court’s order in **CA No. 14369/2025, National Insurance Company Ltd. v. Smt. Thungala Dhana Laxmi & others**. The circular requires insurers to implement a **four-layer motor insurance structure** for **private vehicles only**—specifically **cars and two-wheelers**—so that vehicle owners are offered clear, distinct choices for cover: **(i) third-party liability, (ii) legal liability to occupants, (iii) personal accident cover, and (iv) own-damage cover**. The purpose stated is to make policy options clearer to the vehicle owner and enable an informed purchase decision.

The circular also requires insurers to put in place an **option form** and to issue a **mandatory Customer Information Sheet (CIS)** in connection with these private vehicle policies. It references implementation within the framework of the **Insurance Act, 1938 (including section 14(2))** and the **Motor Vehicles Act, 1989**, indicating that the change is not optional but a compliance direction flowing from the Supreme Court’s ruling and IRDAI’s regulatory authority. The document indicates that IRDAI has acted in consultation with the **General Insurance Council and insurance companies**, implying that insurers should align product design, sales processes, and disclosure practices with the agreed framework.

Although the OCR text is partially truncated, the circular clearly signals that insurers must treat the four-layer structure as a required implementation for the affected private vehicle business and must ensure appropriate product offering and disclosures are available to customers. A compliance team should read this as requiring prompt review of policy wordings, proposal/option forms, sales scripts, customer disclosures, and CIS issuance processes for private car and two-wheeler motor products to ensure the insurer can present the four cover layers distinctly and document the customer’s choice.

IRDAI/F&I/CIR/MISC/142/11/2026), consolidates and clarifies the forms and procedural requirements under the IRDAI (Registration, Capital Structure, Transfer of Shares and Amalgamation of Insurers) Regulations, 2024, as amended by the 2026 Amendment Regulations. The circular applies immediately from the date of issuance and is applicable to all insurers except Foreign Reinsurer’s Branches, as well as all applicants seeking registration to carry on insurance business.

From a compliance perspective, the document’s main purpose is to specify the exact statutory/regulated forms to be used and to provide clarifications on how the 2024 Registration Regulations should be implemented in practice. The table of contents shows that the circular covers “Applications to be submitted” and “Clarifications, Submission of Returns and Transitory Provisions,” indicating that firms must align not only initial filings but also ongoing procedural submissions with the updated framework. The annexures identify the prescribed forms included with the circular: Form IRDAI/NOC, Form IRDAI/R4, and Form IRDAI/ToS (Application for approval under section 6A), so insurers and applicants should use these forms where required rather than relying on older or informal formats.

The document does not, in the excerpt provided, set out new capital thresholds, shareholding limits, or amalgamation ratios, but it does make clear that the registration/capital structure/share transfer/amalgamation regime has been updated and formally consolidated through the 2024 Regulations as amended in 2026. Compliance teams should therefore verify that all applications, approvals, and related return submissions are mapped to the correct current form and regulatory citation, and should remove reliance on any circulars listed as repealed in Schedule I. Because the circular is effective immediately, entities that are in the middle of registration, share transfer, or amalgamation-related filings should treat the new circular as governing from 02.11.2026 onward and confirm that any pending or future submissions comply with these updated requirements.

IRDAI has migrated two health-related regulatory functions to the upgraded **Integrated Business Analytics Platform (BAP)**: **submission of Health Regulatory Returns** and **generation/modification of Health Product UINs**. The change is described as part of a broader BAP upgrade intended to provide a more integrated and streamlined regulatory reporting and product-functionality platform, and these functions are now available through the **Health module of the BAP portal**.

For **Health Regulatory Returns**, **all concerned insurers** are now required to file the following through BAP: **Health Regulatory Returns for FY 2024–25**, **Health Regulatory Returns for FY 2025–26**, and **RET 197 for Q1 and Q2 of FY 2026–27**, with the specific exception that **RET 197 does not apply to life insurers**. The circular also states that **all subsequent reporting periods** must be submitted through BAP in accordance with the applicable requirements. Practically, this means compliance teams should treat BAP as the mandatory filing channel for these health return submissions going forward and ensure internal reporting workflows, sign-offs, and filing responsibilities are aligned to the new portal process.

For **Health Product UIN generation and product changes**, the circular says that the BAP Health module now covers **generation of Unique Identification Numbers (UINs) for new Health Insurance Products** as well as **modification of existing Health Insurance Products**. The document does not specify a separate deadline for these product-related actions, but the compliance implication is that insurers seeking UINs for new health products or changes to existing health products must use the BAP workflow rather than any prior process.

The circular is addressed to **all insurers excluding reinsurers, FRBs, AIC, and ECGC**, so compliance obligations apply to the stated insurer population only. It is dated **30 October 2026**, with reference number **IRDAI/HLT/CIR/MISC/141/10/2026**. A timing note appears in the text indicating **“02 2026”**, but the excerpt provided does not clearly explain whether that is a separate rollout date, a release marker, or another administrative reference; the clearest operative requirement in the text is that the relevant functions are now available and submissions must be made through BAP.

IRDAI specifically encourages REs to supplement these activities with **mass awareness outreach through multiple media channels**, including **television, community radio, radio jingles, reels, memes, and SMS**. The circular does not prescribe a fixed number of events or a quantitative threshold, but it clearly expects REs to organize awareness efforts and disseminate cyber-safety messaging using broad communication methods.

A further compliance obligation is the submission of an **Action Taken Report (ATR)** to IRDAI. The ATR must be sent by **3 November 2026** to **infosec@irdai.gov.in**. This means compliance teams should not only carry out the awareness activities during October, but also document what was done and ensure the report is submitted on time to the specified email address.

rows.summary:
IRDAI has repealed the 3 January 2020 “Guidelines on repatriation of dividends by insurance intermediaries having majority by foreign investors” for all insurance intermediaries. The repeal is effective from 30 July 2026, the same date on which IRDAI notified the **IRDAI (Insurance Intermediaries) (Amendment) Regulations, 2026**.

The reason for the change is that the 2026 Amendment Regulations were issued to align the insurance intermediary framework with the **Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha (Amendment of Insurance Laws) Act, 2025** and the **Indian Insurance Companies (Foreign Investment) Amendment Rules, 2025**. Under those amendments, IRDAI has **removed the requirement to obtain prior approval from the Authority for repatriation of dividends** and has also **removed the condition relating to related-party payments**.

For compliance purposes, this means the 2020 dividend-repatriation guidelines no longer apply from **30.07.2026** onward, and insurance intermediaries should stop relying on that circular as the governing framework for dividend repatriation. Any internal policies, approval workflows, board papers, treasury procedures, or compliance checklists that were built around seeking IRDAI prior approval for dividend remittance by majority foreign-owned intermediaries should be updated to reflect the new regime. The circular itself is addressed to **all insurance intermediaries** and was issued with approval of the competent authority on **22 September 2026**.

rows.summary:
IRDAI has issued a circular dated **27 August 2026** to **all insurers** permitting investment in **New Development Bank (NDB) “Maharajah INR Bonds” / onshore rupee bonds** as part of insurers’ **approved investments**. NDB has requested this permission to support issuance of bonds with a proposed total size of **INR 25,000 crore over a five-year period**, and the stated use of proceeds is for **general corporate purposes** and **financing/onward lending for sustainable development, sustainable infrastructure, and green/social projects in India**.

The circular clarifies that these NDB onshore rupee bonds are treated as **“securities” under the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956**. IRDAI’s permission is not unconditional: insurers may invest only if the bonds are governed by **any applicable Government of India norms**, the **public issue is duly approved by SEBI**, and insurers comply with **Section 27E of the Insurance Act, 1938** when making the investment. The bonds must also satisfy the **rating criteria for “Approved Investments” under Schedule III of the IRDAI (Actuarial, Finance and Investment Functions of Insurers) Regulations, 2024**, as amended from time to time; the circular further notes that where **SEBI exempts the rating requirement** because the bonds have been rated by an **international rating agency**, that SEBI position is relevant to the compliance assessment.

For compliance teams, the practical impact is that NDB onshore rupee bonds are now eligible for insurer investment, but only within the existing statutory and regulatory framework for approved investments. Insurers should verify, before investing, that each issuance has the necessary **SEBI approval**, that any **Government of India conditions** are satisfied, that the investment remains consistent with **Section 27E limits/requirements**, and that the issue meets the applicable **Schedule III approved-investment rating standards** or a valid SEBI exemption applies. The circular is a **permission to invest**, not a relaxation of existing insurer investment controls, and there is no separate date-specific operational deadline beyond the effective applicability of the circular from its issuance on **27 August 2026**.

On claims handling, insurers are directed to use **special, empowered district desks** so claims can be processed quickly in the affected districts. The document’s focus is operational readiness and speed of service delivery rather than changing policy coverage terms: the compliance obligation is to ensure rapid claim intake, escalation, and settlement support for customers impacted by the Assam floods, with visible local points of contact and continuous assistance availability.

rows.summary:
This IRDAI circular, dated 14 July 2026 and addressed to all insurers, issues additional clarifications on implementation of Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS), building on Circular No. IRDAI/F&I/CIR/MISC/45/4/2026 dated 1 April 2026. The stated purpose is to ensure consistent implementation of the regulatory framework and it specifically clarifies three areas: the role of the Appointed Actuary, the requirement for independent validation, and the use of Ind AS-compliant financial statements for consolidation.

On the Appointed Actuary’s role, the circular says that under Clauses 6 and 7 of Part II of Schedule I of the IRDAI (Actuarial, Finance and Investment Functions of Insurers) Regulations, 2024, the Appointed Actuary must provide actuarial expertise and support for preparation of financial statements under applicable Ind AS, but this role is limited to actuarial inputs and valuation-related support; the Appointed Actuary is not the person responsible for actually drafting or signing the financial statements. The circular then clarifies that the insurer’s management remains responsible for the preparation and approval of Ind AS financial statements, while the Appointed Actuary contributes required actuarial inputs, assumptions, and valuations.

A major change concerns independent validation and timing. For the financial year 2026–27, and for every year thereafter, an independent validation of the insurer’s Ind AS financial statements is required before finalization. The circular specifies that this independent validation must be completed by 31 August 2026 for the 2026–27 financial year, and similar timelines will apply in subsequent years in line with the year-end reporting process. The validation is intended to cover the proper application of Ind AS, including actuarial assumptions, policy liability measurements, and consistency of disclosures, and it must be carried out by an independent professional or firm with the relevant expertise and no conflict of interest.

The circular also clarifies how Ind AS-compliant financial statements are to be used for consolidation. For any insurer that is part of a group, the Ind AS financial statements prepared by the insurer are to be used for group consolidation purposes, provided they are prepared in accordance with the applicable Ind AS and have undergone the required independent validation. The document implies that insurers must ensure their subsidiary/parent consolidation packs are based on validated Ind AS numbers rather than on separate local-compliance figures.

Finally, the circular indicates that insurers must align their internal processes, governance, and reporting timelines with these requirements immediately for the 2026–27 cycle. Compliance officers should ensure the Appointed Actuary’s responsibilities are properly documented and limited to actuarial support, that an independent validation mechanism is in place well before the 31 August 2026 deadline, and that finance, actuarial, and consolidation teams are coordinating so that the validated Ind AS financial statements can be used for reporting and consolidation without delay.

This IRDAI circular, dated **8 July 2026** and addressed to **all insurers and reinsurers**, updates the **formats for publishing financial results under SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015** for listed insurance entities. It explains that SEBI’s master circular on financial-results publication already required listed insurers to use IRDAI-prescribed formats, but those formats now needed revision because of the **adoption of Ind AS by insurers**. As a result, the circular says the **unaudited/audited quarterly financial-results formats submitted to stock exchanges have been updated** for **all listed Life Insurers, General Insurers, Health Insurers, and Reinsurers**.

The updated requirements apply specifically to listed insurers/reinsurers **that are required to prepare financial statements under Ind AS**. For these entities, **quarterly financial results must be presented in the format set out in Annexure I**, and the **segment-wise Revenue, Results, and Capital Employed** must also be reported along with the quarterly results, in the format prescribed in **Annexure II**. The circular also refers to a further format in **Annexure III** and indicates another annexure tied to **SEBI LODR Regulation 47(1)(b)**, implying additional publication-format obligations where applicable to listed entities.

The circular also notes an important exception: insurers that have been granted **forbearance for Ind AS implementation for FY 2026–27** are treated differently, because the format changes are driven by Ind AS adoption and therefore apply to the entities that are actually operating under Ind AS. It further references earlier IRDAI directions/circulars from **25 January 2016** and **30 January 2017**, indicating that the current update is a replacement or revision of prior publishing formats rather than a wholly new reporting regime. For compliance purposes, listed insurers should ensure their stock-exchange financial-result disclosures are revised immediately to match the new annexed formats, including the quarterly statement and the required segment reporting, so that their disclosures remain aligned with IRDAI’s standards under the SEBI LODR framework.

rows.summary:
The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) has extended the transitional arrangements governing **payment of annual fee and issuance of Certificate of Registration** for insurance intermediaries, and for surveyors/loss assessors where applicable. These arrangements had originally been issued by Circular **IRDAI/INT/CIR/MISC/41/3/2026 dated 16 March 2026**, with applicability extended to surveyors and loss assessors by Circular **IRDAI/INT/CIR/MISC/54/4/2026 dated 7 April 2026**. The earlier transitional framework was due to expire on **30 June 2026**, but IRDAI has now decided that it will continue **beyond 30 June 2026 until the date the relevant amended Regulations are notified**.

More specifically, the circular amends the timing in the earlier circulars so that the period referenced in **paragraph 4.3 of Circular 41/3/2026** is extended from **30 June 2026 to 31 August 2026, or to the date of notification of the relevant amended Regulations, whichever is earlier**. It also states that **paragraph 4.1 of Circular 54/4/2026** is to be read in line with this extension. The practical effect is that entities covered by those circulars should continue following the interim process for annual fee payment and certificate issuance until the new regulations are formally notified, rather than assuming the transitional mechanism ends on 30 June 2026.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that firms in the affected categories must keep using the existing transitional arrangement and should monitor closely for the notification of the amended Regulations, because that notification will end the transitional regime even if it occurs before **31 August 2026**. No new fee rate or threshold is introduced in this circular; the only substantive change is the **extension of the interim compliance period and related operational process** pending the final regulatory amendments under the **Insurance Act, 1938**, as amended by the **Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha (Amendment of Insurance Laws) Act, 2025**.
